translations.text: The Book
On the Knowledge of Truth
Or, On the Cause of All Causes.
On contemplation and trust, and on the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one true God, who has neither beginning nor end.
A note on this book about the Cause of All Causes, the Creator of All Creatures, and the Maker of everything visible and invisible. A book for all the peoples under heaven.
In it, instruction is given about the knowledge of truth and how it is known. First comes the first discourse, which contains ten chapters. These are the subjects of this book.
They are as follows: 1. First, what a person ought to know and learn, on page [?]. 2. How certain truth is known, page 8. 3. What truth is and what falsehood is,
on page 10. 4. How it is known that God exists, page 11. 5. Whether he is one or many, page 16. 6. What sort of being he is and how many attributes he has, on page [?]. 7. Whether he has a name

that is precise or not, page 23. 8. Whether he is the Cause of All Causes and the Creator of All Creatures, page 27[?]. 9. Whether he cares for, governs, and looks after everything or not, page 28. 10. Whether

God can be comprehended or is incomprehensible, on page 32. The second discourse, containing eight chapters: 1. Why he created creatures and established the worlds, page 36. 2. What his purpose is in creation, page 37[?]. 3. Whether there is
another world besides—here he speaks about the human soul—this visible, existing one, page 39. 4. If there is another world, what it is like and what it is: material and visible like this one,
or spiritual, subtle, and invisible, on page 40. 5. What the order and function of the other world are, which now exists besides this one, on page 42. 6. Whether there is

an end to this world perceived by the senses, on page 43. 7. Whether another world will arise besides this one, on page 44. 8. If another world will arise and is yet to come into being, what its order,
purpose, and function are, on page 46. The third discourse, containing nine chapters: 1. Why the human being was created, page 51. 2. What human nature is, page 54. 3. How a person ought to think,
what a person ought to do, and how a person should live in this world, on page 57[?]. 4. What will become of the human being,
what a person's expectation is, and what sort of hope a person should have, on page 61. 5. How a person can know God, on page 64. 6. Whether a person can
know him precisely as he is or not, on page 65. 7. Whether a person's knowledge of God always remains the same,
or whether, as a person's knowledge develops in accordance with their conduct, their knowledge of God also increases and decreases
within them, page 66. 8. What the reason is that, although God is one and his nature and essence are one,
knowledge of him differs among all peoples, in every rank and at every level, in every human being.
Even within a single person, it changes at all their different stages, on page 66. 9. Whether it itself changes—that is, knowledge about God—in relation to all those mentioned,
or whether the change is in them and comes from them, while it does not change at all, on page 68. The fourth discourse, containing five chapters: 1. Whether the written text
and writing that came to be written in the world are true and useful, on page 68. 2. Who invented writing and [?] it, and what necessity [?] him, on page 69. 3. Whether the Book of Creation is true,
that is, the Torah's account of the world's coming into being, or not, on page 70. 4. When this world was created, since when it has existed, where it came from, and from what it was formed,

and how the opposing elements were joined together and everything visible was formed from them, on page 52. 5. How opposing natures were joined together and everything visible was fashioned from them, on page 2. The fifth discourse, containing seven chapters: 1. How light was created.
And what it consists of, on page 83. 2. And when the heavens were stretched out, and what they are.
And what the firmament above us is, on page 86. 3. And what the constellations are like, and how many they are.
And how they are bound to one another, on page [?]. 5. And how many firmaments there are, that is, the spheres of the zodiac, on page 88. 6. And what the sun, the moon, and the rest of the stars are.
What they came into being from; what their nature is; how they are arranged; what their use is; and what their locations are like.

And what their activity is, and their entire governing order, page 98. 7. And what causes eclipses, that is, the darkening of the sun and moon, on page 101. Discourse Six, containing [?] chapters. 1. What lies below the entire zodiac
and the region of the stars; what the fiery ether is like, and why, on page 102. 2. And what lies below the ether, and what this air is like.
And what the streaks of light are, that is, the shooting stars seen in the air at night, on page 103. 3. And how the clouds are arranged.
And what makes them increase and become dense, and how they disperse, on page 106. 4. And where lightning and the sounds of thunder come from, on page 106. 5. Where rain and showers come from,
and why; and what causes snow, hail, and ice, on page 108. 6. And what causes the changes of the seasons: spring, summer, and autumn,
that is, the months of Tishri, and winter, on page 109. 7. And why the changes of the seasons come gradually and in an orderly way, rather than happening suddenly, on page 112.
Discourse Seven, containing five chapters. 1. Why there are kinds of [?] and birds, where they come from, what benefit they provide, and what their significance is.

And concerning the kinds of fish and all the creatures that swarm in the water, on page 114. 2. And what the nature of the earth is, and the many differences within the earth—in its soil and stones—and their effects.
And what all the substances from the earth are composed of, such as gold, silver, iron, copper, and so forth, together with the rest of the minerals,
that is, things extracted from the earth, on page [?]. 3. And what causes the hot waters found in various places.
And why, together with other waters, [?]; and the many other differences among waters, although there are only two kinds of water:
one, the salt water of the seas, and the other, fresh water for use, on page 4. And what trees, grasses, and the kinds of seeds are,
and why and how they exist. 5. And where wild animals and livestock come from, and why.
Discourse Eight, containing five chapters. 1. How one ought to think about all these things that have been mentioned, and whether there is a single knowledge concerning these created things,

and a single understanding and contemplation of them; and whether, as a person acquires and advances in conduct and knowledge, knowledge of these things also advances within that person, and contemplation of all these created things also becomes more refined for that person.
And what a person gains from true knowledge of these things. 2. And what conduct and training elevate a person's mind and raise it

through the degrees, levels, and accurate knowledge of [all] these things. 3. And through how many levels a person rises and is elevated in conduct. 4. And how far a person rises and reaches in knowledge. 5. And whether knowledge of the truth has an end or boundary,
or whether it is without end and lasts forever. Discourse Nine, containing [?] chapters. 1. And what the kingdom of heaven is, and the delight and blessings promised to those who do good,
and to what extent they can be known. 2. And what Gehenna is, and the torment of those who do evil. 3. And whether there is a single order and degree of delights and torments,
or whether there are many differences among them. 4. And whether these different delights and torments remain perpetually in one order or change. 5. And whether
there is an end to the judgment of sinners, as some have supposed. 6. And whether there is an end to judgment, as others have shown. 7. And whether both sides are true.
and how they are true, when they contradict one another. Then he begins again to show how the generations and families of humanity multiplied.
And why people's languages [?] differ; and why their faces, voices, and visible appearances differ, although the order of their nature is one.
And whether their desires and thoughts differ in the same way as their appearances, and why
there are these many differences in people's outward and inward characteristics; and how kings arose in the world,
and when and why; and why governors of regions and cities were appointed in the world,
and judges and lawmakers; and why cities and fortresses are built, and bitter hatreds [?].
And why people learned warfare and armed combat, and armies were organized for slaughter and [?].
And how each of these orders ought—that is, kings, lords, governors, judges, lawmakers, and armies that wage war—
to conduct themselves and act, each in their own rank and service; and why nations were separated from one another.
And how different religions arose, and when and why; and how many principal kinds of religion there are in the world,
and into how many kinds, forms, and differences of opinion each has divided, although its general kind is one.
And in what respects all religions contradict one another, and in what respects, in turn, they agree and are alike; and which is more certain and stronger:
the disagreement or the agreement of religions; and why leaders of the faith and chief authorities were appointed in all religions,
and what they represent and signify; and what the order of the priesthood and its purpose are, what its dimensions are like, and what they resemble.
And how religious leaders and priests ought to conduct themselves in this world, whom they should imitate, what they should await, and what their hope is.
[And how the rest of humanity—farmers, merchants, and the other craftsmen—ought to conduct themselves.] And how the governors who rule the world ought,
together with religious leaders and priests, to deal with the rest of humanity who are subject to them.
And how, in turn, people—farmers, merchants, and craftsmen—ought to deal with their temporal and spiritual leaders,
in deeds and thoughts; and, after all these things, what it is right and fitting for all people to do and practice,
which is the [?] and protection of them all, and is necessary and obligatory for them all.
These are the subjects of this book, together with other beneficial matters,
and the discourse of knowledge interwoven among these subjects, as the grace of the generous Giver bestowed it and imparted wisdom and complete perfection to the weak and deficient author,
for the benefit and help of the many who will encounter and study these things. Whoever reads this book carefully and intelligently,
in silence and tranquility, with a collected mind and thought, and repeats it a second and third time without growing weary of it, will be filled with all knowledge of the truth,
and will advance, be raised up, and become perfect. And, to speak precisely—even if it is a great thing to say [?]—he will become divine and be purified, and his mind will become clear.
And he is united with his Maker, and sees his Maker within himself. And all these things that have been mentioned, which cannot be contained in ten thousand times ten thousand worlds like this one—
all are contained in him and are within the human being, in a place so small that nothing is smaller than it, namely, in the center of the heart.
And for anyone who attains these things, all the power of this world, its glory, its greatness, its wealth, and its possessions—
are like worthless dust to him. And after his Maker, there is nothing in the world so loved and cherished by him as another human being, who shares his nature.
In him he sees his Lord, and in him he gains his Creator—but not by being close to him, rather by keeping away from all human conduct and dealings.
These things are enough up to this point. Nine discourses have been completed in this book.
And throughout, there are chapters indicating the subjects, as marked at the beginning of each discourse, one after another in order.
These are the six headings that should be placed before the book. 1. The purpose of this book is—
to teach the perfection of the knowledge of truth. 2. It is useful for the study of all peoples and suitable for every rank and every degree,
because it is clear and open, its meaning is easy to understand, and there is no obscurity in it.

3. The book bears the title: “Universal, for All Peoples.” 4. It is divided into discourses and chapters, in which it makes every kind of knowledge known. 5. It is the writing of a stranger, persecuted and harassed, who practiced asceticism in silence and solitude on a desolate mountain,

and burned with love for all human beings and was consumed by love for them, because he had come to know their nature and their dignity, as this book makes known in its main body and at its conclusion.
6. The proper way to approach this book is to read it in silence and with a clear mind, together with knowledgeable people
who are free from every passion of envy and love of empty glory, so that the reader and the listener may benefit,
and the speaker and the writer may receive mercy. These are the six headings that should be placed before every written work.
From here he begins this written work, relying on God, heavenly strength, and the Lord’s help. First: a prayer of supplication,

that is, a petition to the Cause of all causes, the Creator of all creatures, and the Lord of all lords, so that the structure of the teaching may rest on the foundation of truth and may help the speaker, the writer, and the reader,
to the praise of the one Lord, the eternal Being, who has existed from eternity without beginning,
and exists continually and at all times without change, and remains the same from generation to generation and forever and ever, without end:
the first and good Cause of all causes, the wise Creator of all creatures, and the rich Lord of all lords,
the Maker and Fashioner of things visible and invisible, hidden and incomprehensible,
and without limit, the Ruler and Provider, the Giver of life, the constant Caregiver, the Guardian and Protector.
You are the Lord, the King, and the Ruler, good and wise, rich and lacking nothing, merciful and compassionate, abounding in kindness
and overflowing with good gifts, who [?] and made and brought everything into being through his goodness, and is concerned for everything,
and governs everything in his wisdom, and cares for everything and provides for everything from the abundant and rich treasury of his lordship.
You alone are God of gods and Lord of lords, and ruler of all the worlds, visible and invisible.
I acknowledge you, my Lord, my God, and my Maker; I believe in you and hold fast to you. I praise you, exalt you, and magnify you.
I worship you and bow down before you. I prostrate myself before your lordship.
Before your footstool, O hidden and incomprehensible one, I bow the neck of my soul, my spirit [?], and my body.
I kneel, and I ask and plead with the vast extent
and immeasurable reach of your grace: give me, my Lord, from the great treasury of your compassion, from the great and boundless sea of your wisdom in its many forms,
a clear mind, a serene soul, and knowledge of the truth. Create in us a pure heart, renew an upright spirit within us, and sanctify our impulses.
Enlighten our thoughts and make our ignorance wise, so that according to your will, according to what pleases you, and according to the power of your truth,
we may think and speak, and write about you. For everything comes from you, everything is in your hands, and everything is for your sake.
You are the Father, Lord, and Maker of our souls, the one who forms and sustains our bodies, the source of all our good things, and the helper of us all.
We all together worship and praise you—that is, all whom your lordship has created—now, at all times, and in all the ages to come, forever and ever. Amen.
The reason for this composition: why it came to be, whose it is, and to whom it was written—to all the peoples under heaven.
Brothers, kinsmen, and members of one another, children of one race and one lineage, sharing one common nature consisting of a rational and spiritual soul capable of understanding and knowledge,
and a physical body composed of the four material elements: peace and tranquility be upon them all, from the Lord of true peace.
May you all have complete health, well-being, and preservation of life in the light of the knowledge of the truth, without which there is no true life,
no well-being, and no complete health, but only darkness, falsehood, the bewilderment of error, and the death of destruction. May all of us together be delivered from it. Amen.
May we all live and rejoice in the light of the knowledge of the truth, through the grace and mercy of the good Lord of us all, the wise guide of our souls and the generous provider for our lives.
To him be continual praise from us all, upright thanksgiving, and true and spiritual worship, at all times and throughout all generations and ages, forever. Amen.
The least brother of all, a small member sharing human nature with you all,
a weak man from Edessa, the city in Mesopotamia situated in the upper part of the region between the great rivers Euphrates and Tigris,
in [?] of true love and in divine affection, makes known to your honored selves and to your true wisdom
that I, your lowly brother, was somehow brought forward to the office of leadership at the head of the people.
Whether this was by the will of God or through human agency, glory be to him who alone knows everything.
I continued in this ministry at the head of my people for about thirty years.
I was tested in many things and endured great distresses, many afflictions, hardships, and troubles.
Amid the conduct of this bewildering and darkening world, as leaders of the people and shepherds commonly suffer at the hands of the flocks and the people under their authority.
After I had often fallen and risen, suffered and been tested, fled and gone far away, I was called back again, returned, and was overcome by the turmoil of the world.
I considered that unless I fled altogether and withdrew completely from the world and all its ways, my soul would grow dark, my mind would become blind, and I would lose the true life.
Again I was tested in my thoughts and became doubtful: perhaps this thought did not accord with the power of the truth.
Or perhaps, after I moved away, I would again be compelled, whether by love for people, by force, or by some trial,
and return once more to the world. While I was greatly distressed by these thoughts, I pleaded with the good Lord, who cares for his creatures,
to establish my thoughts upon those things that please him, accord with his will, help my soul, and lead me to the light of the knowledge of the truth.
Then my thoughts became firmly established in the resolve to flee and withdraw from the world.
Furthermore, I was helped and encouraged much more, and became convinced that this thought came from God.
For at that very time many bitter trials of different kinds came upon me, and certain people were stirred up and became my opponents,
because I was admonishing them for their neglect of the knowledge of the truth and lovingly reproving them for their shameful deeds
and their darkness, according to the custom and order of shepherds who admonish and teach the people, as they are obliged and commanded to do. In this way there grew harsher against me
a trial that became so severe that I had no refuge left except flight, withdrawal, and retreat from the world and all its deceitful conduct, full of favoritism.
And that is indeed what happened. I turned my back and fled, moving to a desolate mountain and a barren wilderness, cut off from people,
hidden and far from any crossing or path and from anywhere near human habitation. I lived in stillness and solitude,
near two or three solitary monks whose way of life was like mine. Whenever I remembered the world and recalled its conduct and the judgment within it,
I would shake and tremble. I dreaded it and recoiled from it as from a blazing fire or a turbulent, destructive sea.
The longer I persevered in stillness, solitude, and distance from the world's affairs and its harassment,
the more my heart gained strength and became firm, and my mind grew courageous. Great joy and abundant consolation began to settle upon me,
because the light of truth began to shine upon me. After that my thoughts became firmly established, and I would prostrate myself before the good Lord
and give thanks for the great and indescribable grace he had shown to my lowliness. My heart came to feel deep affection and love for those who persecuted, oppressed, and greatly distressed me.
I prayed and pleaded for their help and their deliverance from the darkness of ignorance. For although they hated and persecuted me,
it brought me great good and abundant help. In return for the insults and injustice I suffered, I found abundant mercy
and was visited by divine grace, and the light of truth dawned upon me. After I had remained a short time in that stillness and seclusion,
a thought about creation and the Creator arose within me, and I spent much time pondering and reflecting on these things.
And I desired nothing at all for myself except to be given knowledge of the truth.
When I had prayed much, pleaded, and begged for this, my Lord saw that I had asked rightly, and that good Lord gave it and bestowed it on me.
It was not because I was worthy, but in keeping with his own indescribable goodness. And as he is a king, his gift too is royal and abundant.
His glory is magnified all the more by this: he does not withhold his grace even when its recipients are unworthy, just as he makes his sun rise on the good and the wicked.
In this way his mercies extend over all human beings, and everyone who asks him rightly receives what is very good and abundant,
provided, indeed, that he asks rightly. When the Lord acted in this way and helped my weakness through his grace, from the experience within my sorrowful soul
I perceived and understood the great love and abundant care that the good Lord, the wise Creator, and the generous Provider has for his beloved creation.
And when I considered the great dignity of human beings—what their origin is, what stock they come from, and what they are being kept for,
and what transformation awaits them after the end and completion of this world, their place of training—
I was engulfed in great love for them, and a fierce [?] fire of love for all human beings under heaven blazed within me.
When I think of the good and knowledgeable, those who are truly wise and walk in the light of knowledge,
my heart rejoices and grows strong, and my soul is glad far more than at any good thing that comes to me.
But when I remember my negligent friends and companions, those deprived of the light of the knowledge of truth,
who therefore walk in darkness and in the confusion of error—and, what is still more bitter, do not even know it,
and do not long to see the light—I suffer and am distressed, my heart groans, and my soul is sorrowful to the point of death.
I have no other distress or sorrow except this alone. And out of the pain of my heart and the sympathy arising from our shared nature,
and the great love I have for my fellow members, and divine love for all human beings, those of my own race,
I resolved to write these things to all nations, so that wherever there is someone lazy and negligent like me, he may read and hear these things,
and awaken from the sleep of faithfulness [?], and flee from the darkness of the night of ignorance,
and walk in the way of the light of truth [?], and reach the city of the heavenly kingdom.
There he may rejoice and delight with the great King and Lord of glory, whose door is open to everyone who knocks on it, and whose kingdom welcomes all worlds
and has room for all creatures. But if these things trouble my people and those who hold to my confession, and the foremost men and leaders of our faith become angry with me,
and those who are wise and knowledgeable in the truth reproach me, asking why I am handing over the bread of the children of the household to foreign children,
I beg and implore their greatness not to be angry with my lowliness or reproach my inadequacy, because I have not done these things by my own will, but through the action and will of the Lord,
who is good and is the wise Creator of us all, the generous Provider of our lives, who cares for the help and well-being of us all.
He who makes his sun rise on the good and the evil, who sends his rain down on the righteous and the unjust.
He who stretched out the heavens equally above us all and poured out this life-giving air equally for the [?] and the breath of life of us all.
The wings of his grace are spread out and [?] over us all, and his mercies flow abundantly over the good and the evil alike, without grudging and without restraint.
That good, merciful, and compassionate Lord, to whom all the hidden things of our deeds, our words, and our thoughts are revealed.
Yet before his glorious majesty we sin and act wickedly. Our wrongdoing is against him, and he is the judge of us all.
He has authority over our life and death. Not only does he bear our injustice and put up with us when we sin and do wrong,
remaining patient and not destroying us, but he also gives us life and preserves our lives. He does good to us and provides for us. He cares for us and never neglects our welfare.
He desires that all people should live and come to the knowledge of the truth, and he does not desire the death of the sinner,
nor that a single person should perish away from the path of truth. How much, then, ought we, wretched as we are, to love all people
and help them with all our strength and to the full extent of our ability! Whoever loves the Creator, is mindful of him, and fears him
should also love his image, what he has formed and created. From everything given to him from above, he should give and provide for all his brothers, his fellow human beings.
Anyone who does not do good and help others, whether in word or deed or in whatever way, and withholds his kindness from anyone at all,
whether that person shares his faith or is a stranger, whether righteous or sinful, whether a believer or an unbeliever,
is himself an unbeliever, an unjust person, and a hater of humanity. Whoever hates human beings also hates their Creator.
These things are enough for anyone who knows that he has a Lord and Creator and needs God's mercy and the help that comes from him,
and needs him to pardon and forgive his offenses, preserve his life, and do good to him during his life and after his death.
For it has been said and commanded—and all nations testify that this saying is true—
namely: Just as you want other people to do to you, do to others.
What you find hateful for yourselves, do not do to others. And just as you long for and desire the Creator to act toward you, act
toward all creation yourselves, in whatever ways you can. And so on.
Therefore everyone who fears the Lord, loves him, and needs his mercy and help
should, when he encounters this general letter, drive from his soul every evil influence of the hateful passion of envy, which murders human beings,
and all deceit and favoritism, and all hatred, faultfinding, and accusation against others. He should clothe himself in divine love,

which is known through love for human beings. He should arm himself with love for the Creator's image, strengthen himself with heavenly hope, and become firmly established in the knowledge of the truth,
with humility that raises one up and voluntary self-abasement, together with natural compassion. He should increase his goodness and his help for everyone.
Let him illuminate this written work [?] and expand it well. Let him copy it and write it in other books as far as he can, and correct it wherever there is an error.
Let him supply what is missing, carry it from place to place, and pass it from nation to nation and from language to language,
and from book to book, so that the grace of the good Lord, the generous giver and wise provider, may flow and overflow
over all nations and languages, so that we may all share in this good thing and this benefit for everyone.
And whoever, with love, humility, and fear of God, takes care to do good, writes these things and copies them into other books, and carries and passes them from nation to nation,
and from language to language and from book to book, may he too receive help from his Creator, the good Lord, who desires life and salvation for us all.
May heavenly good things pour down upon him, and may divine blessings be multiplied for him. May the light of truth dawn upon him,
and may he become wise through true knowledge. May his body be sanctified in holiness, and may his soul shine with grace. May his heart be cleansed of all sinful passions,
and may his mind be cleared of every spectacle of wickedness. May he receive help from the Lord of heaven and earth, and may he be strengthened by the great power that overcomes all powers.
May divine favors abound upon him, and may he overflow with spiritual gifts. May he be comforted by his Lord in heaven,
and may he rejoice in his Maker, the Lord of all. May his righteousness dawn like the light, and may his faith shine like the sun.
May he be protected, rescued, and delivered from every injury, affliction, and evil adversity that occurs in this world.
May he be found worthy of a good end, a blessed conclusion, and a peaceful departure.
May his resurrection be with the upright and righteous, and his rising from the dead with the good and merciful. May he delight in heavenly blessings
and inherit eternal life in the heavenly kingdom, in spiritual joy, in the garden of Eden,
before the divine Majesty, in the presence of the fatherly Cause, the ruler of all ages, the Cause of all causes,
who sustains all created things, whom we all worship and praise, exalt and bless,
and whose [?] we await and look for. We ask him for mercy and entrust our souls into his hands.
To him are fitting and due praise, thanksgiving, worship, honor, exaltation, and acclaim from all heavenly and earthly beings,

from everything that has come into being and exists and that his Majesty has created, now and at all times, throughout all generations and all the ages that have been and shall be, forever and without end, for ever and ever. Amen.
Here ends the introductory discourse explaining the purpose of this universal book on the knowledge of truth, addressed to all nations under heaven.
Again, strengthened by the good Lord and made wise by his divine goodness,
we begin the first discourse on the knowledge of truth, addressed to all nations under heaven. It contains ten chapters.
Chapter, that is, the first section: On what a human being ought to know and learn. A human being, then, is a rational, mortal living creature,
composed of a living and rational soul, beautiful and radiant in its nature.
And for this reason it is capable of receiving understanding and knowledge continually and without limit; and from a material, heavy body composed of four elements.
From these this entire visible world is composed and ordered. And because he is not like the other animals, which lack reason,
but shares in the reason that brings knowledge, and has within him a nature capable of receiving knowledge as wisdom is given to him,
he can rise and ascend through his knowledge and understanding to immeasurable and boundless heights.
These he learns and knows not from writing or from hearing, but from the glorious order of virtuous conduct that he displays in his own person.
He ought continually to seek, investigate, and learn what his own human nature really is, what he exists for, and why.
For everything has an order. He too ought to proceed in an orderly way and know what he should first learn and understand,
where he should begin in learning the knowledge of truth, what first foundation he ought to lay, and what kinds of buildings
he should build upon it, and how high his building should rise and ascend.
And where he should begin on this path of the knowledge of truth, which distinguishes truth from falsehood and light from darkness,
and truthfulness from lying, and knowledge from error. For everyone who walks in the light neither goes astray nor becomes confused,
but knows how he is walking and where he is going. He reaches where he wishes to go, and the purpose he has set in his mind is fulfilled.
He receives what he hoped for, his undertaking reaches a good conclusion, and his entire way of life comes to a fine end.
But someone who travels in darkness does not know where he is going. His journey does not reach a good conclusion; instead, he wanders in confusion.
And his ruin leads to destruction. Such is the knowledge of truth, and these are the distinctions between truth and falsehood,
between good and evil, and between light and darkness. For truth, goodness, and light exist and are established realities.
They have a beginning—that is, an origin—and existence. Falsehood, evil, and darkness, however, do not exist.
They have neither substance nor existence, but are the absence of something—that is, its removal.
For example, if someone says that the day is bright, this is true. But if he says that the day is not bright,
this is nothing and is not true. At night, however, when the world is deprived of the sun and its rays are withdrawn from the earth, darkness occurs.
Yet darkness is not anything in its own right, but an absence of good. These are transient accidents without substance,
not accidents that persist by nature, like light in the sun's sphere, whiteness in snow, and blackness in a raven.
And because darkness, falsehood, and evil have neither substance nor existence, they possess no strength either.

Rather, they are weak [?] and easily overcome, if only we are willing and choose, with the natural freedom resembling God that was given to humanity, the good [?], and hate evil. Then his freedom is genuine, and his will resembles [?] in its nature.
But if he neglects the good or does not desire it, evil enters him as an accident. Then he becomes enslaved to the evil that has gained dominion over him.
By his own will, he destroys his freedom and does not remain in his nature, nor does he resemble his Maker. Whoever is like this and has not stood firm in the truth of his nature and his creation
is a liar, walks in darkness, and is bound to destruction. On these matters we do not need to say much or demonstrate them through words and proofs,
because they are clear, evident, and known to many, both by nature and by instruction.
Now, then, it is known and evident to everyone that truth is light, is good and real, and exists.
Falsehood is darkness and evil; it does not exist and is not real, but is an oppressive and thieving accident.
Therefore we ought to choose and desire truth, which is the light that leads to true, blessed, and eternal life, and reject falsehood, which is darkness
leading to everlasting destruction. Therefore we ought to take care and first investigate truth thoroughly.
And when we see the light of truth, then we walk well wherever we wish, like those who have laid a sound, deep, and firmly established foundation.
Their whole building is supported and completed as they wish. Now, my friends, my brothers, and my fellow members—all people who hear these things—
know that anyone who undertakes any task ought to start at the beginning and proceed in order, so that his task reaches completion.
But if he does not begin in an orderly way and from where he ought to begin, but confusedly, from the middle of the task or at its end,
he gains nothing but loss and confusion, and does not reach completion. His labor is in vain.
Therefore we must all begin where we ought, where the task begins: we with speaking, and you with listening.
This, then, is the beginning: let us all imagine that we were created today and entered this world.
This is a true and certain beginning, suitable for all peoples, since it is accepted by them all.
No one can refute it at all. Now, we were created by someone, whoever he may be,
and we were all placed in a certain very broad plain, in which there was as yet nothing at all: no mountains or caves,
no trees, crops, buildings, or possessions—[?] only ourselves, naked.
We see that we have a body susceptible to suffering, and above us are the sun, the other heavenly lights, and the changing air.
Below us are earth and water. We perceive that there is another nature within us, beautiful and luminous: this rational soul
and understanding mind. There is life within us. Then this body begins to suffer from the changes in the air above us.
At one time the sun burns and scorches us with its heat; at another, the air lashes us with its fierce cold and makes us wet with dew and showers.
The earth beneath us, too, mixes with water, becomes mud and mire, and soils us. When we suffer these things, we seek protection from these things that cause the body suffering.
Then this inward thing within us—that is, the understanding mind—begins to generate thoughts and devise ways to protect its partner, the body, from these sufferings.
And we said that we are supposing this. It considered that there ought to be some shelter above us.
to keep the sun’s heat and the violence of the weather and rain away from us. This was the first idea that we human beings conceived.
Afterward, we also considered that this covering needed walls to support it. Then we considered that these walls also needed deep, firm foundations on which to rise.
Here the planning of the construction of the dwelling called a house was complete. And where planning ends, the work should begin.
And where the planning first began and took shape in the mind, there the work reaches completion. This is called the end that is conceived beforehand.
This is indeed known to many. Likewise, regarding the soul, should we not consider
that we see it has painful and stupefying passions, namely the darkness of ignorance and the error of falsehood?
These passions are thieves that enter the soul in the darkness of the night of error. And when they happen to enter it,
they produce in it all the other evil passions, and so on, leading to complete destruction. And just as we devised protection against the injuries that threaten the body,
and made a house for it and sheltered it there, and it was protected from these things that hurt it, along with other injuries that would have befallen it
had it not taken shelter in the house, behind walls and doors, so we should take even greater care for the soul, which is the mistress of the body,
and make it a house of refuge from the injuries that come upon it at all times. And just as this house built for the body
protects it from heat, cold, and rain, and from being soiled by clay and mud,
and from harmful animals, deadly creeping creatures, thieves, and enemies, and after saving it from all these things also provides it with comfort in all
its needs, so too the house prepared for the soul protects it from many injuries greater than these, as we are going to show with the help of God, who guides and gives wisdom.
With these words the first chapter is concluded, with the help of God who guides.
Chapter Two: How the Truth Is Known with Certainty. Now that we have shown what a person should first know and learn,
namely, to investigate the truth carefully and distinguish it from falsehood,
we say further that this book before us was written for all peoples in general, with the good intention of true and divine love,
for the great benefit of the soul and the protection of the body of those who will hear it, and for a favorable remembrance of its weak and needy writer,
but for the praise and honor of the one Lord of all, the Maker, Creator, and wise Provider, from whom comes every perfect good.
He gives the speaker words of true knowledge, and the hearer understanding and accurate discernment,
provided, that is, that both conduct themselves with the intention of love, humility, and the fear of God, free from every hateful passion of envy,
the deceit of wickedness, empty glory that is abhorrent to God, and impure pride that contends with God.
For great opposition has arisen among all the peoples throughout the world, and with the passing of time and the course of years,
the opposition has increased and hatred has arisen, leading to many evils that have unexpectedly come upon the human race like thieves in the night.
And immediately division arose among them, and they would not be reconciled to one another.
From these things, these estranged brothers, sons of one good and kind father, were brought to great hostility and the destruction of one another.
Servants of one great, merciful, and exceedingly wealthy king, and disciples of one faithful and exceedingly wise teacher of truth.
Each turned aside in a different direction and made for himself a book, a confession of faith, laws, and customs. They have conducted themselves according to these down to the present day.
In some of these things they differ from one another, while in others they agree and are united, as we will show with God's help, each matter in its proper place,
and as is appropriate to it. Since, then, one of the peoples has its own separate books, laws, customs, and confessions of faith [?],
this one does not accept that one's book, nor does that one accept this one's, nor the laws,
nor the customs, along with the rest of the other things. We will show where this division came from, if the Lord of us all wills.
Thus, when we bring them out, the masters of the house will remain without fear, at rest and free from worry.
Let the reader understand. Because the peoples differ from one another and do not accept one another's confessions of faith, books, and laws,
it is neither possible nor right for us to use a proof from one of the books, or to bring testimony from one person's law and confession of faith against another.
For he does not accept it: first, because of the orientation of the confession of faith he holds, and second, because of the pattern of conduct, teaching, and law in which he was brought up,
and because of their distance from one another and their lack of association and dealings with one another. For this reason, from the very beginning of this book,
we have never used even a single word of [?] toward any of our peoples, nor with an aim tied to a confession of faith, or to custom and conduct.
The wise and knowledgeable understand as they read. For someone who, with the aim of true and divine love, wants to teach another about what he loves,
should engage with him through something he can hear and his mind accepts, to which his understanding and his nature bear witness.
Likewise, someone who wants to say something to a person should speak to him in a language that person knows, so that he may recognize and understand what he says.
And someone who wants to refresh a person with food should refresh him with the kinds that suit him.
That is, if he is an infant, with milk and water; if he is sick, with drinks and medicines; and if he is weak, with vegetables and seeds.
And if he is a fully grown and healthy man, with substantial foods: bread, meat, and the other dishes.
Likewise, a father speaks with his infant son in the infant's own language, using the names the infant himself gives to father, mother, brothers, and other things,
and not in the mature speech of adults. How, then, should someone act who wants to refresh and help all peoples alike with a message of knowledge,
when he does not use the words of a book as proof or testimony? For my part, I say this,
as I also believe: according to a person's aim, thought, and will,
it is given to him from above. That is, if his aim is true [?] and divine love, in a spirit of humility and with an upright purpose, free from every hateful passion and deceit.
A person wishes to help his brothers and fellow members, the creation and handiwork of his Creator, because of the love and goodwill
of the Lord of all himself, who loves his creation and what he has formed. He is that good Lord who loves humanity
and desires life, good things, and help for everyone. He gives him knowledge, intelligence, and [?].
And he puts a helpful word in his mouth for the speaker whose intention is upright, and, for the blessed and humble listener who is free from all envy,
understanding and discernment, for the praise of the Giver's name and for the benefit of all parties.
Now, my beloved, since we cannot and should not yet use an argument or testimony from Scripture, let us rise and ascend in our thinking
to the source from which Scripture was born and received. From the source from which Scripture receives the [?] appropriate to it, let us also receive what is useful to us all,
and let us provide for one another with it. Who, then, is this, and where is he? We say that the father of Scripture is with us all, and that the one older than Scripture is the father of us all.
The father of Scripture is the mind. It gave birth to Scripture and to all teachings, branches of wisdom, and crafts,
but through the hidden activity and sovereign gift of the good Creator, who is rich in gifts and wise in what he bestows.
The one older than Scripture is the father of us all: nature, which brought us into being and existence.
So, as we ask the Maker of [?] to give wisdom to our ignorance in this writing addressed to you, dear and beloved ones and honored brothers, from nature itself, the father of us all,
let us draw on it throughout the discussion of this course set before us, until nature itself teaches us that Scripture is true
and comes from nature itself, though it is foreign to us, and our intelligence and thinking accept it. Then we shall also use the word of Scripture as is fitting,
or rather, wherever it wills, and as the grace of the Lord of nature, Scripture, and us all grants.
If this work had been written by one of the wise and famous people in the world, or by one of the Gentiles,
or by one of the distinguished teachers, or by one of the great men known in the world,
or by one of the kings who have won renown on earth, it would not have been a great matter. Indeed, it would not even have been believed or accepted among all the Gentiles,
because envy and opposition would have arisen against the work. But through this the praise of the Giver increases,
and the writer is believed and accepted, receives compassion and mercy, and is helped through prayer,
because he is a small and insignificant person, despised and ordinary, uneducated and pure in heart,
so that everyone who sees him or hears about him has compassion on him, loves him, and prays that he may be helped.
For he did not compose and write these things for material gain, nor for worldly acclaim and empty, fleeting praise,
nor because of any evil and deceitful passion, but solely because of divine love and for the common benefit of all humanity.
Rather, it is because helping his creation pleases God, and because it serves the praise of his glorious and worshipful name, and not because he writes to an ordinary person.
And if you benefit, take delight, and rejoice in hearing it, give praise and thanks to the good Giver, the wise Teacher, and the generous Provider.
Pray for help for the needy writer, for the humble man who wrote it solely out of his good will and sincere love.
And thus the good Lord has shown himself to act from the beginning of the world: through people who are despised, of low birth, pure in heart, and ordinary,
he has worked and given a message of help, and has sent those whom we are going to mention to the rest of humanity, wherever our Lord deemed fitting and desired.
In this way the praise of the good Lord increases all the more, and the message is believed and accepted as coming from him.
For he does not send his message through the wise people of the world, renowned teachers, and great men, but through simple and uneducated people
and those who are pure in heart. These remarks are sufficient for this purpose, even though the discussion has grown longer than necessary.
But the subject required these things to be said first. Now let us go on to explain how the truth is known with certainty.
Let us proceed systematically through the discussion. We said above, and explained in the preceding chapter,
that just as the nature of the body compels and obliges us to shelter it from things that cause it suffering, and our mind devised and built a house to protect it,

so it is right that a house belonging to the soul—that is, a spiritual house—should also be built for our spiritual soul. And what we have just spoken of and called a house belonging to the soul and a spiritual house
are not one but two: one belonging to the soul and the other spiritual. Together with the first, the house for the body, they make three in all.

We have built that first house for the body, and we continue to build it as long as it is needed. Likewise, we must build the house belonging to the soul; we are able to do so, and [?] for us. But God builds the spiritual house, provided that we too
are willing, take care, plead with him, and prove worthy. We will speak clearly about these things when the good Lord wills and we reach the appropriate place for them.
Now, however, we ought to prepare a house to shelter and protect our soul, just as we have established a house for our body. And just as heat scorches our body,
so we see that the heat of desire and anger, implanted in our nature, scorches our soul.
And just as cold and damp torment our body when the sun's rays are absent,
so the cold of negligence and the damp of lusts drown our soul when the rays of the knowledge of truth are absent.
And just as harmful animals injure the body when it is outside the walls of the house, so hateful passions injure the soul when it is outside the walls of true wisdom.
These are envy, resentment, hatred, vainglory, anger, contentiousness, and sorrow,
and the love of money, together with the rest of such things. Stronger than all of them is pride, which contends with God,
along with arrogance and conceit. And just as thieves snatch and plunder from a house that is not fortified with walls and doors,
so too the passions of deceit and ignorant error enter a soul that is not fortified with true wisdom
and plunder from it all the good things that belong to its nature, as well as those it has acquired through its own diligence.
Therefore we ought, with still greater diligence and much care, to gain wisdom, devise a plan, and establish a house of knowledge.
And let us strengthen ourselves through it. This knowledge requires practice and learning, and this is attained through inquiry into truth,
so that it may be known and distinguished from falsehood. Hence we ought to begin building our knowledge of truth, which is light and grace,
just as we begin with the foundations when constructing a house, the body's shelter. As for how this is known,
we have already explained it to anyone who has understood. Again we say and make clear: light is something, and it has individual existence and essence,
and it is situated in the sphere of the sun, although other lights exist naturally in stones, pearls, glowworms, and other kinds of things.
Darkness, however, is not something that subsists, but an absence. This world and the human being exist, and they are individual entities,
and they have a nature and an essence. Then, for someone to say that the world does not exist, nor the human being, and that nothing exists, along with many similar things—
therefore truth certainly exists in the world. It is light, which is the knowledge of truth. And truth itself is a nature
that is firmly established and present. And nature brought everything into being. Therefore, the nature that brought everything into being and existence
is itself certain truth. Therefore, let us hasten to the book of nature,
and read in it, and learn from it about everything that we need and ought to learn. With these words the second chapter is concluded, through God who guides.
Again, with God who gives wisdom: Chapter Three. What Truth Is and What Falsehood Is. After the two chapters that have been set forth,
concerning what a human being ought to know and learn—that is, to investigate truth carefully and distinguish it from falsehood—
and how truth is known with certainty, namely, through the soul's clarity, by which it looks carefully into nature and measures truth,
let us now say what truth itself is and what falsehood is. We say that truth is something that exists,
and falsehood is something that does not exist. Truth stands on its own and is confirmed as such by the fact that it exists.
Falsehood, however, does not stand on its own, because it does not exist. Just as darkness is the absence of light,
and evil the absence of good, so falsehood is the absence of truth. Light and good exist, but darkness and evil do not exist;
rather, they are described as the absence of these things. Truth, however, is more powerful than these, because it exists continually and stands on its own.
And where truth exists continually, falsehood cannot exist at all, because there is no time when truth does not exist.
See, it has been shown that falsehood does not exist at all, whereas what is true certainly exists. And this is the wonder:
how something that does not exist at all can be spoken of and have a name. This, however, happens among those who are deprived of truth.
And if this statement were not hard for the hearers, I would say that most of the world is outside the truth, and those who have found the truth are few.
Those who have found the truth have been united with it and enlightened, and have reigned on earth and in heaven. He has absolutely no enemy, no opponent, and no one who hates him,
nor any hindrance, because falsehood [?] has neither robbed him nor gained power over him, since he is always in the light.
And this person became like his Creator and confirmed his own creation and the statement that has been made: that he is created in the image of his Creator.
This is a great mystery, and it cannot be explained now, because the beginning of the book is like milk for infants.
As the infant grows, so does his food, until he reaches maturity, the full stature of all our kind.
We have said, and continue to say, how the truth becomes known. But what the truth actually is cannot be known from hearing words or reading books.
But the person who has found the truth and knows it is recognized by these signs: he loves all people and does good to them.
He is above all hateful passions. All the power of this world, its glory, and its possessions—
he considers them nothing. All hidden things are revealed to him, and he knows the power, the activity, and the hidden mystery concealed in everything that exists on earth.
Everything obeys his will and command: rational beings, living and lifeless things, the elements, and everything made from them.
For they see in him the true image of his Creator, pure, beautiful, and unchanging.
But the person who has not reached this state and has no awareness of these things has falsehood contending with him, and darkness entangles him, along with wickedness.
These are thieving and intrusive passions that have entered the pure and beautiful nature. Therefore, my beloved brothers, since these things are so,
and this is the order of our nature, and our origin is from that [?] purity and great goodness,
we can rise there again, and it is easy for us if we wish. That evil is [?] and utter destruction.
And if we neglect this great and limitless goodness found in our nature, and cling to thieving falsehood,
which has no existence at all and is not found in our nature. With these words this third chapter has been concluded through God, who gives wisdom.
Again, with God as guide: the fourth section, or chapter. How it is known that God exists. Glorious and true God,
you who are the eternal Being, who cannot be comprehended or approached, who cannot be explained or spoken of by a tongue of flesh,
who cannot be grasped by the mind's thoughts, encompassed in speech or writing, or touched by the wings of thought.
Why should I multiply words and chatter before your lordship? For even speech about your incomprehensibility and hiddenness has no limit.
Yet you grant pure minds the ability to know you and enlighten them, according to their capacity and the measure of their purity.
Rather, it is as you wish and in whatever way you wish. And the greatness of your knowledge, which knows everything that has happened and happens from eternity, knows
as though it were before your eyes, without change, what helps those who know and are capable of knowing.
Praised is your great and glorious name, praised continually with its glorious and praiseworthy praise. Your majesty is worshiped. Thanks
to your lordship! O you whom all created beings are neither sufficient nor adequate nor able to praise fully, for you are glorious, perfect, and complete,
and you lack nothing, O good Lord, wise Creator, and generous Provider. Give us a pure mind and an enlightened soul.
And create in us a pure heart, so that through you we may speak about you and for your sake, as your majesty wills and your grace grants.
Your wisdom knows what we are able to say and capable of hearing. Yet we, wretched as we are, venture into things of which we are unworthy.
But you, O Good One, wished to make your creatures aware of your being. For this reason you created them: that they might know you and be enriched from your inexhaustible treasury.
And that they might become wise through your boundless knowledge and delight in you continually and without end.
For these reasons, my Lord, you created your creatures, and not so that they might praise you, for you are glorious, high, and exalted above all the praise of those who praise.
Rather, they themselves are needy and lacking. They therefore praise you so that they may draw near to your majesty.
And so that they themselves may be helped and grow through the praise they offer you. Blessed is your glory by all, and you are worshiped by all.
And your name is praised, [?], and exalted forever and ever. Amen. Truly, my beloved, everyone says and believes that God exists.
And not only human beings, but demons too believe, and quake and tremble before the glory of his awesome and glorious name.
But most people say only in words that God exists.
They know him with a simple and very limited knowledge. Very few indeed are those who are aware of him, and even these have grasped only a little.
It is like a single drop from the whole great sea throughout the world, or a single grain from all the sand on the earth, in the seas, and in the rivers.

And when a little of the splendor of his glory shone upon them, they were consumed and set ablaze by the fire of his love. They were aflame with love for him and forgot themselves and their own nature.
And they became like madmen to [?], who did not understand or perceive what they longed for. But, my brothers and beloved ones,
because we have already said above that we should think of ourselves as though today we had entered this world, all of us together,
and had gathered together on some deserted plain, as we said, and wished to investigate together,
and to examine the matter in our thoughts, find the certain truth, and follow it, we must therefore investigate carefully and learn whether
there is a God, Lord, and governor of this universe or not, from accounts and testimonies that are reliable, confirm the matter, and bring conviction to all the peoples under heaven.
These must be such that everyone's mind can accept them and their understanding can grasp them, and they can hear, understand, and believe the truth.
That truth is revealed and made known to them and established in their hearts, so that they may all agree about it, bear witness to it, and acknowledge it.
And as we explained above, when we found ourselves on this deserted plain, we devised ways to deal with things that caused our bodies suffering.
We thought it through and built a house to shelter us. What we conceived first, namely the roof, was the completion of the work.
And the last part of the plan we conceived was the beginning of the work, namely laying the foundation of the house.
Likewise, we also thought that we ought all the more to build a house of knowledge for that knowing and subtle thing within us, namely our soul.
And just as the roof of the house is the completion of the work, though it was conceived first.
Thus the perfection of the mind is the completion of the works and practices of virtue that we considered earlier.
And just as foundations are the planning of two [?], and also the work of two [?], for supporting a roof,
so too are good works and deeds, pure thoughts, and the rational practice of virtue
a means of drawing near to the attainment of perfection. And just as foundations are the completion of planning and the preparation for action, so the knowledge of truth is
the foundation and beginning of all the good things that raise and lift the human mind and bring it near to complete perfection.
And just as someone who lays a firm foundation and works in the light of day naturally advances and reaches a good and beautiful conclusion,
so too someone who begins to know, investigate, and discover the truth, and whose mind walks and proceeds in the knowledge of the light of truth,
advances and reaches a good and beautiful conclusion, up to the exalted height of perfection. Therefore, my beloved brothers,
from here, from this firm foundation, we ought to begin in an orderly and wise manner,
and rationally, on this bright path of our spiritual and enduring building, which rises to the exalted height of heaven.
What, then, is true truth, illuminating light, perfect knowledge, exalted wisdom, eternal being, and exalted essence?
He existed, and he exists continually, and he remains the same forever. But these things that exist now—
there was a time when they did not exist, and there will be a time when they will not exist. But he always existed and exists,
and he will exist. Therefore, the one who exists continually is more real than those things that do not exist continually.
Therefore, he is true truth. And everything that exists apart from God is nothing—that is, falsehood.
Now we ought, with hope in him and trust in the one who truly exists,
to begin, investigate, venture, and examine carefully whether he exists and how it is known that he exists.
That is—even if the statement is bold—how it is known with certainty and believed among all nations,
and accepted through true testimonies and demonstrations that bring conviction to the mind and understanding of them all,
whether or not there is a God, a Lord, and a governor of this universe. This is the beginning of all our knowledge, the foundation of all our wisdom,
and the reason for seeking all our good things. Now let us gather our mind away from distraction and our thoughts away from confusing concerns.
Let us live in a peaceful dwelling and in a quiet place, free from disturbing noises, troubling reports, and the turmoil of this world, with its many
storms, full of afflictions and disturbances, and piled high with tempests and dark clouds.
Let us pay attention to what is said in this book, and let us also consider the movements of the natural thoughts that our mind produces.
For the soul's nature is clear and bright, and when it is purified of the alien passions that disturb its clarity,

Subtle movements and wonderful, instructive thoughts that reveal the truth. [?] How, then, should we know whether there is a God—that is, a creator and governor of everything? In what book should we read?
From which teacher should we hear? From which wise person should we learn? Which truthful witness should we believe?
On the testimony of which ancient elder, who came first and understands and knows everything, should we all take our stand and agree, and testify that his teaching is true and acceptable?
For suppose that we have all entered the world today, and no one else has preceded us: no prophet, no teacher, no scribe, and no book,
from whom we could all hear and believe. For we have already shown that the truth cannot gain universal belief among everyone through the books possessed by the nations,
because they contradict one another and are not accepted throughout the inhabited world. There are also many who have not read books and have no awareness at all of how
the world was created, or of what has happened or is going to happen. Therefore, the true and trustworthy witness is the one who can demonstrate the certain truth:
the one who does not need another's help or testimony, whether that of a book or a teacher, but whose own truth bears witness to itself.
For he is the true witness, the reliable teacher, and the ancient book—the father and teacher of us all.
But how? Let us listen with understanding, as we said above—or rather, let us begin and investigate from the proper starting point,
which is the beginning and the reliable teacher. We human beings, then, are rational and are by nature capable of understanding and knowledge.
We see two things, visible and perceptible, worthy of great and [?] wonder,
because hidden knowledge and great wisdom lie concealed in them. These are the two visible and perceptible worlds:
one is this great world, consisting of heaven and earth and all these created things between them; the other is the small, twofold world, which is the human being.
That is, we ourselves, who are constituted from the four elements that constitute this great world,
and from another nature, spiritual and subtle, which is hidden within us. It is continually alive and active within us: the living, rational, spiritual soul, capable of receiving wisdom.
When we found ourselves in this broad expanse of the world, this hidden, rational thing within us began to work through
these outward senses, namely sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch, bringing through them much information into itself,
into the hidden courtroom of the just judge in its heart. It compares this with five other, inward faculties, namely intellect, knowledge, thought,
understanding, and discernment. There it makes a great syllogism—that is, a gathering of thoughts—and begins to investigate and examine each matter,
considering it carefully, to know and learn what this great mystery of nature is, and the order established within the human being.
It is continually active. Because it is living, rational, subtle, and spiritual, it neither stops nor rests from its activity,
which is the investigation of hidden things, in keeping with its own hidden and mysterious nature. First, it looked upward and saw this glorious vault,
stretched out with great wisdom and abundant wonder. It began to contemplate the intensity of the sun's light, the changing radiance of the moon,
the bright gleams of the stars, their regularity and orderly arrangement in the different courses of their configurations and their rays.

In the marvelous opposition of their motion to the revolution of the zodiac, under another constraining impulse, by which they are carried along with the zodiac backward in its forceful revolution, and swifter than the zodiac’s lightning [?], in these occurrences and signs that appear in it.
And as outward sight and inward understanding [?] with it. Again, contemplate this air and the vastness of the firmament, the blowing of the different winds,
the arrangement of the clouds, the terrifying sight of lightning, the mighty sounds of thunder, the abundance of rain and showers, the months of the moon,
the changing course of the sun, the cycle of the seasons, and the marvelous ordering of everything mentioned and of many other things like them.
Again, look and gaze at the kinds of winged creatures that fly in the air, at the many species of birds and flying creatures, at their shapes, their colors,
their voices, their songs, their chirping, their seasons, their activity, their usefulness, and the entire ordering of their nature.
Again, look at the different animals and the many beasts on the earth. Some are destructive, powerful, and immensely strong.
Some, again, are large in size and combative. Some eat flesh, and some graze on grass.
Some are gentle and harmless. Some are peaceful and can be kept as possessions. Some can be yoked and used for work.
Some carry burdens, can be ridden, and can be tamed. Some are wild and cannot be [?].
Some can be eaten and used for nourishment, while others cannot be eaten. Some are affectionate and can be kept as possessions.
Some are cunning and crafty. Some are innocent and gentle, though there are differences among them.
And those without fruit, and of plants, shrubs, leaves, and many grasses, and kinds of seeds, greens, and vegetables, and the differences
—the many differences in their nature, that is, in their colors, their scents, their tastes, their effects, and their distinctive properties,
along with the many other things in them. Again, as you look here and there, see the many creeping creatures on the earth. I mean,
great and powerful serpents, kinds of vipers, and venomous snakes that discharge deadly poison,
and scorpions, mice, worms, beetles, and ants, together with the many other creatures that spring from the earth, kill and destroy human beings, and cause much harm.
And as you travel about the earth, here and there, see its many, immeasurable variations, and how they contain hidden mysteries that can scarcely be grasped.
I mean the great height of the mountains, the elevation of the hills, the flat expanse of the plains, the breadth of the deserts,
the different kinds within the earth’s own substance, which differ greatly in their nature and effects, in their colors and tastes,

and in what they produce, together with the radiance and splendor of precious stones, seal stones, crystals, and costly pearls, splendid in color and brilliance, along with other substances: gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, iron, and things like these.
And again, as you wander through creation, approach the impassable seas.
Contemplate them and marvel at their vastness, their expanse, their depth, their movement, their brightness, and their taste.
And as you gaze into them, see the many moving creatures in them, the different kinds of fish,
which are great in body, varied in shape, and numerous in species.
and their number cannot be grasped, along with other species and kinds whose harmful effects differ.
of the depths, such as snails, oysters, turtles, and crabs, together with the rest of the other creatures.
Again, as he traveled, he encountered many rivers, large, medium-sized, and small. He saw springs, streams, fountains, and torrents,
and the many irrigation channels and pools in the inhabited world. In these too he saw many moving creatures and other kinds of fish, frogs, and toads,
and many other things that surpass the power of speech, the capacity of counting, and the comprehension of knowledge,
which exist and are found in this world. And when the human being saw all these things

and considered them in his mind, examined them in his understanding, and reflected on them in his thoughts, he was astonished, amazed, and filled with wonder. Then he put to work the hidden power of the rational nature within him,
and began thinking about and investigating all these things that are seen in [?] and on earth, together with all the other marvelous variations in creation and the established order
and unchanging arrangement by which the world subsists: Where, then, did all this come from, and when? From what, and for what purpose, and how,
and until when? Does it exist of itself, or was it established by another? Does the beginning of its existence stretch back to eternity,
or is there another who is first and earlier than it? While the human being was occupied with these things through his inner senses and the movements of his mind,
and since the hidden nature within him is clear, pure, luminous, and receptive to understanding and knowledge, it resembles a mirror:
the more its surface is worked so that it becomes smooth and polished, the more every shape, color, and form before it appears in it accurately and without alteration.
So too, the more that subtle nature within the human being considers things intelligently and reflects with understanding,

the more it becomes purified, clear, and luminous, and sees and grasps matters, powers, natures, knowledge, and wisdom that it could not grasp before. And the more deeply it enters into its thoughts and exercises its understanding,
the further it advances and rises without end. Then other insights dawned in his mind, and he began examining himself and investigating his own being,
and reflecting on himself with astonishment and very great wonder. He said, “Why should I marvel, wonder, and investigate this world,
which is so great and vast, beyond comprehension because of its greatness and abundance? I will examine my own being and reflect on my own nature: what exactly am I?
For look, I myself am a marvel and a wonder without limit.” He began first with his outward form, investigating, considering, and marveling:
How was this body put together, built, and arranged? How was the head fixed in place, and these many marvelous things fashioned within it?
Where did the hair grow from, covering and adorning the egg-shaped skull? How were the eyes opened,
and this marvelous light placed in them? For look, the pupil is as tiny as a mustard seed,
yet it sees this entire vast expanse and discerns things at a great distance.
Why does it contain so many variations and astonishing wonders? How were the ears fixed in place and their openings pierced
in the head, within the temples, opposite the brain, winding like a snail shell? And how, again, were passages for ascent made in the nostrils, from below upward?
And not from above downward, lest something fall into them and injure them. How taste is in the palate, articulation in the tongue, and the voice comes from the windpipe.
And the firmness of the grinding molars, and the orderly arrangement of the cutting teeth. How the brain dwells like a king in that inner chamber.
Under this splendid dome, inside these gates that admit wondrous reports and send out astonishing actions.
Why are there all these many, countless variations in the head and its parts?
So much so that even physicians of the body have been unable to encompass them in their many books and discussions, treatises and teachings, varied and numerous.
How, again, the neck is firmly established between the shoulders that support it, together with the rest of its structure and the things within it.
How the upper arms and forearms extend, with joints between them for bending and straightening, together with the veins and sinews within them.
How, again, the hands are formed with [?] and fingers and the many things within them, together with the marvelous operations, skilled activities, and various kinds of writing performed with them.
For the great power and ordered working of reason are made known in them and through them. How the chest, the breasts, the belly, the back, the ribs, and the remaining organs are formed.
How, again, the buttocks, thighs, knees, lower legs, ankles, and feet are formed, with their joints and toes.

And the many things within them, together with the rest of the arrangement of the organs, bones, and sinews that make up the body. Then there are the internal organs, which surpass the power of speech and the understanding of the mind.
How the heart and lungs, the esophagus, the stomachs, the bellies, the intestines, the fat, and the other things associated with them hang from the windpipe.
How, again, the liver is placed in a commanding position on the right, the spleen on the left, and the kidneys on either side.
And the bladder and the organs of reproduction, together with the marvelous operations of the rational soul within them.
I mean the mind in the brain, understanding and thoughts in the kidneys, anger in the heart, and desire in the liver.
Together with the many other things that reason accomplishes through them; without them, the activity of that part is suspended.
Where are the four humors, or mixtures, and how are they situated—namely, blood, phlegm, and red bile, that is,
[?], and black bile—together with all the many other features of the body's formation and the arrangement of its external and internal organs.
As is discussed in the many books of Hippocrates and the school of Galen, and of the other physicians who wrote about these matters very extensively and precisely.
And these are only considerations concerning the body, about which one of those skilled in the body's needs and the sufferings caused by its diseases has said:
The whole span of a person's life, he says, is short and small, and insufficient to learn and understand the length, abundance, and breadth of the art concerned with the diseases of the body alone.
But concerning the greatness of the living, rational, and spiritual soul—that is, the knowing mind within us—and concerning its nature and excellence,
Its passions and perceptions, its distinctive properties and operations, and the rest of the knowledge and discourse concerning it: what words would suffice?
What treatises could encompass it? What books could contain it? Who could do it justice? And who could speak of it and make it understood?
For not even all the ancient sages of the house of Nimrod, the disciples of the keen-minded Jonitus, could do so.
And much knowledge. Not even the ancient philosophers, beginning with Agathodaemon and Asclepiades,
and the school of Hermes, wise in everything, the Thrice-Great, and those of Pythagoras and Plato,
and Aristotle’s [?] of words and his rational, subtle, and many-sided teaching, together with the many who came before them, alongside them, and after them,
were able, in their many books, writings, and discourses, to define the nature of the rational and intelligent soul,
and the knowledge and wisdom that it can know and grasp. And how could the people of this world set limits
to something that this whole world can neither contain nor limit—namely, the human mind?
In a single brief moment it travels around the whole inhabited world, reaches all its boundaries, and ranges through all heights and depths.
It plunges into the deep abysses of all the seas, descends beneath the whole earth, and rises above all the heavens.
And if there were tens of thousands of other worlds like this one, it would be in all of them within a single hour, without being delayed.
Nor would they suffice for it. Indeed, it is also in its nature to ascend and rise to immeasurable heights and to comprehend limitless natures. And when a human
being looked and considered all these things in both these worlds—the great world, which is this creation,
and the small world, which is the human being himself, within whom dwells something else greater than the whole creation—
and saw and understood in these two worlds many things, their differences, natures, arrangements, and the beauty of their structures,
and other things without limit, which cannot all be spoken of now, not even a portion of them,
lest the discourse become too long, grow excessive, and burden the listeners, he was amazed, astonished, bewildered, and filled with wonder.
