Then he began to think more subtly and to investigate more clearly, saying, “Where do all these things come from?
“I wonder, all these incomprehensible and limitless things that belong to me and are within me, in my nature and my individual being—
where do they come from? Who created me? Who made me? Who fashioned me? Who arranged and placed all these things in my nature?
Where does this boundless wonder come from? Where does this limitless marvel come from?
How did these things come together within me? Where do I come from, and who brought me into existence? I did not create, make, and fashion myself.
For I know and remember nothing from before my birth, nor am I aware of anything. I did not exist by myself or through my own power, yet I came into existence.
And into this glory and great marvel! Certainly, there is someone else who created me, made me, fashioned me, and brought me into existence.
Truly, I have a maker, and not merely one who created and fashioned me,
but one who continually provides for me and cares for the preservation of my life, without neglecting me even for a brief instant.
And this hidden, luminous, intelligent thing within me bears witness and confirms to me that this is so.”
And I have a Lord and Creator, a Maker and Provider. And the very nature of this spiritual, rational, and luminous element within me,
with all its activity and all its power, directs its desire and longing toward its Creator: it yearns, longs, and desires.
It seeks him and loves his nature naturally and affectionately, since its nature has a close kinship with the nature of the Lord and Maker.
And it has within it something of his likeness and image. Thus it has been established and made known that I have a Lord and Maker,
I, a human being. Again, when I considered this great and spacious world in which I stand,
and the great wonder of its order, the great marvel of the beauty of its constitution, and all these things mentioned above—that is, the human being reflects
and says, “Where do all these things in the world come from? Or rather, this world itself and the things within it—does it exist of itself, like something spontaneous, arising of its own will?
This is not credible, given the great wonders, the ordered arrangements, the natures, and the variations within it.
There must certainly be something else that precedes it, which brought it into existence,
created it, made it, fashioned it, and arranged it in this wonderful and beautiful harmony. And the luminous and subtle nature within me bears witness that this is so.
And just as I have become certain and know that I have a Lord, a Maker, and a constant Provider,
so also this great and spacious world has a Lord, and this glorious and beautiful city has a King,
an Organizer, a Governor, and a Provider, who is constantly concerned with its course, its continued existence, and its order.
He cannot neglect his care for it for even one brief instant; otherwise, it would all perish and fall into ruin.
He is very near it and is within it. Throughout the entire world, the Maker is wholly present and near, like the soul to the body
and like warmth to a living body.” Look, beloved and dear brothers throughout the inhabited world:
it has been made known and established truly, certainly, and without doubt that there is a God—that is, a Lord, Maker, and Creator of this universe.
We have investigated, examined, and considered the book of nature, and we have also read the volume of understanding. We have learned and come to know that this universe has a God.
He is near it and is within it. Therefore he is able to provide for it and is sufficient to exercise his care over it all.
There is no stumbling block or further doubt concerning this Lord, Creator, and Provider, who brought everything into existence and has power over everything.
These things, then, have been demonstrated in this chapter from nature and natural knowledge: that God exists, and further, [?] he is the cause of all things and the Creator of everything.
We will demonstrate much more about his existence in all the chapters and discourses ahead, and about the many things concerning him that our nature can comprehend,
which it is absolutely necessary for us to know. As for our mention of the great and small perceptible worlds, and our statement that one is the great world:
this universe is the great world, and the other, the small world, is the human being. As for how the human being is a small world,
the discussion will explain this in the sections ahead, as the Creator and Fashioner wills, and will also address many things that are needed and useful for continued existence.
Of the Image of Truth. But if anyone among the learned and lovers of polished language
comes across and reads this general account and sees that it does not employ language polished by the wisdom of philosophers, with brief expressions that contain lengthy ones,
and compressed statements that unfold into very extended ones, according to the method taught by grammarians and sophists of the school of Aristotle and his companions,
whose obscure words are like a tangled thicket, as are the constructions of their dark verbal intricacies, and like those of the other poets and writers among the Greeks,
we implore his wisdom not to proceed to accuse the simple and limited author. For his concern is not with these things: to embellish polished words,
to compress discourses, pack meanings together, construct figures of speech, employ verbal intricacies, confuse readers, and deprive many people of accurate understanding.
For philosophical language and grammatical composition are loved by only a few individuals—if indeed they are even useful.
But for many people, or rather for the majority of humanity, they are difficult to understand and unhelpful.
Simple, ordinary language and clear composition, however, are lucid and easy to understand,
and accessible and useful to the whole human community: to the learned and the uneducated, to the knowledgeable and the ignorant, to the shrewd and the simple.
Our purpose arises from divine and sincere love toward our brothers and fellow members, all human beings, who are equal to us in creation, nature, and race,
and are under the authority, care, and governance of the good and merciful Lord, who desires all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
We are not concerned with flattering praise or with passing gains. For tomorrow we will be released from this passing life
and depart from this material and composite world. Praise will not benefit us, nor will gains reach us,
but only a kindly remembrance in the prayer of everyone who comes across these writings.
Whoever he may be, from any of the nations, let him ask mercy for us from the Creator and Maker of us all,
to whom praise, thanksgiving, worship, and gratitude are due from everyone. Praised is his glorious name; blessed is his lordship.
Exalted is his dominion; worthy of worship is his majesty. He is glorious in his work, wonderful in his creation, blessed in his will, wise in his knowledge, rich
in his gifts. His greatness is unlimited, his being is incomprehensible, and his activity is immeasurable.
You, our Lord, our Creator and Maker, we praise, thank, and worship. You we exalt and honor,
and we bless and magnify you, acclaim and glorify you. We believe in you, that you are the Lord, King, and Ruler of us all.
Do not be angry with us, my Lord, because we have dared to investigate your being. Do not condemn us, my Lord, because we have sought to examine your lordship.
Do not drive us away, my Lord, because we have approached to investigate your creative power. You, my Lord, created in us a bold and unrestrained nature that strives to rise toward you.
You, my Lord, fashioned in us a rational mind in the likeness of your glorious and holy image, which is incomprehensible, invisible, and beyond explanation.
You, my Lord, gave us sovereign freedom, ruling and unconstrained, which dares to confront all great powers and ventures against everything fearful.
Through that love, my Lord, we have taken courage to draw near to your accessibility. With ardor, my Lord, we have been set aflame, and we say that we will ascend to your immeasurability.
We have trusted in the hope of your kindness, O good and kind one, merciful and compassionate, so that we may rise toward your incomprehensibility.
You are blessed by all and praised forever and ever, without end. Amen. With these words, chapter four is concluded through God who has guided us.
Chapter 5
With God who gives wisdom, chapter five: On whether God is one or many—the unique being, the sole nature, and the incomparable and inexplicable essence,
incomprehensible; the hidden Lord and glorious King; the Ruler who has power over all; the good Creator and wise Maker,
and generous Provider. O eternal origin and [?], which has no beginning and cannot be comprehended,
and will have no end! O good cause, the cause of all causes, you have no image that can be known,
nor any likeness that can be seen, nor any representation that can be explained. O eternal being, whose existence has no beginning,
and lofty sublimity, above which there is nothing, nor anything that comes close to it; and depth whose profundity cannot be touched, and whose abyss has no limit!
O you who are unique in your oneness, eternal in your being, and incomprehensible in your hiddenness! O you who are good in your lordship and wise
in your creating, and generous in your providing! O you who are merciful by nature and compassionate in your actions,
and abundant in gifts, give, bestow, and enrich us who are needy, poor, and destitute,

needy by nature, as your will sees fit, your lordship commands, and the wisdom of your mind knows will benefit us, help us, and make us wise, though we are unworthy, concerning the uniqueness of your lordship, your authority that is shared with no one, and your hiddenness that has no likeness.
You are good by nature, our Lord. You are wise in your actions. You are rich and abundant in your gifts. We do not inquire with presumption,
nor investigate aggressively, nor examine contemptuously. Rather, we confess without stumbling,
and believe without doubting, and praise without ceasing. But we ask of your mercy, good and kind Lord of us all:

My Lord, give wisdom to our ignorance concerning the uniqueness of your sole lordship, so that continually and without end we may give thanks, worship, and praise your unique kingdom, the kingdom of all kingdoms and the mistress of all ages.
For you hold all authority forever and ever. Amen. In the preceding chapter it was demonstrated from nature and from the natural thoughts within us
that God truly exists—that is, the Lord, Creator, and Provider of this universe. Now, again, for the sake of certainty about the truth,
the discussion investigates further, the mind examines, and thought inquires whether the Lord, Creator, and Provider of this universe is indeed one,
or two, or three, or many, with each of them creating, making, and providing for particular things,
and each of them holding and exercising authority and dominion over what belongs to him. For we see many differences in the world:
light and darkness, winter and summer, abundance and deprivation, existence and disappearance, health and sickness,
stability and decay, composition and dissolution, harmony and opposition, fire and water, earth and air, life and death.
Along with many other things that cannot be confined within a limit or brought within a number that the mind can calculate, contemplate, or investigate.
But now, from whom shall we learn? From whom shall we hear about these things? Whom shall we believe? From where shall we gain knowledge?
What shall we rely on for certainty, and how shall we become wise? For look: we do not listen to one another, and we do not believe one another.
Nor are we persuaded by one another, since we do not accept one another’s books, agree to examine things, or assent to what is said. So then,
from where shall we learn? In what book shall we read? What volume shall we study? There is no writing that is reliable, no book that is certain, and no teacher who is trusted,
like a true father to us all, a common book for us all, a wise and trustworthy teacher over us all. This, however, is nature,
from which we all come, in which we all exist, and under whose authority and governance we all live. In it [?] let us read; in it let us study; in it let us meditate.
And from it let us learn clearly, certainly, and truly whether there is one Lord, Creator, and Governor, or many.
But how shall we read and study in nature itself? We shall explain. We human beings, then, who found ourselves in this open expanse of the world,
thought things over and built a house to shelter our bodies. And we considered that another was needed for the hidden thing within us, which is our soul.
When we began to build the soul’s [?] house, we began to gather the materials needed to establish it,
namely, teachings and branches of wisdom that perfect in us a sure knowledge of the truth. And when we went about gathering these things within our soul itself,
that is, our understanding mind, from the things visible to us—heaven and earth and everything that comes from them and is in them—
while we were occupied with these things, the thought arose in us: Where do all these visible things come from, and we human beings,
that is, our outward and inward being, our visible and hidden being? And we discovered and became certain that we all have a Lord, Creator, and Governor.
And when we wish to know further, look: for many thousands of years there has been no general change in this universe.
And these particular changes that occur, those we mentioned above and others like them,
are not changes that oppose nature and transform it completely. Rather, they persist and continue within nature itself, coming from it and through its activity.
These proclaim all the more loudly and show clearly the stability and permanence of nature, which is firmly established and unchanging,

because those changes continually display and bring about the very same process, in a harmonious and unconfused order and a splendid arrangement that proceeds in an orderly way, without disruption, corruption, or [?].

Look: ever since heaven was stretched out and began the swift revolution of the zodiac, its course has never stopped for even a single instant. The sun has not concealed its light, nor has the moon been held back
from its service. The stars have not darkened their rays, nor has the law governing their course changed.
Heaven has not become earth, nor [?] earth heaven; the seas have not become dry land, nor dry land sea; and the waters have not extinguished fire.
Nor has the air [?] the dust. Winter has not become summer, nor summer winter, nor day night,
nor night day. Rather, look: the course of the world proceeds [?] in an orderly and splendid way, without change or confusion.
From these things we learn that there is one Lord, one Creator and Maker, and one Provider
and Governor, who has no companion, partner, equal, or opponent, because he is almighty and has no need of a helper
or a partner. Moreover, we see that every lordship, kingdom, administration, or government of a people,
or craft or teaching in which two or more people share together,
inevitably contains opposition. Where there is opposition, there is also conflict and strife.
Where these things exist, there is no firm, unchanging stability, nor any order free from confusion,
nor any arrangement free from disruption, but rather change, confusion, and disruption. Since we entered the world,
we have seen no confusion in its order. Therefore, there is only one who sustains it, orders it, and governs it.
He alone continually provides for it and cares for it. Just as every country or people that has many judges and governors
is constantly involved in wars, [?], and disputes, and neither stands firm nor develops fully, neither thrives nor prospers,
so too, if created things had many lords and governors, they would not endure at all.
And just as, where there is one king, one ruler and governor, who is powerful, wise, rich, good, [?], and capable of doing whatever he wishes,
his entire dominion enjoys prosperity and peace, under one good law, with splendid order and protection,
so too, because there is one Lord, Creator, Maker, and Governor of creation, it exists in peace and good order.
And just as, where there is one powerful king, perfect in all the qualities we have mentioned, who governs his kingdom justly and wisely,
he is therefore mighty and feared by all the people in his dominion and under his authority,
and because of the fear of him and the order established by his laws, no one can harm his neighbor,
or seize his office, rank, or honor, nor can anyone encroach upon his neighbor’s domain and property,
along with many admirable and upright practices that are preserved through fear of the mighty king—so too the many natures within creation,
although strongly opposed to one another, have never been able to cause harm, because there is one Lord, Caretaker, Governor, and powerful and fearsome King.
I mean, first of all, the elements, the parents and sustainers of the world, which are strongly opposed to one another in their nature and activity.
I mean fire in relation to water, air in relation to earth, and the sea in relation to dry land, along with many things arising from these elements,
which not only did not produce opposition [?], but instead produced harmony, order, and stable existence.
And all the individual differences and oppositions mentioned earlier, concerning which and because of which thought was divided, wondering whether perhaps there was more than one Lord,
themselves all the more confirm and testify to his oneness and lordship, because their opposition is a sustaining and enduring law.
And not a new and universal change. Nature, indeed, preserves everything well, in an orderly way and without confusion.
Just as that one wise and powerful Maker constituted it, created it, and ordered it. Therefore there is no room for further doubt about this.

Rather, we must believe and acknowledge, according to the force of the truth that has been demonstrated and firmly established, that there is one Being alone, [?], the Creator and Governor who rules over everything.
Again, we offer another, stronger argument.
We human beings, who find ourselves created and made in this expanse of the world, see that there are wild animals alongside us in creation, powerful and mighty in strength.
There are also deadly and destructive creeping creatures. Who, then, restrains these from harming and destroying?
What else but the command of that one Lord and Governor? Who subjects the mighty sea, with its towering waves and turbulent billows,
to a human being, so that he may ride on its back, tread upon its surface, master it, sail across it, and go wherever he wishes?
Who protects him from terrifying sea serpents and great, mighty whales,
and the other dangerous creatures that inhabit the depths of the sea? Who keeps the dry land peaceful despite its many dangers,
and protects human beings from lions, vicious leopards, ravenous wolves, venomous snakes, and the other harmful animals and vicious creeping creatures?
Who guards and shelters children from the many dangers around them and among them, especially during sleep and at night,
when people camp among foliage and in fields, and sleep like the dead from exhaustion?
Who is the watchful guardian who stands guard over them, shelters them, and delivers them from harmful animals and rational creeping creatures?
More than we rational beings, they serve and carry out the will and command of the mighty Lord.
They see his image in us, tremble and fear before our weakness, and even submit to our lack of strength.
Who has subdued before us the mighty elephants, the burden-bearing camels, the oxen and powerful buffaloes, and the swift horses, along with all the others?
Who else but that one Lord of us all? They see his image in us, fear us, and submit before us. There is no other beside him.
Nor can there be another partner with him in his kingdom. These things have now been demonstrated concerning the fact that God is one and alone.
Yet there are very many other things that show and confirm that he alone is God. We know this from the heavens, the air, the arrangement of the clouds, and the ordered patterns of rain and dew,
the formation of hail, the pounding of spring and autumn downpours, the mighty sounds of thunder, and the terrifying flashes of lightning,
along with many other things. These will be demonstrated further in the chapters ahead of us, with the Lord who guides and gives wisdom,
each subject in its own place and where it belongs. But if someone among those who have not been trained in the branches of knowledge that give wisdom and guide one toward certainty about the truth,
still doubts the oneness of the Lord and says, “If there is one Lord, Creator, Ruler, and Provider,
and he is good by nature and does good things, and everything he created and made is good and beautiful,”
Where, then, do these evil and hateful things that exist and are found in the world come from, along with the others that arise and happen?
Who made these things that exist? And who produces and brings about the things that happen, when that one is good and does good things?
Who created and made devouring lions, vicious leopards, and ravenous wolves? When they run wild, they become even more destructive and deadly.
Who made destructive wolves, man-eating hyenas, and contemptible foxes,
along with the rest of the animals that destroy people, livestock, and property? Where do the terrifying dragons come from,
and the deadly snakes, the [?], the vipers, and the scorpions, along with the rest of the venom-spitting [?]?
Who sends out [?] the locusts, the crawling locusts, and the blight called [?], and the ravaging locusts, along with the other things that destroy crops and ruin people's hope of a livelihood?
Who strikes with hail, destroys with frost, drowns with floods, and buries people through tremors and earthquakes? Who opens the earth so that it swallows many people?
Who burns with lightning, scorches with thunderbolts, suffocates with fierce summer heat, torments with heat, and sears and kills with snow and cold?
Who stirs up wars and conflicts, unleashes swords and disturbances, and brings about quarrels and battles,
and causes killings and dreadful plagues, and brings about captivity and marauding bands?
Who lays cities waste and uproots prosperous fortified towns, along with many dreadful things like these—devastating calamities and utterly destructive evils—
when there is only one ruler and governor, and he is merciful, good, and compassionate?
He is good by nature, merciful in his disposition, and generous with good gifts.

How does he cause these great calamities and evils that lead to widespread destruction, injustice, wickedness, and lawlessness, as commonly happens through wars, battles, and the capture of boys, children, women, and virgins,
and the bitter enslavement of freeborn men and women, the uprooting of their households, and the destruction of their homelands?
Who, again, brings these many afflictions and disorders upon human bodies?
I mean severe pains and incurable illnesses, such as frenzy, madness, and evil possession,
wasting disease, elephantiasis, ringworm, leprosy, scabies, white skin patches, paralysis, a bent spine, and lameness,
crippling, blindness, deafness, muteness—that is, inability to speak—and stammering, along with many devastating and incurable pains.

A death that came once, in a single moment, would be far preferable to these, rather than continual torments and daily death in this life full of afflictions and bitter suffering, along with many other such things that a doubting mind [?] and brings forward:
Perhaps there is not one creator and governor of all these many different things. Rather, just as the good one created and made good and beneficial things,
so there is also another, an evil one, who created and made these harmful evils, just as there are light and darkness in creation. Or perhaps, again, there are many
lords, and each one created and made something, and now governs and manages it according to his own nature and will.
It is to doubtful thoughts like these that we speak, bringing certainty to their doubts and healing their sickness.
And we strengthen their weakness through the power, help, and strengthening support of radiant truth, which enlightens everyone who wishes to walk in its light.
For this reason, we have already demonstrated above, in the preceding chapters, the certainty, existence, nature, and individual being of truth through many proofs.
And we have demonstrated the falsehood of falsehood, its nonexistence, and that it has no nature, essence, or individual beings. Rather, it is something that does not exist.
Darkness, too, is not a thing, but the absence of light and the shadow of a body. Likewise, evil does not exist by nature and has no existence.
It has no nature, individual being, or essence. Rather, it is simply the absence of good.
It does not come into being from itself or through itself. How could it come into being when it has no existence, nature, or individual being?
Rather, the mind—that is, the will—and the movements of free choice bring it into being when they become deprived of good.
And once we are certain that evil has neither nature nor existence, how can we say of anything that it is evil by nature?
Therefore, all these things mentioned by those with conflicting ideas are not harmful evils, but helpful goods.
These very things show and confirm to us all the more clearly and certainly that there is one Lord, Creator, and Governor of both us and them. And they are described
rather as disciplines that set right and correct the conduct of our lives, so that, fearing such things, we may conduct ourselves properly and please our Lord according to his will.
This upright conduct and pleasing of his will do not benefit him, since he is neither needy nor lacking anything.
Rather, they greatly benefit and help us ourselves, so that we live in peace and harmony with one another,
in safety, well-being, rest, and tranquility. And these things prepare endless blessings for us,
everlasting rest, and life that does not pass away, as we shall demonstrate through the Lord, who wills, guides, and gives wisdom.
Therefore, fatherly disciplines and corrections that impart wisdom are not called evils, but rather goods, because they produce and bring about good things.
Evil, however, has no existence in nature at all and does not exist. Rather, free choice gives birth to it when that freedom is used wickedly.
Someone who kills and strikes another person does evil by his own choice. Someone who kills and strikes in accordance with the law, as the lawmakers have prescribed,
does good to the whole community. There are many similar cases about which much can be said and examined, and they are known to everyone,
especially those experienced in the world and those who hear the laws. This world is a place of discipline—that is, a place of instruction—like a school for children.
Is a child educated for the sake of his conduct and activities within the school, as though he were to remain there forever?
No. Rather, it is so that he may learn there the wisdom and knowledge of how to conduct himself in the world, return to his parents’ house, inherit from them, and remain in his inheritance.
Therefore, God has another world, and that is our everlasting inheritance.
He is the one who disciplines and corrects us through all these disciplines that have been mentioned, so that we may fear and not sin,
but do good things in this world that passes away and inherit the blessings of that world which does not pass away. And if these disciplines, hardships, and terrors
Rather, destructive and ruinous; good lords and creators. And opposites are things that consume and destroy one another.
They abolish and wipe out, rather than establish, preserve, and govern, as with light and darkness,
health and sickness, peace and war, and many things like these. And if the world had many lords,
in their opposition to one another they would destroy one another—that is, the strong would destroy the weak—or they would all be consumed
by the opposition among them, or the weak among them would be. Yet we see and know from experience, throughout all these thousands of years,
that nothing has disappeared from the world. Rather, all created things are preserved, each in its own nature and according to its own order.
Nothing has been disrupted in the arrangement of heaven and earth, the cycle of the seasons, or all the natural things composed of the elements.
Therefore there is only one Lord, Maker, and Governor. Again, just as with the kingdoms in this world:
although there were strong and very powerful ones among them, nevertheless, because of the opposition that arose and continually arises among them,
many of them consumed and destroyed one another, uprooting and wiping out their memory from the earth. So it would be if there were many gods and lords.
We have not written these things without reason. We know very well that all the nations on earth acknowledge one God,

Lord, Maker, and Governor. Nevertheless, they habitually entertain evil thoughts, speculate, blaspheme, and ponder whether perhaps there are lords and governors besides the One, so that through this they may grow lax,
and falsehood and sin may reign over them, and they may be lost from the light of truth
and go into everlasting darkness. Again, there are others who act arrogantly without knowledge of the truth.
As though they were exalting the good God, they magnify him and say, “Far be it from the good God, the [?] and the giver of light,
to create or make such things! And how can he bring about and punish with these devastating blows?”
They do not know that through these hateful thoughts and contemptible notions they are denying the truth and diminishing God's power.
They do not know how to distinguish truth from falsehood, or evil things from good things. There is no evil at all by nature, but only what is done through the choice of human free will.
Nor is there any other agency that forcibly overcomes and compels human free will to do evil.
There are, however, enticements and suggestions in one's thoughts from an evil agency, which was not evil from the beginning in its nature and creation.
But the doing of evil belongs to free will, solely through the movement of one's own will and not through compulsion. Therefore there is no evil at all by nature, nor anything evil.
Rather, everything came into being and comes to be for goodness and benefit. And there is one God, the Creator, Maker, and Governor of all,
Lord of all and capable of all things. He provides for everything through the great wisdom of his providence over all and his care for all.
Him we praise, bless, and magnify. Him we acknowledge and believe in, and in him we take refuge. On him we rely and set our hope,
and we wait for him. And we say with all our strength and all our soul, with all our sincerity, knowledge, and confession:
That there is one Being, eternal and everlasting, without beginning or end, but existing always: one God.
One Lord, one Creator, one Maker, one King, one Ruler, one Sustainer, one Guardian, one Guide.
One Provider, one incomprehensible nature, one inexplicable essence, one eternal being,
and everlasting, to whom belong glory, thanksgiving, and worship from all peoples, clans, and families, and from all rational and non-rational beings,
[animate] and inanimate, visible and
invisible, now and throughout all the ages, forever and ever. Amen. With these words the fifth chapter ends, through God who gives wisdom.
Next, with God who guides, the sixth chapter. On how many persons and distinctive properties there are in God.
The great Mind and essential Wisdom, living and life-giving, who gives life to all who share in life, both intelligible and perceptible.
You alone are the sovereign Mind, the Creator of all minds. You are the great Wisdom, mistress of all wisdom,
who makes all wise rational beings wise, both bodily and bodiless. You are living and life-giving, the source of all life,
and the giver of life to all who share in life. We praise you, we bless you, we magnify you. We petition you as we worship.
We ask [?] as we give thanks. We entreat you and plead with you as we kneel before your lordship.
Again we dare, though we are unworthy, to approach your unapproachability. Again we rise to search your unsearchability.
Again we boldly attempt to comprehend your incomprehensibility. In faith, my Lord, we draw near.
With great hope we search. With burning love we are set ablaze; in the fire of love for you we yearn
to comprehend whatever your hiddenness wishes to reveal to our thinking, and whatever your concealed being is pleased to show to our blindness,
and your will is pleased to teach our ignorance—not as you are in your nature, for this cannot be known by created and made beings,
but insofar as our knowledge, given by your wisdom, can comprehend and understand what strengthens our heart in right faith in you,
and in true thanksgiving and acknowledgment of your lordship. The little mind that your great and boundless Mind created now dares to know you and praise you.
The rational knowledge that your great and immeasurable Wisdom gave us now yearns to become wise in you and exalt you.
The life within us and our breath are stirred by your life, O giver of life to all. They now strive to live spiritually in you and to savor life from your being.
Give to us, O you who abound in gifts. Enrich us, O you who are rich in blessings. Supply the need of our poverty,
O refuge full of abundance, who enriches all who are in need and remains without deficiency. Blessed are you, my Lord, and worthy of worship is your glory. Thanksgiving be to your lordship
from all of us, created and made beings whom your divinity created, always, at every time, and forever and ever. Amen. Now that we have all come to know and have been assured, my beloved,
from our own soul and nature and the discernment of our understanding, and from the nature of this world in which we were created.
We have come to know that we and all creation truly have a Lord, Creator, and Maker, and that he alone is one.

Furthermore, in keeping with the rational nature within us, we ought to investigate and examine with our understanding, and consider with this mind capable of receiving knowledge, which has been [?] to us, whatever our knowledge and the reach of the mind within us can comprehend about our Creator.

Especially those things that our Lord and Maker himself has given and gives us, knowing that we are capable of them and that the mind he created within us can grasp them, and that they please his will and benefit our nature.

Thus the mind, that hidden, rational, and subtle thing within us, reflects further. It rises and becomes more subtle according to its nature, never ceasing or resting from its upward ascents and elevations,
as far as it is permitted, and especially in proportion to its purification from passions and worldly ways.
What, then, is our Maker? We have become certain that he exists and that he is one. But is he life?
Is he rational? Is he mind? What, then, is he? Even though he is an eternal being, without beginning and without any end,
his being cannot be comprehended, his greatness cannot be bounded, his nature cannot be investigated, and his providence cannot be searched out.
Nor can his judgments be traced or his ways be known. Yet we ought to know what our God is—
those things that he himself wishes to make known to us. For unless he gives us knowledge and understanding of his lordship as he pleases,

we, weak and darkened as we are, cannot possibly look with the thought of our mind toward the exalted height of his incomprehensibility. Otherwise we are dazzled, and the light of our presumptuous mind grows dim,
just as the eyes of bodily sight are dazzled when they gaze intently at the orb of this visible sun.
Where can we ascend and rise with our mind, since his exaltedness cannot be comprehended? And how can we think about him, when the subject of him astonishes every mind?
And where can we read and hear about him, since all books, writings, discourses, and words are insufficient to speak of him?
Let us therefore return to our ancient father and teacher, that is, to nature, which brought us all into being.
This is the wise teacher whose teaching no peoples, languages, races, or families can possibly dispute.
When we first examine ourselves, we see and perceive this immeasurable mind within us: how it dwells and sits like a great king in our head,
visiting places, reaching the farthest limits, and seeing heights and depths through its rational thought and its own nature.
Through the life stirred within it by the living spirit within that life, it looks into the great and expansive mirror of its own nature.
There it sees the image of its Creator, who in his goodness and mercy [?] it in the image of his greatness. It reflects and says in its understanding:
“If I, created and made, possess this great and glorious mind, then what must the Creator be like—that intangible depth of his mind?
A great and incomprehensible mind, and the source [?] of all minds! He brought forth and made all minds, while he himself [?] was born and made from another mind.
Therefore the Lord and Creator, the God of us all, is a great mind and the Father of all minds, both spiritual and embodied.”
Again a person reflects and says in his understanding: “If I, created and made, have a mind that brings forth within my heart this wondrous thought, that is, a rational word,
and it is continually within me, coming from its great father, the mind, the source and begetter of every word and thought—
Then my Lord and my God, who gave me this wise power of speech and the understanding thought that my mind continually generates—how wise his Word must be, and how great his thought!
And if I am a creature and the handiwork of the Word who is wise in everything, my own word is neither exhausted nor limited when it moves within my spirit.
How, then, can the Word of my Lord’s mind—that is, his thought, moving within his Spirit—be comprehended or limited by the speech of us human beings?
We will shortly show whether the fatherly mind of my Lord and my God possesses an understanding Word, wise in everything—that is, a great thought.
Again, a person reflects and considers in his mind, saying, “If I, a creature and a thing made, am alive in my spirit and my body,
and move through both—that is, through the vitality of my body and the thoughts and movements of my spirit—
and have within me this vitality, that is, my own life-giving spirit, then the Spirit of my Lord—
how great and glorious is his vitality, which gives life to all who share in life, those known by the mind and those perceived by the senses, rational and irrational!”
Therefore, the holy and glorious Spirit of my Lord is truly living, life-giving, and the giver of life.
From these natural and true thoughts, we have indeed become certain that our Lord is living, and that he has a great mind, the source of all minds and the Father
of the Word and wise thought through which he created and made all creatures. And within him is a living Spirit, through whom he moves of himself
and sets in motion everything that moves. These three realities are present and exist essentially and eternally in our God:
namely, mind, Word—that is, thought—and the living and life-giving Spirit. We have learned these things with certainty from our own nature, which he created in his image.
There is no room to doubt these things. And the mind continually generates thought.
Because he lives through the activity of his vitality—that is, his living Spirit—his thought acts, creating and making everything it wishes.
Just as we have a mind that continually generates thought—that is, a word—in our hearts, and it is entirely hidden within us
and unknown to others, and whenever we wish, through the vitality within us—that is, through our spirit, which is our breath—
we bring it into bodily form through the sound from our bodies, and it becomes known to everyone, so too our Lord:
his mind naturally generated thought, that is, the Word. Nor does thought exist where there is no mind.
Where there are mind and thought, there is life, because without vitality, mind and thought cannot exist.
But because the mind is the cause and source, the name of fatherhood properly and necessarily belongs to it, since it is the sovereign Father.
What does “sovereign” mean? It means that he has no other like him, resembling him, who can be called by this glorious name of fatherhood.
For he is always Father, because the mind is not the offspring of another, so that it would have been a creature—that is, the offspring of another—
and only then have become the father of another. Rather, the mind is always the Father of the Word, that is, understanding thought.
Therefore, he is properly and truly the sovereign Father, with no other father resembling him. From him every fatherhood in heaven and on earth takes its name.
But every father or head of others who was himself a child and subject to another according to the established order became, when he grew older, a father and head of others

who came from him and after him. Such a person is not called a father in the proper sense. Thus it has been recognized and established that there is one Father in the proper sense, from whom all fatherhood takes its name.
He is the great Mind of the Godhead and the first cause of all causes.
Now the Word of the Mind, that is, his thought, is called his offspring, because the Word is born from the Mind—not newly or afterward.
Rather, his Word exists with him in his very being, eternally and forever, and is in no way bounded or comprehended.
The Word is the image, likeness, and radiance of the eternal Mind, of the same nature as he and from his own substance, without division and without

any separation, equal in glory, being, and power. He is called, and is, the offspring of the Father—that is, the only Son, the Son in the proper sense, of the sole Father, the Father in the proper sense.
For there is no other offspring like him, and the Mind, the Father, has no other Word except him alone.
For it is impossible for God to have two Words or two thoughts, or even for an angel [?] a human being.
Thus the Word of God is one. He exists of himself and is eternal, and he is equal to the Father in glory and honor, because he is not something else outside him.
Nor is he younger or smaller than he is. Rather, he is his Word, his Wisdom, and his Thought, through whom all the worlds were created.
Through him they endure and exist. He is called God, and the power and wisdom of his Father. He is called the offspring—that is, the Son [?] in the proper sense—of the Father in the proper sense.
For he is always the Son, because he is the Word born from the Mind. And he, the Word,
cannot change and become a mind and give birth to another word, so that the Word would have a word, and Thought a thought.
Rather, the Word is always the offspring of the Mind, and not the begetter of another word. Therefore, fittingly and truly, he is the offspring—that is, the Son in the proper sense,
for there is no other offspring, that is, son, like him. From him, being begotten—that is, sonship—takes its name
in the proper sense. He is not, nor was he, nor will he be, the father of another word.
Nor is this possible. Thus he is always the offspring in the proper sense, equal to the Father, the Mind, in being, lordship, power, will, glory, worship, and praise.
The whole Word is in the Father, the Mind, and everywhere, without separation, division, or limitation.
But as to how this is, listen briefly, insofar as we can speak and you can hear.
Look within yourself. See and understand that within you there is a great mind, the source and begetter of every word, wisdom, and thought,
in the image and likeness of your Lord and Maker. And this word—that is, the thought born in your mind and hidden in your heart,
which is the bosom of your mind—when you want it to come out into the open, you set yourself in motion by your spirit, that is, by your life.
You join the spiritual nature of your word to the bodily nature of your voice, which is air blown from your lungs through your windpipe.
And you make your word, spiritual and hidden in the bosom of your mind, audible to me and to everyone who listens.
Or you give bodily form to your hidden, spiritual word in ink and paper, and its spiritual nature becomes known spiritually through the means
of this combination of ink and paper, to me and to many others. It is passed from one person to another by voice and in writings, and the whole world is filled with it.

In the ears of listeners and in the hearts of readers, it is present with each person fully and completely, without diminution. Likewise, it is all present with you in the bosom of your mind, fully and completely, without departure or change.
And if, though you are a created and made being, your word, born of your mind, exists without limitation, and this whole world has been filled with it,
and even if there were tens of thousands of other worlds like it, it would neither be limited nor depleted by them all, nor would it depart from you or undergo any change,
then how much more is this true of the Word who is God and the Wisdom of the great Mind, the source of all minds,
who is the Creator, Maker, and Giver of every word, wisdom, and thought! How could he be limited or depleted by all the worlds?
While he is hidden and concealed in the bosom of his Father, he is wholly present everywhere, in his fullness, without departing from his Father’s bosom.

In the same way, your word, with which everything has been filled, has not departed from your heart, which is the bosom of your mind. And just as your spiritual word, which is hidden spiritually in your heart,
is not known to others unless it is set in motion by your spirit and given bodily form in sound or in paper and ink,
so too is the Word of God, who is called his offspring, who is his Power and Wisdom, the Son of his nature and the Son of his being.
As long as he was hidden in his bosom, like your word in your heart, he was unknown to any created being. But when, in his love and grace, he wished
to make known to his creatures the mysteries of his hiddenness and the nature of his being, he set him in motion by his Spirit, that is, his holy Life.

He clothed his Word in sound and spoke with us through likenesses and in portions over time, as he pleased, and as we were able to hear, know, and understand, according to what would help us and was suited to our time,

each period in its own time. But after the world had been instructed by the utterances of God and had heard his words, had become accustomed to divine conversation, had become aware of its Maker and had come to know its God,

at the end of the ages the Word himself, who is God, took bodily form in our flesh, sharing our nature, just as our word takes form in paper and ink. And behold, he is a human being like us, and became like us in everything except sin.
And this work that he accomplished when the Word himself, who is God, became flesh through the action of his Holy Spirit—
we will explain it at length later, as his grace grants and his lordship wills. And the Word who became flesh was wholly present in the flesh that he had put on, and everywhere
and with everyone who heard the news of him and believed in him. In the heart of everyone who believed in him, he was wholly present with each one, and in heaven and on earth,
and with the angels, and wholly with everyone. And he was wholly present in the bosom of his Father, without departing at all, changing, or becoming different.
In the same way, your own word has not departed from your heart. It is wholly present with you and in your mind, and everywhere, and everything has been filled with it.
Reflect and think in this way about the Word who is God, the Creator and Maker of all words and all wisdom,
the incomprehensible and unlimited one, who wished to reveal himself to his creatures—not as he is in his incomprehensible greatness,
but as created beings are able to know him, each according to the measure of his knowledge,
or rather, according to the purity of his soul, the refinement of his understanding, the serenity of his mind, the clarity of his thoughts, and the purity of his heart.
This Word of his—that is, the wisdom and thought of the great Mind and first Cause, who is the eternal and sovereign Father—
was itself also called and named the only-begotten Son and the sovereign offspring of the one sole Begetter and sovereign Father.
Now the life of God is his Spirit, because he is the Spirit and life of God.
He is called holy and is holy, and is God, likewise sharing his nature, being, and eternity. And how could he exist
if the Mind and Word had no life within him? His life is his Spirit, and this Spirit of God is holy and is called God,
because he moves of himself, and no other moves him. Just as the life within you moves you, and no one else moves it within you except your Creator.
But the glorious God himself has no other creator or maker who moves his Spirit within him. Rather, his Spirit moves of himself and moves everything in heaven and on earth.
There is absolutely nothing, either in heaven or on earth, that moves of itself except the Holy Spirit of God. Through him God moves and lives and exists eternally.
Through him, his Spirit who proceeds from him, and through his activity, the begotten Word was revealed, who had been hidden in the bosom of the Mind, the Father.
At times he was joined to a voice and was heard in forms and portions. Afterward, the Word himself was embodied in flesh through the activity of the Holy Spirit and became known to created beings.
Just as the spirit moves you, and you join your word to a voice and make it heard by others.
Or your spirit works through your hands and moves them so that you embody your word in ink and paper and show it to everyone. In the same way acted the Spirit
of the great Mind, God the Father. And his Word, who is the offspring of the Mind, became known and was revealed to all created beings:
at times through voices and revelations that came upon the prophets in every generation, and afterward through the flesh that the Word put on through the activity of his Holy Spirit.
This is the true God, the Creator and Maker of all, who is acknowledged, worshiped, and glorified by all.
He is the great Mind, the source of all minds, and is called the sovereign Father, the first Cause of all causes.
He has a Word who is called his offspring and the only-begotten and sovereign Son, the source of all words and the giver of all wisdom.
There is life in him; that is, he is alive. This is his life, and it is called his Holy Spirit, who proceeds from him.
And together with the Word's being begotten from his bosom, these three persons exist in one Godhead: Mind, Word, and Spirit.
The distinctive property of the Mind is begetting. [The distinctive property of the Word is being begotten.] The distinctive property of the Holy Spirit is proceeding.
The name and rank of the Mind is Father; that of the Word is Son; and that of the Spirit, who is his life, is Holy Spirit. Three persons, three names,
three distinctive properties, but one nature, one lordship, one activity, one eternal being,
one will, one power, one authority, one Godhead in Trinity, and Trinity in one Godhead.
This is the Holy Trinity confessed by Christians: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one true God,
who is worshiped and glorified by true believers. This is the glorious name of the worshipful Trinity.
In it Christians—that is, followers of Christ—are baptized and born from water and the Spirit, with a new and spiritual birth.
For now, these things suffice concerning the mysteries of the Trinity: the persons, names, and distinctive properties of the one true God.
And those things that are still lacking, which ought to be spoken, believed, and confessed,
concerning the great and glorious mystery of the worshipful and holy Trinity, we will write afterward, if the Lord wills and permits,
when we reach the subject of the distinctions between the confessions of all nations, in the discourse and chapter concerning the faith and confession of Christians.
With these things the sixth chapter is completed, through God who grants wisdom.
Chapter 7
Again, with God who guides: the seventh chapter, concerning whether or not God has a precise name.
Blessed, praised, and exalted is the worshipful, awesome, and holy name of the Lord, Maker, and Creator of all things intelligible and invisible, perceptible and visible, who is the eternal Being,
who has no beginning and will have no end; who is incomprehensible [?] to all created beings, heavenly and earthly, intelligible and perceptible.
He cannot be investigated or explained, nor can an account of him be bounded. He is the eternal Being and is before all things.
There was no one before him to give him a name, as he himself created the creatures and gave them all designations and names,

by which he made them known and distinguished them, each one by their names, designations, natures, individual beings, ranks, distinctive properties, and work. How, then, can a name be known for him [and a designation be given to him by creatures that do not] comprehend him?
Nor can they investigate him, explain him, or speak about his eternal and inconceivable being,
and give him a name and designation, unless he himself gives himself a name and makes a designation for himself known.
Otherwise, no one among his creatures can do so, nor can anyone comprehend or know how to give him a name.
As for all the names by which they have called him and which they have given him: 'Lord'—that is, the 'Lord' by which they have called him—comes from the term for lordship.
Anyone who is master of the world, or of property, or of a place, or of other such things, is its lord—that is, its master.
As for 'God,' it likewise comes from the designation 'gods,' which the nations from the beginning heaped upon everyone who proved outstanding in the world,
whether through valor, might, prophecy, wisdom, or fluent speech in teaching,
or through the performance of [?] and wonders, or through victory in battles and the athletic prowess of accomplished competitors,
or through asceticism and solitary dwelling in mountains, deserts, and desolate places devoid of human habitation,
or through abstinence, fasts, vigils, standing in prayer, and prayers before the Maker and Provider of all,
or through courage and unwavering adherence to the ancestral confession, and the endurance of many tortures and afflictions on that account, even to a violent death.
For everyone who distinguished himself in one of these things or in things like them, and departed from the world, was acclaimed and praised by the people of his time.
And they named him such-and-such a god. They continually kept his memory alive, and they also made a picture of him or erected a statue in his likeness to honor him.
They held a commemoration for him, recounted his victories, and honored his picture or his statue.
Just as even today they call anyone who displays any kind of victory a saint or a true martyr, so too those people of earlier times
used to call him a god. And someone who achieved many victories, or who was the leader and foremost among others, and the cause, inspiration, and encouragement of their victories,
they used to call lord and god. From this custom they came to call the Maker God. Those who spoke precisely called him God of gods.
That is, they named him the god of gods. Likewise, the powers in the zodiac—that is, the great lights in heaven—
such as these seven wandering stars, namely the sun, the moon, Kaiwan, Bel, Nergal, Beltis, and Nebo,
they used to call gods. They also erected statues and pictures of them, with prayers and petitions.
From practices like these they became accustomed to calling that Maker and Creator God. Others called him the First Cause and the cause of all causes.
Others called him the Hidden God; others, Ohrmazd; others, the Eternal Being, because of his existence and his eternity.
Others called him Creator because of his creating, and Maker because of his making, and Good because of his [?] goodness.
And Rich because of his abundance, and Wise because of the wisdom of his deeds, and Merciful because of his mercy.
Likewise, the other names they give him come from the qualities they have seen and learned that he possesses, such as Guardian, Watchful One, Protector, Nurturer, Provider, and Governor,
and Life, Compassionate, Patient, Almighty, Lord of All, Upholder of All, Powerful in Everything, and Wise in Everything,
and Knower of All, Blessed in Everything, Praiseworthy, Worthy of Worship, Holy, Just, Judge, Giver of Life, Discerning, and Nourisher,
and Giver of Wisdom, Guide, True Light, Consuming and Immaterial Fire, Warrior, Mighty, and Mighty in Strength,
and Strong, Majestic, Exalted, Lofty, Sovereign, King, King of Kings, Lord of Lords, Sabaoth, Elohim, Adonai, and El Shaddai,
along with the other names and titles by which all the nations of the earth used to call him, each in its own language and according to what was honorable, lordly, and great in their eyes.
All these names were assigned and applied to that Lord and Creator on the basis of the customs, arrangements, and activities in our world.
There is no name for his being and no title for his eternity, because he is above these things.
He is incomprehensible, unsearchable, and unlimited, and above goodness
and mercy and holiness. Every name that is named on earth and in heaven worships, acknowledges, and praises him. And every
tongue of spiritual and bodily beings magnifies, extols, and blesses him. Moreover, his greatness, his lordship, and his creative activity are praised and made known,
and his wisdom, by all creatures that live, move, creep, have sensation, are seen, and are known.
Who, then, can know his name precisely? Or who has the ability and knowledge to give a name to that eternal and incomprehensible Being?
Or how can we compose and utter his name in our speech, which is composed of words and sound breathed from this air?
The one who is simple and not composite, who moves everything but is himself moved by no other. He is beyond speech, since no discourse can encompass him.
The mind cannot grasp him. Thought cannot search him out. Understanding cannot touch him. He cannot be investigated, encompassed, or expressed.
For he is beyond every movement of thought, every flutter of understanding, and every perception of the mind. He is above everything.
Below everything, on this side of everything, within everything, outside everything. He himself is everything, and everything is from him, and everything is in him.
For everything begins from him, everything stands firm in him, and everything returns to him. Glory to him for his incomprehensible judgments.
Glory to him for the greatness of his gifts. Glory to him for the abundance of his grace. He who cannot be comprehended or encompassed,
or conceived by the mind, created the human being in his image and revealed his likeness in him—that is, in this mind we possess, which cannot be seized or grasped by thought,
or encompassed. And we are our own masters, since we have the freedom to carry out our will, like him and in his likeness.
We will explain these things broadly and more fully in the other discourses that lie ahead of us, through God who gives strength.
What, then, is the precise thing we should do? How should we call upon and name our Creator and Maker? By what names should we call him?
By what titles should we pray, make requests of him, and implore him? How should we praise him, bless him, and exalt his name?
For look, he is beyond every word the tongue utters, and beyond every movement of your fluttering in thought.
And he is deeper within than every thought the mind produces. But what is precise and fitting for us to say when naming the incomprehensible one
is this alone: namely, ‘He who always exists.’ That is, he existed from the beginning.
Not that he came into being from the beginning, but that he existed without having any beginning apart from himself.
And he remains himself, existing always, at every moment, without change. And again, he remains himself forever and ever, without end and without conclusion.
But as for angels and human beings, there was a time when they did not exist. They are subject to change and are changeable.
Some changed from radiant angels at one time and became dark demons. And human beings are sometimes good and sometimes righteous,
and sometimes wicked. As for the other created things that are made from the elements, there was also a time when they did not exist.
And there will also be a time when they pass away and no longer exist. But the Maker and Creator, the eternal Being, existed and always exists.
And he will continue to exist forever and ever. This is the true and precise name by which we can name the one who cannot be comprehended or encompassed,
and who is beyond every name and title named in heaven and on earth. But when, with the intention of prayer, we offer him praise, thanksgiving, and worship,
and petition, supplication, and entreaty, whatever name you call him by, he accepts your prayer,
when you offer your prayer from a pure heart and an upright soul, with an upright [?], humility, clear faith, and wholehearted simplicity.
While you do not imagine him at all as a composite likeness and image, nor conceive of him as any form,
or as a likeness drawn from visible things—not of heaven, nor of the firmament, nor of the air, nor of the sun, or the moon, or the stars,
nor of this visible light, nor of this bodily fire, nor of the sea, nor of dry land—you must not imagine him as anything at all,
or think of him in such terms: he is simple and not composite, and does not fall within thought, perception, or understanding.
For he created all things, visible and invisible, and everything is filled with him, yet he is neither depleted nor limited.
And even if there were a thousand thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand other creations and worlds like this creation,
they would not limit him at all, nor would he be depleted by them. He is wholly present everywhere, without transition, without change, and without disturbance.
How could anyone conceive of him as any likeness or form at all that thought could grasp?
Yet he dawns and shines upon the understanding of clear minds and pure hearts, according to their clarity and purity,
and their refinement and lucidity. These people understand and are enlightened in their minds through subtle movements and spiritual thoughts,
and through what cannot be spoken by a tongue of flesh, or explained by a bodily tongue, or expressed in a composite voice. And concerning
these things we will give a clear explanation again in the appropriate place, as his grace allows. There are also three titles by which it is fitting to designate
him who is above every name and title. But from his actions toward his creatures, we have learned to designate and name him by them.
These three names embrace and encompass every name and title by which he has been named. They are these:
Good, Rich, and Wise. These three titles encompass all the names we have mentioned above,
as well as those we have not mentioned in this book, which apply to him in the proper sense, because he is perfect, complete, and true in them all.
For he is good and the fountain of all good things. From his goodness alone he brought all these things into being, both visible and invisible,
without anyone asking him, persuading him, or telling him to do so. For there was no other nature or other being before him or alongside him to ask anything of him.
Rather, because he is good by nature and is entirely goodness—or rather, is above all goodness—in his grace he made all these things and brought them into being.
And after creating and establishing them, he did not leave them in an ordinary state, but exalted and honored them,
and did good to them and enriched them with every blessing. Continually, without ceasing, he does good to them, because he cares for them,
and provides for them, guides, protects, and saves them. Therefore he alone is good [in the proper sense, never departing at all from his goodness,
because he is good by nature] and a giver of good. Likewise, he is rich in the proper sense and the fountain of all riches,
and the giver and bestower, the perfect enricher who has enriched and continues to enrich everyone, while he himself is neither diminished nor lacking anything at all.
And more than recipients are eager to receive, he is eager, willing, and longing to give. He enriched the angels with gifts.
And the heavens with lights, and the zodiac with powers, and the air with clouds, and the whole firmament with different kinds and species of birds and flying creatures.
The earth with trees, grasses, and plants; the meadows with blossoms, flowers, and lilies; the mountains with cedars and cypresses.
And springs and fountains; the plains with rivers and streams; the depths with caverns and impassable seas.
The seas, too, and the rivers with countless swarms of fish, whales, and sea monsters.
The dry land, too, with wild animals, livestock, horses, cattle, sheep, mares, and herds of every kind.
He also brought precious substances out of the earth for human use
and for the world's continued existence, such as mineral deposits—that is, sources and mines of gold, silver, tin, copper, lead, and iron, together with countless other kinds;
along with fine seals and precious stones: beryls, jacinths, emeralds, carbuncles, sapphires, and jasper, in a treasury of secrets, and [?] and [?], together with the rest that are known and found.
He also brought up from the sea fine pearls of great value, together with other shellfish, purple dyes, and beautiful colors.
He also enriched human beings, horses, and livestock with strength, might, courage, and endurance,
along with tens of thousands of noble and precious things and deeds with which he enriched the intelligible and visible world,
without anyone persuading him or asking him. He is the sovereign rich one who enriched everyone abundantly, [?], and perfectly.
Yet he has never lacked anything, nor does he lack anything or suffer any decrease in his complete riches. Wise. That is, he is called wise in everything, and so he is.
For he is perfectly and supremely wise, complete in wisdom that belongs to his nature, because all wisdom flows from him and all knowledge is given by him.
And who can measure or comprehend his wisdom, which is full of every kind of discernment, and his knowledge, which knows every deed and every kind of knowledge?
And who can measure or comprehend his wisdom, which is full of every kind of discernment, and his knowledge, which knows every deed,
and every word and every thought that has existed or exists, openly or secretly, even within the hidden and deep chambers of hearts
and the minds of all rational beings, as though they had already happened and been completed, just as they are destined to happen
or to be stirred in [?] and thought? He knew them beforehand, before the foundations of the world.
And he gave and bestowed upon angels and human beings the spirit of wisdom, intelligence, understanding, knowledge, and advance revelation of future events. With great and wondrous wisdom,
utterly incomprehensible to created beings, he created and established the heavenly powers.
He ordered their ranks, their troops, their assemblies, their work, and their service. He stretched out the heavens and encircled the zodiac.
He arranged the lights and determined their courses, their movements, their revolutions, and all the laws governing them.
He caused this air to blow for the sustenance of everything that lives and moves, for the continued existence of creation, and for the orderly arrangement of clouds, rains, and showers.
And he regulated it through wonderful variations, for preservation, growth, and a flourishing existence.
and the course of the world. With great and incomprehensible wisdom, he arranged the seasons, years, months, weeks, days, nights, hours, and appointed times.
He created and fashioned human beings, livestock, wild animals, birds, creeping things, and the remaining kinds of everything that lives, crawls, and moves, with their distinctive characteristics.
And their species, individual beings, colors, varied combinations, sounds, habits, activities, functions, fertility, and offspring,
and their nourishment, growth, mingling, separation, gatherings, and dispersal, along with the many other things belonging to their natures and distinctive characteristics.
With wonderful wisdom he spread out the earth, broadened the plains, raised the mountains, and lifted up the hills.

He adorned them with trees, plants, grasses, blossoms, and flowers of every varied kind, which amaze those who see them through the diversity of their colors, scents, and tastes, along with their other effects.
Yet the earth from which they spring has a single nature and has neither color, taste, nor scent.
Consider also the vaulted surfaces of the seas, and reflect on their [?], their height, and their piling up.
Marvel at how all their movement, and the towering of their waves and surges, are confined
within a boundary of loose, scattered sand. Consider also the multitude of kinds and species of fish and the many creeping creatures in their depths,
along with the splendid pearls and precious stones in their depths. What more can I say about this wisdom, full of distinctions and beyond investigation,
when all the angels and human beings cannot search out and comprehend even a tiny part of the great abyss and immeasurable depth of the wisdom and knowledge of him who alone is wise in everything?
Leave aside the countless, limitless things that the wise Maker established, made, arranged, made, and arranged through his incomprehensible knowledge.
Turn to yourself, examine yourself, and consider your own creation. Be amazed and marvel at yourself: how all created things, both intelligible and perceptible, are contained within you,
both rational and irrational, both sentient and insentient. And what is greater than all these, more astonishing, and worthy of great wonder,
is that you are made in the image and likeness of your Maker, and you are a bond that gathers and unites all created things and the Creator.
Even if you lived in the world for tens of thousands of years, you would not be able or have the capacity to learn the great wisdom of your own constitution and creation.
So, concerning your Creator, the rest of his creatures, and the great mysteries and wonderful wisdom hidden in natures and existing things,
how can you grasp or encompass knowledge of them? Think about yourself:
how your soul, spiritual, luminous, subtle, and receptive to intellect and knowledge, is united with this body of yours, which is dense, material, heavy, composite, and made of elements.
Even if, as I said, you lived for tens of thousands of years, you would not be able to learn the nature of your soul, what it is like, or where it comes from,
or what it is, its substance, its senses, its distinctive characteristics, and its effects, or how it dwells in the body and its subtlety is united with the body's density.
Nor, again, can you comprehend the body's nature, its constitution in the man, and its smallness in the woman,
the formation of its shapes in the womb, and the placement of its internal and external organs,
the arrangement of its senses, their distinctive characteristics, effects, natures, and activities, and how it receives nourishment, digests, and grows.
And how the humors, that is, the bodily fluids, are present in the flesh, bones, veins, arteries, skin, hair, and nails.
And how the nourishment from food and drink flows throughout the whole body, from the hair to the nails.
And how the power of medicines and the power of roots act upon the body's humors, composition, and nature.
Along with many other things whose names we cannot even list. The same applies to all the bodies of other living creatures.
And to all the natures and beings on earth, in the seas and rivers, in the air, in the firmament, in the zodiac, and in heaven.

And above the visible heavens, in the dwelling places of the angels and the rest of the heavenly powers, the great wisdom of him who alone is wise in everything truly cannot be measured or comprehended.
He is the wise, perfect, and complete one, and he alone deserves to be designated and called wise.
Thus it has been established that he is supremely wise, with no limit to his knowledge and understanding. Through these things, then, the incomprehensible one is known, designated, and named.
That is, he who exists eternally and is good, rich, and wise, perfectly and completely.
And to him be glory forever and ever. Amen. With these words the seventh chapter is concluded, through God who strengthened and helped us.
Next, chapter eight, with God who gives wisdom. On whether he is the cause of everything that has a cause and the creator of everything created.
Previously, with the help of God who gives wisdom, the argument demonstrated—in the chapters, or sections, above
that were discussed—and examined through natural reasoning, with intelligence and understanding, on the basis of existing things and the nature of this great world,
and the nature of the human being, who is a small world, that there is a Lord, maker, and creator of this universe, and that he is one nature,
and Lord and ruler, known in three persons, that is, distinct properties: Mind, Word, and living Spirit.
Their distinct properties are begetting, being begotten, and proceeding, and they are designated Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
An adorable Trinity, one glorious Godhead, one eternal Being who exists forever
and is good, rich, and wise. And since we know and have established from nature and reason that he alone is one,
and that he is the eternal Being who exists forever, with none before him and none to come after him,
but that he exists without beginning and without end, from eternity and forever and ever,
therefore, truly and without doubt, he is the cause of everything that has a cause and the creator of everything created.
First, since he is living and rational, and because he created everything living and rational along with the rest of creation, he is the great Mind.
And Mind is the cause of the Word, that is, thought, and of life, which is the living Spirit—not that they came into being after him,
because Mind cannot exist apart from Word and Spirit. Rather, they exist with him and in him by nature and in essence.
One will, one power, one authority, one lordship. Rather, they exist with him and in him by nature and in essence.
One will, one power, one authority, one lordship, one divinity, one essence.
A Trinity that is undivided, indivisible, and unmingled. The Father, who is Mind, is called the cause.
And the Son, who is the Word, and the living and holy Spirit are called effects [?] the cause and together with the cause.
This is the one eternal Being who is known in three—that is, the Trinity. He alone is the one who exists perpetually.
He is the cause of everything and the creator of everything. He is the cause of everything because, by his existence, he brought everything into being.
And he became the cause of everything that came into being. He is the creator because he created and fashioned everything that came into being out of nothing.
And when we said that he created and fashioned creatures out of nothing, it was because there was nothing else besides him from which he could create and fashion creatures.
The discussion of this subject is extensive, hidden, mysterious, and concealed from the impure. For the natural person does not accept spiritual things.
They are foolishness to him. But the spiritual person knows everything and judges justly and correctly, as it is, with abundant understanding.
For his mind is clear, his soul serene, his heart pure, and his understanding cleansed of
all the murkiness and darkness of empty thoughts and the disturbances of this world. Someone whose sight is clear
sees clearly, by the light of the sun, all creatures and the entire form of this world.
But someone whose sight is diseased, weak, and feeble sees the things of this world dimly and indistinctly.
He cannot look toward the intense light of this sun, because his feeble sight becomes still dimmer when he is dazzled because of the weakness of his vision.
Therefore, my beloved, let us take care to keep our hearts pure and to cleanse our understanding of sinful passions,
and to keep our souls serene and our minds clear. Then we see everything clearly and correctly with the eyes of our understanding,
and comprehend it with our minds, and perceive it through our subtle and spiritual knowledge. Just as a mirror,
the more it is polished, becomes clear and bright, and a person sees in it his face and all his features clearly and accurately,
down to the fine veins, the strands of hair, the eyelids, and the eyelashes on them,
so too, in the mirror of his soul, when it is polished and purified of all the materiality of the passions,
the soul sees everything spiritually, understands, becomes assured, and gains conviction about how everything came into being out of nothing.
And it marvels and wonders at that eternal Being and wise Creator, before whom there was no one and after whom there will be no one.
Everything is from him, everything is in him, and everything is in his hand. Everything comes from him, and everything returns to him. Everything exists in him,
and he exists in everything, like the soul in the body, like warmth in a living body, and like light in the air.
That great and boundless mystery [?], that hidden and inexplicable marvel, that profound wonder and spiritual wisdom.
And whoever has been found worthy to understand him and perceive him through his purity, the holiness of his body, and the clarity of his soul sees his light and tastes his power.
He rejoices in love for him and burns with his love. He is set aflame and kindled by the gladdening fire that burns within him, and he forgets the world and everything in it.
He is continually captivated by him, meditates on him, turns inward, and is raised to the immeasurable heights of true and spiritual knowledge.
He perceives, understands, and gains certainty about everything that cannot be spoken by a human mouth or expressed by a tongue of flesh.
It cannot be recorded with ink and paper or contained in a discourse or narrative, because what he sees and understands is not something composite,
to be explained and made known through composite speech or the material substance of paper. Rather, it resembles the spiritual vision of the angels, who are spiritual and not composite,
in keeping with the experience of vision and contemplation in the new world that is to come, in which the good and righteous will delight.
