Thus, truly, the primal Good is one, and is the cause of everything in heaven, in the firmament, in the air, on earth, in the seas, and in the depths.
It was and is the cause of all causes and the creator of all created things. Nothing existed, exists, or will exist
apart from that first cause, which exists eternally. There is nothing above it, nothing beyond it, nothing outside it,
and nothing on this side of it. To put it all briefly and conclusively: there is nothing apart from it. Thus he is the cause of all causes
and the creator of all created things. To him be glory and thanksgiving from all. Amen. With these words the eighth chapter is completed, through God who gives wisdom.
Again, with God who guides: Chapter Nine. On whether he cares for and governs everything and is concerned for everything,
or not—he who exists eternally, the eternal Being, the cause of all causes, and the creator of all created things.
For he alone exists eternally without change, and he created and established everything from nothing, as he alone knows,
along with those who are worthy and to whom he wishes to reveal it. Because he created and made everything, it is necessary and incumbent upon him—
all the more since he is able—to care for and govern everything according to his will and as seems right to him, that is, to be concerned for everything.
For he is the Lord of everything and holds everything in his power. And if a natural father and mother in this world
diligently care for and oversee the upbringing of their children and provide what is needed for their lives,
and are deeply concerned for their health and protection, never neglecting them either by day or by night,
because parental love for them, tender affection, and delight in them are naturally implanted in them,
then surely the natural parental affection within them compels them to care diligently for their children and guide them well,
to bring them up with great care and sustain their lives at every stage, each in its proper time, according to their age and the measure of their growth:
at one time with mild milk, then a little later with drinks and gruels made from flour and milk, and afterward with soft and tender foods,
and finally with food of every kind. Likewise, with baths, oils, wrapping in swaddling bands, and little cradles.
To bear burdens and disturbances; and in times of illness to give treatment, to bandage and heal whatever illness there may be, and to train them in teachings suited to them.
And to teach them trades by which to support their lives, along with the many other things that fathers do for their children with great care and much concern.
As is known to every [?] from nature and experience.

And if earthly fathers have all this great concern for their children, guiding them knowledgeably and without neglect, providing for their livelihood, and taking great care over their upbringing, protection, and instruction,
then how much more does that merciful and compassionate Father, that good and generous Lord, with natural love and spiritual love—
that Creator, Maker, and wise Fashioner who made us in his image and likeness—care and provide for us and for his whole creation.
He is greatly concerned for the continued existence and preservation of everything. He does these things without toiling, growing weary, or being worn out by worries as created beings are.
Rather, his command guides, provides for, sustains, preserves, causes to grow, nourishes, and gives life to everything.
And just as a person cares for and directs his life with knowledge and wisdom, as far as he can and his understanding reaches, and provides well for himself,
and is concerned about sustaining his life, the health of his body, and its preservation, with all its requirements and needs,
even more does that good, rich, and wise Creator care for, guide, provide for, preserve, and sustain his creation and the work of his hands.
If, indeed, we also speak of hands in relation to God, and, as far as possible, [?] his body and limbs.

Although speech is bold to speak of composition in relation to him who is simple and not composite, nevertheless this is according to our ability to understand the spiritual nature of the matter through composite speech.
We and the whole creation are his possession and inheritance, and he possesses nothing apart from us. Therefore he is greatly concerned for our well-being.

And just as a person wants and longs to be wise, perfect, complete, and without bodily deficiency, together with the fulfillment of all his other wishes and desires, so God wills this—and still more, in proportion to how much higher, more exalted, and better he is than we are—and greatly desires our well-being:
that we should be perfect and complete in everything, not merely like the angels, but
he wants and longs for all of us to be like himself, if that were possible, and for us to resemble him as far as possible.
And if you wish to know and understand still more clearly, and to be assured of his unfailing and almighty power,
how he alone can guide and provide for everything—that is, the heavenly beings in all their ranks and orders,
and the companies of the heavenly powers, and the heavens and the heaven of heavens, and all their circuits, and the zodiac with all its configurations and movements,
and the stars, their courses and movements, and the whole order governing them, and the firmament and the fiery ether,
and the air, the clouds, the times and seasons, and all the changes in the course and arrangement of months, weeks, nights, and days,
and all the kinds and species of fowl, birds, and flying creatures, and of creeping things, livestock, and domesticated animals within inhabited places,
and those that live outside in deserts and rocky places, and fish and whales, and everything that moves in the waters and within the earth,
and fruit trees, all the cedars, grasses, lands, blossoms, and all growing things.
And the earth and all its ends and regions, from one side to the other, and human beings, rational creatures made in his image and likeness.
That is, the angels, rulers, authorities, governors, leaders of peoples, and commanders of armies.
And officials, dignitaries, judges, and teachers, and all of them together: peoples, races, nations, languages, tribes, and ranks.
And the occupations of men, together with women and children, and their entire way of life, the sustaining of their lives, and their needs.
And their protection, their growth, and all their activity—in short, everything visible and invisible.
That exists and [?] his dominion, that his power sustains and his will governs. Listen carefully to all these things, as his grace enables them to be spoken
And allows them to be shown and made known. First, know that the great, exalted, spiritual world of incorporeal and invisible powers
Is far greater and more spacious than this world. The great, exalted, spiritual world of incorporeal and invisible powers
Is far greater and more spacious than this world, beyond description and measurement, for its greatness exceeds measurement.
And there is no limit to the number of orders, troops, companies, and legions of thousands and tens of thousands of powers within it.
He is the good Lord and wise Creator, who can do everything, holds everything, and provides for everything.
He is their light, their glory, their food, and the service of their worship. His power is their continued existence and their movement.
And his will is all their activity. In him they live and exist, and he is like the soul in the body, giving life, movement, and sustenance.
He is also the movement of the highest heavens in their circuits, and of the zodiac
In all its configurations, its inclination, and its revolution. He is the light of the stars, their radiance, and their rays.
And his power is their course, their rising and setting, and their entire order. The blazing of his power is the fiery, burning ether.
And he is the moisture in the clouds, gathering and increasing the rain and showers within them.
And he orders each individual drop of rain and dew, snow, hail, and ice. Not a single drop falls apart from him,
But only as he wills, in the way he wills, and where he wills. He is the cycle of the seasons, the span of the years, and the one who distinguishes the months.
And he orders the days and nights and sets the limits of hours, [?], and moments.
He is the life of all the birds of the sky, in all their races, kinds, varieties, incidental characteristics, and individual beings.

He is their nature, the one who moves them, brings them to birth, makes them grow, nourishes them, shapes them, clothes them with feathers, gives them their calls and chirping, teaches them, and orders them.
Thus some of them gather in groups and flocks, and some form a single gathering of countless thousands.
Some are few in number, some fly in pairs, and some singly. Some rise and soar very high,
And some remain in midair, while others stay close to the ground. Some live with human beings, and some in buildings and walls.
And in [?] and in trees; some of them in high mountains, some on cliffs, and some in desolate wildernesses.
And with a great variety of habits, voices, calls, songs, and kinds of species.
And a mingling of splendid and wonderful colors that surpass understanding. Speech cannot encompass them all. He is present like moisture in water.

There is not one tiny [?], nor even one part among these birds, for which he is not its support and the one who orders it: all their species, varieties, forms, movements, habits, and colors, together with everything pertaining to them.
His hidden command is depicted in them, and the pure in heart recognize how he is present and visible in them.
Likewise, he is also the support of the nature of riding animals, livestock, and all animals, both those within inhabited places and those outside in the wilderness; his power is hidden in them.
He has placed in each one distinctive traits, habits, and ways that are varied and astonishing: the mighty strength of elephants and the power of lions;
The load-bearing capacity of camels, their large bodies, their small need for food, and their endurance; the subjection of the stubborn strength of oxen and buffaloes;
And the taming of the proud, swift, and spirited breeds of horses, together with the other kinds of mules;
And donkeys that endure under burdens and heavy loads; sheep and cows, too, that provide nourishment in the form of milk, butter, fat, and cheeses;
And their hides for many uses, and their wool and hair for clothing, coverings, curtains, sacks, and many other purposes;
Together with the many kinds and varieties of useful things, nourishment, and medicines derived from their flesh and bones
And the rest of the body parts of animals and livestock. Those within inhabited places are kept peacefully with human beings, while those outside in the wilderness are untamed and [?].
There is still much more, but there is no need to recount everything and draw out the rest of the discourse at great length, burdening the listeners.
God's power and command guide and provide for all these. Some of them feed on their fellow creatures,
And some on grass and the roots of the earth. As for their other habits concerning conception, birth, and growth, together with their other distinctive traits,
If someone were to examine and learn them all, they would be beyond speech and thought. You are astonished and amazed at the vindictiveness of camels and the pride of horses,
The skittishness of mules, the stubbornness of donkeys, and the affection and discernment of dogs, together with their great perseverance in staying awake,
Their watchfulness, alertness, and barking, together with the many kinds of wonders that are established and found in the nature of each one of them.
His power guides all these and orders them. He cares for them in this way, reaching and encompassing them through his incomprehensible care,
So that not one part of all these species and varieties of wild animals, livestock, riding animals, and so forth
Falls from them apart from him. And in that one small and insignificant part, God is present and exists there,
Not a part of him, as though he were limited and divisible, but all of him, without change. Likewise, the crawling creatures within the earth and in the seas and rivers—
His power, command, and will guide and provide for them. In him they move and exist. Otherwise, how could they endure, and how could they exist,

If he did not order their reproduction, growth, nourishment, and way of life, and also place distinctly within their nature, bodies, and limbs wonderful powers and workings that surpass the power of speech?
And he gave them places to roam, and for protection and safety. To some of them he gave a weapon and a particular property for their protection.
Some with their mouths, others with their fangs, others with their hearts and bellies, and others with their sharp tails and their stings.
And others with their skins, which they shoot from their bodies like an arrow from a bow for their protection, and others with their claws.
Each in a different way causes great amazement and wonder in anyone who pays attention and understands, bringing great praise to the wise Creator and Provider.
Then there are trees, grasses, seeds, roots, and the rest of the blossoms and flowers, and the different kinds and species that sprout from the earth.
Words cannot describe or encompass how, although the earth has a single nature and has neither taste nor color nor smell,
it brings forth and nurtures all these different natures, which exceed the limits of counting. How many varieties of fruit there are within a single species!
How many distinctions and differences there are in the colors, tastes, and smells of grapes, figs, olives, pomegranates, apples, and the rest of the fruits and produce!
The same is true of seeds, roots, and flowers. Where, indeed, did they acquire these powers, effects, properties, shapes, colors, tastes, smells, and great diversity,
although the earth from which they sprout has a single nature, color, and taste, and the garden in which they are all planted, set out, and sown drinks from a single spring?
They receive the same breeze, and it is the same sun whose rays rest upon them.
All these innumerable and astonishing differences in the power and activity within them—where did they acquire them and become endowed with them?
Thought is astonished, understanding is amazed, and the mind is bewildered. Human speech and teaching cannot at all express or explain
one out of the millions and myriads of myriads of instances of divine governance, provision, and care:
how it varies into myriads upon myriads upon myriads, and into limitless differences of natures, properties, powers, effects, colors, and shapes,
and smells, tastes, and textures, although the power, nature, and will of the wise Lord who acts in all these things are one.
But as for spiritual contemplation and true knowledge of the hidden power and great mystery that exists concealed and buried within the beings and natures in creation,
they cannot be learned from paper and ink, nor from spoken words and hearing with bodily ears,
but from upright conduct, emptying oneself of the whole world, stilling one's thoughts from every concern, and living in silence and solitude,
with fasting, keeping vigil, and prayer, and constant meditation on the Maker himself and on his governance, which is full of many inexpressible distinctions.
From here the first gate of knowledge belonging to the first degree of virtue is opened. It is called the contemplation of bodies—that is, of everything that can be seen and touched
and is within this circuit of heaven, which surrounds creation like a membrane, or shell, around an egg. Whoever attains this contemplation knows and understands
all these things as they are, and spiritually knows the whole great mystery concealed and buried within them, and sees the Maker and Creator himself in them all,
in a mystical [?], spiritual, and hidden way, intellectually, with subtle [?] and spiritual understanding.
And if he perseveres in virtuous conduct and proceeds rightly without wavering, he rises and is raised in his knowledge, from contemplation to contemplation.
And from one kind of knowledge to another, higher and more exalted than the first, he enters and penetrates deeper into the divine mysteries.
Until he reaches immeasurable heights and wondrous, inexplicable insights.
He is perfected and brought to fullness, and within his own soul he sees his Maker without limit.
For now, let us leave the discussion of these things until we reach their proper time and place, where we should speak about them as far as we can.
Or rather, as divine grace grants and teaches us—that grace which is rich in everything and enriches everyone without begrudging.
Let us return to the order of our discussion and conclude this chapter about the Maker of all things and his limitless care and providence over everything.
For he did not appoint others to serve and care for his creatures, as the kings and rulers of the earth do and arrange.
This is what certain people, darkened in mind and blind in knowledge, have fancied, saying and teaching it without knowledge or truth.
They supposed that by this they were honoring the First Cause, saying that they did not bring it down to the ordinary services of this world,
and to those regarded as insignificant and contemptible. Instead, they said, he appointed others over these tasks of administration, while he himself remains hidden, high, and exalted in his being.
These dull-hearted people do not know or understand that they are actually diminishing the Maker's honor,
not magnifying him. For if this visible sun, which is one of his creatures,
exercises its power throughout creation, and nothing is hidden from its heat, and its rays fall upon things that are beautiful, pure, pleasant, and clean,
as well as upon rottenness, uncleanness, and filth, yet it is neither defiled nor harmed, nor stained at all, but
rather purifies, clarifies, and cleanses everything, and besides this gives life and growth, and leads and brings all other natures to fulfillment,
how much more, then, can the power and command of the one who can do everything and sustains everything accomplish! Indeed, the sun's light, its nature, and its activity are the Creator's own power,
which accomplishes all these things, since he is in everything and near everything, like the power of the sun in existing things,
like the elements in natural things, and like the soul in the body, giving it life and sustaining it. He is the one who establishes the earth upon the waters,
and he bears them all. He is the breadth of the plains, the firmness of the heights, and the greatness of the mountains.
He is the hardness of stones, the solidity of rocks, the scattering of sand, and the covering of the earth's [?].
He is the expanse of the seas, the hollowness of the depths, and the movement and moisture in the waters.
He is the back that bears the foundations of the world, and the pillar and support of all creation. He is above everything,
below everything, within everything, and outside everything. Therefore he can govern everything, because he holds everything.
There is no place empty of him, nor can there ever be, because he existed when nothing else existed.
Whatever came into being came into being from him and exists in him. Nothing can be spoken of as outside him.
He is also the one who forms human beings in the womb, assembling, building, and binding them together with limbs, flesh, bones, and veins, and distributing their bodily humors.
He makes the blood flow and arranges all the senses, inward and outward, bodily and spiritual.
He clothes them with skin, makes their hair and beards grow, and fashions their statures, likenesses, individual identities, and forms.
He unites and joins the spiritual, subtle, knowing, and rational soul with the dense, heavy, composite body.
Just as the soul is the body's life and mover, so God is the soul's life, mover, reason, knowledge, wisdom [?], and thought.
Through the mediation of the subtle, spiritual soul, made in his image and likeness, he unites himself and dwells.
He is the human being's [?], breath, life, and continued existence. In him the human being lives, moves, and exists.
The human being reasons, knows, perceives, and understands things beyond perception and beyond limits, and is swift and flies, passing in a single instant through all
the farthest reaches, heights, depths, and every region. Moreover, he has given and bestowed on the human being a great and divine gift: self-determination.
In this the human being is the image and likeness of his Creator: he does whatever he wills, desires, and plans. For this reason a law was laid down for him.
For he possesses freedom and self-determination. But the other animals, because they possess neither reason nor freedom,
have had no law laid down for them. By the very fact that a law and a commandment were laid down for the human being to observe, his freedom and self-determination were made known.
If he wishes, he observes it, obeys, and submits by his own free choice. And if he wishes, he does not observe it, but rebels, disobeys, and refuses to submit.
For this reason life and death were decreed for him: if he obeys by his own free choice, he lives forever in delight.
But if he rebels by that same free choice, he dies a spiritual death and is tormented forever.
Like a watchful and diligent father and teacher who never neglects him for a single instant, God cares for him, provides for him, and is deeply concerned for him,
from the beginning of his formation in the womb, throughout all the stages of his growth and development and his way of life, whether awake or asleep,
whether acting rightly or sinning, whether enjoying delight or suffering torment, whether being tested or finding relief,
and in all his conduct. He is so close to him and so present within him—more so than the soul within the body, to put it briefly.
In this way God is present throughout his entire creation, like the soul in the body and like warmth in a living body,
like moisture in water and like light in the air. There is absolutely no place empty of him, nor can there be,
nor can such a place even be spoken of or named. For this reason he sustains everything, moves everything, and cares for everything.
He is concerned for everything, gives life to everything, does good to everything, and preserves everything. Praise, thanksgiving, and worship are owed to him by all,
forever and ever. Amen. Here ends chapter nine, through God who gave strength and help.
Again, with God who grants wisdom: chapter ten. On whether God can be comprehended or is incomprehensible.
That God exists, and that he alone is the one Lord, Maker, Ruler, and Upholder of all, and that there are [?] three persons:
Mind, Word, and Spirit, who are called Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—one worshipful, holy, and glorious Trinity,
self-existent and eternal, without beginning and without end; and that his name is one, he who exists forever.
He is the cause of everything that has a cause, and the Creator of all created things. He cares for them, governs them, and provides for them,
and is concerned for all, since he upholds all and is almighty. This has already become known and established among us, and has been believed and confessed,
through the preceding syllogisms and the collection of arguments and natural demonstrations that cannot be disputed or overturned.
Now, however, the discussion again examines and urges us to consider whether it is fitting and possible for that Maker and Creator, who is called God, to be comprehended and known by his creation,
especially by rational and intelligent beings who share in mind and knowledge; and, if he can be comprehended by them, whether he is comprehended completely and fully,
or partially; as he is in his nature, or as he wishes to make himself known to them, according to their worthiness, purification, and clarity, and their capacity to comprehend;

or whether he is altogether incomprehensible and inexplicable; and whether other, non-rational creatures also perceive him and there is—altogether incomprehensible and inexplicable; and whether other, non-rational creatures also perceive him and have knowledge of him,
or not. It is neither lawful nor permitted for minds that are not clear, hearts that are not pure, and thoughts that are not clean,
to meditate, reflect, and think about him who is holy in every respect, worshiped by all, and upholds all,
who governs all and is almighty, who cannot be comprehended, conceived, spoken of, or explained,
nor compared, investigated, or encompassed by the minds of created and made beings.
Someone whose eyesight is weak and feeble cannot gaze at and examine the rays of the radiant sun.
If he presumptuously dares to gaze and examine them, he is dazzled, his vision grows dim, and flickering images spread across his sight.
He becomes bewildered, stupefied, and tormented. So too with someone who has not been purified and made clear of evil passions and hateful thoughts,
and whose body has not been sanctified and cleansed through purity and holiness, who has not been trained in ascetic discipline, in fasting, abstinence, vigil, and prayer,
whose mind has not been cleansed of the world's cares, who has not withdrawn from all its activities and forgotten every remembrance of it,
and has not lived in silence and tranquility, refraining from all associations except those that are pure and virtuous,
and has not stripped himself of every created possession except the necessary, simple, and scant provision sufficient to keep the soul in the body,
and has not persisted in gazing upon God spiritually and intellectually, and in meditating on him, his providence, and the nature of his creatures,
with supplication and petition to him. Whoever dares, apart from these things, to meditate on that nature which is blessed in every respect—wrath blows against him, and blinds

his mind and darkens his heart. He sees illusory images and dreams, mistaking one thing for another; he becomes foolish and deranged, and his understanding is disturbed and confused. He is bewildered and terrified, becomes frenzied, [?], and goes out of his mind.
For it is not for us, who are created and made, to presume to investigate and probe that blessed and incomprehensible nature.
But anyone who longs first to know himself, and then to perceive his Maker and know him as far as he can be comprehended,
should first attend to the [?] of his heart, the serenity of his soul, and the clarity of his mind.
These come through disciplining the body, upright conduct, purification of the mind, and purity of thoughts, as we said above,
together with abandonment of, distance from, and estrangement from all the world's distractions.
Then, in proportion to the excellence of his conduct and his integrity in divine service, spiritual meditation, and training in true knowledge,
he [?], rises, enters, and penetrates into the divine mysteries, and hidden and secret mysteries are revealed to him.
He grows, is renewed, becomes strong, and is firmly established in the things made known to him. He receives great gifts that had never entered his mind.
The great power of truth overshadows him and gives him understanding, insight, knowledge, and discernment to distinguish truth from deception,
and truthfulness from falsehood, and heartening certainty from confused error and a spirit of bewilderment.
Then he begins to enter through the gate of the knowledge of truth, to ascend through the successive degrees, and to penetrate into spiritual contemplations.
From these and through them, he begins to see the Invisible One, as that One wishes to reveal himself to him,
according to his measure, his conduct, and the capacity of his knowledge to comprehend, and according to the clarity and purity of the mirror of his soul.
And when the soul ascends to the height of knowledge, rises to the summit of perfection, and reaches a great measure,
then, as he gazes upon that realm of purity and the radiance of truth shines upon him, he sees a vast expanse,
exalted and immeasurable heights, wondrous and inexplicable insights, inexpressible wonder, and boundless amazement,
immeasurable greatness and incomprehensible Being. And when he perceives that blessed [?] sovereignty,
which is ineffable, and does not reflect on himself and his nature—who he is, what he comes from, and how he exists—
he despises himself and becomes small in his own eyes. His mind is humbled, and he considers himself dust and ashes beside that greatness,
and filth and uncleanness beside that holiness, and a contemptible, despised worm beside that exalted blessedness.
Then, just as it is the nature and property of a magnet to draw iron to itself, so the grace of Being draws him to itself.
Consider the wonder and the great lesson for contemplation in this magnet: the clearer and purer it is of other substances, the more swiftly it draws iron to itself, and the iron clings to it.
But if it is smeared with other substances, such as garlic, onions, and similar foul-smelling things, its power becomes inactive, and it does not draw iron at all,
until it is again tended, washed with strong vinegar and clean water, and cleansed of all the dirt and foul smell that have clung to it.
Then it returns to its original nature. Likewise, the clearer, cleaner, and purer the human soul is of the materiality of evil passions and hateful thoughts,
the more it is drawn toward its Lord and joined to its Maker. But if it becomes entangled in these evil passions,
It becomes defiled and blinded, departs from what is proper to its nature, and draws away from knowledge of the truth and awareness of its Creator.
But if it is washed clean of the filth of its stains and cleansed of the foulness of the passions and the pollution of thoughts through the purifying power of the labors of repentance,
and the pure waters of tears of remorse, and returns to its original nature and the clarity of its own being,
then it again becomes aware of its Lord and clings to its Maker. And when the mind is purified and cleared of the passions,
it is cleansed and freed from all the materiality and theatrical display of the world.
It ascends, is raised up, and turns inward through spiritual contemplation, as was shown above, and attains complete perfection.
Then no desire, wish, or thought remains in it except one alone: namely, to be aware of its Maker,
to reflect on him and meditate on him. From this it rejoices, takes delight, exults, gains strength, is gladdened, and is enlightened. Even if the whole world were given to it,

it would despise it like worthless ashes and foul manure, and would not be inclined even to look at it. Its inexpressible delight, as we have said, is meditation on [?]. But how this is so, a little out of much—
or rather, as much as can be spoken and heard—we will explain. When, therefore, a person becomes perfect,
and his heart is purified, his mind becomes clear, and he becomes aware of his Creator, he begins to reflect on him, to investigate, and to seek him.
And because he has no other place and knows no other path to follow in tracing him except through his creatures,
he roams and wanders among them, boiling with love for him and aflame with affection for him. He seeks the one who, more than anything else, is lovable and beloved, good and beautiful, rich and wise.
For in the beings and natures of created things he sees his footsteps and the traces of his tracks. Because of this he becomes still more transported and inflamed, and runs without stopping.
He roams about, consumed with love for him, and seeks the one who, more than anything else, is lovable and beloved, good and beautiful, rich and wise.
For in the beings and natures of created things he sees his footsteps and the traces of his tracks. Because of this he becomes still more transported and inflamed, and runs without stopping.
He roams about, consumed with love for him, and seems to think that he is now close and has reached and overtaken the Beloved. And when he sees the traces of his footsteps,
and from time to time something like his shadow—and because he is still bound in the body and his dwelling is on earth—he begins his search from there.
As he travels over the earth, he sees his footsteps and the traces of his tracks: how he spread it out, made it firm, and established its foundations by the command of his power.

As he wandered and sought him, mountains and hills met him. He climbed them in his search and found the marks of his hands, where he had piled them up, set them upright, raised them, and lifted them high.
As he roamed among thickets, trees, and gardens, and walked over meadows variegated with the colors of blossoms and flowers,
he saw his beauty upon the trees, received his taste from the fruits, breathed in his fragrance from the flowers, and saw his splendor upon the blooms and lilies.
As he traveled and roamed in his tranquility, absorbed in his Lord, seas and rivers met him, and he saw his shadow in the waters,
his power among the waves, and his footsteps upon the backs of the billows. The mind, burning with love for him, ventured forth, leaped, and entered the sea.
It was tossed among the waves and battered among the billows. The disturbances did not bring it down, nor did the surging waters bewilder it.
It saw his ways within the seas and his paths in the mighty waters. It plunged into the depths and descended into the abysses.
It found his footprints at the bottom of the abysses, as he brought forth, raised, nourished, and ordered all the creatures moving in the depths.
It saw him there engraving fine gems and precious stones, fashioning splendid pearls. [?] his beauty in their nature,
and his radiance on their surfaces. The mind descended beneath the foundations of the world. It saw his arms carrying his creation, and his power
supporting it so that it would not tilt to either side. It rose from there in search of him, burning and aflame with love for him.
Eager, urgent, and zealous, it ran after his footprints. It was not held back by the seas, hindered by the waves, or left behind in the abysses.
It began to ascend and rise above the earth in its search for him. It drew in his breath from the air. It saw the diversity of his forms in the different kinds of birds:
his dyes in their wings, his colors in their bodies, his songs in their voices, his utterances on their tongues, his praises from every kind.
It also saw his canopy in the clouds, the downpours and droplets flowing from his springs, his hands fashioning balls of hail,
his blasts hardening water, bringing down snow like wool, and casting ice like morsels; his mighty voices in the thunder,
his powerful light in the lightning, the traces of his footsteps upon the backs of the clouds, the gleam of his bow amid the downpours.
Again the daring mind ascended and rose higher, burning with love for its Lord. It saw the heavens proclaiming his glory,
and the firmament displaying the work of his hands. It saw his forms in the sun, his light in its rays, his power in its heat,
his will in its activity—in a word, his likeness and his image there. And just as three aspects can be seen in the sun,
namely, its sphere, in the likeness of the mind, the Father; and its rays, like the Word who comes from the mind, who is the only-begotten Son;
and its heat, like the spirit and life in the mind and the Word, who is the Holy Spirit;
so in it can be seen the one Trinity, worshiped and glorified, one Lord who holds all things.
It also saw his radiance in the moon, his bright rays in the stars, his law in the constellations,
his movement and command in the revolutions of the stars of heaven, the greatness of his power in the highest heavens of heavens. And while the mind dwelt there above,
it saw the Beloved: his whole form and likeness, the image of his glory and the radiance of his majesty were there.
It peered from there, from that exalted height, and gazed into the abysses below. It looked down beneath the foundations of the world.
And the very same power and might of his majesty was there, carrying the foundations of the world.
His arms supported the bases of the world. He is wholly below and wholly above, wholly within and wholly outside,
wholly in the sea and wholly on dry land, wholly within the earth’s hollows, within the solid mass of rocks and cliffs, and within the heart
of stones, trees, grasses, and flowers. He himself is the radiance of their surfaces and the beauty of their colors, and he is beneath the earth.
And while he is above the earth, he is the [?] of the air. He is its light, and he is what moves it.
He brings forth the birds of heaven, raises them, and makes them fly. He gives them their forms and the splendid coloring of their wings.
He is in the gathering of the clouds, and wholly in the moisture of their droplets. He is wholly in the firmament and wholly in the zodiac.
He is wholly in the stars and extends along with their rays. He is wholly in heaven and wholly in the heaven of heavens.
And when the mind contemplates him, the Maker who cannot be bounded or comprehended, who is wholly present everywhere without division,
wherever it looks and contemplates, there is his overshadowing presence, and the traces of his footprints and his steps. His care and his provision are everywhere.
He is near everything and present with everything, within everything and beside everything, and everywhere. He cannot be bounded or comprehended.
He cannot be grasped or measured, held back or made to stay. His voice roars like thunder, and like lightning he is swift and escapes from sight.
He is near like a breath and distant like storms. He seems to be in one's hand, yet passes away like a whirlwind. He is near, caring and providing.
He supplies and prepares food for everything. He guards and rescues; he nourishes and causes growth. He brings everything into being,
gives life, and governs. He takes away spirits and causes death, and he guides as he wills. And when the mind sees him in all these things,
and contemplates him who cannot be grasped or bounded, it is astonished, amazed, filled with wonder, and bewildered at the depth of his judgments, which cannot be comprehended or searched out,
or traced: how he is near everything and provides for it, is present in everything and governs it, and cares for everything and guards it.
This reflection and vision of wonder, amazement, and astonishment at the Creator's provisions, full of wisdom and knowledge,
is called by those perfected in spiritual wisdom the contemplation of judgment and care—that is, of providence. And as the mind reflects on its Maker,
it again soars here and there and roams in search of the beloved and cherished one, the good Lord who sets everyone ablaze with love for him.
In keeping with its swift nature, it flies everywhere unhindered. It soars and runs, cannot be grasped, and does not remain still, swifter than a light wind, [?], as it flies unhindered.

It soars and runs, cannot be grasped, and does not remain still. It travels and hastens faster than the wind, swift as lightning and without delay. It was not held back within this creation or detained
among visible things. It did not remain with things that are [?]. And because its nature is spiritual and like the substance of angels,
it turned its face in that direction, to ascend in search of the Beautiful One. It saw his paths in the lofty heights,
and his dwelling places above all the heavens and the heavens of heavens, visible and invisible.
It ascended and rose to the heights. It grew and reached the immeasurable dwellings. It soared and flew and settled among the heavenly assemblies.
It knocked, opened, and entered the city of spiritual beings without being held back, and mingled with the companies of spiritual beings.
It moved among the beings of the heavenly powers. It walked among the fiery ranks. It began searching and investigating,
seeking and asking about the one who cannot be seen, about the one who cannot be traced, about the one who cannot be comprehended.
He was not burned by the blaze. He was not scorched by the flaming coals. He was not consumed and destroyed by the terrible conflagration.
He did not tremble before their ranks or shrink before their orders. He did not fear their companies, nor was he blinded by the great brilliance of their rays.
O love, how intent you are! You do not know how to be still. To what heights have you raised the created and fashioned mind in its search for the Creator
and Maker! To what heights have you ascended! How high you have risen! How did you gain strength and come here?
How did you dare to leap into the realm of spiritual beings? How did you become so bold and take courage to seek that blessed and uncreated nature,
that exalted and unmade essence, that eternal and incomprehensible being?
With what movements do you move, and in what order do you stand? But these things are accomplished through unwavering faith.
Through steadfast hope these things are sought; through perfect, unblemished love these things are boldly attempted. The mind entered, armed with three impenetrable breastplates:
faith, hope, and love. It dwelt among the assemblies of flame like one mad and delirious, absorbed in burning love for the one loved above all
and cherished above all. It began to seek him among their assemblies. It entered the city of angels,
the heavenly Jerusalem, the dwelling place of spiritual beings. It walked among her streets, traveled and wandered through her squares.
The daughters of this Jerusalem—that is, the heavenly hosts—met it. It asked and inquired about the Beautiful One. It saw his image upon their faces,
the radiance of his glory upon their countenances, his movements in their hearts, his stirrings in their thoughts, his sounds in their mouths,
his utterances on their tongues, his melodies in their throats, his praises in their speech. Their ministries were blessings of him;
their service was to proclaim him holy; their deeds were his will; their watchfulness was to keep his commandments; their life was longing for him.
His very being was their nourishment; his radiance was their light; his praise was their honor; his exaltation was their songs of praise. He was seen among them all
and known to them all. He is the Father of them all. He sustains them all. He speaks through them all. He provides for them all.
He guides them all. He is worshiped by them all, praised by them all, acknowledged by them all, exalted by them all,
and acclaimed, blessed, proclaimed holy, celebrated, and glorified. Yet he is not confined. He does not remain in one place or linger to be seen,
nor can he be grasped by thought. When the mind saw all the radiance of his greatness in the first company—that is, the order belonging to the rank of the congregation of angels—
it ascended again and rose to the second company, in which was the second order of the rank within the congregation of archangels.
And behold, once again all the splendor of his glory was with them, among them, and upon them. He had been wholly there, and here the mind found him wholly present.
Yet he had not departed from there, nor had his nature changed. He is not far from any place, and he is present everywhere.
Again it rose to the third order, that of the lofty rulers belonging to the ranks of principalities. And behold, all the glory of his majesty was there,
and the image of his glory was upon their faces. And when the mind, bold with burning love, had searched among them all and wandered among them all,
It did not understand him precisely, nor was he grasped by it, and it did not persist in investigating him.
He was not comprehended by its thought. Again it rose and was lifted up to the second city. It entered the second assembly.
It saw three other companies of the children of light standing there. Three orders of the watchers on high were arrayed there:
Authorities, dominions, and powers, praising, honoring, and exalting the sovereign lordship.
The Beloved is made known through their praises, glorified through their honors, and celebrated through their exaltations. Here too, likewise, he is present in his entirety.
He is known among them all and holds them all, guiding and providing for them. He does not dwell in a location and is not confined to a place.
None of them can fathom him. Again it was strengthened and fortified. [?] dwells, and is not confined to a place. None of them can fathom him.
Again the sovereign mind was strengthened and fortified. It ascended and was lifted up to the highest company. It boldly entered the third assembly of the children of
flame. There again it saw three ranks bearing the marks of fire. The radiance of their faces flashed, and embers fell from their wings.
The order of thrones, another of six-winged seraphim, and the third of many-eyed cherubim. All of them had faces and wheels of flame.
They burned with fire and blazed with flames. The first offered praise, the second proclaimed holiness, and the third offered blessings.

All the praises of the first and middle orders ascended to this third company. All the thanksgivings, honors, praises, exaltations, songs of praise, and proclamations of holiness were gathered together.
They mingled with the blessings of the cherubim, above whose backs that sovereign chariot was arranged and set in great radiance and glory.
Harnessed to it were fearsome, speaking living creatures, blazing with fire beyond the mind's understanding.
Above it was glory that cannot be spoken, radiance that cannot be explained, light that cannot be bounded—that realm which has no likeness.
That place cannot be trodden by the created mind or comprehended by thought. There the mind was bewildered.
The understanding was confounded; knowledge stood amazed. Thoughts ceased; movements grew still. Those who could speak fell silent; speech vanished.
An impassable boundary stood there. An unbreachable fence intervened. That realm was surrounded by an impregnable wall.
Gates that cannot be opened were set over it. A watchful guardian stood over them, neither slumbering nor sleeping, holding a fearsome spear.
He grasped a blade full of terror, turning fearsomely amid great astonishment and wonder filled with trembling, so that you, thought, might not enter there,
and you, speech of inquiry, might not tread in that realm. Fearsome is the realm, and awesome its authority. There a great silence dwells.
Unspeakable wonder reigns. The movements of thought are neither authorized nor permitted to tread in this realm, which is beyond quality
and beyond quantity, incomprehensible and unapproachable. And as the mind stood amazed, trembling and bewildered,
quaking and silent, afraid, shuddering, and confounded, mercy supported it again, and it was strengthened. For it had not ventured boldly by investigating,
nor had it acted presumptuously by probing, nor had it risen through disputation. Rather, it was made firm through faith, encouraged through hope, and strengthened through love.
And from there, from the immeasurable height, from that exalted realm, from that place where no foot can tread.
The mind sent its gaze flying, rose high, and descended to the lowest depths. It traveled in every direction and ranged through every region.
It looked intently and saw him everywhere and in every place, wholly as he is, without movement, without disturbance, and without change. And behold, again,
he was wholly present in all the assemblies of spiritual beings and in all the immaterial orders,
and with all the ranks of immaterial fire and incorporeal spirit, the children of flame. And all the glory of his honor was above the chariot,
the radiance of his majesty above the exalted throne, the splendor of his praise above the seat of majestic power.
And as the mind stood astonished, amazed, and silent, its reflections ceased and its movements grew still.
Its thoughts were quiet. And suddenly it heard an immaterial voice; an awesome intimation whispered in its ears.
A spiritual word spoke to it, sweet and pleasant, full of encouragement and strengthening its understanding, so that the soul would not perish from fear.
The Creator cannot be fathomed, and the Maker cannot be comprehended. The eternal Being cannot be explained.
He who exists forever cannot be grasped by the mind. Praise, thanksgiving, and worship are fitting for him, rightfully his, and owed to him
by all created and made things, intelligible and perceptible, animate and inanimate, sentient and insentient,
at all times and forever and ever. Amen. With these words the tenth chapter is completed, through God who gave strength and help.
The first discourse on the knowledge of truth, containing ten chapters, is completed.
Again, with God who grants wisdom, we write the second discourse on the knowledge of truth, containing eight chapters.
Chapter One: Why the Creator Created Creatures and Established the Worlds.
Let us praise, bless, and exalt him who alone is the Being who is praised, blessed, and exalted.
He is exalted, in need of nothing and lacking nothing. He supplies everyone's deficiencies and meets their needs; he gives, bestows, and enriches.
Yet his fullness is not diminished. Now if this visible sun, created and made, illuminates the whole creation,
warms and sustains creation through the power of its heat, ripens and brings to maturity the fruits and the genera and species of plants, and preserves nature in life and freedom from decay;
and again, if springs and fountains continually pour forth and send out streams and rivers that water the lands and cause things to sprout and grow,
while they themselves never run short, nor does their flow cease—how, then, is it possible that that glorious, perfect nature, lacking nothing,

the Creator of all these things, their sustainer and provider, who can do everything, should lack anything at all, or that his fullness should be diminished, or that there should be any deficiency in his nature
requiring something to complete it? Far from it! Why, then, did he create this wonderful and richly varied creation
and establish the rational world, the intelligible and spiritual, and the perceptible and bodily? Many have held and handed down various views.
Some of them said that it was so that they might praise him and exalt his glorious nature. Others said:
That creation itself should be a reason for praising him: when discerning and wise people see the great beauty of creation, it should be a reason for praising him.
When discerning and wise people see the great beauty of creation, they will praise and acclaim its maker.
Others thought that it was so that there might be rational living beings who would serve his will and fulfill his commandments.
The remaining creatures would serve the needs of these rational beings. Others proposed other explanations. And the deniers, that is, the unbelievers—
those whose understanding is dull like that of wild animals and livestock without knowledge, and whose minds are darkened by error and ignorance of the truth—
thought that this world exists of itself, something spontaneous that has neither beginning nor end. And they say there is no world of spiritual beings.
We have already opposed these people and rebuked their error in the discourse preceding this one. We demonstrated conclusively, from nature itself and the ordering of the world,
that there certainly is a Lord and governor who is the creator and maker. He has neither beginning nor end, and he alone is one.
It is utterly impossible that there should be another alongside him. He created the worlds, established them, and arranged them according to his sovereign and uncoerced will.
We say that he did not create the worlds so that they might praise him, bless him, and exalt him.
For he is glorious, blessed, and exalted, and his glorious nature cannot be raised and exalted any further beyond what it already is,
since his worshipful and exalted nature is perfect and complete, lacking nothing at all.
If his nature were deficient or in need, he could not be the maker, creator, and almighty one.
Anyone who is deficient and in need is a creature and something made, not a creator and maker. And although the creatures themselves too—
each one is complete in its own nature with respect to that in which and for which it was created.
Nor did he need rational creatures to serve his will and fulfill his commandments because of any need of his own
or any lack of power, but rather for their own perfection and their advancement toward sovereign blessedness.
The certain truth, then, is this: because he is good, rich, and wise,
[and perfect and complete in every respect. And one who is good, rich, and wise] certainly does good to others out of his goodness,
and enriches them from his inexhaustible wealth, and reveals his wisdom through his works. For this reason he created the creatures, though he had no need of them.
He established the worlds through his grace and showed his power through his works, which are made with great wisdom, with many distinctions and variations.
Just as it necessarily belongs to the sun by its nature to give light, warmth, and life,
and to a spring [?] to overflow and flow continually, so also the good, rich, and wise Lord—
it belongs to his nature, by his own will, to do good, to enrich, and to perform works full of wonder and great wisdom.
Not like created things, which have distinctive qualities in their nature as fixed and natural attributes, like the sun, springs, and so on.
Rather, God is good, rich, and wise by his will and by his nature. And from his wonderful works, full of wisdom,
and the good gifts and great endowments he has given to rational beings, and the good properties he has placed in different natures and kinds,
and the good, helpful, and beneficial effects he has produced through them, his goodness, wisdom, and riches have become known to everyone.
Therefore, it was not for any other reason that he—the Creator, Maker, and true Lord—created creatures and established the worlds,
but because of his goodness, his abundant riches, and his great wisdom. And not only this,
but also something still more wonderful, great, and exalted: that those very beings whom he created, established, and brought into existence by his grace,
he might, out of his abundant riches and in his great wisdom, graciously make sharers with himself in these great properties of his nature, without begrudging them,
so that they too might be good and blessed, rich, complete, and perfect in true wisdom.
Oh, this indescribable goodness! Oh, these inexhaustible riches! Oh, this great and boundless wisdom!
Oh, this good nature of the sovereign being of this Lord, who is merciful and abundant in grace!
Who is equal to praising him? Who can speak of him? Who can give thanks, praise, and honor to this glorious Creator as he deserves?
If creatures praise him, look: they themselves are created and made by grace. If mouths sing and exalt him, look: from the wealth
of his treasures they are filled with gifts and great endowments. And if tongues give thanks, praise, and honor, he himself arranged them in his wisdom,
gave them utterance, and set them in motion to express the word composed and embodied in sound,
so that it might be heard by ears, understood by minds, and grasped by intellects.

It is like a pen that draws written characters and, through marks, composes words with paper and ink, making known hidden mysteries that are held immaterially in the brain and mind, laid up in hearts, and concealed in their chambers.
Therefore, let us give thanks, worship, and praise to him from whom everything comes, in whom everything exists, and in whose hand everything rests.
Let us offer him what is his own. Let us not be ungrateful, conceal his grace, hide his gifts,
and cease to praise him. With these words, the first chapter of the second discourse is completed, through God, who strengthened and helped us.
Again, with God who gives wisdom: the second chapter of the second discourse, on what God's will is in his creation. Just as every created and made nature
has a distinctive property in its nature, by which it is recognized as being precisely what it is.
That is, just as fire necessarily has the property of burning, heating, and rising upward,
although its upward movement comes from the elements of air mixed into the substances through which it spreads.
And likewise, water has the property of sinking, along with the other natures, each of which is recognized by the dominant quality within it.
Thus the good, rich, and wise Lord is abundant in mercy in his essence and nature. It belongs to him to do good, enrich, perfect, and bring to fulfillment.
These things cannot be fully accomplished except through fellowship with him. This, then, is his will for creation:
that all rational beings should be perfected in goodness and brought to fullness in riches and wisdom. The perfection
and fulfillment of these things are joy without distress and eternal life,
radiant in God, with no anxiety or worry, no stumbling or doubt, but peace, tranquility, and wonder at God.
For God himself, who is good and beyond goodness, draws those [?] who have been perfected into wonder at him.
And when there is no longer any work there, nor worry, distress, stumbling, doubt, or any other thought or meditation,
but only wonder at God, sustained by great love, burning affection, and longing
that ardently reaches toward that nature which is blessed in every way and perfects everyone in blessedness,
from these things come union with him and the deification of rational beings through their union with their Lord and God,
by whom they were created and established, in whom they exist, and in whose hands they are. They return to him and are united with him by his grace, through their love for him.
They acquired this love through perfection and fulfillment, and this came about through keeping his commandments and fulfilling his laws.
No one can know these things precisely, perceive them, and taste them in his mind and understanding
unless he reaches them in his own person and rises and grows strong in the order required for them,
which is the keeping of the commandments. [Through the work of keeping the commandments] nature is refined
and clarified of the disturbance and filth with which it was stained through lawlessness and unnatural conduct, which are sin.
Sin came upon the pure, beautiful, and beautiful nature as something incidental; that nature was created by the Good One, who is pure, clear, and beautiful.
And when that nature returns to its own proper condition, which is purity, serenity, and clarity, it is united with the pure, serene, and beautiful One who made it.
This union is sustained by love, affection, and great longing.
Through these things it is perfected in joy, peace, harmony, and tranquility, which are wonder at the One who is loved.
But how can these things become known to us, whose understanding is dull, who are entangled in passions and darkened by the disturbance and smoke of sin?
It is possible only through things that are compelling and dear to us, because they suit our bodily ways of life, which crawl along the ground.
It is not improper for us to use fleshly and material illustrations, because they suit us, since we are entangled in such things.
And we yearn for them with great longing as long as we live in a bodily and earthly way,
because the very nature of the flesh gives them strength and reinforces our affection and longing for them.
For they are planted and exist in him. Suppose, then, that a young man is a king’s son or belongs to the great and wealthy people of the world.
The powerful excitement of youth stirs within him, and he marries a woman who is likewise young, beautiful in appearance, and the daughter of wealthy and renowned parents.
They abound in wealth and possessions and have plenty of everything in this world. They have no worry, trouble, or distress,
and no lack of anything at all, nor yet any concern about children or worry over them. At that
first period of their marriage, when both have come from virginity [and an honorable state], which everyone loves,
they rejoice greatly in their marriage and are absorbed in their love for one another, with affection, ardor, and longing that boils like a blazing fire.
It is as though their souls are woven together and united with one another. Therefore, once a man is joined to a woman, they are no longer called two but one. They are one flesh, not two,
because they have been joined to one another. This joining is called unity.
The equivalent of this unity is love and affection, with passionate longing and eagerness.
And if this bodily, fleshly, and perishable unity is so aflame with affection, so sweet, delightful, and pleasant to those who possess it,
then how great must be the delight, sweetness, and pleasure of that spiritual unity, pure, clear, and imperishable!
For it unites not body with body, but mind and spirit with the good Creator, the Maker and Beloved,
who sets those who love him ablaze with his eternal, imperishable, and unchanging love.
This longing and great pleasure of desire were not placed and planted in the bodily nature of human beings
except to serve as a likeness of that unifying desire and incomparable love toward that Nature, blessed in every way,
who captivates those who love him by his love. Through this perishable desire, one [?] is stirred to long for that imperishable desire.
As one subdues and quenches the fleshly desire, the spiritual desire awakens.
Through it a person rises and is lifted up in this world, until he tastes in his mind and perceives through his understanding the great joy that will be his in the life to come.
This is wonder at his Maker, love toward him, and union with him. Thus it has now become truly clear that this is God’s will for his creation:
that rational beings should conduct themselves rightly and keep his commandments, so that they may become perfect in his love and be filled with affection for him,
so that they may be worthy of union with him. For this reason he first created them in bodies and placed them in this deficient world,
in which there are pains, illnesses, afflictions, sighing, sorrows, and worries that cause suffering and grief,
so that, by conducting themselves rightly in it and keeping his commandments and the laws he established and prescribed for them as rational beings,
they may be refined, purified, and raised to the purity of their nature, become perfect in his love, be filled with affection for him, and be
in his perfect world [?], which is free from pains and illnesses and raised above afflictions and sighing, and in which there are no sorrows or worries that cause suffering and grief.
Rather, harmony, peace, joy, and life are united in God, who perfects all things, united in that blessedness belonging to the Lord.
And if someone should say or think that, since God is good, rich, wise, perfect, complete, needing nothing and lacking nothing,
he created his creatures out of his goodness and established the worlds,
why did he not create all rational beings in that perfect blessedness and completeness which will be theirs in the renewal to come?
We answer him: For many reasons, of which we understand only a little.
Those who have been perfected understand still more. From them, in turn, we will understand these things and know them precisely,
when we are brought to completion in that renewal, in union with our Lord. What we now understand is as follows:
If the Creator had created rational beings from the beginning in completeness and perfection,
with the things he is going to give them after they are perfected by keeping the commandments and brought to completion in love for him,
this would not have been at all fitting, nor would it have been secure. Rather, they would have regarded the blessedness in which they were created as something belonging to their own nature
and as their own possession. And because they had not first toiled, hungered, and thirsted,
they would not have known the worth, strength, and pleasure found in rest and tranquility, in fullness, work, and freedom from want.
Just as food is greatly cherished, loved, pleasant, desirable, and sweet after intense hunger, and drink after burning thirst,
and health after a long illness, abundant wealth after distressing poverty, and light after darkness,
so, and far more than this, the renewal of the world to come, which endures in harmony, peace, and joy, is greatly cherished,
after this world, which is full of troubles, pains, and sighs. Indeed, we see that anyone who acquires something easily carelessly loses it, because it is not precious to him,
since he did not acquire it through hardship and toil. He is like someone who finds great riches,
or receives them freely from a king through his mercy and generosity: he takes no care of them, because they are not precious to him, and he does not know their worth,
because he has suffered no hardship for them. But someone who acquires something through his toil and the labor of his hands, or through trade on long journeys to distant places,
or through arduous work on the land, cherishes and values it greatly.
He takes great care of it and does not squander it easily, because he knows with how much toil, hardship, and danger he acquired it.
Likewise, if the Creator had given us that complete blessedness from the beginning, it would not have been precious to us, nor would we have enjoyed it
as we will after the great toil, labor, and hardships we endure in this world. From these few examples, let us understand many things,

and be assured that it is very good, beneficial, and helpful that we were first created in a world of hardship and want, and will afterward be in the new world, which is joy, delight, rest, and perfection.
Let us acknowledge the justice of God's judgments, praise his inexplicable wisdom, and give thanks for his inexpressible grace.
With these words, the second chapter of the second discourse ends, through God, who gave strength and help.
Again, with God who gives wisdom: the third chapter of the second discourse, on whether there is another world besides this visible, existing one.
We see, understand, and know that our nature as rational human beings is constituted and exists from something subtle and spiritual and something else that is dense and bodily.
These are the soul and the body. As long as this life continues in us, the subtle dwells in the dense.
But when this composite is dissolved and this life ceases, they separate from one another—the soul from the body.
And just as the body returns to its own nature, that is, to its elements—dust to dust and breath to air,
and moisture to water and heat to fire—so too the spiritual and subtle soul
returns and goes to dwell in a place suited to it, that is, a spiritual place, invisible to bodily eyes. The body loses none of what belongs to it,
nor is the soul dispersed and destroyed. Rather, the body leaves each of its parts in the elements from which they originated, preserved and undiminished.
For there is no other place or region in which they could be dispersed. Likewise, the soul dwells and is preserved in a spiritual place suited to it and corresponding to its nature,
until the time of renewal. Then it takes back from the elements the parts it left in them
and puts on the body it took off, the very same body, having been [?] and having acquired glory and incorruptibility through renewal.
This subject belongs to the order of resurrection and renewal, which we will also discuss below in its proper place,
providing firm assurance that puts the mind at rest: creation will certainly be renewed, and there will be a resurrection.
What dies will become immortal through renewal, and what decays will become incorruptible.
Therefore, just as the body's parts are preserved in the elements, so the rational and spiritual soul is preserved in the place of rational and spiritual beings.
There is, then, truly a place for spiritual beings—if indeed one may speak of a place in the spiritual realm—which is the invisible world.
Let us understand this: the creation that God created is complete, not deficient in any way and needing no addition. Nor is it diminished or altered at all until the time of the universal renewal.
Its matter remains as it is, namely, all four elements,
which continue in the same weight and measure in which the Creator created them, neither increasing nor decreasing at all.
They act upon one another, dissolve into one another, and are effaced by one another, and each returns to its own nature,
without anything being diminished at all, since none of them can leave this region and world within this celestial sphere.
Wherever they circulate, they return again to their own nature. So too, when the soul departs from its dwelling in the body,
it goes to dwell in a place congenial and suited to it, which is subtle, spiritual, and invisible, corresponding to its own nature,
and rational and knowing. For every place necessarily has inhabitants corresponding to its nature, suited and congenial to it.
And if the dense, heavy, non-rational elements each have their own inhabitants corresponding to their nature, suited and akin to them—as birds dwell in the air,
and on the earth there are wild animals, livestock, swarming creatures, worms, and creeping things, and in the waters many kinds of fish, creeping creatures, sea monsters, and whales,
and within fire, too, there dwell birds called amianton, that is, “unburnable”—
people catch them, take their down, spin it, and make cloths; and when they throw these into the fire,
the dirt in them burns, but they themselves do not burn at all. Instead, they remain as they are, becoming white and beautiful.
then certainly the place to which souls pass, which is subtle and spiritual,
also has inhabitants suited and akin to it: subtle, spiritual natures, rational and knowing.
And if you say, “Since these subtle, spiritual natures were created in complete perfection, why was the human being not likewise created perfect and complete?”
we say that the very nature of the human soul is perfect in its purity and clear brightness, but a condition of susceptibility to suffering came upon it.
While it remained in its spiritual state, it could not be purified, become clear, and return to its natural condition.
A dense body was given to it, to dwell in and be united with, and in it to undergo hardship and toil until it is purified and made clear.
It was not those spirits themselves that were darkened by the fall that put on bodies, but others of the same nature as they are, namely our souls.
And although we say that the nature of spiritual beings, who are rational, knowing, and invisible, is perfect and complete,
it is only in comparison with our deficiency, caused by the condition of darkness that came upon us through negligence,
that we call them perfect, and not in comparison with [?] that nature which is blessed in every way and brings everything to completion and perfection,
which neither lacks anything nor diminishes, and whose nature admits no change or alteration. And just as they are superior to us and higher than us in perfection and completeness,
so that nature which is blessed in every way is thousands upon thousands and myriads upon myriads of times more exalted than they are, more perfect and complete, and higher than they are.
Therefore they too are called deficient and incomplete. And because they are living and rational,
and there is a realm above them to which they can be raised, they continually ascend, rise higher, and advance.
Through these changes of ascent they have continual joy. That is, they are continually and always in joy and making progress.
Nevertheless, even in their progress they are not perfect and complete before the universal rejoicing shared by us and them.
Rather, they remain under a certain fear because of an alien and contrary condition that came upon many of their companions.
Some of this fear has been removed from them, but not entirely before the universal renewal and complete perfection.
We will explain these things precisely when we reach the appropriate point for them.
Therefore there certainly is another world, invisible, besides this visible world that exists.
These things are also known from the many workings that we see actually taking place in this world.
For something from that invisible world is constantly being seen and carried out in it. And the dreams that we see—we do not see them with bodily eyes.
For the body is sunk in sleep, still and silent, and all its senses are shut.
It is the soul that sees dreams, individual beings, events, and actions suited to its nature.
These belong to the invisible world. Moreover, many workings actually take place before the eyes of
everyone: beneficial and adverse workings, revelations and visions that announce and disclose beforehand events that, after a long time, are revealed, take place, and become known.
Then the revelations that were seen, which foretold these events long beforehand, are also confirmed.

These revelations, visions, dreams, and disclosures are revealed and shown to us from the invisible world through living, rational, spiritual, and subtle beings, who are sent by the sovereign command of the Creator and Lord of all.
He signals to them to carry out whatever his command directs, everything that he wills and that pleases him.
And those whose faculty of understanding is sound, if they examine the world carefully and pay attention to its movements, its revolutions, and all its activities,
understand, know, and become firmly convinced [?] that over a ministry, an order, a people, a country, a kingdom, and a craft,
there are individual beings appointed from among the rational, intelligible powers of the invisible world.
They direct, guard, watch over, and administer every people, country, and kingdom, and also oversee the seasons and the changes of the years,
the air, clouds, rain, and dew, and the rest of the world's activities and affairs, and the care required for its continued existence and preservation,
according to the command, direction, and will of the Lord and Maker. And just as he is hidden and invisible—
indeed, not even comprehensible—so too are the powers, servants, and ministers of his lordship in his invisible world.
They too are not visible to everyone, but only to someone whose mind is clear and pure.
Thus, from these many things of this kind, it has become known that there is another world of rational, intelligible, spiritual, and invisible beings.
With these words the third chapter of the second discourse is completed, through God, who gave strength and help.

Again, with God who gives wisdom: the fourth chapter of the second discourse. On the question: If there is indeed another world, what is it like? Is it material and visible like this world of ours, or spiritual, subtle, and invisible?
We believe that in the preceding chapter, which is the third of this second discourse, we explained a little out of much about the other world, which certainly exists.
It is subtle, spiritual, and invisible, for it cannot be material and bodily,
but spiritual and subtle. For everything that is composed of the four elements
depends for its subsistence—depends for its subsistence—on them, since it is from them, the elements, and necessarily
is material, bodily, and visible. But that world is subtle and spiritual, and is a dwelling place for spiritual beings, souls, and spirits.
It is not made of the elements, nor does it depend on them for its continued existence. And whatever is not made of the elements
neither sustains nor is sustained by them. It is not sustained. It is neither nourished nor bodily,
but spiritual and simple. And whatever is spiritual and simple, and is not composed of elements,
has neither beginning nor end. Therefore that world of spirits, which is subtle, simple, and spiritual, accords with the nature of its inhabitants, spirits and spiritual souls that are not composite.
It does indeed have a beginning, because it is a creation, and its beginning dates from when it was created.
But it has no end, because it is simple and not composite, and because its Creator wished it to endure and not pass away.
For this reason he created and established it as simple, subtle, and spiritual. [So that it might be a dwelling for simple, subtle, and spiritual natures.]
Changes and opposing conditions do not occur in it. There is no distress or anxiety in it, nor alarm or fear, but rest and tranquility.
Nevertheless, it is not the place of perfection and fulfillment, because the spiritual world of spiritual natures
is created and made. But the world of perfection is God's world: communion with him, wonder at him, and joy with him.
The world of spirits, however, is greatly inferior to and lower than that of God.
Nevertheless, all the work and service of its inhabitants are directed toward God: God's will and his service,
which consists in each one remaining unchanged in the condition in which it was created.
But it is destined to be further perfected and exalted at the renewal of everything. And the spiritual, rational, and understanding natures in the invisible world
are not all of one rank and measure, but belong to many ranks, degrees, and measures—not in terms of regions and places,
but in understanding and spiritual knowledge. Each of these ranks is made the head and leader of the one after it,
and it conveys to that rank gifts and a varied divine endowment. For there is one kind of gift
and endowment poured out from the Godhead, the Creator and Lord of all, upon all created and made beings.
But each one receives according to the capacity of its knowledge, and is enriched and delighted by the endowment,
and becomes wise, enlightened, helped, and improved. Similarly, this visible sun is one in its nature, and one
is the kind of its light, as its rays spread throughout the inhabited earth. In its light all the beauty and splendor of the world are seen.
Those who look see them, are enlightened, gain knowledge of events and their course, and take delight and pride in all the splendor and adornment of this world.
Nevertheless, not everyone sees, is enlightened, and takes delight equally, but each according to the clarity and clearness of the sense of sight.
Someone whose pupil is clear, unclouded, and bright sees everything clearly and accurately, takes delight, and benefits.
But someone whose eyesight is weak does so to a still lesser degree. Then there is someone whose eyes are feeble and whose sight is impaired by whatever affliction it may be.
He can barely make out solid bodies and move and walk straight; but someone who is completely blind—
night and day, light and darkness are all the same to him, although the light of the sun’s rays is one and unchanging.
But it varies for those who see, although the light of the sun’s rays is one and unchanging.
But it varies for those who see, the cause lying in them. Think in the same way about that blessed and sovereign nature,
and about his divine gifts and enriching endowments, which continually, at every moment and at all times, flow and pour forth from the sea of his mercy
and spread over all his creatures. All rational beings, both those perceived by the intellect and those perceived by the senses, receive them and are greatly enriched by them,
