beginning with the higher ranks, which are near and exalted toward the [?] of divine lordship,
through contemplation and knowledge, as we have said. Do not imagine this in terms of place and location, in a material and sensory way.
These pass first from one to another through all the heavenly ranks, orders, and companies. The last of them all is close to us,
and it conveys them to us, since it has been appointed and established to oversee our care and to exercise concern and solicitude for us, through the power and working of the Lord and Maker.
In this way all of us human beings receive heavenly gifts, each of us according to the capacity and knowledge he acquires through the excellence of his conduct,
and according to how well he keeps the Lord’s commandments and fulfills the laws, and according to the clarity of his understanding and the intellectual light in the pupil of his mind’s eye.
And although, through all these countless and unlimited thousands and myriads of spiritual and invisible beings and bodily and visible beings,
that divine gift passes, filling, perfecting, and enriching them, it is never depleted or diminished. Rather, it remains as it is, in its fullness and abundance.
And just as all the stars are placed and arranged in the firmament of the zodiac, and in a single orderly revolution
are yoked together, yet one far surpasses another in glory, brightness, and radiance, so think also about all rational beings, both those perceived by the intellect and those perceived by the senses.
Thus, from nature itself and the activities that occur in this world of ours perceived by the senses, we have gained firm assurance concerning that world perceived by the intellect:
that it is a spiritual world, invisible, subtle, and uncompounded,
just as this visible world of ours is bodily and material, dense and composite. With these words the fourth chapter ends, through God, who gave strength and help.
With God, who gives wisdom: the fifth chapter of the second discourse. On the order, purpose, and service of the other world that now exists apart from this visible one.
When we look at the governance of this world, we perceive clearly with the eyes of our understanding how it is ordered and established,
and how it proceeds, is provided for, and is governed, and how different natures opposed to one another are preserved within it
without being corrupted and destroyed by one another, although they are all adversaries and enemies of one another,
beginning with those that are our parents and sustain us, namely the elements: fire, water, earth, and air,
which are opposites and adversaries of one another. In this way everything has been composed and established.
Human beings, I mean, and livestock, wild animals, creeping things, birds, and flying creatures—all are opponents of and harmful to members of their own kind and of other kinds.
Even those primary elements themselves consume, destroy, and annihilate everything.
Fire burns and destroys. Water drowns, devastates, carries off, sweeps away, and destroys. Earth buries, annihilates, and destroys.
Air uproots, devastates, scatters, and destroys in many ways. The changes of the seasons, too, are likewise opposed to one another.
Nations oppose nations, peoples oppose other peoples, language groups oppose language groups foreign to them, and kingdoms oppose one another.
Authorities, rulers, administrators, judges, craftsmen, laborers—all the ranks of humanity, and the other dangers that surround them,
from above, from below, and from every side: those of the air [?], of destructive wild animals, and of harmful creeping things,
and of countless other things. And likewise all kinds of animals, flying creatures, creeping things, and things without life,
and everything that exists in the world, have many opponents and destructive, consuming dangers.
Yet although all these opposing forces exist in the world, look: it is preserved and continues to stand firm.
It is governed in an orderly way and managed fittingly. All these things are accomplished through the Lord's almighty care and divine providence,
which holds everything together. And look: kingdoms and authorities, judges and administrators, military commanders and workers are arranged within the world,
along with ranks, orders, measures, and services, clearly defined and not confused; and leaders of nations, teachers, and guides,
lawmakers, keepers of the laws, those who subject others and those subjected to them, masters and slaves, instructors and pupils, craftsmen and laborers,
travelers on the roads and merchants, those who sail the sea and sailors, together with all the orders and varieties found in this world.
Others, however, inhabit the mountains and wander in the deserts with herds of camels, horses, cattle, and flocks of sheep, and with vast possessions beyond number or limit.
For this is the great wonder and marvel about these people: although they do not live in cities, within walls and gates,
nor under the authority of kings and rulers, and are not bound under the laws of judges and administrators,
nor are they instructed by teachers and scribes through books and written, clearly defined regulations,
nevertheless they themselves have organized themselves and established beneficial laws and customs for themselves.
In summer they go up to the north, and in winter they go down to the south, numbering countless thousands and tens of thousands.
They take with them their wives, their children, their camels, their horses, their cattle, their flocks of sheep, and all their baggage.
They camp in meadows and pasturelands, beside springs, fountains, and rivers,
in an orderly and well-arranged way, without confusion, neither quarreling nor fighting with one another,
as though the land had been divided among them and marked out with measuring cords and measurements. The way these people live and maintain their existence is a marvel.
Although they are not one race, tribe, and language, but many, differing in dress, custom, and language,
and in their whole way of life. Among them are Arabs, Turks, Kurds, [?], Alans, and Khazars,
and Russians, Scythians, Vlachs, Serbs, Slavs, and Albanians, along with many others.
Each people has tribes and clans, along with many who live far from us in the east and south
and in every region. All these whom we have mentioned do not inhabit towns, cities, and villages,
but wander and move about, living in tents and shelters in deserts and mountains. They all maintain established rules and laws and clearly defined customs.
In this way the world is preserved and endures, and is not destroyed by all the opposing forces within it. Pay thoughtful attention, reader.
And if this confused and corruptible world, which is filled with and constituted by all these opposing forces and violent occurrences,
and is surrounded by all these injuries and harms,
which affect every race, species, and nature within it, coming from members of its own race, species, and nature
and from others—even though its very [?] comes from mutually opposing parents—is so well ordered, and its functioning proceeds,
and it endures and is governed without confusion, is bound under laws and limits, and is preserved and carried along in a wonderful arrangement and glorious order,
how, then, could that subtle, simple, uncompounded, and invisible world of spiritual beings lack a glorious order, a good law, and a clearly defined service?
Certainly the inhabitants of the invisible world have a glorious and majestic order. There is no opposition in it at all, nor any obstructive harm.
No injury or corruption approaches it, nor anything at all that harms or opposes, but only peace and great tranquility.
Its order consists of distinct persons, rational and intelligent, spiritual and subtle, who are arranged, divided, and assigned their limits.
Some of them are first among all the orders; others are last, second, and third,
with many more following one after another: heads of orders, commanders of hosts, dominions, authorities, and principalities,
along with ranks, divisions, companies, and legions without limit or number. Their quantity cannot be known to us who are made of dust,
but only to the one who created them and knows their number and quantity. They are neither mingled nor confused, but ordered and assigned their limits,
each order in its own region and each division in its own place, and each company and legion wherever it was assigned by the wise Creator and glorious Maker.
The last are subject to the second, who are above them, and the second to the third. In the same way, each order is subject to the one above it,
which serves as its head and high priest. There is no envy or arrogance among them, nor any insistence on their own will,
because neither among them nor in the nature of their world are there causes that produce these passions. Their aim is to gaze upon, contemplate, and marvel at their Creator,
and to hold their will, desire, and gladness ready to do his will and fulfill his commandments.

And although free beings can accomplish these things, since their nature is subject to their will, because there are no obstacles or accidents or anything at all hindering their will from fulfilling their Lord’s will,
it is only voluntarily and not under compulsion, since they are free and masters of themselves, as befits the order of rational beings.
And every rational being who is not free and is not master of himself—an irrational animal
is what he is, not a rational living being created in the image of his Creator. For he exercises mastery over himself and his freedom like a lord, and directs his will according to his desire.

Their service, moreover, consists of oversight, administration, and care for the movement, revolution, order, and laws of the heavenly lights, and for the elements and the preservation of the existence of everything composed of them;
for the blending of the air and the changes of the year, seasons, and times;
and for seas, rivers, and springs, and for plains, palaces, mountains, hills, and all the dry land;
and for seeds, plants, trees, fruits, winds, dews, and breezes; and for the government of kingdoms, the organization of armies, wars, and critical occasions;
and for countries, regions, climatic zones, fortified towns, and cities; and being sent to individual human beings;
and announcing future events, revealing hidden things, showing concealed things, and teaching mysteries;
and proclaiming and making known their Lord’s will. For this reason they are called angels, that is, those who are sent, or messengers.
For this is their service: being sent, carrying messages, and exercising oversight.
And this is their purpose, which is composed of them. Concerning the blending of the air and the changes of the year, seasons, and times;
and concerning seas, rivers, and springs, and plains, palaces, mountains, hills, and all the dry land;
and concerning seeds, plants, trees, fruits, winds, dews, and breezes; and the government of kingdoms, the organization of armies, wars, and critical occasions;
and concerning countries, regions, climatic zones, fortified towns, and cities; and being sent to individual human beings;
and announcing future events, revealing hidden things, showing concealed things, and teaching mysteries;
and proclaiming and making known their Lord’s will. For this reason they are called angels, that is, those who are sent, or messengers.
For this is their service: being sent, carrying messages, and exercising oversight.
And this is their purpose, their will, and their desire: to fulfill their Lord’s will and carry out his commandments.
All their care, administration, oversight, and concern for their service are carried out and accomplished through the sustaining and sovereign power of their Maker, which accompanies them,
and not through any power of their own. They are all under orders, not those who give orders. They are servants and subjects of their Creator, as beings created and made,
and not sovereign masters. Nevertheless, their created nature is beautiful, serene, clear, pure, lofty, and exalted above all created things.
There is much to say about them, beyond speech and explanation, and it cannot be contained in a book or scroll.
Human beings, being of dense substance and bodily, cannot grasp knowledge of the subtle natures and orders of the invisible world of spiritual beings.
Except for those who have been purified and cleansed of the turmoil of the flesh,
and of the body's shameful passions, and have returned to stand in the created order of the pure and understanding soul,
by being perfected through the labors of virtue and brought to fullness through keeping the Lord's commandments and the spiritual laws.
Even to these, only a certain portion of knowledge concerning the world of spirits is given, and not complete knowledge in its entirety [and fullness.
After the general renewal,] it is given to human beings, when they are released and freed from the harassment of the passions of the gross and earthly flesh.
But the Creator's world, which is prepared for all who keep their Lord's commandments and have done and fulfilled
his will, is one of the things that those perfected in rational and spiritual perfection can grasp and understand to some small extent and in small [?]. May the Lord make us all worthy of it. Amen.
With these words the fifth chapter ends, through God, who gave strength and help.
Chapter Six, with God who gives wisdom: Whether this visible and perceptible world has an end or not. This faculty of knowledge, that is, rationality, which God has given to the human being,
is something, and a glorious image of the Creator who is wise in all things, and a likeness of the spiritual powers endowed with reason and understanding.
Through it we can distinguish truth from falsehood, and things that truly exist, as they are, from things that do not exist at all,
and things that endure and remain from things that dissolve and pass away. Through this same understanding, or rational vision, which is the capacity for thought,

we have been able to investigate, examine, know, comprehend, and establish with certainty that there is a God—that is, a Lord, maker, creator, and arranger of this whole universe that is seen and perceived,
and of everything that is known but not seen; that he alone is one; and that he is three persons, namely, Mind, Word, and Spirit,
who are named Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: one glorified and worshiped Trinity, in which none is greater or smaller,
nor older or younger, but one eternal being, one God, one nature, one power, one essence, one royal dominion,
a simple and uncompounded nature, without beginning or end. He created and established the simple and spiritual world of the heavenly powers,
which had a beginning but will have no end, because it is simple and not compounded.
What is simple and not compounded does not dissolve. And because these subtle and spiritual natures of the invisible world
are close to and resemble the Creator's own nature, so that it should not be thought that he cannot create and make something unlike his nature,
he composed and established it from four opposing elements, for a certain purpose that his will desired:
namely, to place in it the physis, that is, the nature of the soul, [as in a place of training and discipline], as a temporary resident for a certain limited time,
so that in the world it might learn and gain wisdom from the nature of its contents and its constitution,
and from its own self and from the nature and mixtures of the body in which it dwells, about who its Lord and maker is,
what it owes him, and what things are right and fitting for it to do and offer him as long as it dwells in the compounded body within the compounded world.
that when this composite structure is dissolved and this cycle, way of life, and bodily activity cease,
the very nature of the soul, which is simple, not composite, and not subject to dissolution,
will remain and enjoy what it gained and worked for while it was joined to the composite body, whose structure, belonging to this world and its activities, is dissolved.
And we have understood and become certain that all simple, noncomposite natures are neither subject to dissolution nor perishable.
And all dense, bodily natures, composed of opposing elements,
necessarily have their composite structure dissolved, decay, pass away, and come to an end.
This whole world is composite and bodily, apart from the nature of the soul. Therefore this world will certainly be dissolved,
and its way of life will cease, pass away, and come to an end, apart from the nature of the soul, which is not composed of these elements.
But even though the composite structure of this world is dissolved, ceases, and comes to an end,
nevertheless, along with its dissolution and end, it is to be renewed. From being composite, dense, bodily, and material, it becomes
something else: simple, subtle, and spiritual, remaining forever and ever. Never again will it undergo dissolution or come to an end,
as we are going to show, if the Lord wills. With these words, chapter six is completed, through God who gave strength and help.
Chapter Seven, with God Who Gives Wisdom: On Whether Another World Exists Besides This One.
The argument in the preceding passages has shown, through investigation and syllogism—that is, the assembling of thoughts—by means of the rational power of knowledge within us,
that there is a Creator of this universe, and that he created and established another, invisible world.
From this visible world and the ways it is ordered and governed, we have gained a precise understanding and become certain about that invisible world.
And again, from this very world itself, its natures, its changes, and the things that happen in it,
and from the rational nature within us, we have understood that after the dissolution and end of this way of life, nature will necessarily undergo renewal.
And again we have understood that after the dissolution and end of this way of life, nature will necessarily undergo renewal.

And again we speak plainly and bring conviction to discerning people through demonstrations and indications that [?] has shown us, teaching us and giving us certainty about the universal renewal of all nature.
Look, in this world we see many natures belonging to genera
and species that decay and perish, and then are renewed and established again more gloriously.
For where can the body of something that decays [?] and perishes go?
Nothing can go outside the sphere of this air: neither a dense, physical, solid body,
nor flame, vapor, or smoke, which is an airy and subtle body. Rather, all natures composed of elements pass into one another, destroy one another, and cause one another to decay.
And this decay and destruction that befell them in their [?] is itself the cause of their renewal and their rising again.

First, human beings, livestock, wild animals, creeping creatures, birds, and flying creatures—even though they decay and perish through the dissolution of their bodily structure and the death that befalls them,
yet through the birth of others from them, like themselves and belonging to their own nature, they are continually renewed.
And they arise more gloriously than their aged progenitors, and this renewal depicts the mystery of the universal renewal.
Trees, too, and fruits and seeds themselves depict, display, and proclaim, without a voice, the [?] mystery of renewal.
In winter, trees are stripped of their leaves and deprived of their fruit, and they remain black, scorched, ugly, and repulsive to look at.
Throughout the winter they are battered by cold, snow, and ice, and they deteriorate and waste away. But when Nisan and the spring weather arrive,
and the earth grows warm to bring forth [?] the different kinds and varieties of seeds and the plants that have been planted, set, and sown in it,
then those old things that had decayed are renewed. They sprout, rise, and flourish, and appear in glorious and beautiful colors:
white, green, red, yellow, variegated, patterned, and blended. They acquire different and wonderful flavors as well as colors,
and aromatic and pleasant scents, astonishing those who see them with their beauty, taste, and fragrance.
And there is another, very remarkable wonder: the powerful effects they produce in the physical bodies of human beings and other animals.
Some of them bring health and healing for various diseases and severe pains, while others cause sickness and injury and are deadly,
causing death and destruction. How, then, did all these differences, powers, and effects come about,
and these colors, tastes, and scents, which surpass understanding in their multitude and variety?
In a single tract of land one can see [?] many trees, including the vine, with many kinds of grapes—white, black, and green—whose varieties are beyond counting,
as are their tastes and colors, although they all belong to the vine. The same is true of olives, figs, pomegranates, apples, and every kind of fruit.
Although the soil in which they are planted and the water that makes them grow are of one nature, many differences appear in them:
colors, tastes, and scents that are too numerous to count and beyond the power of words.
Likewise, seeds, grasses, growing plants, and all vegetation decay, perish, wither, and deteriorate year after year.
Then they are renewed again, sprouting and flourishing with great radiance, splendor, and glory. And if these small and ordinary things,
all of which were made for human beings, for their use and their needs, are renewed, how much more will human beings themselves be renewed when their time arrives,

and the life-giving air [?] reaches them! Then they sprout, rise, and are renewed, clothing themselves in radiance, splendor, and great glory that will never again change or decay. And all the renewals that take place in the world each year,
whether of trees, plants, seeds, and growing things, or of wild animals, flying creatures, creeping creatures, livestock, and all the kinds and varieties of creation,
depict and display beforehand that great and universal renewal. Then all those renewals will reach their limit and their end.
And that universal renewal is one and unique, enduring forever, never again decaying or passing away, because it becomes clear and refined.
And it becomes something pure, clean, and spiritual. The very same elements and nature of heaven and earth are renewed and undergo a transformation into a clear and refined state.
And the very same bodies of rational human beings rise in great glory, simple, refined, and spiritual.
For that pure, simple, and refined thing that dwelt in them, namely the nature of the soul, is preserved and continues unchanged.

And the very same soul takes to itself the body composed of those very same elements, its parents, from the place where it had left it. It rises anew and is renewed [?] in appearance, likeness, image, and form.
But it is pure [and no longer decays or dissolves, because that pure], clear, and clean part of created natures blossoms and endures.
And all its coarseness and [?] become refined, purified, and wonderfully renewed.
And this perishable nature puts on imperishability. And if you should say, “Perhaps that renewal and that refined and clear transformation

will again become coarse and heavy, grow old, and decay, like the annual renewal of trees and plants and the offspring of animals and birds, which we mentioned and from which we supplied an illustration and comparison for the universal renewal.”
We say in response to this doubt:
If rational human beings who perished in death were themselves renewed and rose after a year, or more or less,
there would be grounds for thinking this. But that is not how the matter stands, since human beings, as we see, increase through birth and reproduction.
And those who pass away and perish in death have not yet been renewed, nor has even one of them appeared in the world.
Their bodies have not been renewed and risen and put on the very same appearance, as seeds do; nor has the soul of any one of them put on a body, been renewed, and appeared to human beings.
These renewals of seeds, trees, animals, and birds take place year after year.
They perish every year and are renewed again. But that universal renewal has one appointed time and season.
In it heaven and earth are renewed, refined, and made clear, and in that renewal human beings undergo a spiritual transformation,
one that is not perishable at all, like the nature of the rational spirits whom we mentioned above.
Thus we will then be able, through our knowledge, once it has been purified, refined, and cleared of all materiality, to draw near and commune with our Lord and Maker,
and to delight with him in his great, invisible world, which neither passes away nor dissolves. And even the invisible world of spirits that now exists,
in that universal renewal, will itself be renewed and become clearer than it is now. For the whole creation of heavenly and earthly beings,
invisible and visible, intelligible and perceptible to the senses, will acquire in that universal renewal a state more excellent than the one they previously possessed.
And the entire nature of rational beings will be further exalted and raised up in knowledge of its Creator in that renewal. Then all rational beings together—
I mean all the spiritual natures, the ranks, orders, companies, and legions above,
and all the races, families, and languages of human beings who have existed and who exist throughout the inhabited world.
who recognize and know that [?] he is the Lord, Maker, and Creator of them all. They all acknowledge him and render him praise and worship.
They all testify and cry out that the Lord, the King of glory, is one. But each person, according to their conduct in this world,
receives repayment there. Those who have done good enjoy delight with their Lord and are close to him, and are called [?] to the gathering of his majesty.
But for those who did evil while they were alive in the world, the sight of him becomes a great torment.
Because they willingly wronged themselves and did not keep his commandments, they are justly deprived of the joy that is in him.
All the companies of the righteous and the sinners cry out and say, “The Lord is righteous and good; upright are
his judgments.” Thus another world truly exists, besides that invisible world of spiritual beings which exists now,
as the discussion has shown briefly. But discerning people understand much from a little.
Give a wise person an opportunity, and they will become wiser still. With these words the seventh chapter ends, through God who strengthened and helped.
Chapter Eight, with God who gives wisdom. Concerning this question: If another world does indeed exist, how is it ordered,
what is its purpose, and what is its activity—that is, its way of life? How can a bodily being, subject to suffering, yoked and entangled with the passions of heavy, dense, corruptible flesh,
speak and explain something spiritual, subtle, and incorruptible? And how can a material being, composite and subject to dissolution,
give an account of what is immaterial, simple, and not subject to dissolution? And how can one who is small and limited speak about what cannot be measured or limited?

How can an understanding imprisoned within the clay of the theatrical body comprehend, learn, and reveal the hidden things of the secrecy of the mysteries stored in the concealed and locked treasuries of the Godhead?
Minds that crawl among earthly things are neither authorized nor permitted to study the books of the Spirit, interpret things unheard, and explain things that cannot be spoken.
Who, indeed, can leave behind their material nature and enter the clear realm of spirituality?
Who can rise from their dunghill to immeasurable heights and ascend the high and holy mountain that overlooks the new world?
Who can become subtle and clear of all earthly defilement, so as to see the clear and pure realm that is not a realm,
and the place that is not a place? Who has been freed from all the heaviness that sinks and drags downward,
and acquired wings of fire and pinions of wind, flown in understanding, and gone far beyond all material heaviness and density,
and settled and dwelt among the branches of the tree of new, everlasting life, tasted its fruits, and provided for their companions?
Someone bound and fettered in the shackles of the body cannot travel and reach the realm of spirituality.
Someone weighed down and dragged along by material existence cannot peer out and catch sight of the world that is exalted above spirituality,
just as the world of spiritual beings is exalted above the world of bodily beings. A mind darkened and obscured by the mists of this troubled world cannot grasp
the contemplation of perfect clarity, radiant purity, and complete tranquility. All of us, my discerning brothers, who are concerned with the knowledge of the truth, those who
Who seek true life for their souls, who take care to purify their hearts and long to see their Lord,
As far as a created human being can see God the Creator; who wish to approach his holy mountain and ascend to the height of his holiness,
And to escape all the destructive beasts: foul thoughts and evil passions.
Those who are joyful and eager and ready to go to the city above and to see the [?] of holiness, [where the Lord’s kingdom dwells,
And to hear words] that cannot be spoken, tongues that cannot be translated, mysteries that cannot be explained,
Matters and events [?] and wonders that cannot be grasped—come, let us all leave the body and strip off its bodily coarseness.
Let us withdraw, ascend, and rise above all the material nature of the flesh. Let us purify our senses, sanctify our bodily members, and clarify our thoughts.
Let us be renewed in spirit, become radiant in soul, and be perfected in knowledge. Let us leave absolutely no share of earthly things within us.
Instead, let us seek what is above and think about what is above. Let us ascend above and rise beyond every thought, impulse, and movement,
So that we may find the ability and grasp enough, even if only a little, very imperfectly and faintly, to speak about the world to come, to show, to hear, and to understand.
As we cry out and plead with our good Lord and our kind and merciful God, who loves humanity, that he may open the eyes of our hearts,
Enlighten our thoughts, and purify our minds, so that we may be able to grasp spiritual meanings that reveal the hidden and concealed things and the glorious mysteries of his new world, let us say:
Good Lord, bountiful Creator and wise [?] Maker, eternal Being from everlasting, and King of kings forever,
God of gods and Lord of lords, giver of authority and strength and wisdom and true knowledge: you are the one who is from everlasting, continually, and forever.
There is none above you, none outside you, and none apart from you. Everything comes from you, everything stands through you, and everything is in your hands.
You are in us, and we are in you. Yet you are hidden from us by our unnatural passions, the offspring of our minds’ thinking, [which keep us] from seeing you, knowing you, and wondering at you.
You, our Lord, are Lord of everything that exists and comes into being, that is seen and known and has existence.
Give and grant to us, your servants, your creation and the work of your hands, knowledge of the truth and the light of spiritual wisdom,
And a pure heart and a radiant and holy mind, so that we may know and perceive your new world, which you will give as an inheritance to all who keep your commandments,
Who do your will and fulfill your laws, where every rule and authority ceases and every dominion is made subject,
And one alone is Lord of those in heaven and those on earth; where the Lord’s Presence dwells, where the divine kingdom reigns,
Where mighty justice is revealed, where the Being alone is worshiped, praised, and exalted—
The Being who is eternal and everlasting—by all creatures and created things, intelligible and perceptible, and by the whole creation.
He has enriched the human race exceedingly and beyond words with great gifts and endowments, to the point that he made it in his image and likeness.
Oh, the great wonder that cannot be spoken! The marvelous mystery that cannot be explained!
That a servant, made and created, formed from clay, should be in the likeness of the Lord, Maker, Creator, and Fashioner.
Yet this created and fashioned being is in the image of the Creator and Maker through this great and wondrous mind that the good and wise Lord placed within him.
Like its Lord and Creator, it cannot be explained, bounded, comprehended, or measured. It is broader than the world.
It is greater than the sea, higher than all the heavens, deeper down than the lowest depths, and brighter than the sun.
It is swifter than the whirlwind, faster than the wind, and quicker than lightning. The whole creation cannot bound it.
The whole world cannot contain it. It cannot be seized, grasped, bound, or measured. It cannot be searched out except by its Creator alone.
For it is in his image and resembles him in this wondrous, spiritual, and Godlike nature that the Creator, who made us in his image, placed within us.
Through it, see, we ascend and dare to investigate, seek out, and contemplate things above us,
and things concealed, hidden, and veiled from our understanding and our thoughts. And because it is made in the image of its Lord,
and armed and girded with this sovereign name and the divine likeness of the eternal Being, see, it soars and rises.
It flies and travels through every region and among all peoples. It ascends and rises above every height, reaches every world, and looks toward every farthest limit.
It converses and debates with all kings, rulers, and lords. Because it is the great image of the divine Being, it acts boldly and is not restrained.
It ascends and rises without being stopped. It investigates and examines without being constrained. It seeks and finds, asks and receives, and presses onward with unhindered force.
In its course it is swifter than lightning, until it reaches the dwelling place of the sovereign Presence of the eternal Being, who created it in her image and likeness,
and bestowed on it this great authority and a boldness that astonishes the worlds
and leaves the incorporeal heavenly powers amazed when they see the created servant, dwelling in [?], leap and ascend above their heights,
and pass beyond all their ranks and rise above all their orders. It did not rest or settle, nor was it stopped in the impetuous rush of its course,
swifter than lightning, until it reached the meeting place of the Limit that bounds everything in its boundlessness.
There the ship of the mind, the image of its Lord, came to rest in the peaceful harbor of sovereignty, the mistress of all worlds.
It entered the city of sovereign kingship. It reached the eternal citadel that holds all worlds. It entered into the royal treasure houses
of the source of its nature. It was deemed worthy to enter the chamber of the eternal King. It stood before the throne of the one who holds all authority, and drew near as it advanced.
It gazed as it pondered. It contemplated the glorious throne of the King of kings, hidden from every mind in heaven and on earth.
It gave thanks and praised, extolled and exalted, blessed and glorified, crying joyfully and calling out with an incorporeal mouth, and proclaiming with a tongue not made of flesh:
"How glorious is your name, our Lord! How wondrous and incomprehensible are your works! Glory to your being, worship to your sovereignty,
and thanksgiving to your divinity! For how you have created and fashioned me in a small, bounded body of three cubits!"
Me, whom the world and all created things cannot contain. And how, without envy, you honored me and exalted me, even to the point of making me in your image and likeness.
So that I might be master of myself, exercise my own free will, range in every direction, and travel to every boundary.
And I rise above all the orders and ranks of the hidden powers above.
While the temple of my body remains standing on the dust heap, its mother. And here is another wonder beyond explanation: while in all the regions and directions,
and the immeasurable heights and depths, and the hidden, inaccessible dwelling places of spiritual beings,
I travel and pass through, reach out, see, and contemplate it, I remain and dwell in that same lowly dust of mine, without moving away and without interruption.

How much can I say or investigate about what cannot be expressed? Just as its Lord cannot be comprehended or fathomed at all, neither can the one made in his image and resembling its Creator be explained at all.
And if even now, while our mind, this image of God, still resides and exists in this heavy and troubling body, it is continually clouded with smoke by it and darkened,
through the ugly passions it pours out, staining the purity of the royal image, and is continually pressed by its density and dragged down by its weight,
it is light and flies, ascends and rises, neither settling nor being held back, neither remaining nor lingering, until it reaches its meeting with the limit of all limits,
who encompasses all boundaries. Then, after the great renewal by the Lord of the whole company of heavenly and earthly beings,
when all this materiality and theatrical display are removed, and this density becomes fine, and this murkiness of the body becomes clear,
and the shadow of the heavy body is lifted, and it is renewed and becomes clear, transparent, spotless, pure, light, and fine,
spiritual and luminous—the whole nature of humanity—what world, then, can contain the exalted mind, the great image of the Godhead?
There is no way to state, explain, or define the history, nature, and creation of this exalted nature, the image of its Lord.
Now let us look wisely and reflect with understanding, with our thoughts gathered away from distraction and cares. The image of its Lord.
Now let us look wisely and reflect with understanding, with our thoughts gathered away from distraction and cares and from every
recollection of worldly things. This exalted and unbounded nature of the human mind, which is the image of the wise Creator
and resembles his inexpressible likeness—where, then, is it destined to dwell and reside after the universal renewal
and release from the weight and passions of the body that is subject to suffering? For even now, while it still dwells in it, it is neither bounded nor confined.
Where, then, will it be bounded, and how will it be confined? And if someone says, “The mind dwells and resides there in the invisible world of spiritual beings,”
look, we have experienced, know, and affirm, each of us personally,
that even now, while it is still wrapped in a bounded and heavy body, it cannot be bounded or confined within the invisible world of spiritual beings.

And when it flies in its lightness and reaches there, it neither rests nor settles, neither is stopped nor held back, but darts, leaps, and passes onward, ascending and rising until it reaches that impassable boundary
of the incomprehensible Being. There its swift and unrestrainable rush is checked and halted.
And just as the sea is churned up and swells, and its waves rise and cannot be stopped or held back,
but when they reach the edge—that is, the sand on the seashore, which has been set as a boundary that cannot be crossed—
there the mighty waves are restrained and stopped, and turn back,
so too the swift mind, the image of greatness, when it is churned up and swells amid all the waves of the visible world
and the ranks of the world of spiritual beings, flies and passes over them all. It does not linger or stop until it encounters and reaches the great boundary,
which is thought concerning eternal Being. There it is restrained, [?], and brought into order, and it is no longer permitted to go beyond.
Now we have all been assured by all these convincing demonstrations, which each of us has personally experienced and knows with certainty,
that the invisible world of spiritual beings that exists now is not the new world that the righteous, who loved their Lord and kept his commandments, are to inherit.
And it is called new because it is not old [like this world of ours and like the world of spiritual beings. Nor is it called old].
Rather, it truly exists, but its order has not yet been made known or revealed to created beings, since no eye has seen it and no ear has heard it.
It has not stirred in thought or entered the heart. But at the renewal of all things it will be revealed and made known, and its gate will be opened.
And it is called the new world because it will be newly made known and receive inhabitants.
And if someone should further say, concerning the spiritual powers in heaven, that is, in the invisible world:
“Are they not subtle, clear, and luminous minds? And because they are not entangled with dense bodies, do they not excel all the more
in spirituality and purity, remaining pure and clear in their nature? And does their mind not extend like ours, and indeed much further,
because it has not been darkened by the body? Where, then, is the place of these beings?” This world is one kingdom.
But within it there are army commanders, judges, and governors who stand in high positions beside the king and constantly share in his confidential counsel.
There are other rulers and officials who are lower than these, but who are also close to the king’s council,
though not like the first. After these come others: commanders of thousands and commanders of troops; then soldiers and workers
further down; then attendants and servants further on this side; and those who have business and approach the judges
further over there; and many others assigned to numerous services and tasks, among bakers and cooks, over storehouses and supplies of bread and wine.
Others are entrusted with the royal treasuries; others with the stables; others with the herds of mares, cattle, and sheep.
And many others are engaged in the many affairs of kings and rulers. All of them are within the royal household,
and constantly see the king’s face. From him they receive their livelihood, support, and provision. Think of the new world in this way:
it contains many ranks, degrees, places, and chambers. And each of the orders of rational beings
Whether spiritual or bodily, it has a particular place suited to it, even though the region is one and the kingdom is one.
But within it there are countless ranks and degrees, just as the sun is one in its light and its nature,
but each of us enjoys seeing it according to the soundness of our sense of sight. And those deprived of sight
are tormented in darkness. Likewise, those deprived of spiritual sight, which is contemplation of the sovereign Being,
which is acquired through the praiseworthy practices of virtue, are tormented in the darkness of ignorance,
because they are far from the glorious region of the kingdom, and the gate of life is closed in their faces.
They are deprived of the delight of seeing the life-giving tree and of the sweetness of its desirable fruits, of which one can never have enough.
Now that we have become convinced that, beyond any doubt, another, new world, apart from that invisible world of spirits,
is what the righteous are destined to inherit, we should investigate and inquire what its order is, what its purpose is, and what service takes place in it.
Although no eye has seen it, no ear [?] has heard it, nor has any thought of what it is like entered the heart,
we ought nevertheless to investigate and learn whatever our nature can grasp and know of the things that will exist and be put to use in the new world.
For this exalted nature of the mind within us, which is the great image of the Godhead, itself
ventures, searches, investigates, and discovers these things, because it has been given authority to go, reach out, ascend, and rise wherever it wishes.

And if it is purified of the theatrical display of the body in which it dwells, becomes clear and illuminated, stands in the order proper to its nature, and recognizes its dignity, nothing in heaven or on earth is hidden from it.
It sees the image of the Creator depicted in its own image, enters the great treasury of hidden things, brings out spiritual treasures, and provides for its fellow servants.
Let us pay attention and gather our thoughts here, since we know and have become convinced that this mind is the great image of the Godhead.
It is neither bounded nor confined to a place, nor can it be restrained or contained within the whole visible world or the invisible one,
because it is far greater than the world, far more spacious than creation, and high and exalted beyond measure.
And if this, which was created from the eternal being of the glorious Godhead, is so high, exalted, great, and glorious, and is neither confined nor bounded,
how much higher, more exalted, greater, and more glorious is the adorable Lordship itself, which the worlds cannot bound!
It is not confined and cannot be measured at all, and everything is filled with it, both visible and invisible,
that has been known until now, that is known now, and that will be known after the renewal, when the perfection of fulfillment is revealed.
And there is no place or region that is seen and known, or that is yet to be known,
that is not filled with the glorious Godhead, even if there are, or come to be, myriads upon myriads of other worlds,
and each one of them should be far greater and more spacious than this visible world of bodies and than the invisible world of spirits.
Tens of thousands of times ten thousand are still too few and cannot encompass the sovereign Being, and there is nothing above Being.
Nor is there anything outside Being, or apart from Being, since this is how it is. And there is nothing outside God.
Nor can there possibly be. Why do we wander aimlessly and become confused by speculations and thoughts that have no foundation?
And why do we imagine that the new world and the heavenly kingdom are something else apart from God?
Look, the mind has gathered its thoughts, forced itself onward, dared to pass beyond its rank and measure, revealed hidden things, and disclosed secrets.
It has explained the great, hidden, glorious mystery and committed to writing something great that it was neither permitted nor authorized to commit to writing.
Nor is it permitted for those who crawl upon the earth and live in the flesh to touch these things or even encounter them.
But even if people of this sort look and read, they see without seeing; they read without
perceiving. They hear without understanding at all, because their hearts are dull and their knowledge is darkened
by the darkness of vile passions that incidentally came upon their clear and pure nature, disturbing and obscuring it.
But those whose senses are sound and whose minds are enlightened in their hidden vision,
let them come, meditate, and enjoy this spiritual table prepared by a lowly and needy host.
Not from his own possessions, but from his Lord’s rich treasury, he has dared to take and set before the discerning guests reclining at the table.
Love does not know how to keep still. Because he loves, he dares and steps beyond his measure. Just as a musical flute
and the strings of a lyre are ordinary instruments, [but the praise and glory belong to the musician and the lyre player,]
so too with the writer and composer of the discourse: the praise is not his, because it is not from his own nature that he brings forth new things and produces explanations.
Rather, he receives from the Lord of nature and from the teachings of others through whom the Truth has acted and spoken.
He is strengthened, becomes rich, and provides for others. Thus, truly, there is nothing outside God or apart from God,
nor anything without God. Everything is from him, everything is in him, and everything is in his hand. Everything has its being from him, everything returns to him, and everything exists in him.
Even the hostile and rebellious powers, and wicked and unjust human beings, cannot live apart from him, because it is by his power that they endure and exist.
For they were created by him and were good and beautiful, but by their own will, through their negligence, they were deprived of goodness.
And evil came upon them incidentally—evil that did not exist and has no being, but arises from a slack will and negligence.
And since everything is in God and God is in everything, he himself is the heavenly kingdom; he himself is the world to come.
He himself is the life that does not pass away, the blessings that never end, the delights that never cease, the everlasting splendors, the joys without end.
In him the righteous reign; him the just inherit. He himself is the dwelling place of the saints. We know that he is all these things.
But what that blessedness is like and how great it is—the nature of its delight and the extent of its joy—cannot be expressed.
No eye has seen it, no ear has heard it, nor has it entered the heart. Who knows the nature of something that has not yet been revealed?
Who can explain the hidden depths of a concealed and secret mystery? A door that is shut and a treasury that is sealed—
who can speak of the hidden and limitless riches stored within it? Whoever is purified and made clear through upright conduct in keeping the Lord’s commandments,

and subdues and wears down the body and stills its impulses, strengthens and empowers the soul, enlightens its thoughts, and restores it to the natural order in which it was created, peers inward through
hidden doors at limitless riches.
He rejoices and exults in his hope and becomes assured of the unfailing blessings awaiting him. And when he perceives these things, neither height nor depth nor the kingdom of the world,
nor all its glory, neither possession of the whole inhabited world and the desirable things of this age, nor sword nor fire,
neither death nor life can any longer separate him from the love of the good Lord who has prepared and made ready for him these glorious and limitless things.
And all the power, glory, possessions, and beauty of the whole world

he considers worthless dung compared with that great glory and unfailing blessedness which he has perceived in his soul that he is to receive at the universal renewal, when the bodily covering is folded away.
He perceives these things in hope and expectation, though he has not yet received or possessed them. Then, when he experiences them and is perfected and brought to fulfillment in them,
how great his blessedness will be, what his joy will be like, and how great his greatness! May we all be found worthy of these things through the grace of our Lord. Amen.
Now that we have become assured that our Lord and God, our Maker and Creator, is the world to come and the kingdom that the righteous inherit,
and the delight and joy of the perfect, we ought, if possible and insofar as it is possible, to know and learn what the order of that transformation is,
and what the aim of the new people’s way of life is, and what their service is in God’s new world, after the universal renewal,
when all materiality and coarseness are taken away and removed, and all nature is made clear
and refined and perfected in fullness. There is no longer any need or deficiency, no distress or dejection,
no anxiety or worry, no fear or sorrow, no stumbling or doubt, no confusion or turmoil,
no weariness or affliction, no pain or sickness, no anguish or sighing. Rather, this is the order of God’s new world:
peace and harmony, joy and gladness, tranquility and rest, cheerfulness and consolation, perfect blessedness,
complete greatness, a celebration that never passes, delight that never fades, a festival that never ends, wealth that never runs out, life that never ends,
a kingdom without opposition, a heavenly inheritance, the fulfillment of the hope and expectation of the saints who kept the Lord’s commandments
and conducted themselves uprightly during this short time in which they lived as temporary residents in this passing world. The aim of God’s new world
is the renewal of natures—that is, that everything should return to its own nature. Oh, how great and glorious is this wondrous mystery!
That is, that everything should return and become as it was; that created beings should be united to the Creator.
That things made should mingle with their Maker; that everything should become one; that all duality and number should cease; that there should be brought to perfection
all of nature, and it should become clear, return, and be united to the beginning; that the word should be heard, ruling the ages, encouraging rational beings, and uniting servants to the Lord.
Instead of the saying, “You are dust and come from dust, and to dust you will return,”
the saying, “You came from God and are in God, and to God you will return”; and, to say it all together boldly, “You will become God in God.”
Then the saying of one of those perfected in God will be fulfilled: “Then God will be all in all for us.”
And that of another among created beings: “Everything came forth from him and returns to him.” This is the goal of the new world.
Or rather, it is the will of the Lord of the ages, whose glory is worshiped and whose name is praised. The worship offered in God's new world by those who have been deemed worthy of it consists of:
spiritual praises, holy songs, thanksgivings to the Lord, pure hallelujahs,
radiant cries of joy, clear declarations of holiness, glorious psalms, magnificent acclamations, splendid exaltations,
sweet melodies, wonder at the Maker, amazement at the Creator, a glorious vision of the Lord,
full of hope and consolation in the Lord; celebration, festivity, and priestly service in the church that is Jerusalem in heaven,
which the Craftsman of the ages built and completed for his beloved ones. He himself is the priest and the high priest. He himself is the sacrifice and the altar.
He himself is food and nourishment. He himself is refreshing drink. He himself is the nurturer and the nurture. He himself is delight and the giver of delight.

He himself is the treasure that enriches. He himself is the holy temple and the one who sanctifies. He himself is the chamber and the lodging place. He himself is the perfecter and the one who brings to completion.
He himself is the one who renews and the one who unites. He himself is joy and the giver of joy. He himself is gladness and the giver of gladness. He himself is the first, the middle, and the last.
He himself is the beginning and the end. He himself is without beginning [?] and without end. He himself is from eternity and forever.
He himself is the tabernacle and the dwelling place for all generations. Beyond this, pen and ink have neither authority nor permission to depict anything on paper.
Beyond this, there is no command to venture further and reveal hidden things. Beyond this, it is impossible to convey it fully in writing. Beyond this, the mouth cannot speak.
Beyond this, the tongue does not know how to interpret. Beyond this, the mind cannot comprehend as long as it is confined within the covering of flesh.
Beyond this, the ear cannot hear unfamiliar sounds. Beyond this, the heart cannot receive unspeakable words. From here onward there are amazement and wonder.
From here onward there are stillness and silence. From here onward there is great astonishment: movements without slackness, subtle utterances, unmixed thoughts,
lives beyond quantity, ways of life beyond quality. Everything is one. Everything has been united. God is one, and there is no other
besides him. Bodies have been taken away. Stumbling blocks have been removed. Numbers have ceased. There is no longer anything that is not he, but God
alone, he who is. He was and is, and he will be. With these words the eighth chapter is completed, through God who strengthened and helped.
And blessed be our Lord. Amen. The second discourse on the knowledge of the truth is finished. It contains eight chapters on spirituality and theology.
Next, the third discourse on the knowledge of the truth.

In it he speaks about the creation of the human being, his nature, his rank, and his purpose. It contains nine chapters. Chapter One. With God, who gives wisdom: On why the human being was created. Lowly dust, molded from ashes, gives you thanks,
because you have so greatly exalted and honored it, even to the point of making and fashioning it in your image and likeness.
We praise you, the Praiseworthy One, whom all gloriously praise. We bless you, the Blessed One, whom all blessedly bless, and you are blessed forever and ever.
We kneel and worship before the awesome throne of your lordship. You are worshiped by all and receive the worship of all, though you need nothing and lack nothing,
but so that you may exalt them through their worship. Thanks be to your perfect [?], which perfects everything, for though you have not become smaller or diminished,
you hear the thanksgiving of all for their help and exaltation. Who is able to give you thanks, my Lord,
or to proclaim and recount the glorious [?] of your lordship? When we did not exist, you created us, fashioned us, and brought us into being.
And in your indescribable grace, entirely free from envy, you made me in your image and likeness.
But through my own evil will I grew slack and careless, and did not understand my glorious and exalted honor.
Because of this I became like cattle and resembled the beasts. What shall I say, and what shall I do? No one grieves and cares for what has been molded
except the one who molded it, or for creation except its Creator and Maker. After he had made it and fashioned it in his image and likeness,
and it had, by its own will, become corrupted, defiled, and stained, he is ready to renew it again, cleanse it, and make it pure, until he restores its splendid beauty
and it returns to its glorious nature, so that it may be worthy to become a chamber, a tabernacle, and a dwelling place for its Maker forever and ever.
He needs nothing and lacks nothing: the good and wealthy Lord, the wise Creator who created and fashioned creatures although he himself had no need,

but because of the exalted nature of his goodness, which cannot remain without doing good, enriching, and displaying his great wisdom through his works, as we have explained these matters at length above.
And we have provided assurance concerning everything we have said from the beginning
of this book, and also concerning everything we are going to say, with God, who gives wisdom and guidance.
Now when he willed and resolved to create creatures and fashion the world, these things had been in his thought from the beginning:
that he thus willed and was prepared to make, create, and fashion an invisible world of spiritual beings
and another, visible world for bodily beings. He did not conceive these things as something new, nor does he conceive anything new.
Rather, he is perfect and lacks nothing. And everything that has happened and happens—whether he himself has done it or does it,
or whether free will, which is its own master and resembles God, has done it or does it, whether in deed and action,
or in an audible word, or in a hidden thought—and all the other things that have taken place and happened in the world and continue to happen forever.
All these things are known to him beforehand, as though they had already happened, even before he created the worlds.
He is not like us, thinking of something new that he did not previously know. Far be it from that great, perfect, and complete wisdom to have lacked anything that it only recently came to know.
Nor is it as those unlearned people say: “The Lord does whatever he wills, and changes his will anew.”
Rather, whatever he wills, he has willed from the beginning. And even those things that he does not will, he knew beforehand, before those who do them came into being.
And if he is prepared to put a stop to them, that too has been known to him from the beginning; and if instead he allows free will to conduct itself according to its own wishes,
this too is completely known to him. And if you, a human being, change the will of your freedom tens of thousands of times in a single day,
some of these changes come from you yourself, through your desire and the movement of your free will, and some from circumstances that press upon you.
The one who knows everything knew them all beforehand, just as they come about, happen, and take place—neither more nor less.
This Lord of ours, then, who can do everything, knows everything, and is wise in everything, created the worlds when it pleased him, from no other thing.
For nothing existed, nor does anything exist or come into being, apart from him, except sin. Therefore, from himself he created and established the worlds.
These existed in his thought as part of his being, not as something new. Nor was it because he was in need, as we have amply shown and explained above.
Rather, because of his goodness, he willed to establish the worlds through his wisdom and enrich them with the abundant, inexhaustible riches of his lordship.
And the thought and will of the God of all became a deed, perfect and complete in everything, lacking nothing.

Thus the invisible world of spiritual beings was created, the world that exists now and whose existence we have confirmed through natural demonstrations, discoveries, and effects that occur in this world.
As we showed in the discourse preceding this one, everything was created together in a single instant.
The world of spiritual beings, with all its ranks, orders, and divisions: spiritual powers endowed with reason and knowledge, companies, legions, and hosts.
Thousands and tens of thousands beyond counting, not in confusion or [?], but in order and arrangement: those of the first rank, commanders of the powers, and those of the second rank,
and those of the third and fourth ranks, up to nine orders, ranks, and companies, divided and arranged in three spiritual assemblies.
They all have names, positions of leadership, and ranks, and they proclaim holy, bless, and praise the exalted nature of the substance of the being of the Godhead.
It is designated by three names: Mind, Word, and Spirit, which are named Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Not one after another, as is customary in the speech of our tongue, but all three together are names of the one God, who is known as a Trinity.
These three spiritual assemblies were established, and in each assembly there were three companies of living, rational beings.
Above all these was another, exalted rank, portraying the one Godhead, which is one lordship,
one kingdom, one authority. This tenth rank was exalted above them all.
It was the first to receive the divine gifts and the Lord’s favors that flowed from the eternal Being.
And he would convey these to the other assemblies. And these divine gifts would pass through all those immaterial orders.
And they were conveyed from one to another, as far as the last, while all were filled and made complete by them and perfected through them.
And those gifts were never exhausted or diminished. Rather, just as they went forth and flowed abundantly from the sovereign Being,
so they reached the last of those incorporeal powers.
Yet each received these gifts according to the strength and capacity of its nature and rank.
And as they were being made divine and perfected through these divine gifts,
they all uttered and repeated discourse about God—that is, [theology]—concerning the Trinity worthy of worship, of the one glorified Godhead.
Some of them cried, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts, Sabaoth!” And some shouted, “Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place!”
Others repeated, “Hallelujah, hallelujah! Glory to you, O God!” Some offered praise, while others shouted for joy.
Still others offered honor, others acclaim, others exaltation, and others thanksgiving and worship.
And all the praises of glorious discourse about God ascended from one order to another,
and from one rank to the one above it, and from one company to the one more exalted than it, up to that exalted order above them all.
Because of its glory, its exalted position, and its nearness to the meeting place of the dwelling of the divine Being, it was called the Morning Star.
That is, just as the morning star of the firmament is near and is a messenger of light, and comes before the rising of the great sun, the king of the heavenly lights,
so he too was stationed before the intelligible Sun, the King and Lord of all the rational powers of fire and spirit.
And he would present and bring before the divine Lordship the theological praises of all the orders of spiritual beings.
He in turn would receive the Lord’s gift and convey it to his companions in these three sovereign assemblies.
By nature he was pure, beautiful, radiant, and master of himself, in control of his freedom and in control of his will.
He resembled his Lord, commanded like his Creator, and governed like his Maker—this great and exalted ruler of all the powers.
This one, great in rank, exalted in honor, and glorious in greatness—this Morning Star—stood at the gate of the kingdom,
bringing in and taking out like the chief steward, the commander of the army, and the king’s deputy. By a movement of his own freedom, he turned aside and thought wickedly.
He brought upon his good nature the occurrence of evil, which had not existed. He reflected in opposition and thought rebelliously.
He considered things arrogantly and said to himself, “Since I am placed above all the powers of fire and spirit,
and I am near the dwelling of the eternal and sovereign Majesty,
and all the praises and discourse about God from all the orders of spiritual beings ascend to me,
And I present offerings before the sovereign Lordship, and I also receive divine gifts and blessings from the eternal Being.
And I bring them out and convey them to the other orders and companies. Therefore it is right that I too should have a royal throne,
and that it should be set above all these intelligible stars, these spiritual powers in heaven,
which is the city of spirits. And I will be like the Most High, since I am also close to, joined to, and like the Lord Most High.
But the wretched fool did not understand or consider that he was a creature, not the Creator; something made, not the Maker; and something limited, not the one who sets limits.
All this greatness was given to him by grace; it did not belong to his nature eternally.

When he entertained these arrogant thoughts, he turned away from the divine contemplation that had been given to him. He ought to have entertained these thoughts of lordship only about the essence of the eternal Being,
and lowly and humble thoughts about himself, as a servant who was made and a minister of greatness. Because he turned aside, he was called Satan.
And because he exalted himself, he fell through the passion of pride. This was the first sin to enter, as an accidental occurrence,
into the pure and beautiful creation made by the good Creator. Therefore there is no sin greater or more powerful than this passion of pride, which opposes God.
When he became puffed up with this proud thought and wished to rise still further and exalt himself to a place that was not rightfully his,
his luminous mind was darkened by the darkness of this hateful passion, and he contended with God.
He was cast down from his exalted honor into the lowest depth of mental darkness. Therefore he was called and named a demon—that is, one cast down, because he was cast down from his honor.
When he was cast down and fell from that exalted height of his honor, he passed through all the companies, orders, and ranks of the spiritual powers,
plunging, tumbling, and descending without stopping at all, because of the terrible command that was hurling him down sharply and swiftly.
His fall was so swift, as he was hurled down and fell from heaven, like swift, flashing lightning.
But when the heavenly powers in all the assemblies, and all the spiritual orders and ranks, saw him
passing and tumbling down through them all, they stood in amazement and great bewilderment,
because they were afraid and trembled, thinking that perhaps they would all fall and tumble down in the same way. Some say
that many of them, from all the orders, tumbled down and fell with him—that is, those who had themselves also entertained an arrogant thought.
Others say that there was no tenth order apart from these nine orders in the three assemblies.
They say that those who thought arrogantly and fell belonged to these orders. But the accurate account is as we have stated above:
there truly were ten orders. Those nine portray the holy mystery of the sovereign Trinity,
while the one remaining order signifies the one Godhead and Lordship of the eternal Being, who is three in persons.
He was exalted above all the orders of the powers on high, and he was their head and foremost among them.
and second to the Godhead. For this reason he was called the morning star and ruler. And because his position was very high and exalted,
his fall was therefore very terrible and severe, with no rising again from it, no recovery, and no restoration.
And that order alone [?], the one who created them, or even the powers who were their companions. And this while they were falling and tumbling amid a great upheaval,
and all the heavenly powers were standing in amazement, fear, and great alarm,
lest they too should be overthrown with them. Then a command was signaled from before the throne,
the awesome throne of the sovereign Being, to one of the commanders of the spiritual powers.
And he cried out with his spiritual voice, in his language, an uncompounded word that is translated [?], and said, “Let us all stand firm in fear and holiness.”
And at this utterance each of the orders was established firmly in its place. Their minds were strengthened, and they took courage.
Again they began to praise, bless, and declare holy. Each continued in its ministry and service, down to this day and forever.
Fear did not remain in their hearts until later times, as we shall show below, if our Lord wills.
And those rebellious powers who had plotted and fallen—when the utterance came, “Let us stand firm,” each of them remained in its place,
but far below, in the dark and lowest depth, very far removed from the assembly of all the spiritual orders and ranks, the children of light.
And so occurred the fall of Satan [?], that is, the one who turned away from God. He was named the rebellious demon because he was cast down from his rank
and was overthrown and fell because he rebelled and was removed. But his glorious, high, and exalted throne
and his glorious and honored place remained empty and deprived of inhabitants.
And the Creator, Lord and God of all, and Lord of the powers, because he is good and rich and abounding in mercies (in gifts),
his goodness could not endure that this exalted throne and glorious place, from which Satan had been estranged and overthrown, should remain without inhabitants and heirs.
And to create other beings, likewise spiritual, like those who had fallen, and establish them in the place and on the throne of the one who had been overthrown from it,
so that [?] that high and honored place in the sovereign kingdom, and to entrust it to them
suddenly and hastily, as he had given it to others—they would by no means have been able, or have understood its honor, so as to preserve it and become firmly established in it.
Rather, they would quickly have lost it, become estranged from its glory, and been deprived of its blessed and sovereign ministry, like those first ones,
who did not understand their honor and did not preserve the order in which they were created. It is just as we see in this world: people who suddenly become rich and rise to greatness
and acquire wealth belonging to others, for which they have neither labored nor toiled—whether it is given to them by someone else,
or they find some treasure—quickly and easily squander it recklessly, throw it away, and lose it, because they do not know its worth,
since they have not labored and toiled for it. But those who acquire wealth through the labor of their hands and the sweat of their faces,
And with great personal hardship, they guard it carefully and use it wisely, hiding it in a
secure treasury, under locks, seals, and signets, concealed and hidden away, because they know how much hard work, great exertion, and hardship it took them to gather and acquire it.
And how many afflictions and hardships of winter and summer, of working the land and much drudgery, or dangers on distant journeys,
and fear of raiders, thieves, and robbers, or the great terror of sailing among waves and towering billows on seas and rivers,
and deaths every day and every hour, or exhausting and compulsory hired labor, wasting toil, personal hardship, and the exhaustion of their strength.
As everyone knows from experience, whoever acquires wealth without hard work quickly squanders it, because he does not know its value,

since he did not exert himself for it. But someone who acquires it through hard work and hardship takes great care of it and guards it, because he knows its value, since he exerted himself greatly for its sake.
Likewise, if someone is a naive youth who has not yet experienced the world, or an insignificant and uneducated person, not yet mature in understanding and knowledge,
and he is given high rank and authority to govern a large population and a city, or a great number of troops,
he exercises his leadership badly and without discipline. He quickly falls from his position of honor (his rank) and is removed from his authority
because of his lack of knowledge and training. Or he destroys himself and those with him because of his ignorance.
Likewise, the Creator, who is wise in everything and knows everything before it happens, considered this,
knowing it as though it had already happened, been completed, and passed away: if he created others like these and entrusted that honored place to them,
and appointed them to the exalted service from which [?] the ruler who was overthrown because of his pride had been deprived and excluded,
they too, because they did not know its value, would quickly lose it, be excluded from its dwelling, and be deprived of its great blessedness,
because they had received it freely, without [?] and without weariness.
He who is blessed in everything and alone is wise, knowing everything, resolved to create many rational beings like these,
and first to place them in a place of drudgery and many hardships, so that they would exert themselves there and endure afflictions and dangers,
with great hard work, weariness, anxiety, and much fear, for its sake—that is, for the sake of that honored position and that glorious and exalted place
in his heavenly and eternal kingdom in his great world, from which the first rebel and originator of evil was excluded and deprived, who by his own will
became darkness. And because subtle, immaterial spirits have no hard work, hardship, or drudgery in their nature, nor exertion, weariness, or anything like these,
he resolved to make another creation, composed of matter that had already been created from the beginning, together with the creation of the spirits, and kept aside.
For he who is wise in everything knew through his foreknowledge that things would happen as we have described,
and that he would need to make a rational living being composed of spirit and matter. He therefore created matter beforehand, from the beginning, together with the creation of the spirits.
And all these things he created, established, and made in a single instant. Yet they do not become known to us all at once, because of our perfection.
But with much discussion, in the recounting of a long, narrative discourse, so that through the materiality and density belonging to this composite, rational living being,
you may be able to endure and bear toil and struggle willingly amid weariness and hardship,
and through the exercise of freedom and self-determination, so that you may justly and rightly earn a reward and receive recompense,
which is the inheritance of the throne [?] and the glorious place from which that pampered one, who became sick with pride, was estranged.
And because he was lifted up, he became dark and was cast down. And so that, when you receive just recompense and inherit that lordly place in the kingdom,
you may guard that freedom for the royal inheritance with great care and vigilance, knowing its honor and greatness,
because you endured much humiliation and hardship in the arena of struggle for its sake. And when you come to be and live in this way,
you will remain in that indescribable blessedness forever, without change and without disturbance.
As for the nature of that blessedness, there is nothing one can say, because the feeble eye has not seen it, nor has the ear heard it.
Nor has the nature of that lordly blessedness and delight in the kingdom of eternal Being entered a material heart that has not been cleansed of passions.
This is the reason why the human being was created as a rational living being, composed of a spiritual soul sharing the nature of spiritual beings,
and a material body constituted from the four elements, the progenitors of the world. With these words, the first chapter of the third discourse is completed, through God who gives strength.
Chapter Two, with God who gives wisdom and guidance: On what human nature is. Because the Maker, wise in everything, is exceedingly great, glorious, and wonderful,
and cannot be comprehended by created minds, or measured, or bounded, and weak natures cannot attain knowledge of him, so too the whole creation, great
and glorious and wonderful, is incomprehensible, because it contains many distinctions, variations, genera, species, and individual beings that cannot be bounded or comprehended at all.

Who among human beings, dense and material, [?] with the flesh their companion and crawling upon the earth their mother, can comprehend, know, and learn about the wonderful and incomprehensible creatures,
filled with great wisdom, which the wise Creator created and fashioned? Only someone who has withdrawn from the world's disturbances, gone far away, and settled in stillness,
kept silence and gathered his mind and thoughts together, wasted his body through ascetic discipline, and become refined and clear in mind and knowledge,
purified his heart and cleansed his mind of every passion and impurity, meditated on nature in many ways, examined it with his mind, and reflected on the Creator,
and occupied himself with him alone and meditated on him, until he was enlightened by him in mind and knowledge, became wise, and comprehended the nature of all created things.
From his creatures he also [?] came to know the Creator himself, insofar as a human being can know God. When he learns all these things and becomes wise and knowledgeable,
then a human being can know himself and examine his own being: what his nature is, where his beginning comes from, and toward what his end is directed.
Apart from this, anyone who has learned and knows anything has knowledge that falls far short of true and exact knowledge of nature.
And now, because of our imperfection, we say a little out of much before imperfect people like ourselves,
