so that we may not be entirely deprived of knowledge of the truth. Through this little that we present, we also exercise ourselves and undergo examination, making no confident claims at all.
Truth itself has revealed its certainty to us, from itself and through itself. And we say that human nature is something twofold: a living being composed
of a spiritual and a material component. On the spiritual side, there is a living, rational, and knowing soul, sharing the nature of spiritual beings.
It has two powers, the vital and the rational, and is luminous and clear by nature. The more it meditates on knowledge, the more it advances, grows wise, and rises.
There is absolutely no end or limit to the knowledge it can receive, because knowledge of the truth has no end.
And nothing prevents the rational soul from receiving knowledge and advancing in it, both in this world and in the world to come, and so on forever without end.
The more it rises and advances in knowledge, the more it delights and rejoices in pleasures and joys that are incomparable and indescribable.
If knowledge of the truth had only one level, and had a limit and an end, then, once someone reached
it and remained in it for a certain length of time, he would become satiated with it, and it would become like a habit and a fixed, unchanging nature.
He would not delight in it as he does in something new, something he encounters afresh each time, as we experience with many natural and incidental things in this world.
But since he alone is perfect and lacks nothing, all rational and knowing creatures ascend in him
and rise higher and grow wise. Yet they cannot attain or reach the limit of his perfection and completeness.
On the material side, a human being has a body composed of four elements: a complete living being, sharing the nature of all animate creatures.
It has a blood-based soul that sustains the body, like the other living creatures. This soul has two powers, desire and anger.
The body also has its own properties, namely weight, nourishment, growth, and the other conditions and changes.
Both together—that is, the rational and knowing soul and the living body—have discursive reasoning.
This means the gathering together of thoughts, reflections, and deliberations. Neither has these apart from the other.
For the rational soul is luminous and clear by nature, and perfect according to the natural order of the spiritual powers.
It does not need to deliberate, think, and weigh thoughts to determine which is good and which is evil,
which is fitting and which is not, or to select those it desires and wants and reject those it hates. These things do not belong to the nature of spiritual beings.
And so that chief of evil, as soon as he thought rashly, fell from the height of his honor.
If he had possessed discursive reasoning by nature, he would have deliberated and gathered his thoughts,
weighed them, and chosen those that were fitting and sound rather than those that were harmful and unfitting.
Then he would not have suffered that great fall of his. But the gathering together of mixed thoughts does not belong to the nature of spiritual beings.
For the Creator created them perfect, closely resembling his own nature, and not easily prone to falling.
And if a fall [?] does happen to them, there is no rising again for them, because of the great distance and the exalted height at which they stand.
For this reason God created the human being as a composite being, so that he would have the power of reasoning to gather thoughts and examine them, choose those that help, and reject those that harm.
And if he becomes proud because of the exalted nature of the rational soul, then, by considering the nature of the body—coarse, filthy, heavy, and subject to suffering—

he should humble and lower himself and regard himself as insignificant, rather than perish and be overthrown by the passion of arrogance and pride. And again, whenever he becomes excessively contemptible
in his own eyes because of the body's ugliness and foulness, its illnesses, and the repulsiveness of its sufferings, he should again take comfort and be lifted up in hope,
by considering the glorious nature of the soul, clear and radiant, which produces ideas and actions, reveals new things, and brings forth teachings,
and discovers crafts and methods that it has not learned from others. Thus he should not lose hope and perish in distress.
Just as he falls through the body, he can rise through the soul. And if he falls into an illness of the soul,
the body's lowliness and susceptibility to suffering heal him. This is the great reason why divine Wisdom created and fashioned this composite living being and called it a human being,
and named it its image and likeness, because of its freedom, self-government, and will. We also speak of another hidden mystery.
For the wise and perfect Creator knew beforehand that the composite and material creation would become enslaved to futility,
and would worship its fellow creatures and assign to them, as borrowed titles, the names of the glorious God,
and would even regard them as gods, creators, and makers, through the error that was destined to befall it. It would therefore be necessary for him to reveal himself and show himself to his creation,
and teach it and give it understanding of his eternal existence, his lordship, his divinity, and his oneness,
and establish it in these things firmly and convincingly, without doubt or change. And since this creation was composite and clothed in matter,
it could not see the Creator, converse with him, gain conviction, and become firmly assured about him unless he too became composite and clothed—or rather, mingled—with material existence.
For this reason, in the very image, likeness, form, mind, and appearance in which he was destined to reveal himself and become visible to his creatures,
he created and fashioned the human being beforehand. For this reason he called him his image and likeness, as we shall see more clearly
concerning the certainty of these things below, with God who guides and gives wisdom. He also established in human nature that the rational power of the soul, which governs the living being,
should subject to itself the powers of the blood-based and material soul, namely anger and desire,
and use them rationally and intelligently, that is, courageously and chastely,
and not allow them to be stirred in a brutish and irrational manner, like the other irrational animals, which use these two powers boldly and without restraint,
as their nature requires for its preservation and continued existence. But the composite and rational human being was not [?] and established in this way,
to use them brutishly, but rationally, as we have said, for
the preservation and proper maintenance of his rational nature. The proper maintenance of the rational human being consists in becoming perfected and complete in righteousness.
Righteousness is the perfection of the human being, his knowledge of the truth, and his discernment of divine matters concerning the Lord and of the natural properties of created things.
which apportions and gives to each what is due to it—that is, to God, praise, worship, and thanksgiving, to the one nature of the one divine and sovereign being.
And as for created things, the wise person should examine them and know them as they are, according to their nature, and comprehend them.
Others, however, among those trained in philosophy and the study of various disciplines,
named three powers belonging to the rational soul: namely, thought, which is rationality itself, and desire in its nature.
The soul, however, has two powers that belong to it specifically and principally: the vital and the rational. These are subdivided into others.
The vital power means that the soul is alive in its own being, clear and luminous. The rational power is divided into five spiritual senses:
mind, knowledge, understanding, comprehension, and discernment. Bodily life has two powers: desire and anger.
These occupy an intermediate position. If intelligence directs them rationally, the human being will be perfected in righteousness.
But if the body itself uses them in a beastly way, according to its own properties, that human being is a brutish animal,
and not a rational one. As it is said of him somewhere: “The human being did not understand this honor of his rational and beautiful nature.”
That is, he did not conduct himself properly and rationally, according to the order impressed upon his nature. He was handed over to the beasts and became like the animals.
The human being is understood in three aspects: spirit, that is, the mind, a rational power; and the animal soul, which gives life to the body and sustains it,
as with all the other animals. It is called the blood-soul, that is, the subtle and refined part of the body;
and the body itself. The human being has three levels: the bodily, the psychic, and the spiritual.
He ought to conduct himself in them properly and rightly, rising and advancing from one to another until he ascends and reaches the exalted rank of spirituality.
We shall speak about these things more clearly at their proper time and place, through the Lord who guides us.
But we ought to investigate and learn how the spiritual nature of the rational and intelligent soul is united with the material nature and density of the heavy body:
how something subtle and spiritual can be united and joined with something dense and corporeal that is foreign to its nature
and is its opposite. Worshiped and praised be the wise Maker and wonderful Creator, all of whose creatures are wonderful and a great marvel!
How he joined opposing natures and united them! His glorious command established and fashioned all the beautiful and diverse creatures.
It is like metalworkers who forge and fashion a single magnificent work of craftsmanship from masses of gold, silver, bronze, iron, and other such materials.
They join and unite the different kinds with one another by means of another preparation, which they call “kolla,”
that is, an adhesive, and in Arabic, “laḥm.” With this they join the different kinds to one another,
and fashion a magnificent object or image through their rational craftsmanship, which is given by God.
In the same way, the wise Creator and skilled Craftsman of the world created and made diverse natures.
And again, he joined and united them to one another through his wondrous craftsmanship.
From them he fashioned and established other composite natures, wondrous and full of great wisdom.
He did the same with the human being, the king and lord for whose sake all visible creatures exist, for he created and made him composite.

First he fitted and united the subtle, spiritual nature of the rational soul with the subtlety of the blood-based soul that gives life to the body, which is somewhat close to it and suited to its subtlety.
And through the mediation of the subtlety of the blood-based soul, which served as an adhesive—that is, like a smith’s solder—
the subtle, rational soul was united with the density of the material body.
And it exercised its spiritual properties within it; that is, the five spiritual senses were united with the five bodily senses.
The intellect took up residence in the brain, discernment in sight, understanding in hearing, insight in [?], and knowledge in the heart; and also these two animal powers:
anger in the liver and desire throughout the whole body; thoughts in the kidneys, along with other wondrous combinations, full of marvels,
of the nature of the soul and the nature of the body, together with their properties and activities, and a multitude of wondrous variations.

For if we wished to speak about the nature of the soul and its powers, and the rest of its properties, its arteries, its illnesses, its pains, its afflictions, and the rest of its many and varied activities,
these things could not be encompassed in many books and discourses. Indeed, people have tried and spoken a little: some about the composition of the human being,
and some about the nature of the soul, its properties, and so forth; and some about the body’s pains, illnesses, and states of health,
such as those physicians who followed the schools of Hippocrates, Galen, and the others.
Likewise Hermes, Pythagoras, Agathodaimon, Plato, Aristotle, and their colleagues spoke at length about the soul, nature, and existing things, but could not encompass them.
For human nature cannot know these things precisely before the renewal. Therefore the wise Maker is wonderful and glorious.
With these words the second chapter of the third discourse is completed, through God, who strengthened and helped.
The third chapter of the third discourse, with God, who guides and gives wisdom. On how a human being ought to think,
and what we ought to do and how we should conduct ourselves in this world. Previously we showed that human perfection, according to the true order of human nature, is justice.
Justice is that which judges wisely, weighs correctly, and distinguishes rightly, so that you reckon and give to God what belongs to God,
and to nature what belongs to nature, distinguish truth from falsehood, drink in and hold fast to truth, and reject and drive away falsehood.
This is how a rational human being ought to act, conduct himself, think, and wisely judge the words and deeds of natures and created beings.
He should weigh and assess everything correctly with his intellect and knowledge, according to what it is,
and assign to each what is fitting and proper to it. By this he is distinguished from irrational animals,
and is recognized as a rational human being possessing intellect and knowledge. First, then, let us consider: what, indeed, are we human beings?
And where we come from, and for what purpose, and where indeed we are destined to go, and the path laid out for us, so that, when we know these things,
we may do what is right and conduct ourselves as we ought. Let us consider what his beginning is and what his nature is,
and what his existence depends on, and why he was created, and what is required of him, and what his service is,
and indeed how long his sojourn and residence last in these two worlds, one being the small and limited world of his body,
and the other the great world of creation; and how he was put together, and how, in turn, his dissolution takes place.
And after dissolution, what then? Is there a renewal of these things, or does everything cease, disappear, and pass away?
Each of these matters calls for extensive investigation, reflection, logical reasoning, and lengthy discussions.
And anyone who takes an interest can, from the discourses and chapters before us—those already past, that is, and those still to come—
learn, gain understanding, and become firmly grounded in the true knowledge of all these matters. And when he knows these things, and where his beginning comes from, and how
his conduct ought to be, and where his end lies, let him choose and hold fast to those things that are true, enduring, and beneficial to him here and hereafter.
And let him reject, thrust aside, and abandon those things that are false and do not last, but instead harm him and hinder him from virtue, here and hereafter.
And once he has become certain about his creation—why he was created and what his nature is—as was shown in the chapters before this one,
let him examine this world. For look: three general passions wage fierce war in it, and their outcome is destruction and great ruin,
and deprivation of the blessedness of the full knowledge of the truth. These are gluttony and love of the flesh,
and love of the flesh and love of money. Let him judge them fairly in his heart, consider them rationally, and say:
“Look, we see that these three have absolutely no satisfaction, no limit, and no end. Gluttony is never filled
or satisfied. Even if you give it abundant food today, with a variety of delicious flavors,
and fine, clear, intoxicating wines, tomorrow it again demands just as much, and so it continues forever.
Every day it grows and expands, as the intestines are stretched and distended, and it grants neither peace nor rest.
Instead, a person is constantly made its [?], its slave, and its diligent cook. Along with these things, many evils flow from it for both soul and body.
For the soul: darkness of mind, dimness of understanding, confusion of thought, forgetfulness, bewilderment, instability,
lack of a firm footing, and disorder, along with other things like these. For the body: severe pains, prolonged illnesses,
an unhealthy constitution, damage to the stomach, dizziness, weakening of natural sight, heaviness of heart, slackness of the limbs,
trembling of the hands, weakness of the feet, along with other afflictions involving bodily foulness and unruliness, and the unrestrained pursuit of impure desire,
wantonness and ugliness of thoughts, and burning of the heart. And the outcome of all these things is hateful ruin and great destruction.”
Therefore it is very necessary and helpful to discipline it from the outset, deprive it of excess, and give it only what it needs.
That is, whatever can preserve the body's life and health. Likewise, its nourishment should be measured and carefully chosen, so that it does not harm the mind.
Such as onions, garlic, pungent foods, vines, coarse meal, and heavy foods that the stomach cannot digest quickly.
And like meat, which makes the body unruly and strengthens desire, and wine, which makes desire boil and blaze up and darkens the mind,
and causes many evils. Oh, how helpful and greatly beneficial it is to measure and select foods with knowledge and discernment,
when the food is small in quantity, light, and nourishing. But love of the flesh, which is strengthened by gluttony,
and to which most of the world is yoked, supposedly for the propagation and continuation of humanity—even this cannot be satisfied.
Even if someone mates with many women every day, tomorrow he wants much more again, and so on forever, without end.
Likewise, it produces many evils for the soul and body, along with crimes, murders, jealousy, and hostility over females, in the manner of wild animals and livestock.
Besides these things, when children become numerous, there are the worry and care involved in raising and providing for them, accompanied by endless afflictions, distress, and troubles.
Then neither reason, knowledge, understanding, nor discernment remains, but only agitation, confusion, madness, destruction, and ruin.
Therefore it is beneficial for a person to guard his body from the outset, subdue his limbs, and never indulge in fleshly desire and sexual intercourse.
If someone says, “How, then, will the world carry on and be sustained?” let him know that even if nine-tenths of humanity abstained from sexual intercourse,
the remaining tenth would sustain the world, provided they engaged in it properly, according to the rule appropriate to rational beings, without licentiousness or greed.
Quite apart from the fact that not even one in many thousands of people actually abstains from sexual intercourse. And if a few do, it is not with discernment and knowledge.
If people had conducted themselves properly from the beginning, according to the Creator's will, the propagation and reproduction of rational beings would have taken another form,
and would not have been like this, according to the manner of wild animals and livestock. If you ask how this could have been possible, it would have been entirely possible for the Creator of nature.
Indeed, there are many kinds of animals and birds in the world that do not mate, yet reproduce and multiply.
Consider the bird called the raven, that large black bird, and others like it: they do not mate at all.
Instead, they pick up tears from one another's eyes, and through these they conceive and produce offspring—that is, eggs—and hatch chicks.

Again, consider all the kinds of fish and creatures that move in the seas and rivers, among which are bodies so large that they surpass description and measurement. But when the time comes, according to the order established for them,
the male releases his seed into the water, and the female comes and swallows it, conceives, and gives birth.
There are many kinds of creatures in the world that do not mate, and those experienced in the study of nature know these things well.
Therefore it is very helpful for a person to abstain from sexual intercourse and keep his body in purity and holiness,
and [?] from the body's passions and compulsions, from the unruliness of desire, and from the great anxiety and worry over children, their upbringing, and their support.
So that, when he keeps away from all these things, his thoughts may become still and quiet, his inner movements may be enlightened, and purification may come to
his heart, his mind may become clear, his soul may become radiant, and his nature may become serene. Then he will be able to examine his soul, know himself, and reflect on his nature,
and arrive at knowledge of the truth. Again, the love of money and the acquisition of the wealth of this passing world
are likewise utterly insatiable, and there is no point at which you can say, “Enough,” as we plainly see happening in actual experience.
Look and consider the kings and rulers of the world. A man who possesses one province, that is, a territory containing ten cities with their villages and farms,
strives and struggles through wars and battles, gathering armies, drawing up battle lines, great toil, schemes, and cunning, and through everything his strength and knowledge can accomplish,
until, if he can, he extends his boundaries, enlarges his territory, and makes them twenty cities.
And if he acquires them, takes possession of them, and rules over them, he becomes still more exalted and powerful.
Again he longs to acquire more and add to them from the territories around him, and to seize some of his neighbors’ cities.
And so it goes, without limit, without satisfaction, and without end. Even if he could acquire the whole earth, he would still not be satisfied.
Instead, he would devise further schemes to seize even heaven, though this is impossible.
And if he possessed this entire visible creation, he would still strive and struggle to seize even heaven, if possible.
And if he possessed this entire visible creation, he would still strive and struggle to acquire another like it, if possible.
Yet out of all these things he needs only what meets his necessities: daily bread and a covering for his body,
just like the man who meets his necessities through the labor of his hands and the sweat of his brow. Indeed, this latter man has more rest than the former,
because he has no great anxiety, alarm, or fear, since he has no haters or enemies,
no one who envies him, and no one who thirsts for his blood. There is also this further point: even if someone possesses the whole inhabited world, his possessions will not save him from death.
There is therefore no limit or end to it. The more a person acquires, the greedier he becomes, and the more he longs to acquire.
So it continues until his end. This too is an evil passion that penetrates the soul and darkens it, turning it away from its duties,
and drives it onward through love of wealth, although an abundance of wealth brings no profit or benefit
or help, but rather great harm to soul and body. Again, because of this evil passion come
envy, hatred, enemies, quarrels, lies, and denial, even murder and destruction.
For this reason, truly wise people have called it the root of all evils.
And because of the great anxiety surrounding it, the mind becomes still darker and knowledge grows dim,
the understanding is blinded, the heart becomes heavy, and thought is confused. It also brings great toil upon the body in gathering wealth.
In hiding it, in guarding it, in keeping watch over it, in staying awake on its account.
In great fear, in distress over whether it will be seized, in vigilance lest it be snatched away, wherever it may be.
And as soon as it appears, countless evil thoughts arise in hearts that had not been prepared for them, concerning its seizure and the [?] and destruction of its owner.
Woe because of this passion, which kills and destroys both soul and body!
Yet there are many in the world who do not indulge in it. They manage properly with the little they possess and make good use of it, only as need requires.
They live calm, peaceful, restful, and quiet lives, in complete ease and contentment, without any burdensome anxiety,
or exhaustion and distress, together with the countless evils that spring from possessing it and never having enough of it.
And many good things are gained from not possessing it. Therefore, it is very good and [?] for a person not to possess it at all,
and not to concern himself with accumulating it, since he is never satisfied, and there is no end or respite to the anxiety over it.
The needy and downtrodden in the world have lives far more restful, quiet, and calm than the rich and propertied people in the world.
And everyone whose mind has been enlightened by the knowledge of the truth, from among all the peoples and languages in the world,
if he possessed anything, quickly distributed it and freed himself from its burden. He emptied himself, found rest, and emerged into the light from the darkening anxiety over it.
And if he possessed nothing, he did not concern himself at all or long to acquire anything. A rational human being ought to reflect on these things and others like them.
Then he should also consider what he ought to do and accomplish in this world where he is a sojourner, because he is a temporary sojourner and a passerby,
and not a permanent resident or an heir who remains forever. He is like a boy entrusted to a place of instruction—that is, a school—or to any sort of craft,
so that he may receive instruction from the teacher of that craft, learn it, and become proficient in it, and then return to his parents’ home and manage his household and his own affairs,
and become heir to his parents’ possessions and household. But if the boy should remain in that place of instruction, or in the school, forever,
and lose his parents’ inheritance and become estranged from them and deprived of their possessions,
while he sees other boys applying themselves and learning the teaching for which they came to the teachers, then returning and going back to their parents’ homes and becoming their heirs,
while he himself remains miserably in the school until they forcibly drive him out of there,
surely that boy deserves ridicule, deprived of understanding as he is, since he did not distinguish and recognize what benefited him and what harmed him.
Such is every human being who has entered the world as though entering a school and a place of learning, to learn there and become wise
about the things that benefit him—that is, to acquire the good things that remain with him, which death cannot seize and snatch away from him.
These are the knowledge of the truth, in which all the good things that benefit a human being and endure are contained.
For after he departs from this world, which is like a school, he goes to his Father—that is, his Creator.
And there he inherits what the Father of the ages has prepared for those who fear him, those who have loved him and kept his commandments.
A rational person ought to reflect on these things and others like them until he is purified and freed from these three evil bodily passions.
There is also a passion of the soul called vainglory: a person longs to be praised and glorified in this world.
It attaches itself to all the good deeds a person does, so that good deeds are done for the sake of praise and acclaim from onlookers, rather than with an upright intention.
Anyone who desires and thinks this way is miserable and labors foolishly, wasting all his labor and toil over good deeds.
In the world to come, no reward remains for his good deeds, because he has received his wages and reward from this world—that is, the praise and acclaim of onlookers.
And he is deprived of the reward that lasts. But if he does good deeds with an upright intention, solely for the love of God—
for this is what he commands and teaches us everywhere: to do good deeds and keep away from evil deeds—
and does not desire the empty and worthless praise that comes from people, has no wish at all for such a thing, and does not occupy his thoughts with these things,
then God himself increases his honor and makes him more distinguished in this world than others who are praised and acclaimed in accordance with their contemptible desire.
And again, in the world to come, after the renewal, he pays him a good reward many times over.
A rational person must therefore be very much on guard against this evil passion as well.
With understanding and great care, he should quickly uproot it from his heart, from the very moment it begins to stir in his mind.
For if it lingers and grows old with a person, it grows strong and great and produces the evil passion of pride, which denies its Maker.
For the relationship between vainglory and pride is like that between a blossom and its fruit. Just as a blossom first appears on a tree,
and, if it continues, remains, and [?], it grows, becomes strong, develops, and becomes fully formed fruit, so it is with vainglory.
If it remains in a person and grows old, it becomes strong and turns into pride. Pride.
Now it is an evil passion and the first sin that entered the pure and beautiful creation of the good Creator.
When the angel of light and chief of the heavenly hosts became sick with it, he was darkened, overthrown, and fell from his honor, and was cast down
from his throne. He became the chief of evil and the teacher of every hateful thing. Then pride gave birth to envy within him.
Envy, in turn, gave birth to murder. Thus pride truly contends with God and opposes him.
Pride considers all the good things that God has given to nature to be its own, its own achievements and possessions.
For this reason it is opposed to God. And anyone whose enemy and opponent is God—how great is his torment, and how great his woe!
This is the passion with which Satanael became sick and was cast out of heaven. Everyone who is sick with this passion and persists in it is his companion and is tormented with him.
A person ought to reflect continually on all these things and remain watchful and alert against evil and destructive thoughts.
5. The desire of the flesh, gluttony, and the love of money and empty glory destroy good things.
Pride destroys both soul and body, distances a person from God, and brings him into fellowship with Satan. After he has properly considered these things
and turned away from their wickedness, he ought to do deeds that help him, benefit him, and endure. He should not cease doing good things.
This is the work a person ought to do: every deed that pleases God and accords with his will,
that helps sustain a person in this world, and for which a reward is also kept for him after his departure from here. This is what a person ought to do continually.
But as for something that remains here and does not accompany a person to remain with him after his death, why does he worry about it, exhaust himself, and suffer distress?
Because of it he neglects the service of God, and afterward leaves it to others, while he himself goes away empty-handed, stripped of everything.
We speak of a people living at the eastern limits of the inhabited world, who undertake or carry out no earthly work at all.
Instead, they live among the trees and feed on their fruit. They drink water from springs and rivers, and they make no use of clothing,
because their climate is temperate throughout the year. They merely tie loincloths made from the skins of wild animals around their waists.
Their women live separately. They come together on one occasion and then separate again.
If one of their women conceives and gives birth to a boy, after three years they give him to the men, and he lives with them according to their way of life. If the child is a girl,
she remains with the women, and they raise her. Throughout their lives they have no other occupation
except the study of knowledge, prayer, and spiritual worship. They fear nothing at all and are subject to no other kingdom.
They possess nothing at all about which to worry or on account of which to be troubled. This is their work and their way of life:
spiritual service, meditation on God, reflection upon him, and wonder at him. They commit no injustice or sin at all, nor do they even know them. There is no buying
or selling, nor any commercial dealings. King Alexander, son of Philip, who conquered the whole earth, went and reached them in order to subjugate them.
But when he saw their way of life and their occupation, he himself submitted to them. He greatly honored and praised them and commended their way of life.
Why, then, do people seek superfluous things that they do not need, but that instead disturb their lives
and hinder and burden them, keeping them from the genuine search for and discovery of the knowledge of truth?
God wanted all the human beings he created to live like those we have described,
so that the good and righteous might become numerous, and the number of those who fell [?] with Satan their leader might be made up,
and this world of worries and distress might pass away, creation might be renewed, and a new world of delights and joys might arise.
For until the number of the good and righteous is complete, matching the number of those who fell, this world of afflictions will not pass away,
because it was for this purpose that God established this material world, which is full of toil and sighing.
And in it he created human beings, rational beings composed of different elements, so that they might become fit through it and be refined through training in righteousness.
And so that they might go and inherit that glorious and exalted place from which Satan and his entire rebellious host were cast down and fell, as we explained above.
And when that number is complete, this cycle will cease and there will be a renewal. So, my beloved, why [?] above.
And when that number is complete, this cycle will cease and there will be a renewal.
So, my beloved, why do we busy ourselves with buildings, possessions, plantations, farming, and trade? Look, Satan stirs people up and strengthens them in these things,
so that their lives may be troubled and their minds darkened, and they may have neither the leisure nor the peace to know the truth and follow it, because of hateful, destructive greed.
Human beings came to hate one another, each seeking to rob [?]. Because of such fear, they built themselves fortresses and walls and rose against one another, each seeking to secure his wealth
and protect his possessions, as we intend to explain precisely concerning all these things in the appropriate place, if the Lord wills.
Therefore, a person ought not to do or work at anything other than what brings him near to God his Creator
and does not hinder him at all from divine service, which consists of knowledge of the truth and deeds of righteousness.
As for how a person should conduct himself in this world, we say that he should love everyone and honor everyone,
that he should live in harmony with everyone, and that he should never make an enemy or someone who hates him in this world because of [?]. That he should honor everyone,
that he should live in harmony with everyone, and that he should never make an enemy or someone who hates him in this world over anything that passes away.
And how can this be possible for someone who is entangled in the world, bound by its affairs, and yoked to its bustle?
Therefore, it is very necessary and right for us to keep away from unnecessary things and avoid many evils.
For anyone who has people who hate him and enemies in this world lives a bitter life full of sorrows, since he is constantly anxious and afraid of his enemy.
All the time he devises schemes, thinks, and contrives ways to escape his enemy’s harmful acts,
or, if possible, how he himself might find a way to harm and destroy that enemy. He is roasted and burned by these consuming and darkening thoughts.

Anyone who occupies himself with these things and broods over them tastes death every day, and something more bitter than death. His mind is darkened, his understanding blinded, and his conduct confused and disordered.
And if he remains like this, his end will be an evil one of ruin and destruction. Blessed, therefore, are the poor, ordinary, and unknown people in this world,
for although they are lacking and poor in possessions, they pass their lives in this world in peace and rest. And after their departure from here,
they inherit blessings and delights that never end. And even if there were no other world, no renewal, and no resurrection,
surely in this world the ordinary and unknown live in rest and tranquility, with lives full of peace—not leaders or rulers [?] of others.
And if you say, “How, then, can this world continue without these things?”
Greed, excessive possessions, hatred, enmities, and envy—these are not what sustain the world, but rather what devastate and destroy it.

Therefore, a person ought to withdraw and keep away from every way of life and behavior that harms him and disturbs the serenity of his life. He should conduct himself properly, quietly, peacefully, simply, and humbly.
And inconspicuously. He should keep away from all excess, and his dealings, conversation, and close association should always be with those who are good, truly wise, and upright in their conduct.
He should shun corrupt and troubled people who are entangled in the affairs of the world, who love its positions of authority and acquire its wealth, and flee from them as from a deadly dragon.
And he should always choose ways of life filled with peace, rest, quiet, and tranquility—from a deadly dragon.
And he should always choose and follow ways of life filled with peace, rest, quiet, and tranquility.
So that he may be able to find the knowledge of the truth that raises him to immeasurable heights. With these words, chapter three of the third discourse is completed, through the awesome God.
Chapter Four of the Third Discourse, with God, who gives wisdom and guidance.
Concerning what is to become of the human being, what his expectation is, and what hope he should have: in the first chapter of the discourse we briefly explained these things,
And why the human being was created. Now once again we speak, examine, and investigate through this rational understanding that we have from our Creator:
What, then, is destined [?] to become of this living being, composed of rational spirit and dense matter?
And what is the prospect toward which the human being himself looks and waits? What hope should he hold on to, and through it
Take courage and gain strength, relying on it firmly and without doubt? If the human being were like the other animals that lack reason,
His blood-based soul would perish with the decay of the body, and every element would return to its own place, and that would be all.
If, on the other hand, he were only a rational soul stripped of materiality, he would be like the other spirits and would dwell with them,
And would remain in all their characteristics. But we see that he is a mixture and a composition of both kinds and natures. Moreover, he has an abundance of thoughts,

And the ability to discover new knowledge, learning, and crafts that he has not been taught. Rather, through contemplation and the activity of his thoughts, he discovers them from the nature and distinctive capacity given to him by his Creator.
He has authority over himself and over the exercise of his freedom, which is his will. In these things he closely resembles his Creator,
Just as he has also been called the image and likeness of his Maker. Although the human being himself is mired in his dust and crawls upon the earth, his mother,
He does not clearly comprehend these things. Yet if he recognizes his dignity, considers and reflects upon his origin, with his mind clear, his heart pure, and his spiritual vision bright,
He understands well and becomes firmly convinced about his nature and his creation: that he was made and fashioned in the image of his Creator.
And if he cannot grasp and know these things by himself because his understanding has not been cleansed of the passions that darken it,
Let him examine his own nature and the other creatures, his fellow creatures, and see and learn how they are placed and how they stand in relation to him.
His ignorance is rebuked and condemned by these irrational beings themselves, for they recognize him and see in him the image and likeness of the Maker and Creator.
Yet he, wretched as he is, neither perceives nor understands. We will explain how these things are indeed true, with the help of our Lord, who gives wisdom.
Let him consider the irrational animals that are subject to the human being: the mighty ox, the [?], that is, the buffalo of great strength.
which has the strength of many people, yet a single boy harnesses them to a yoke and prods them with a goad, and they fear him and submit to him.
They bear and endure the pressure of the yoke on their shoulders, and for fear of the goad and the blows they furrow the ground and cultivate it.
Why do these creatures submit to all this harsh servitude?
They are oppressed by the harshness of the yoke and harness, and endure all this great humiliation until death.
If they wished, they could turn on the person who drives them and forces them along with a goad and blows,
and kill him, along with twenty, thirty, or even forty men like him.
But they see the image of the Creator depicted in him. They consider this very human being their lord and maker, and fear him as they fear God. They are restrained and enslaved.
Likewise, camels carry all that weight. And how donkeys, mules, and packhorses endure all that suffering beneath their loads, bowed down, sweating, and panting!
If they did not see the Maker's image in those who subject them, they would rebel and would not bow down at all. Instead, they would kick them, bite them, trample them, and kill them.
But out of fear of the image that they see in us and understand better than we do, they submit and are afraid.
Again, how these proud, swift, spirited horses submit to a single boy, allowing him to put a bit in their mouths and a saddle and covering on their backs!
He climbs up and rides, or puts a heavy burden—that is, a load—on it, and strikes and lashes it with a rod. The animal fears him and submits to him.
And [?] speak of these tame animals, when there are also the bold and predatory creatures among the wild beasts,
such as the bold wolf, the foul-smelling hyena, and the fierce leopard. Even the mighty lion, the king of beasts, fears human beings.
People rear and subdue many of them, bind them with chains, and raise them in cities, and they become accustomed to human beings.
They no longer rage. Because of the glory of the image they see in us, they fear and submit. Likewise, dragons, vipers, and the rest of the snakes
are very afraid and flee from human beings. Likewise, the various kinds and species of birds:
people tame them and rear them, and let them fly in the air. They go away a great distance, but when people call them again, they come and submit.
And what shall I say of these, when even the mighty and astonishing elephants, through the tremendous strength they possess and the firmness of their enormous bodies,
uproot walls and carry great weights? How they submit to human beings!
Especially when people skillfully give them strong wine mixed with frankincense to drink, they become enraged and immensely powerful.
People place a wooden tower on their backs, and many fighting men sit in it with weapons and coats of armor.
They advance in battle to attack the walls, and these elephants stretch out their trunks,
and with their tusks breach the walls, demolishing and uprooting them. They cause great devastation in battle before their masters,
along with many other things that people devise and carry out in buildings, excavations, rivers, and water channels.
And the construction of ships and boats, and sailing among the waves and billows on the surface of the sea,
as they steal and capture the wind to make it serve them and carry the great weight piled up in the ships. They also devised another thing:
they crossed mares with donkeys and produced mules, an alien animal that was not fashioned by the Creator along with the rest of creation.
And the images they raise up, and the great statues, monuments, steles, and pillars they erect—
all these things and others like them clearly indicate and demonstrate that they bear the image and likeness of the Creator.

And someone whose nature is such, who can do all these things, discover, devise, learn, demonstrate, explain, establish things in the world, and leave behind him an everlasting remembrance and memorial—
what, then, is [?] to become of him? Is he to decay, dissolve, and be scattered among the elements like the rest of the irrational animals, which he himself subdues?
This cannot be believed or accepted. Rather, he lives, endures, and is preserved in the original state of his nature.
And when the world's winter comes to its end, and [?] the season of the great April of renewal,
which all the Aprils, spring growth, and renewals of each successive year foreshadow and announce beforehand,
nature itself is also transformed, blossoms, and is renewed gloriously and more fully (more sublimely).
And nature rises clear, pure, subtle, and spiritual, fit and suited to be united and mingled with the very Cause of its origin,
through a certain mediation that is desired and longed for with the natural love that nature had acquired from the completion of renewal.
Here is the boundary of spoken language. Beyond this point, the tongue is no longer permitted to interpret, nor pen and ink to write on a scroll.

But the mind that has become clear and enlightened and has taken its place in the order proper to its nature through upright, virtuous conduct, which purifies and cleanses it of the incidental filth that has come upon it—
it is permitted, from this point onward, to speak, hear, learn, and know spiritually, in great wonder and subtle contemplation,
apart from every movement, combination of thoughts, and mental image. Here we stop, because of our inability to express it.

For this great stature and exalted rank, to which the human race is destined to rise, discerning people polish and purify their nature with great care and without negligence, removing what is contrary to nature, namely the filth of sin.
And they clear the mind of materiality, because there, after the renewal, their origin returns and is united with the first Cause, the Cause of all causes.

Everything is from it, everything is in it, and everything is in its hands. To him be praise from all! Let us look toward this perfect hope, which brings our nature to completion, and make it our goal.
Let us direct and straighten our thoughts toward this great goal, which unites creation with the Creator.
We are destined to reach this great exaltation and perfection, if we are willing. In this state,

that is, this great transformation, the nature of composite rational beings who have conducted themselves rationally in this world of training and school of discipline takes its place. There are two realms and dominions.

One belongs to the sovereign Lord, who by nature and essence is Lord and eternal Being. Within himself, by nature and sovereign right, he possesses dominion and a blessed kingdom filled with blessings, delights, and everlasting light.
The other belongs to the rebellious and overthrown slave who insolently seized for himself the title of lordship.
And he has a tyrannical, gloomy kingdom, full of afflictions, groans, and bitter torments in everlasting darkness.

Through the envy that his pride produced toward the nature of this composite creature, the human being—for he perceived and knew that the human being was destined to rise to the rank from which he had fallen,
and to inherit his place and reign in the realm of the kingdom from which he had been estranged—he planned to kill him, so that he would not attain and reach these things,
but would instead be overthrown and cast down like him, and inherit his torment and destruction in the everlasting darkness called outer darkness, that is, outside God.
These are the evil branches that bear deadly fruits from the tree of death, which is pride that contends with God.
Pride gives birth to envy, and envy gives birth to murder. These are the three deadly sins that are evident among all nations.
This is Satan’s tyrannical trinity. With these he wages war against humanity, drawing on his own experience of evil.

With the fruit that he ate and died from, he deceived others so that they would die and become his companions and partners in Sheol, the abode of the dead, which is everlasting torment in outer darkness.
Now everyone who listens to him and eats the fruit he offers should expect and prepare to inherit with him and be tormented in everlasting darkness.
As for the trees that produce these deadly fruits, the soil that nourishes them is piggish gluttony; the water they drink is love of money,
a strangling snare and the root of all evils. The wind that blows, fattens the fruits, and brings them to maturity is vainglory.

When this grows strong, increases, and reaches its fullness in a person, it brings him to his end and destroys him through the deadly passion of pride, the mother of envy, which gives birth to murder,
destruction, and despair. Now everyone who conducts himself properly and rationally in this world,
and plants within himself from the luxuriant planting of the [?] of life, and cleanses the soil of his heart from the filth of shameful passions,
and clears his mind of the darkness and [?] of sin, and restores his nature to its own proper order, as it was created
by the Maker, pure and radiant, should expect great, indescribable blessedness. For his origin is destined to be united with the first Cause itself,
and he will reign with the good and true Lord, who by his very being, eternally, and by his essence possesses lordship and a blessed kingdom in everlasting light.
This is what awaits the human being if he recognizes his dignity and remains in the proper order of his nature. But the person who conducts himself in this world like an animal and without reason,
that is, in feeding the body and being preoccupied with it, and in the hateful passions of soul and body that we mentioned above,
and plants within himself from the detestable and evil planting of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which is the tree of death,
and has not cleansed his heart of foreign weeds and the evil seeds of shameful passions, nor cleared his mind of darkness and what is contrary to nature,
and has changed his pure and radiant nature, making it murky and dark, should expect great, indescribable woe.
For he is estranged and removed from the first and blessed Cause, like a withered branch that has been cut off from the vine and thrown
into a burning fire. This is the evil prospect awaiting the person who did not recognize his dignity, but became like wild animals and livestock,
and corrupted the order of the glorious and beautiful nature with which he was created. Now we must explain what hope a human being ought to have.
Let us contemplate nature itself, the great book, the father and teacher of us all.
From it let us also learn about hope: its order, its aim, its measure, and its distinctive character. And if we pay attention and contemplate rationally and clearly,

we learn and become convinced that all the activity, practical affairs, and conduct of this world depend on hope: through it they stand and exist, are carried along and advance, are sustained and preserved.
In hope of the harvest, the gathering of crops, and the storing of fruit,
the farmer toils and labors, enduring the intensity of summer heat and the biting, numbing cold of winter,
along with the many afflictions and hardships that accompany and occur during these changes.
He wears himself out working the land—in the vineyard, in the second and third plowing, in sowing, watering, and clearing away thorns and weeds,
and the other foreign plants, and in waiting until the fruit is fully grown.
Then comes much more toil: harvesting, carrying, threshing, sifting, winnowing, clearing the threshing floor, and the other tasks that press upon those who work the land.
Likewise, there is also much labor in tending vineyards and trees. For he does not toil on the land for just one year, as with sowing,
but for a period of five or seven years he wears himself out and labors, in winter and summer, incurring many expenses,
including the workers’ wages and their food, along with many other things known to everyone.
He bears and endures all these things because he trusts in hope and takes courage from it.
His hope is the gathering of crops and the storing of fruit and good things in storehouses and [?]. Likewise, consider merchants who travel distant roads,
those who sail on the fearful sea amid violent waves, and those who make crossings over rivers that are swollen and deadly,
builders of great buildings, those who erect splendid towers and ornamented fortresses, diggers of channels who burrow into the earth,
those who bring water from great distances; the gathering of armies, the ordering of battles, [?], and combat,
the shedding of much blood and the casting down of corpses, wounds from swords and spears, injuries from arrows, and wounds of every kind,
together with the great patience and willing kindness of teachers, along with the many kinds of conduct and activity in this world:
all their diligence, their courage, and their great endurance amid severe toil and hardships, even to the point of bloodshed, as we have listed,
are for the sake of hope, and rest on firm confidence that the goal will be fulfilled and that the hope awaited by the person who bears all these things will be attained.
Especially if someone is in a distant country, very far from the royal capital,
and someone is sent to summon him to come and take possession of that kingdom, put on the crown, and reign over it,
how much he would toil, hurry, and labor day and night, going hungry and thirsty, keeping watch, wearing himself out, bearing and enduring hardship without losing heart!
Indeed, all that affliction would be sweet and pleasant to him, because he trusts in the hope he awaits and takes courage from it—that is, that he will become king and put on the crown.
And if people endure all these things, are battered, and bear all these afflictions for the sake of an empty hope that is neither certain nor lasting forever,
but belongs to this passing time, and comes to nothing, vanishes, and passes away, then for the sake of the great and enduring hope that lasts forever and ever—
that great blessedness prepared for the pure who have become clear and enlightened, and that complete and perfect joy of nature and union with the first cause—
how many torments, hardships, and daily deaths should we endure without growing weary, losing heart, becoming discouraged, becoming agitated, or being distressed at all!
Rather, with mighty courage and firm confidence, we should endure everything that presses upon us by force,
as well as the hardships we willingly impose upon ourselves for the sake of the great hope that awaits us.
Through these few indications and demonstrations that we have grasped, discerning people understand many things and examine them broadly.
"Give a wise person an opportunity," it says, "so that he may become still wiser." And these things concerning what is to come and what awaits the human being,
and concerning the aim and order of hope, are sufficient. Let us pray and plead that we may be delivered and saved from the despair that comes upon the weak who lack knowledge of the truth.
For every idle, indolent, and lazy person who neglects the aim of all the disciplines we have set out above
has no confidence and does not expect to gather fruits, crops, and benefits. He has no expectation of rest at all, but is hopeless and miserable,
and lives in distress and dejection. Likewise, anyone who does not make an effort to cleanse his heart of shameful passions,
and does not conduct himself properly and refine his nature, has no confidence in his blessings, does not expect fulfillment, and is without hope.
He is cut off from true life, and already here he is in bitter torment, because he has no confidence and no firm hope.
With these words, Chapter Four of the Third Discourse is completed, through God who gives strength.
Chapter Five, with God who gives wisdom: How this composite human being can know God. Chapter Four of the First Discourse of this compilation [?] on the knowledge of truth:
We showed how it is known that God exists. But now that we have reached this point and have explained the creation of the human being,
why he was created, what his nature is, how he ought to think, what he should do, and how he should conduct himself,
and also what will become of him, what his expectation is, and what his hope is, we ought here, systematically and in proper order,
to examine further how this human being can know his God, so that he may take courage in his confidence and become firm in his hope.
In Chapter Four of the First Discourse, we showed that, by natural means, when a human being uses his reason to contemplate nature,
and carefully considers and examines the world and its circuits, and the human being himself,
his structure and constitution—or rather, where the origin of everything comes from—he can discover, know, and become certain that all these things have a cause.
And that cause itself has a cause prior to it, which is its cause.
Therefore, that first and sovereign cause, which is the genus of genera—that is, the first substance, above which there is nothing, nor can anything be spoken of or be possible—
Because it does not derive its existence from another cause, since it is itself eternal being and sovereign fatherhood.
For it is always fatherhood—that is, an eternal beginning that does not itself take its beginning from another beginning.
Rather, it is itself the eternal, essential beginning, the first cause, the cause of all causes,
and Lord of all lords, God of all gods, King of all kings, Creator of all created things,
and maker of all worlds, ruler over every authority, capable of every mighty deed, and sustainer of all
peoples. It cares for all, provides for all, and governs all. It is all in all.
Nothing is above it, [or outside it,] or apart from it. Yet someone may be outside it by circumstance, not by nature.
Thus, just as in the light of this sun the eyes see the natural beings, things, and creatures of this world,
and delight in them and enjoy them, someone whose eyes are blind is deprived of light, sees nothing, and is deprived of all this enjoyment,
even though he is right in its midst. His being deprived of the sight of the light and the ordered things of the world does not mean that the light, the world, and its ordered things do not exist.
Rather, these things exist, but he is deprived of seeing them by circumstance, not by nature.
The cause of his blindness and his deprivation of the enjoyment found in the light lies in himself, not in the nonexistence of light.
So too, those whose minds are darkened, blinded by sinful passions and deprived of the knowledge of truth,
are said to be outside God and to be tormented in the outer darkness, outside God. Yet apart from God there is nothing.
Rather, they are in darkness with respect to true knowledge and are deprived of his glorious light, like those who are physically blind. They are in the darkness of not knowing him.
From their point of view, there is neither light nor enjoyment. Yet it is not altogether nonexistent: it truly exists, and only for them does it not exist,
because they do not see it. Nor do they understand what it is or what it is like, because of their own darkness. In the same way, God truly exists,
and all whose minds are enlightened delight in the light of knowing him, having been enlightened and purified through purifying conduct and the observance of the divine commandments,
which perfect a person and bring him to completeness in the knowledge of truth. Therefore, we must first struggle against these three fundamental passions, which are gluttony,
love of money, and love of glory. These are what give rise to evil.
From gluttony, impure desire and every kind of uncleanness and licentiousness arise and are nourished.
From love of money come greed, rapacity, dishonesty, hardness of heart, insensibility,
and lack of sympathy. From empty glory, in turn, come conceit, boasting, arrogance, and self-importance.
From these, that destructive pride which opposes God gains strength and comes into being. From this, in turn, envy is born, and from envy murder develops and comes into being.
Unless a person is first freed from these things, he cannot be purified, become clear, and be enlightened.
And unless he is enlightened by the knowledge of the truth, he cannot at all think and reflect truthfully about God.
And if he does try to think about him, his mind is dazzled, and he becomes still more darkened, goes mad, and suffers great ruin because
he dared, while impure, to occupy himself with the Pure One, and to contemplate [?] the Pure One who purifies everything, while he himself is full of filth and the stains of sin.
Just as someone whose eyes are diseased and weak, if he brazenly gazes at the sun’s disk, is dazzled and injured, and his eyes become still darker and he loses his sight.
Therefore, whoever wishes to know God as far as possible, and to delight in the knowledge of him with a delight whose sweetness has no equal,
should first take care to be purified from the material nature of the passions, as we have said. The more he is purified from the passions, the more he is enlightened by God.
And the farther he withdraws from the sea of the world, frees himself from its turmoil, and becomes clear of its disturbances, the closer he draws to God and is enlightened by the knowledge of him.
And he delights in contemplating him. Earlier, in the fourth chapter of the first discourse, we showed how it is known that God exists.
[Here, however, the discussion concerns how a human being can know God—that is, after it has become known that God exists.]
How can we know [?] this one whom we have learned and become certain exists? Our subject resembles an ordinary person speaking about Rome, the great royal city,
and about the arrangement of its beautiful setting, the splendor of its glorious palaces and lofty buildings, and its mighty towers,
and the halls and decorated dining rooms of the royal palace, and about the king’s beauty, the glory of his crown, and the radiance of his appearance,
the gleaming of the precious stones and pearls set in his diadem, the glorious color of his purple robe, and the height, magnificence, and decoration of his chariots,
and the ranks and ordered companies of the illustrious dignitaries before him, and the ranks and degrees of governors, judges, and chiefs of nations,
and the troops of the armies, and the authority of the military commanders over their forces, together with the other glories in the city’s streets and squares,
and its merchants, its craftsmen, and the rest of its inhabitants, and about its lofty walls and splendid gates,
and about the springs and rivers that water its lands, and the gardens and parks surrounding it,
and about the kinds and varieties of trees, fruits, and flowers in them, although the person speaking of these things
has never personally seen a single one of them, but knows them only from hearing the accounts of others.
And although this arrangement truly is as described, he himself has not seen it in person.
And the road leading to the royal city is marked out and known, and many have traveled along it, reached the royal city, and delighted in its beauties.
They have also made it known and given others an accurate account of what it is like.
And many, after going there and arriving, were deemed worthy of illustrious ranks and became heirs in it. They no longer longed for, or even remembered, the rubbish heaps in which they had grown up
in them. And again, many, while traveling along that road without caution or experience,
encountered difficulties, heaps of earth, and steep slopes, or storm-tossed seas; ambushers rose up against them, they suffered distress, and their ship was shattered.
Or they fell into the hands of murderous bandits or plundering thieves, and all their wealth perished. So too we, miserable and uneducated people, crawling on the earth,
and darkened in understanding, are now speaking of great things concerning God and divine matters, although we have had no experience of them at all.
We have not even attained knowledge of them, but speak from the words of others, some of whom personally saw, knew, and became convinced,
while others in turn received these things from other trustworthy people.
Moreover, nature itself teaches us that these things truly are so, as do the many things of which we have had certain experience.
Now the road is marked out and known, the kingdom stands ready, and the King has prepared crowns, gifts, and rewards to give to those who are worthy.
Let us strive, my beloved brothers, members of our race and sharers in our nature,
so that we may not be deprived of the glorious sight of this King of glory, this good and merciful Lord, of the honor of being near him, and of his joyful companionship.
Let us exert ourselves, take care, and cleanse our hearts of the filth of shameful passions and hateful thoughts.
Let us cleanse our bodies of the stains of sin and clear our minds of the spectacle of the world's turmoil.
Let us illuminate our understanding with the glorious light of the knowledge of truth, so that we may be able to know our Lord as far as a creature can know its Creator,
and a thing made its Maker, and a servant of dust his heavenly Lord. That a person knows God through the purity of a virtuous and perfect way of life
is what we affirm and hold to be certain. But how a person knows him, or how he is, we do not know.
Even if we did know, we would not be able to convey this in spoken or written words.
But whoever comprehends and attains this himself knows these hidden and profound mysteries.
May our Lord make us worthy of them. Amen. With these words, Chapter Five of the Third Discourse is completed, through God who gave strength and help.
Chapter Six, with God who makes wise: On whether a human being can know God precisely as he is, or whether he alone is wise in everything and knows himself as he is.
It is entirely impossible for a created and made nature, whether intelligible—that is, the spiritual powers—
or perceptible—that is, human beings composed of dust and spirit—to know its Creator precisely as he truly is.
Even if a human being lived for thousands of years, spending all of them in spiritual worship and the study of knowledge, while keeping the commandments and the rules
of virtue, in stillness and freedom from every disturbing activity, thought, and concern, he would never attain precise knowledge of God as he is.
Rather, he knows only as much as he is worthy to know and capable of comprehending, and as much as that glorious Nature grants him to know: some small measure of the divinity.

But that God exists, we know and have become convinced, both from nature and from the intimate knowledge given to us by grace; and that he is one nature, power, essence, eternal being, will, and lordship.
And we have learned that he is three persons, namely Mind, Word, and Spirit [?],
who are known as fatherhood, sonship, and procession. But how he is, no created and made being can know.
For we cannot say of the divine nature how it is, what it is, or how great it is, but only that it cannot be comprehended,
and that it cannot be bounded or measured. It is beyond speech, beyond the mind, beyond mental activity and thought,
and beyond every manner of expression spoken by the tongue, grasped by the mind, or stirred within one's understanding.
He reveals himself to those whose hearts are pure, whose minds are clear, and whose understanding is enlightened, as he wills and according to their capacity to know,
not exactly as he is, but according to their ability and the reach of their knowledge. But in the new world, after the renewal,
they ascend and rise in him without limit, learning, seeing, and grasping in him at every hour and moment something they had not known before.
Through these things they rejoice and delight without limit or end. In this way, human beings who have been found worthy of that blessedness after the universal renewal grasp and know something
that even the heavenly powers do not now grasp or know at all. But after the renewal, when the whole of creation is brought to perfection, each in what belongs to it,
according to its worthiness and its way of life—glory to him who knows how far the measure of each one's knowledge reaches and extends!
With these words the sixth chapter ends, through God, who gave strength and help.
Chapter Seven of the Third Discourse, with God who gives wisdom. On whether the knowledge a person has of God always remains the same,

or whether, as a person's knowledge develops according to their way of life, their knowledge of God also increases and decreases. Through nature and the contemplation of it, we learn many things and become wise.
He, the Father of us all, is a scribe and a wise teacher. Just as, then, when the air is disturbed by dark, [?] clouds and gloomy mists,
the ordered beauty of creation is not clearly visible to us, and we cannot see anything even a little distance away because of the murkiness of the air,
so, as long as a person's mind is disturbed and their understanding is clouded by darkening passions and empty concerns,
they do not know or understand anything at all of the true knowledge of God. Nor can it be known.
But when the mind becomes clear and is freed from disturbance, and the heart is purified of passions and becomes enlightened in its natural order,
a person begins to know and contemplate that blessed nature of the sovereign, self-existent, and eternal essence.
The more a person rises and advances in the excellence of their way of life, the more they also rise in knowledge. Their mind becomes more refined and enters deeply into the mysteries of Being.
But if some darkness and confusion should again befall them through a breakdown of discipline and the corruption of their conduct, their understanding becomes confused,
their mind grows dark, and they forget what they knew and can no longer grasp it. But when they put themselves in order and live rightly, quietly, and calmly,
restrain their body and guard their senses against harmful sights, sounds, tastes, and arousing touch,
and against empty conversations and idle speech, and gather their mind back from distraction,
and guard their heart against thoughts, then divine knowledge begins once again to enlighten their mind, and they meditate on it.
And the more they remain guarded and watchful, persevering in fasting, prayer, vigils, and the reading of the Holy Scriptures,
And a little conversation with one or two people who are truly wise and guard their senses,
and persevere in stillness and upright conduct. Every day he will advance in knowledge of God, rising higher and entering more deeply into hidden and wonderful things.
His mind grows wise and enlightened, and he grasps something he did not know and that had never even entered his mind.
And when he thinks that he has understood and reached the height of perfect knowledge and become complete,
he sees again that he is still only beginning, because an exalted height and an immeasurable depth are revealed to him.
And when he struggles again, disciplines himself, gathers his mind, and does not look at or turn toward anything else outside it,
he ascends and rises into that height which appeared to him, without being held back or disturbed by any adverse event.
He revels in the glorious beauties that meet him and exults. He rejoices and delights with a spiritual joy that has an indescribable taste.
He becomes confident and courageous and has no doubt at all about his knowledge. And while he is enjoying the mysteries he has grasped and finding comfort in the beauties he has encountered,
then another light bursts upon him like a great flood, still more powerful, shining and flashing, and sets him ablaze with love for it.
It captures his mind, carries his heart away, and consumes him with a great, inexpressible love.
He forgets his own nature and is unaware of it. His nature does not even demand provision for his body's needs.
Instead, he is intoxicated with that burning love, like someone submerged and hidden from the world
that is visible, raised up and drawn inward into hidden secrecy.
And while he is like this, he does not remain at a single level and degree of knowledge. Instead, he continually rises higher and enters more deeply, without limit or end.
This very ascent from height to height and from glory to glory, each more glorious and exalted than the last, produces great joy in him
and burning love. For if his mind and understanding remained at a single level of knowledge, and his enjoyment and spiritual dwelling were in a single place,
after he had spent a little time in that changed state, it would become like a natural habit for him, and he would not enjoy it as he did when it was new.
Therefore, as he rises in his conduct, he rises in his knowledge, encountering new things—wonderful and glorious things that bring him joy and courage.
And [?] is the cause of these endless ascents and this continual rising.
For the eternal Being is infinite, immeasurable, unlimited, and beyond comprehension. So too, knowledge of it,
entry into its mysteries, and contemplation directed toward it have neither limit nor end. With these words, chapter seven ends, through the power of God.
Chapter Eight, with God Who Gives Wisdom. On the reason why, although God is one, and his nature and his craft are one,
knowledge of him differs among all peoples, at every stage and in every degree within each person, so that even within a single person it changes at all his stages.
There is absolutely no variation or change in the essence of the eternal Being.
And when everything is filled with it, and there is absolutely nothing that can be seen, known, or spoken of that is empty of it,
how can it change or undergo alteration? From where could it receive a change, when there is nothing apart from it?
For everything that changes increases and decreases. But these things do not exist in the nature of Being. From where could anything be added to it?
Or where could anything taken away from it go? For there is no place that is not filled with something belonging to one of the natures in the world,
whether wet or [?], whether liquid and soft [?], or hard and solid.

Suppose it is completely filled with it, so that no room remains in it for even a single grain of sand to be added, because there is no room, nor is there any more of that substance with which that vessel is filled.
Nor can anything be taken away from it, because there is no other vessel or place in which it could be put. And if it is something hard
and solid, filling that space like a mold, so that no room remains for the point of a needle to enter between the vessel and what is in it,
how can what is in that house or vessel be transformed or changed?
Rather, it remains like this forever, without change or disturbance, without increase or decrease.
So, all the more—indeed, more than this and above this—is the nature of sovereign Being without change, alteration, or disturbance. It is not merely like something filling a vessel,
but also like the vessel containing what is in it, with its contents being like itself. In this way the sovereign Godhead is all in all, above every word,
above all comprehension, above every composition, thought, form, image, [?], reflection, and conception.
One power, one nature, one will, change [?], never changing at all. That it exists truly, eternally, and continually,
and forever, it has granted us to know. But how it exists we cannot know at all, nor can we define or comprehend it.
Thus the eternal Being of the Godhead is one great and glorious mystery, never changing at all.
Yet the kinds of knowledge and thoughts concerning it are many and beyond number. And why, although it is one, are the thoughts concerning it and the orders of knowledge many?
One reason is its incomprehensibility; another is the many differences among rational beings.
It is set before them as a goal, like a lofty mountain whose greatness and height have no limit.
And many people are striving to climb it, to see and know what is on it: namely, trees of every kind,
various fruits and flowers, stones, soils, mineral deposits, and many solid substances, such as gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, and tin,
and everything that comes from the earth; springs, fountains, streams, and trickles of water; colorful meadows, grass, and herbage of every kind;
wild animals, livestock, and everything that crawls; birds, winged creatures, fowl, and everything that flies, with their many kinds and species.
And the higher and loftier it rises, the more beautiful and desirable are the varieties found on it than those on its lower slopes, its sides, and its flanks.
And all these people are making an effort and traveling onward, hoping, if possible, to ascend to the summit of that mountain.
And each one advances and ascends according to his strength and the capacity of his nature.
Some of them were completely unable to approach and reach the lower slopes of that mountain. Instead, they grew weak and sank down.
They remained wherever they had been able to reach. Others mustered their strength and climbed a little way up its lower slopes. [Others went higher still,
and others higher than these.] Others reached its flanks, others its ridges. Still others mustered their strength and climbed higher.
And others, through the great strength and ability they possessed, went even higher than these, although no one
has been able to ascend to the summit of the mountain, or even to go around the whole mountain and circle it, because of its height and vastness.
Each one reports with certainty what he has seen and verified. Other things, which he has heard from others, he learns and accepts.
Yet he cannot know them as he knows the things he has personally seen, touched, and verified. Such are the degrees of knowledge of the one God.
For although he is one, each person grasps, knows, and understands him according to the capacity of his knowledge.
Every people attains knowledge of the truth about God and grows wise in it according to the character of its conduct, training, occupation, and customs.
There are mountain dwellers, desert dwellers, inhabitants of the plains, and herders of cattle, sheep, and mares,
such as Arabs, Kurds, and Turks, who spend all their time behaving and living like animals, like the livestock they own.
Others are villagers who work the land and labor diligently at sowing and planting,
