whose entire way of life is earthy and material, like the soil they cultivate and constantly tend. Others are soldiers and fighting men of every rank,
constantly engaged in wars, raids, and every kind of combat, along with all the ranks and inhabitants of this world.
The knowledge of each of these differs greatly from that of the others, whether because of his temperament and nature,
or because of the climate and character of the place where he lives, or because of the practice of his trade,
or because of the occupation and training in which he constantly engages, or because of the instruction in which he has been brought up and to which he has been accustomed since childhood.
Thus knowledge exists among human beings in many forms and countless variations.
Likewise, many changes occur within a single person as he grows in stature, and with his diligence, conduct, and occupations,
and changes in his habits. Just as human faces do not resemble one another, neither do their characteristics or their thoughts,
nor their knowledge, although knowledge of the truth is one in its nature, and God is one, his nature is one, and his power is one.
All forms of knowledge bear witness to his truth, just as the sun is one, as are its light, its nature, and its activity.
Yet each person makes use of it according to the strength and soundness of his sight and the nature [?] of his constitution. And all bear witness that its light and its nature are one.
With these words the eighth chapter is completed, through the awesome God.
Chapter Nine. With God, who gives wisdom.

On whether knowledge of God itself varies for all those mentioned, or whether the variation lies in them and comes from them, just as the nature and taste of bread, water, honey, and other foods and flavors remain the same.
Yet each person receives a different taste and different nourishment from them.
Each receives according to the nature of his constitution, according to the humors—that is, the bodily fluids—at work in him, and according to his illnesses and his health.
Indeed, also according to the measure of his stature. Likewise, knowledge of God and his truth is one in its nature and order.
But each of us apprehends, knows, and understands according to his conduct, the purity of his heart, the clarity of his mind, and the brightness of his thoughts.
He also tastes, enjoys, and delights in it. As though receiving nourishment, he gains wisdom through it, is instructed, and grows in excellence.
And all these differences, degrees, measures, understandings, reflections, and many varied thoughts concerning God
exist because of his greatness, his boundlessness, and his incomprehensibility.
Even if a person's life lasted a thousand thousand years in this world and in the world to come—and it is known that life there has no end—

throughout all these stretches and long periods of time, no one could reach the limit and fullness of knowledge and apprehension of the glorious nature of the eternal Being, the sovereign of all ages.
Nor could the pure and spiritual nature of the heavenly powers. Yet in all the ascents and elevations within this knowledge,
one finds perfect delight, exalted blessedness, and complete joy, so that one does not suppose there is anything further superior to the rank at which one stands,
until knowledge of the Being itself—or rather, the divine Lordship itself—raises him and brings him up to yet another glorious and exalted height.
God wishes the entire race of rational beings to live in such an order, way of life, and spiritual service,
so that it may be worthy of that glorious, great, and immeasurable blessedness.
This good Lord of ours possesses great wealth and is very eager to distribute it and enrich all his creatures with it.
What use is wealth that is hoarded and hidden? And what benefit is a kingdom that is concealed and hidden, with no one aware of it?
All the wealth, kingship, delights, and splendors possessed by the Lord, who is good, rich, and wise in everything,
and merciful and abundant in compassion by nature and essence, exist and are reserved for the race of rational beings,
and not for anything else, of which he has no need. For his treasury is overflowing and never runs short,
more abundant than the boundless sea and the unceasing flow of rivers. Nor does he have any heirs or children besides rational beings.

He has entrusted the entire decision and choice to their freedom: if they wish, they become rich and grow great, enter and advance within, ascend and are exalted, rejoice and delight in his eternal and sovereign kingdom.
And if they are deprived of and alienated from these inexhaustible blessings, it is because of their own negligence and contempt.
Therefore, my brothers, let us strive and exert ourselves for a little while, so that we may go and dwell, reign, rejoice, and delight forever and ever with this good and gracious Lord.
and merciful. To him let us offer glory through all generations, forever. Amen. With these words the ninth chapter ends, through God, who gave strength and help.
Here ends the third discourse on the knowledge of the truth, containing nine chapters.
On the creation of the human being, his nature, his order, and his knowledge; and theology concerning the knowledge of divine things and the order of that knowledge.

Next, the fourth discourse on the knowledge of the truth, which discusses reading and writing, the coming into being of this world, and the composition of its elements. It contains five chapters. Chapter One.
On whether the writing and literature written in the world are true, beneficial, and useful. First, a prayer. Blessed are you, our wise teacher.
And praised is your name, good and merciful God, abundant in kindness. We give thanks to your lordship. We worship your divinity.
We exalt your being. We praise your mercy. We proclaim the abundance of your love
and your affection toward our lowliness. How greatly you have exalted and honored our nature! How greatly you have enriched our poverty! How greatly you have made our ignorance wise!

You stooped so far as to become like a schoolteacher instructing children and training little ones, and you concerned yourself with caring for our upbringing. After you created our nature and enriched it with your divine gifts and the inexhaustible gifts of your grace,
you also taught us reading and study, through which we might become wise
and read the testament you wrote for us, and know the extent of the riches, treasures, and inheritances you bestowed on us, and the royal city and the land of the living,
and the garden of blessings you gave us as an inheritance. Who is sufficient to encompass your praises? Who is adequate to give you thanks? Who can recount your kindnesses?
Blessed are you, good Lord, wise in everything and enriching everyone. Blessed are you, and blessed is your glory. Blessed and praised is your name forever and ever. Amen.
Just as a blind person is deprived of light and is therefore denied the enjoyment of the beauty of created things,
so the rational human race would have been, had it not been given the knowledge and discovery of reading and writing:
that great, indescribable gift, that exalted and lordly endowment.
The good Lord, who cares for our lives and desires our well-being, appointed two guides and teachers for us: one is sovereign nature, and the other is the mind.
It wisely devised to make nature a book of memorials for itself, and to inscribe in them deeds, histories, divine acts, wonders, and miracles, like written letters,
so that through them the whole race of embodied rational beings might study, know, remember, hear, and learn about the things of old,
and might itself also record them and make them known to those who arise afterward, forever and ever. Truly, it is a great gift—
reading and writing—to rational beings, for in it are contained all the good things given to them by their Creator.
When the mind examined and read the nature of existing things, it found in writing a treasury for itself, in which to store its treasures
and preserve what had been entrusted to it. It is a strong fortress and a trustworthy treasury, which carefully preserves whatever you store in it, [?] forever.
And with it, continually and diligently, every treasure and every good, precious, beneficial, helpful, and glorious thing that the mind discovered in nature,
it gathered and preserved in the treasury of writing, to serve as spiritual nourishment for the generations and peoples that would come afterward.
And when the tribes of the peoples, nations, and languages that arose in creation came, they found great wealth in the guarded treasuries of writing and the written word.
From it they gained wealth that could neither be exhausted nor depleted. One passed it on to another, and one enriched another.
Until all rational beings abounded in riches from the great treasury of writing, from the things they discovered in nature,
through knowledge and reason. Had it not been for writing, our race would have been blind to the light of truth,
deprived of the knowledge of God, and estranged from all spiritual blessings.
It would have wandered as though groping in darkness, not knowing where it began, how it was proceeding, or even what its end would be.
And it would have imagined that this whole universe existed of itself, as though by chance.
But writing became our reminder, teacher, instructor in wisdom, and guide toward the knowledge of truth,
that is, toward knowing God. Otherwise, everyone would have supposed that the father who begot him was the God who made him.
No one would have known at all how the worlds were created and established, nor the things that happen in the world, nor how generations succeeded one another and tribes passed away,
nor how kings and rulers arose, nor how religious beliefs came to be accepted, nor even what was going to happen.
Times and seasons would not have been distinguished, nor would the year and its changes have been known, nor the boundaries of the months and the days of the week.
Moreover, it would not have been possible at all for the world to endure, proceed in an orderly way, and be preserved through its cycles.
All these branches of knowledge and wisdom were preserved in the treasury of writing, and through it they became known and were learned.
For it is a trustworthy guardian, preserving what is entrusted to it with its stamps and seals.
It has never concealed or hidden the deposit entrusted to it, but has faithfully preserved everything in its own form,
and handed it down to peoples, tribes, generations, and families. Apart from spiritual wisdom and the divine will,

it would never have been possible for this to become known, to take hold of the world, for the world to be governed by it, and for everything to be established. Through writing, kingship is preserved and established.
Through it, priesthood and divine worship are passed on, made known, and handed down. Wisdom, teachings, and knowledge are studied through it. Praises and records of
the world, its establishment, and its course are inscribed in it. Through it, truth is distinguished from falsehood. Therefore, writing is reliable and very good,
beneficial and helpful. Everything inscribed in it with the testimony and signatures of two or three trustworthy people is reliable and very certain, and there is no doubt about it at all.
Blessed is he who taught it and gave it to the human race. With these words the first chapter is completed, through God, who gave wisdom, strength, and help.
Chapter Two of the Fourth Discourse, with the help of God, who gives wisdom. Who invented writing and made it,
and what necessity compelled him who created the human being in his image, fashioned him, and made him in his likeness,
and gave him authority over his own affairs and freedom resembling God's, so that he might govern himself sovereignly by it,
He placed in his nature the ability to perform works, create structures, and bring forth wisdom, knowledge, and learning from himself, like God his maker.
First he gave him nature as a school tablet, and inscribed on it intelligible signs and the forms of created things.

He appointed the mind as his tutor and guide within nature—that is, for the human race. He inscribed for him the alphabet for studying creation on tablets and on a scroll that could not be erased, so that he might constantly study it and become wise.
Through this study, the mind invented the book and made it a teacher and a reminder for generations and families, gathering and storing in it all the riches and treasures
that it had collected and acquired throughout the long course of time from nature and its changes, events, new occurrences, marvels, and great wonders that took place in creation,
so that they might all be preserved, conveyed, and handed down to children and grandchildren who would be born and arise,
so that children and infants might become wise, learn, and gain knowledge—
that is, the simple and uneducated whom future times would bring—and become rich from the treasures that the mind had stored and preserved for them and entrusted to the book, a faithful guardian.
Now that we know and are assured that the mind became wise through the nature of created things, and invented, produced, and perfected the book,
we must also know precisely what need it had for the book and writing.
We say, as we said in the preceding chapter, that it should be a secure archive—that is, a trustworthy treasury—
and that the treasures of learning, wisdom, and knowledge should be gathered in it, which brings forth [?] secure archives—that is, a trustworthy treasury.
And that the treasures of learning, wisdom, and knowledge brought forth by the rational and thoughtful nature within us should be gathered in it,
along with the histories of the world's generations, its institutions and those who established them; and that the laws and commandments of the Lord given to the human race should be confirmed in it;

and that the rules and limits assembled by wisdom for the preservation of nature and its proper maintenance should be inscribed in it; and that it should be a wise teacher, an enlightening guide, and a
truthful reminder and faithful messenger, bringing from earlier generations letters, news, and information about essential matters, namely, upright conduct and rational teachings,
and passing on and entrusting to others ancestral inheritances and enriching treasures, so that they might learn what is true and know what is certain,
and perceive, in the things that happened and took place, the correct insights of the knowledge of truth, and walk in the true paths of upright, virtuous conduct,
and not turn to the right or the left from the royal road of faith in one God, the creator and maker of nature and the one who orders the worlds.
And when they know and learn these things, and are enlightened and made wise through knowledge, they should do them and carry them out in practice,
and interpret truthfully and know precisely what height and depth and length and breadth are:
height is God's exaltedness and incomprehensibility; depth is the unfathomable depth of his wisdom;
extended length is his boundlessness, and spacious breadth is his greatness.

And from his visible creatures the hiddenness of his eternal being is made known, together with the many good things, benefits, and teachings of wisdom that have been preserved and conveyed to us within the embrace of the faithful book.
With these words the second chapter ends, through God who gave strength and help.
Chapter Three of the Fourth Discourse, with God who grants wisdom. On whether the book of creation, that is, the Torah, is true,
concerning the world's coming into being and the ordering of created things, or not. Prayer. O Being who exists from eternity, and Sovereignty that lasts forever,
you who always exist and remain forever and ever, without change or alteration, King of glory, God of every god and object of worship,
and Lord of all lords and authorities, good Lord, bountiful Creator, wise Maker, craftsman of the inhabited world and arranger of created things,
and sustainer of the worlds [?] and their arranger: you who, at the mere signal of your command, established the worlds out of nothing and brought them into being;
you who established countless orders, ranks, and companies of spiritual powers to serve the glory of your lordship;
you who, in your grace and for the glory of your greatness, created humanity in your glorious image and in your sovereign likeness,
and greatly magnified, exalted, and honored its lowly nature, and made it wise and enlightened it with the light of the knowledge of your truth:
you, Lord of all, according to the abundance of your boundless mercies, illuminate our darkness with the rays of the knowledge of you.
Make our ignorance wise through your truth, and guide our minds and our understanding along the straight paths of your teaching.
O you who are full and overflowing with goodness, who have done all these wonderful and glorious things, although you have no need and are not
lacking anything: we continually worship you, give you thanks, and praise you forever and ever. Amen. In the first three discourses we spoke about the knowledge of the truth,

without bringing forward proof from Scripture, because, out of natural love, we wish to benefit our brothers and sisters and relatives throughout the whole world, who share our nature and all its characteristics.
We used the book that is the father of us all, namely nature, which sustains us—the book in which we are constantly reading and studying.
None of us can oppose it or depart from its law. From it we have learned, gained certainty, and become wise in everything that it is fitting for our rational nature
to know and learn. We have learned that there is a God, Lord, Creator, and Maker of everything visible and invisible,
and that he alone is one, known in three properties: namely, the Mind that begets the Word, that is, thought;
the Word itself, begotten from the Mind and not begetting another Word; and the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Mind together with the begetting of the Word.
And there is one power, nature, being, will, authority, and dominion forever and ever.
We also learned that he created created things and ordered the worlds without being in need, and why he created created things and humanity,
what humanity's nature and rank are, what it awaits, what is in store for it, and where its hope lies, along with the many things that we demonstrated and established.
In this fourth discourse, however, we have explained letters and writing: whether writing is reliable and useful, who invented and produced it, and what made it necessary,
and the many benefits that come from it. Now, however, following the order we have adopted and in which we have reached this point through our Lord's power, it is time for us
to examine the written law to see whether it is sound and true, so that from this point onward we may use it, lay the foundations of our knowledge upon it,
and build and raise up courses of wisdom and knowledge—things that it is altogether fitting for us, and incumbent upon us, to know accurately.
Until our building is completed and reaches fulfillment, which is perfection in the knowledge of the truth.
This knowledge unites the Creator with created beings and distinguishes truth from falsehood. It adheres to truth and rejects falsehood.
The first book of the written Law, the reading tablet and scroll of instruction given to the child—the world, that is, rational humanity—
by the wise teacher, Lord, maker, and orderer [?], is the book of the origin of creation, which the great Moses, the wise scribe and faithful steward, wrote.
Now we must first investigate and examine wisely and rationally whether this book is true and its writer trustworthy,
and whether it was given by God, so that we may accept it without doubt or dispute, believe it, and affirm everything recorded in it.
But if it is not true and reliable, we should not use it at all. First, then, we say that there is
in the world an established practice and law among all peoples: concerning any matter litigated among them,
if three trustworthy witnesses come forward, testify, and confirm it, that matter stands, is established, and is believed.
It is accepted by kings, judges, and everyone, and the person bringing the matter, lawsuit, and claim prevails and is vindicated in truth and justice.
Likewise, Moses was the writer and transmitter of the book of the origin of creation and the written Law.

He testified and affirmed that he received and learned from God everything he recorded in it. Now there are witnesses who testify concerning this Moses and confirm his words, declaring that he is trustworthy and truthful:
three groups that hold sway over the world, divided into many branches, with countless individuals in every branch, all trustworthy and truthful.
What makes their testimony still stronger and more credible, true, reliable, and acceptable is that these groups oppose one another.
Their branches too [?] likewise oppose one another in many other matters. But in this matter of testimony concerning Moses and his trustworthiness,
and concerning the reliability and truth of his book, all these groups and their branches agree together, concur, testify, and affirm
that Moses is trustworthy, chosen, and truthful, and that he is a trustworthy and truthful messenger of God,
who is the eternally existing Being, the Lord, Creator, and maker of created things,
and the orderer of the world; and that the book Moses wrote for us is true and reliable, and the Law he handed down is accepted,
because he received, heard, and learned from God everything he recorded in it. These trustworthy groups that testify to and confirm these things are:
Christians in all the branches of their confessions, and Israelites, that is, Jews, in all the varieties of their religious observances,
and Ishmaelites, that is, Hagarenes, in all the varieties of their beliefs.
All these peoples oppose one another in many matters as groups, and so do the branches within each group.
Likewise, these branches themselves oppose one another in other matters. But in this matter of the book of creation and its writer,
they all agree, testify as if with one mouth, and affirm that it is true, reliable, and complete.
And originally it was given by God through Moses, who pleased him and was his true and faithful witness. He himself taught him, made him wise, and entrusted this tablet of instruction to his hands.
He inscribed written letters on it and sent him to the immature child, the world, which had rebelled against the school of its sovereign master and teacher of truth.
And there it was, wandering in the error of empty worship, walking in hateful darkness, in the confusion of ignorance.
Because the world was still immature and inexperienced in divine things, and could not yet receive complete instruction, he first wrote down for it, as
letters, laws, commandments, and judgments, so that through them it might practice, train, and learn until it became wise, grew strong, and reached maturity in the knowledge of truth.
He dealt with it with great wisdom, love, and compassion.
And like a mother who raises the beloved child she bore from her womb, so that she may rejoice and find comfort in him for an appointed time,
and then he may become her heir and the recipient of her property, she first raises him on gentle milk, because he cannot yet take solid food.
After the child raised on milk grows a little stronger, she then gives him other nourishment suited to him, made from flour and water,
and [?], until he grows stronger and develops further. As he becomes established and approaches youth, his teeth for cutting food grow strong, and his grinding molars become firm.
Then he is given solid food. God dealt with humanity in the same way.
Because humanity had turned aside and rebelled against the school of its Creator, and had forgotten the first writing and the natural law through the counsel and influence of the first rebel,
who envied humanity and wanted to teach it rebellion like his own, so that it would become his companion and partner in torment—as we will show with the help of God, who gives wisdom—
another law, a written one, was given to humanity, like gentle milk for a child and like letters for a pupil to practice, so that through it humanity might find comfort and be nourished spiritually,
and might practice and train in laws, judgments, and the observance of commandments, until it grew strong in the knowledge of its Creator and became wise through his instruction.
Then perfect instruction is handed on to humanity like solid food, bringing it toward the knowledge of truth, which makes it wise in the love of its Lord and unites it with its Maker.
In this manner and with this intention, the book of the law was given to the world through Moses, so that it might practice and train through it and draw near to the knowledge of its Creator,
until the time came for it to be given complete instruction, which would perfect it in the knowledge of truth, and for it to be filled with understanding and knowledge.
When the proper time for these matters comes in the sequence of our teaching, we will discuss their precise details at length and clearly.
For now, however, let us return to our subject and once again establish the reliability of the book about the origin of creation that Moses wrote.
Now his book has indeed been accepted through the testimony of all these different and mutually opposed nations, which agreed and testified that it is true
and that it was given by God. They also all testified that the man himself was trustworthy,
and that he was God's messenger and steward of his household, on the evidence of the signs, marvelous mighty deeds, wonders, and great terrors performed through his hands.
He gave commands like God, who sent him, and performed divine and mighty wonders, and the forces of nature obeyed him.
The elements submitted to him, and he exercised authority over created things in the sea, on dry land, in the air, and everywhere. And since we have thus become certain of these things,
Again, we wish to learn more precisely and to gain confirmation through deeds and events.
We [?] concerning the certainty and truth of these things, from the natural knowledge implanted in our nature, just as through this same natural knowledge of ours
we investigated and discovered the things we have written up to now. For through this knowledge of ours, when we examined the nature of this universe
and reflected on its signs, which are created beings, we perceived, knew, discovered, and became certain that God exists,
that he is one, that he has three persons, and that he created the creatures, cares for them, governs them, and watches over them,
together with all the other things we have said and written above, with no doubt or contradiction in them.
Now let us also look at and examine this book [?]. If it teaches what we have learned up to now through understanding and the examination of nature,
and follows that same order, it is true, trustworthy, and acceptable; and the witnesses who testified and confirmed it are entirely truthful.
But if it is contrary to this, let us examine and investigate further until we arrive at certainty about the truth.
What, then, does Scripture say, and how does it teach? Let us listen. It says, “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.”
We ourselves have already testified to this teaching above, drawing on our natural knowledge. For we investigated extensively and discovered that this universe has a Creator—
that is, the heavens and the earth and everything in them—just as we now hear this man saying in his book.
Since, then, he has begun so well to speak and write about the things we discovered in the vast world through extensive investigation, rational understanding, and the examination of nature,
and about which we became certain, the man is truthful and trustworthy in everything he says and teaches in his book, and these things are entirely true and trustworthy,
just as the many witnesses who testified to his truthfulness and accuracy are also truthful.

Now that all these things have come together for us, and we have gained certainty from every side and have become convinced that the book which the great Moses wrote about the coming into being of creation is true,

since it is true and has been thoroughly confirmed, from this point onward let us make it a new beginning for our discourse. Let us build on it a strong tower [?] and a fortress of the knowledge of truth.
Let us gather, fill it, and place within it all the supplies and necessities that are appropriate and useful for this subject, which we have laid out from the beginning [?],
so that all who encounter this book and reflect on it with understanding,
with their minds gathered back from the distraction of this world’s empty concerns that disturb the mind, remaining in quiet and tranquility
and keeping away from the confusing conversations of foolish and ignorant people, may become perfected and complete in the knowledge of truth, and may perceive and know the nature of all
creatures, both those apprehended by the mind and those perceived by the senses, precisely and as they truly are—that is, in the order and manner in which the Creator created and established them.
And from true knowledge of these things, namely spiritual and material creatures, one rises to contemplation of the Lord and to exalted knowledge of their Creator,
as far as created nature is able to know its Maker. When someone attains this knowledge and rises to it in understanding,
he no longer rests or ceases ascending and rising in this divine contemplation, continuing in this way without end.
Neither in the life here nor in the life after the renewal there. That is, when one reaches the full measure of contemplation of our Lord in the life here.
One no longer needs the written law, nor even the natural law. Then there is no longer meditation or study.
The outward senses are shut, and the inward senses also grow still. Movements cease, and thoughts fall silent. That person no longer lives for himself.
Rather, his Lord lives in him, because he abides and dwells in him. He produces in him subtle perceptions beyond compare,
above every combination and image of thought. He gives him joy and makes him grow in love, and sets him ablaze with love for him.
It is no longer permitted to speak or write about these things. Nor is it at all possible for people subject to passions, such as ourselves.
Forgive me, my brothers, for I am being very bold in revealing hidden things that it is neither lawful nor permitted to pass on to people of every degree.
Yet love is doing these things against my will, although I confess that I have not attained even a tiny portion of such things.
Rather, I am like an ordinary painter who depicts through his art many things he has never seen, such as kings, fathers, prophets, and many glorious things,
and still other things that a human being cannot even see: angels, cherubim, and seraphim.
And I am like a poor man who fashions splendid diadems and crowns, although not one of them has ever been placed on his own head, nor can he put one on.
And if he dares to put one on, since he has no right to do so and is not of royal birth [?],
death meets him immediately. For diadems and crowns are fitting for kings and kings’ sons. And kings’ sons are human beings.
Therefore, if human beings so desire, it is within their nature to rise and be exalted until they become sons of the King of glory
and become heirs in his heavenly kingdom. May he make us worthy of it by his grace. Amen. With these words the third chapter is completed, through God who gave strength and help.
Chapter Four of the Fourth Discourse, with God who grants wisdom. Concerning when this world was created, how long it has existed, and from where and from what it was established.
Prayer. Creator of the worlds and maker of created things, their founder and sustainer, their caretaker and provider,
you upon whose command they all depend and stand firm, in whom they live, and in whom they move
and are preserved: direct the steps of our minds along the straight paths of the knowledge of truth. Enlighten our hearts so that they may be cleansed of the darkness of sin.
Make our ignorance wise through the knowledge of your teachings, so that all of us may give thanks and praise you through all our ages and at all times. Amen.

Now we have all become firmly convinced concerning the divine book [of the origin of creation, and that he was a man of God, the one] who wrote it at God’s command, and it was handed down in the world.
He was truly made holy through his glorious conduct, and his humility raised him to this exalted height, so that he conversed with his Lord.
Through his complete fast of forty days, his stillness on that holy mountain, his continual prayer, and his standing before his Lord, his mind was enlightened and his heart purified.
His thoughts were cleared of the entire spectacle of material existence, until even the skin of his face became radiant,
and the radiance of his face shone like the sun, so that the Israelites could not dare to gaze upon that godly face of his.
Then the Holy Spirit, who dwelt in him and performed great miracles through his hands, moved him to begin explaining to the world the creation of heaven and earth.
And [?] God created heaven for the angels and earth for human beings. We have explained these things above, concisely and briefly.
We have established from trustworthy nature, the father and teacher of us all, and handed on to all the nations, our brothers and fellow human beings, that our God is one;
that he created all creatures and established the worlds; why he created them; that he cares for them and provides for them; and that he cannot be comprehended at all
or known; that there is another world besides the material one, and what it is like; and about another world that is yet to come;
and about the creation of humanity, its nature and its order—about the many things we have been able to learn from the great book of nature.
We have given everyone assurance about these things, and there is no room at all for doubt. But now let us recount these things again in their proper sequence,
as they were arranged by the one who worked through Moses, their great teacher. Let us listen and learn precisely how the worlds were established and created things were formed,
from what and in what way, so that through created things themselves we may know the Creator and reach out toward him.
He is a great refuge and a strong tower, the one who gives rest, protects, and brings to perfection. Now let us begin and listen to the holy book of the Law itself.
Let us examine its divine words and proceed in order, with sure hope and trust, which brings us to a good conclusion and fulfillment.
Now, then, it is time to set out the holy words of the divine Scripture, saying: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”
First he showed that heaven and earth have a beginning and have not existed forever. If he had said, “In the beginning
heaven and earth existed,” he would thereby have testified that they were self-existent. Instead, he said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”
By these words he showed first that God exists eternally, without a beginning, and that he created heaven and earth and gave them a starting point,
that is, a beginning. And if you say concerning the creation of heaven and earth, “This thought occurred to God afterward, and he created them;
this thought did not exist beforehand, since he himself had no beginning, whereas these things have a beginning, that is, a starting point,”
we say that God is perfect in everything and lacks nothing at all. His entire perfection belongs to him essentially and eternally.
It involves no process of reasoning, something that does not belong even to the angels, who are his creatures. Nor did a new thought arise in him that he had not known eternally.
Even though Scripture speaks haltingly with us, in a way that we can understand, and speaks of his actions in terms of times and seasons, stages [?] and measures,
thoughts and deliberations, fury and anger, regret and sorrow, and many similar things that have absolutely no place [in the divine nature],
but only in human nature, these things are subject to time and under the control of free will. God, therefore, is above time
and above all these things, and above every human impulse and thought. Everything he created and made, whether earlier or later,
and everything that came about and happened in the world of the angels and in our world, and that still [happens], whether in deed or word or thought,
he foreknew from eternity as though it had already happened and passed. The same is true of the creation of heaven and earth.
which are the world of spiritual beings and the world of bodily beings. It existed in his mind, truly and eternally.
So too did the time at which he wished this creation to begin. It was accomplished, and what had previously been conceived in its finished state came to have a beginning.
But we cannot speak of it or hear it in this way, in a single instant.
Instead, it requires an extended narrative, a lengthy sequence of much discussion. It is like someone looking far into the distance,
who suddenly sees, in the single instant when he opens his eyes, a broad plain before him, with cities and villages in its midst,
and rivers, gardens, woods, and fields. A multitude of troops, cavalry and infantry, is also gathered there.
There are also many farmers and shepherds tending sheep, cattle, and herds of horses. Many mountains surround it, thickly covered with trees of every kind.
Wild animals and many birds live in them. There are also pits, springs, and mines of many kinds in them,
along with many other things that could be in that great plain and in the mountains surrounding it. And all these things
he saw with a single opening of his eyes. Yet they cannot be recounted or heard except over a long time,
just as we ourselves have now been unable to speak, write, and encompass them in a single word. In this way, and beyond this, God gave a sign, and everything came into being in a single instant.
But Holy Scripture babbles to accommodate our childishness, like a teacher thoroughly versed in learning who comes down to a child's level and babbles with him as he practices letters and writing.
With a word containing ten letters, he has him sound it out ten times, one letter at a time, until he becomes practiced and fully instructed.
Again, when a reader opens a book and looks at it, he recognizes everything inscribed in its lines.
But he cannot say everything he sees with a single opening of his mouth. Nor can the listeners hear everything at once.
Instead, the words are read one at a time and brought together into individual sentences. In this way they are explained, interpreted, and made known to the listeners.
In the same way, Holy Scripture babbled with us, recounting and teaching us at length everything that the divine creative power determined and established in a single instant.
For we could not even understand until we had been trained and strengthened in divine teachings.
Then complete instruction is handed on to us, through which we become wise and strong in divine knowledge.
It is also like someone having a newborn son, a nursing infant [?], who does not yet know how to say anything at all, but babbles with his faltering tongue.
He calls his father by a name that he can babble, and likewise his mother and his brothers, his mother's breast [?], water, and the other things and foods.
On his own, using whatever sounds he can form with his tongue, he calls them and gives them other names.
His parents come down to the level of his babbling tongue and speak with him in a way that he can recognize and understand.
As he grows a little taller, he changes the names of things to ones that convey more than the earlier ones.
His parents likewise converse with him using these, until he becomes fully proficient in speech and pronunciation.

This is how our good God and merciful Father dealt with us. In matters that we could know and understand, he babbled with us in our own language and manner of speaking. He trained us through his divine teachings, made our ignorance wise, and appointed for us, after the first teacher, the intellect,
another great teacher, Moses, until we grew strong in learning and knowledge. Then another teacher came to us, with the complete teaching of perfection.
Moses gave us milk to drink as though we were newborns. He babbled with us as though with infants, and, as though we were children learning at school, he taught us to recite the letters
of writing, until we were trained and grew strong. Then we are given the complete book, which perfects its readers and brings them to completeness in the knowledge of the truth.
Let us think this way and understand this way, and first establish this in our minds.
Like infants, newborns, and children, let us accept the things through which divine Scripture deals with us, while we are [?] in divine matters.
Then we are given the complete teaching, which is like a full meal offered to a man who has reached the measure of full stature.
Now let us return again to the holy book. Let us hear how and when the world was created, and from what it was established.
We have already explained and shown above why the worlds, created things, and humanity were created. But now we are recounting and showing in order
when, how, and from what everything was created and fashioned. It is as though someone were to say that a certain king built cities for such-and-such a reason,
and convinced his listeners of the reason, intention, purpose, and desire with which that king built and established these cities.
After the listeners had heard, learned, and become certain of the reason, purpose, and desire for which these cities were built and fashioned,
then he begins again to recount in order when and at what time they were built, and how their buildings were arranged,
and their walls, towers, surroundings, and streets, and from what, and from which kinds of things, the material for erecting the buildings came—
that is, such things as stones quarried from the mountain, timber cut from the forests, and bricks and tiles fashioned from earth—
and the inhabitants and settlers who took up residence in them, and the rest of the craftsmen and organized groups that came into being and were established in these cities.
In the same way, we too have already clearly shown above for what reason and why creation was created and the worlds were fashioned.
We learned precisely about everything that needed to be investigated, from nature, from our own being, and from our creation.
But now it is time to recount in order when the worlds were created, how they were established, and from what they came into being.
“In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” In this statement he included all the created things that God created:
the world of spiritual beings and the world of bodily beings. “The heavens and the earth”—
that is, the nature of the heavens, how they came into being, and the nature of the earth, how it came to be established. “The heaven of heavens” signifies many things,
for everything that is high is called “heaven.” [The upper part of a human mouth is called the “heaven of the palate.”] A roof is the “heaven of the house,” and the firmament is “heaven.”
The spheres of the constellations are many heavens. The waters above all the spheres are called the “heaven of heavens.” The statement
“In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” means that God first created the nature of the heavens and the nature of the earth. And afterward he said:
The earth was formless and empty, and darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters.
We must therefore consider clearly and understand precisely every word and statement spoken by the Spirit of God.
For there is not a single superfluous or useless letter in them. He said that God created the heavens and the earth.
Then he left aside the discussion of heaven and began to speak about the earth: “The earth was formless and empty,” and so on.
It would have been fitting that, just as he placed heaven before earth in creation, he should likewise follow that same order by speaking first about heaven and then about earth.
Now we must ask why he left aside heaven, which was mentioned first, and began to speak about the earth, which he mentioned second.
And which heaven is this that was mentioned? We say that it is not one of these visible heavens.
For these were arranged and established after the light and the stretching out of the firmament.
They were given their name from something higher than themselves, just as the roof of a house was given its name from something more elevated than itself.
Thus the heaven that Holy Scripture mentioned through the Spirit of God is the heaven of spiritual beings.
It is spoken of in the plural because of the many orders, ranks, and companies of the heavenly powers.
Similarly, there are many dwellings above our heads, as we shall see with God's help, and they are all called heavens.
That is, each one is the heaven of what lies beneath it. Likewise, in the heaven of spiritual beings, each rank is the heaven of the one beneath it.
The same applies to every order and every company. This is the reason why Holy Scripture said nothing at all about it, but left it aside and went on to speak about the earth that came after it.
For, as we said above, the Holy Spirit, who speaks with us in this divine book through our great teacher Moses,
gave the world milk to drink as though it were a newborn, since it was still entirely untrained in the knowledge of the one God.
It needed to suck divine instruction as a newborn sucks at the breast.
And again, he babbled with the world as with a little child, since it was untrained in speaking about God.
As to a child, he gave us tablets for practicing the letters of writing, so that we might practice, train, and learn about these divine matters.
And when we become proficient in the words and statements formed by combining letters—that is, in calling on the name of the Lord—
other interpreters are given to us to set out complete writings for us, namely the holy prophets who came afterward.
Little by little, they made known to us the glorious nature of Being, and that God is one, who is
the eternal Mind and has Word and Spirit, that is, knowledge and life.
Afterward, when the world had become fully trained and complete in the knowledge of God, it was given the perfect teaching that raises it, lifts it up, and brings it near its Maker.
This is the holy and adored Gospel, spoken by the mouth of God.
This is the reason why, at that time, the book of Genesis said nothing about the heaven of the angels, which is the world of spiritual beings.
For the world of bodily beings was not able to hear it. Instead, he first gave them divine milk to drink, as to newborn babies.
Then again, in giving the law, he babbled with them as with little children.
Then he instructed them through regulations, judgments, customs, rules of conduct, sacrifices, and drink offerings, like letters written on tablets for children.
Then the holy prophets came—or rather, were sent—to speak in many portions and in many ways, like writing teachers and reading instructors who provide complete instruction in writing and reading.
They made known and showed the world that God is Mind, Word, and Spirit, by proclaiming and saying:
“This is what the Lord says,” and “Thus says the Lord of lords,” and “The Spirit of the Lord did such and such,” and “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made,
and by the Spirit of his mouth all their hosts.” Great teaching was contained in this verse. In it he expressed profound theology concerning the Godhead,
by showing that the Lord God has a creating Word and a working Spirit. In it he also taught about the creation of the heavens
and the making of all the hosts within them. Here he clearly explained the statement in the first book, Genesis:
that when it said, “In the beginning God created the heavens,” it was speaking about the world of spiritual beings. For here the divine psalmist said,
“By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made”—that is, the heaven of the angels. For in the same verse he added to the mention of the Word, saying,
“And by the Spirit of his mouth all their hosts”—that is, all the heavenly ranks and orders.
Likewise, all the holy prophets made known to the world the hosts of angels.
Anyone who has the time should read and study their writings, and in all of them he will find an account of angels.
The entire order of the ministry of the holy prophets was carried out and accomplished through angels,
until the world was perfected in divine teaching. Then the spiritual law is given,
and the order of the perfect and complete ministry is established, not through angels or through prophets, but through the Lord of them all,
just as they all foreshadowed, depicted, and announced beforehand, as we are going to see and confirm, and to establish for the hearer a trustworthy conviction,
one that does not depart from nature and is not contradicted by Scripture. But now let us return to the discussion of creation,
and show how the world was created, when, and from what. And now that it has been established as trustworthy and we have become certain that what
Holy Scripture said, “In the beginning God created the heavens,” was said about the heaven of the angels, that is, the world of spiritual beings, and that “and the earth” referred to this creation,
that is, the world of bodily beings, it is right for us too first to explain a little about the creation of spiritual beings,
and then, in due order, to speak also about this creation of ours. In the second discourse earlier in this book, we spoke a little about the creation of the worlds,
and about the world of spiritual beings, its nature, its purpose, its [?], and its ministry, because the order of the discussion required this.
First, in the first discourse, we will speak about God and [?], and in the second discourse about those next to him, namely the heavenly powers above.
And in the third discourse, about the nature of the rational human being, composed of the spirituality of the powers above and the materiality of the bodily animals below.
And in this fourth discourse, which binds and gathers them all together, we speak about the creation of them all together.
Then, in the fifth, we begin to explain the arrangements of the perceptible world: how the worshipful and glorious Maker established, ordered, and sustained them.
And because in this fourth discourse, which gathers things together and serves as a fresh summary and introduction,
and in it we have explained precisely when the world of spiritual beings, which is the heaven of the angels, was created,
we ought to speak a little more about them, as their Maker and the Creator of us all gives us understanding. First, then, we ought to know:
One cannot say “when” about that time, since there was not yet any extension of time, nor any cycle of years,
nor any ordering of months, nor any boundary of weeks [?], nor any measurement of days, nor any distinction between daytime and night,
nor any counting of hours, nor any indication of seasons. How, then, is it possible to say when they were created?
We know for certain that they were created. But when, only one knows: the one who created them.
Nevertheless, they existed eternally in his mind, for he was going [?] to create and establish worlds in this way. Creating them was not a new thought that occurred to him.
But when he wished, [he created and established them. And in this way] he created and established them in a single instant. As for how, it was as the divine Scripture says:
“In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” He included all the worlds of spiritual and bodily beings in this statement.
But how? Listen: by that divine will and hidden command, when it pleased him, just as it had already been determined in his mind,
the world of spiritual beings, which is the heaven of the angels, was suddenly created and came into existence. And together with their creation, the earth was created,
that is, the created nature, or this perceptible world, which is matter constituted from four
elements. At that time it was mixed together and unformed, like a lump of potter’s clay that has been kneaded and set aside to mature, so that when its time comes,
the craftsman may fashion many useful vessels from it. In this way God created matter together with the creation of the heavenly powers,
so that when the time came—as he knew beforehand, in his foreknowledge, what was going to happen,
namely, the fall that befell Satan—he might fashion and make this world and its arrangements from that matter which had already been created and set aside,
and place in it the living being composed of spirituality and materiality, namely the human being, so that he might ascend, sit on the throne of the one who fell, and take over his ministry,
and reign in his place. For this reason he created beforehand the substance of the earth, which is matter—that is, all four elements—together with the creation of the heaven of the angels,
as the one who knows everything, as though these things had already happened. This is the statement about creation that Holy Scripture makes:
“In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” The heavens are the city of the angels, that is, the world of spiritual beings.
The earth, however, was matter composed of four elements. They were mixed together and not separated.
As Scripture went on to explain, speaking about the earth: “The earth was formless and void.”
That is, jumbled, mixed, and not yet put in order, like a mixture kneaded and blended from dust and water
and from other kinds of material useful for construction. In this way the elements were jumbled together and were formless and void.
That is, jumbled, mixed, and confused with one another in darkness, as it also says: “And darkness was over the surface of the deep.”
Since the elements had neither definite form nor light, they were like some boundless void.
“And the Spirit of God,” it says, “was hovering over the surface of the waters,” to make known and confirm that, even though [?] God [?],
that is, matter, formlessness and emptiness, and a dark abyss, it was nevertheless not abandoned without divine care.
Nor was it left outside the treasury of the kingdom, but within the honored and glorious embrace of his lordship.
For this reason the Spirit of God was hovering over it, protecting it and producing life in it, like a hen brooding over her young to produce life in them.
In the same way, the Spirit of God was hovering with care over the waters within matter, for the sake of the things that were to be born and formed from them.
With this statement he concluded the account of creation, which runs as follows: “In the beginning,” as follows.
“In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was formless and void, and darkness was over
the surface of the deep. The Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters.” And now.
Here he concluded and completed the account of the creation of everything. Afterward he began another beginning, which took place after a long [?],
describing how God arranged the beings and adornments of creation when he wished to create and make the human being. From that very matter which had already been laid down beforehand,
he began to make many kinds and varieties, like a craftsman working from a mixture laid out for him, which he called “already laid down.”
And because Holy Scripture concluded the account of creation here, and then began the formation of beings from matter, which took place after a long interval,
we too will make a break and a space here in the account of creation in general. We will speak first about the heaven of the angels, since it also comes first in the order of the account.
Then, when the time comes, we will speak about “the earth” and the arrangement of this visible creation. As for our statement that heaven came first,

we should understand that it came first in the order of the words, not in the order of creation. Rather, in a single instant there were created the heaven of the heavenly powers, which is “the heavens,”
and the matter of bodily things, which is “the earth.” As for the heaven of the angels, about which the book recounting the origin of creation said nothing,
this was because it was not its purpose to write about the heavenly powers for earthly people who did not yet even know how they themselves had come into being.
Instead, the Creator arranged things this way: first he would instruct them about bodily things, and about how they themselves had come into being and from what;
then they would rise to the knowledge of spiritual things and learn how the heavenly powers were brought into existence.
On the spiritual beings, their world, their orders, ranks, arrangements, companies, and legions, and their work and ministry.
Certain people who speak of divine things have taught us and made these things known to us: those whose hearts were purified of material passions and whose thoughts were cleared of empty concerns.
Their minds became clear and were enlightened by divine wisdom. Some of them were prophets and revealers; all of them distinguished themselves by virtuous conduct.
Their soul was enlightened and stood in its natural order, serene, pure, radiant, and spiritual, just as it was created by its Maker,
sharing the nature of the holy angels. When it is enlightened and stands in its natural order, it sees all the beings that are equal to it.

It knows and understands all their activity, their work, and their order. Nor does it know and understand these things alone. Rather, if it continues to struggle, to be purified, and to be enlightened,
it rises still higher in knowledge and grows wise, to the point that it can teach and speak even about that worshipful and glorious nature of the hidden and incomprehensible Being,
through the radiance of the divine rays that shine upon it and make it wise through revelations of immaterial light, as did many theologians
who lived and became wise in these divine things. Through their teaching they enlightened everything under heaven, and human beings became aware of their Lord and came to know their Creator.
Had it not been for these people, the whole world would have remained sunk in the hateful darkness of great error, and people would have been strangers, far removed from God
and deprived of the light of true knowledge of him. Truly, the difference between one person and another is
like the difference between an angel of light and a filthy pig wallowing in mud and sunk in a dark enclosure, awaiting the day of slaughter.
Therefore, my brothers, since these things lie within human nature, and a person can rise through virtue to this glorious height, until he becomes the equal of the angels,
and knows the order of their nature and all their work, and can advance and rise still further until he gazes into the hidden mysteries of the concealed and glorious Lordship,
why, then, have we so neglected our radiant soul? Through our hateful conduct, full of sinful passions, here we are, sunk in the darkness of ignorance.
Like filthy pigs, here we are, indulging in feeding the belly, that fountain of filth, and wallowing in the foul mud of shameful deeds.
We are deprived of the glorious light of purity that sees God. No, my beloved brothers, let us not neglect our soul and become like filthy pigs.
Instead, let us strive courageously and live rationally, practicing the glorious conduct of virtue, like our blessed and diligent fathers,
who, through their upright and glorious conduct, were deemed worthy of great gifts and were raised up to become companions of the heavenly powers.
Their minds were further enlightened, and they advanced to the exalted height of divine knowledge.
They grasped, knew, and became certain of mysteries that cannot be spoken or explained.
These blessed ones—the holy prophets, the divine apostles, and the spiritual teachers—truly became wise through divine help [?] and power.
They taught the rest of humanity about the reality and power of the world of spiritual beings,
not from hearsay or traditions handed down by others, but from what they themselves had personally experienced, known, and become certain of.
We too all bear witness to their truth: there truly is a world of spiritual beings, in which the heavenly powers dwell spiritually.
Among the many activities taking place in this world of ours are those brought about by the holy angels.
They appear openly to many people, at sea and on land, and in times of distress they help them and rescue them from their troubles.
To others they announce beforehand the things that are going to happen. And they appear continually to all of us through dreams:
sometimes angels of truth, and sometimes angels of deception, who are servants of Satan.
Because all these beings share the soul’s nature, it sees them at all times: sometimes while the body is awake, and much more often when
it is asleep and sunk in sleep. For the soul itself stays awake and does not sleep, because it is spiritual by nature.
It sees spiritual beings when they approach it in whatever manner, although dreams are of many kinds.
But angels are also continually present in this world: in the spasms of children, in the possession of adults,
in the many words they speak through the mouths of the demon-possessed, in divinations, in omens, in familiar spirits, in incantations, in springs,
in thickly branching trees, in stone images, in bronze statues. Sometimes they speak out from the ground, sometimes from dark caves,
among tombs, on desolate mountains, in the darkness of winter nights, in the fierce midday heat of summer days,
through frightening voices, in the shapes of hideous animals, in visions, in apparitions, in mirages, in the formation of deceptive likenesses,

in the fabrication of untrue imaginings, in bringing news from distant places so as to lead the simple astray, along with the very many kinds of activities that demons perform, as each of us has experienced, known, seen, and heard.
It has now been established from nature, reliable experience, and trustworthy reports from those who have themselves experienced and verified it, that angels truly exist and demons exist.
Now let us say about them what we need to know, according to the enlightenment we have received from the tradition of the ancients, true witnesses, proven, perfect, and trustworthy,
and from the experiences that we ourselves are examining and testing. In the second discourse, in chapters three, four, and five, we discussed and established that a world of spiritual beings exists,
what it is like, and how it is ordered and carries out its service. Now, however, we do not need to establish conviction about these things again,
but only to give a simple narrative account of how they were created and brought into being.
We say that the first cause, the cause of all causes, the Lord of all lords, and the ruler of all ages,
because he is good, rich, and wise by nature, created and brought into being, all at once, a great world of rational beings, subtle and spiritual,
luminous by nature, endowed with knowledge, not easily subject to change, firmly established in their nature, masters of themselves and of their freedom.
Their will is good by nature, and they know everything through the keenness of their perception,
except their Maker. He made known to them that he exists; how he exists they cannot know.
He made their freedom—their mastery over themselves—voluntary, not compelled. He arranged them in three orders,
and in each order three ranks. He divided each rank into rows upon rows and companies [companies].
And in every rank he arranged legions, thousands, and hundreds, whose number and quantity he alone knows. And above the nine divisions in the three orders,
he established one exalted order, which stands at the gate of the kingdom of Being, and made it
head of all the orders and all the divisions [of the hosts]. And with it he established legions, ranks, and many companies, as he alone knows.
He completed their number and sealed it with ten. From there the reckoning of numbers took its beginning,
ascending as far as ten. Then it begins again, ascending and multiplying into another ten tens.
And again these ten tens are multiplied a third time and become ten hundreds, each hundred being ten tens.
And so they ascend to thousands and many myriads, without adding anything beyond ten or going outside ten.
Rather, the number ten is the limit that bounds all limits. Thus, there truly were ten orders of the heavenly hosts.
And that exalted one was appointed head and first of them all, closely resembling and depicting the likeness of its Lord.
It is near and stands at the gate of Being, like the second in command of the kingdom. It brings in and leads out like a steward, and conveys and passes things on like a mediator.
It was made chief, high priest, and patriarch over all the other orders beneath it.
It is the symbol of the completion of the number ten. And the three other orders beneath it depict the mystery of the Trinity.
It also depicts the mystery of the oneness of the divinity, lordship, substance, being, nature, and will of the one Lord who holds all.
Likewise, each of these three orders is divided into three divisions, and each division is divided into three companies,
three times in a threefold manner: a sign of the great mystery of the Trinity of persons of the one eternal Being.
And in each company they are arranged and stand rank upon rank, and in each rank are countless legions: a sign of the mystery of the incomprehensibility of the divinity.
A legion consists of thirty-six thousand, making three myriads, and each myriad consists of twelve thousand.
In each legion there are three chiefs, one chief for each myriad, and under him twelve commanders, chiefs of thousands.
Ten centurions, who are chiefs of hundreds, and under each centurion ten officers, each one a chief of ten.
These three orders are nine divisions, making twenty-seven companies. Whether each company consists of three ranks,
and each rank of three legions, which are again divided three times in a threefold manner like the first division, we do not know.
But each legion consists of three myriads, and each myriad of twelve thousand. Others say [ten thousand.
And others say] that a legion consists of thirty-two thousand. And others say
that a legion is itself a myriad. But we have written above according to what we have firmly ascertained.
And whoever does not believe, let him go and see and count and ascertain it, and come and inform us. Otherwise, let him listen and be silent and praise their Maker.
He alone knows their order, their number, and their entire multitude. But we do not need to dwell much on these things.
Nevertheless, numerical reckoning was brought from there into this world of ours: our counting rises to ten
and returns. This reveals a great mystery: through knowledge of these ten orders, the human mind can ascend and be raised up, and be perfected in the excellence of upright conduct.
Beyond that, the mind is no longer permitted to think. There is nothing further it can comprehend. Beyond that lies great wonder:
stillness without movement, silence without speech, amazement without thought. Thus there truly are ten orders of angelic powers.
We will explain these things further and establish them below. And above them all
is the worshipful and glorious nature of the sovereign Being, which all worship, glorify, sanctify, bless, and exalt.
But do not conceive of it as being in a place or location. Rather, with the mind and spiritual thought, spiritually and subtly, understand the exaltedness of that Being through knowledge alone.
Consider its incomprehensibility. It is wholly present in everything, like the soul in the body.
If your mind cannot grasp and understand these things, do not venture to think about them, lest you mistake one thing for another and sink into the abyss of ignorance.
Then you will not even be able to find a way to rise and escape from that darkness of ignorance.
Instead, humble yourself before God. Weep, fast, pray, keep vigil, plead, and ask without growing weary. He will give to you and make you wise in the knowledge of the truth.
But know that without stillness and tranquility, silence and restraint from conversation, fasting and abstinence from wine
and from foods, vigil and prayer together with readings from the Holy Scriptures, and an understanding mind and a wise and experienced guide,
it is entirely impossible to acquire knowledge of the truth. Now the highest order of the heavenly powers was called and named the Morning Star.
That is, like the light that appears at dawn before the sun, when day breaks and the light is near,
so this order was placed and stationed before the divine Lordship, the intelligible sun. And this name of light and dawn was brought from there into this world of ours.
This account reveals a great mystery that was to take place after a long interval: the Godhead was to dawn upon the darkness of creation and illuminate it with the light of divine knowledge.
But since our purpose is not to explain this, but to give an account of creation, let us pass over these things.
Otherwise, the account would become very lengthy. This highest order, which was named the Morning Star,
had countless divisions, companies, and ranks. Their ordering and the manner in which they stood were not precisely known,
because their nature is deeply hidden, just as the Being before which they stood is hidden and concealed, and they [?] its mysteries.
To Moses, that man of God, only a little of the mystery of their number was revealed. For in the hymn “Listen, O heavens, and I will speak,” he says this:
“Listen, O heavens, and I will speak”—that is, the heavens of the angels, you spiritual beings who do not hear with ears.
“Listen to my speech, and let the earth hear the words of my mouth”—that is, human beings, the inhabitants of the earth.
You who hear with your ears and understand with your mind, listen to a discourse composed in the voice that comes from my mouth.
He commanded the spiritual beings in heaven to listen to a spiritual word, and the bodily beings on earth to hear the discourse spoken by the mouth.
After proceeding a little further in the song—to keep us from going on too long—he said, “Remember the days of old, and consider the years of generation after generation.”
That is, the days, or the times, of creation, which are the first days of old; and reckon the years of generation after generation.

“Ask your father”—nature—“and he will show you; and your elders”—the Scriptures—“and they will tell you. When the Most High divided the nations”—that is, in his mind he divided all the nations that were to exist in creation.
And when he separated human beings, the righteous from the sinners, he established the boundary of the righteous nations according to the number of the sons of God.
This is how it is written in the accurate Septuagint. That is, he established in his mind the full boundary of the righteous nations, so that it would correspond to the number of the sons of God,
those who were overthrown and fell, so that they might serve him in their place. “For,” it says, “the Lord’s portion is his people.”
That is, the Lord’s share, chosen for him from all humanity, is that people whose number corresponds to those who fell. But the rest,
the unjust, the wicked, the unbelievers, and the blasphemers, are not the Lord’s portion, or his share, but the share of the Adversary, their master. They are added to him and are tormented with him.
The number of the righteous is also destined to be completed according to the number of wicked human beings who are added to the number of those who fell.
These become a share belonging to God, that is, the Lord’s portion. He gives them as an inheritance not only the place of the one who fell, but also a place higher than it,
the place that Satanael himself—that is, the one who turned away from God—was to receive, if he had remained in the rank proper to his nature and had not exalted himself and risen above his Lord.
Because of this, he began this struggle of great hostility against the human race, out of the hateful envy that his pride produced in him.
He was burning, roasting, and growing bitter with envy toward them, devising ways to kill them through sin, so that they would die apart from God
and be added to his number and be tormented with him. My brothers, let us fear pride, which drives us away from God and is the mother of murderous envy.
Let us struggle courageously to escape the portion and company of our Adversary, so that we may belong to the portion and share within the company of our good and merciful God.
These things have been disclosed to us from the holy book of the godly Moses concerning the number of Satanael’s rank, his companies, and his legions:
that human beings were created for this reason, to inherit his place. And when the full number of the righteous nations is completed, corresponding to the number of those
who fell and of those wicked people who are to be added to them, this cycle of time will cease.
There will be renewal and rest for all created beings. Then the spiritual way of life of the other, new, and everlasting world will begin.
See how glorious and [?] was the place where the morning star stood,
and with what radiance, glory, and honor he was stationed at the gate of the self-existent, eternal, and everlasting kingdom, which is like a great, unfailing abundance.
A thousand thousand times over, like the rivers Gihon, Pishon, Tigris, and Euphrates, divine gifts and spiritual endowments poured forth and flowed from that Being without limit and without ceasing.
He was the first to receive them, and he carried and passed them on to those after him, and from one rank to [?], down to the last.
Just as the laying on of hands that the patriarch receives from the Godhead through the assembly of bishops.
Then he passes it on to the orders of the Church, [which are] the catholicoi, metropolitans, and bishops.
And the middle order consists of priests, deacons, and subdeacons; and the third order consists of readers, singers, and exorcists.
Others say that it consists of members of the covenant—that is, monks—and readers and singers. But we think that this is not so.
For the honored order of monastic life has another purpose and represents an exalted mystery.
Indeed, members of it are found in all the orders of the Church. There are patriarchs who are monks.
And there are catholicoi, metropolitans, and bishops, as well as priests, deacons, and subdeacons, who are monks.
The same is true of the rest. But only Christians know these things, whereas our present discussion concerns all nations.
The heavenly orders, meanwhile, were arranged in this way in three assemblies. Within the first order, three ranks were arranged.
The first is that of the Angels; the second, above it, is that of the Archangels; the third is that of the Principalities.
In the second order, which is in the middle assembly, the Authorities are arranged first, above the Principalities; and above them are the Powers, who are also the Hosts.
Above these are the Dominions, who are also called commanders of the Hosts. And in the upper assembly, which contains the third order above,
the first rank, above the Dominions, consists of the Thrones; and above these are the six-winged Seraphim.
Above them all are the many-eyed Cherubim, who are also called the speaking wheels,
because they are yoked to the fearsome chariot upon which the great radiance of the glory of the Godhead is carried in majesty.
The discourse and explanation concerning each of these orders is extensive, and not everyone is capable of treating the subject.
Above all these is the exalted order of the Morning Star. [The praises of all the ranks of spiritual beings used to ascend from one to another higher than itself,
and from one order to the one above it, until they reached the Morning Star.] And the exalted ruler who stands at the gate of the heavenly kingdom—he would bring
the praises, blessings, and acclamations of holiness of the assemblies before the Majesty. And he would receive the beams and rays of the Godhead,
and with them the divine gifts and exalted endowments from the eternal sovereignty of the Godhead.
He would convey and pass them on to the orders beneath him. And so they were conveyed from one to another in a wondrous way.
Each of them would receive in a divine manner according to his strength and capacity, while those divine gifts and rays neither ran out nor diminished.
We will write at length about all these matters in another book, on the spiritual ministry of the heavenly beings, with the help of God, who gives wisdom and wills it.
But this chief of the heavenly hosts, that exalted and lofty Morning Star—a thought of pride stirred within him, and he reflected and thought:
“I have been placed in all this greatness, and all the praises of the hosts of spiritual beings are raised to me.”
And all the divine gifts are conveyed to them through my hands. It is right that, above all the stars in heaven,
that is, the angels of light, a royal throne should be set up for me, and I should be like the Most High.
Spiritual beings do not reason as we do, gathering thoughts and examining them in their minds. If their free will chooses them,
their will brings them into action and makes them manifest. But if their free will does not consent to them, their will drives them away, and they are scattered and come to nothing.
Others like us do not perceive these thoughts when they do not issue in visible action.
But the natural order of spiritual beings is not like this. Rather, a spiritual being’s thought is itself its will, the movement of its free choice, and its completed action.

At the very instant when a thought stirs within it, all the thousands and tens of thousands who share its nature see and know it fully. And when this thought of wickedness and arrogance stirred in the head of their order,
they all consented to it and desired it through the movement of their free will. Together with the thought and the consent of his companions,
he was abandoned by the power of providence, which holds everything and sustains everything.
At that very instant they were all overthrown and fell from their authority. This whole affair happened as swiftly as a flash of lightning.
Even though we cannot hear and understand in this way, because we are composite beings,
spiritual beings communicate to one another in a single instant everything that we recount over the course of a day or a month; they make it known to one another and carry it out.
This was how the Morning Star and all his hosts fell from the heaven of his glory, like lightning falling from the vault of heaven.
Oh, the pride that brings one low! From what an exalted height, great honor, abundant glory, radiant light, spiritual service,
