and lordly rank it overthrew, drove away, and hurled the Morning Star into the lowest, bottomless depth and into the outer darkness, where there are no rays of light!
And if an angel of light was overthrown, fell, and was brought down to such utter lowliness because of the single passion of pride,
then into what great destruction must someone descend who, along with pride, a passion of the soul, also has other passions of the body,
unless he takes himself in hand, humbles himself, and considers himself dust and [?] and foul mud—as indeed he is, a house full of filth.
We have hope of repentance because of the flesh we wear. In the nature of spiritual beings there is neither repentance nor turning back.
Rather, along with the evil thought come rejection and separation from God,
and everlasting destruction and bitter torment in the outer darkness, just as happened to Satan: he fell and was lost forever.
We cannot possibly know the length of that interval, as we explained in the second discourse and at the beginning of the third.
Afterward, when the good Lord wished to appoint others to the service of the one who had fallen, and to give them his place and honor as their inheritance,
or rather, even to raise and exalt them to the glorious height that had been reserved for him, had he not exalted himself against his Lord and rebelled against his Creator in his arrogance,
and desired in his pride to seize it before his time—this was the reason why the human being was created.
But when the time came to create the human being, as it had previously been possible for him to come into being,
this composite being needed a place to live, to do his work there for a long time and apply himself diligently there, and then to go and receive his reward in that exalted place.
First he determined to prepare a place and a dwelling for him and to supply him with everything he needed.
Then he would bring the inhabitant into being and settle him in the dwelling of his temporary residence. Thus, from that time began the creation of this visible world.
Its formation was from matter, namely the earth itself, which had previously been created together with the heavens.
It was formless and empty, dark and unprepared. It was from this very earth, which had been laid aside and kept like a potter’s lump of clay,
which matures until the time the craftsman knows and desires, when he knows that the moment has arrived.
As had already been settled in his mind, at that time God created this world for the human being.
He established and fashioned it from the earth itself, which is the matter he had previously created together with the heavens,
that is, together with the world of spiritual beings. This matter, namely the earth itself, is all four elements, as we shall explain in order, with the help of the Lord, who wills and guides.
With these words the fourth chapter is completed, in which much of substance was said through God, who gave strength and help.
Chapter Five of the Fourth Discourse, with God, who grants wisdom.
On how opposing natures were united and everything visible was fashioned from them. From the beginning of this book until now,
we have used demonstrations drawn from nature, the father and teacher of us all: matters that are suitable and acceptable to all the peoples under heaven.
There is no room at all to doubt them or to argue against them. Now nature itself bears witness concerning the book of the coming into being of creation, which Moses wrote,

that it is true and entirely reliable, and that it was written at God’s command and through his activity. Three well-known groups of peoples, foremost on earth, have testified to these things and confirmed them.
These are all the varieties of Christians, and all the divisions of the Jewish people,
and all the different groups among the Arab people. Each confession is divided into many varieties and into many different peoples.
They all testify and affirm that the book of the Torah was given by God. Now that we have all become assured of its reliability and truth,
from this point onward we shall compose and arrange our entire account from this book itself and from nature. For Holy Scripture says:
“In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was formless and empty, and darkness was over the surface of the deep,
and the Spirit of God hovered over the surface of the waters.” We have already spoken about these things in the preceding chapter. Now we ought to explain them again and set them out,
so that they may be understood easily. A long time after the creation of the first world, that of spiritual beings, Satan’s fall occurred.
This fall cast great fear upon the rest of the hosts in the nine heavenly orders.
They were in great anxiety and terror until the way of the holy ones was revealed. Then their fear was lifted from them.
But not completely until the universal renewal, when he kills every ruler and every authority, and the enemy, death, is abolished.
Then one alone reigns: the one to whom belong the kingdom, power, and authority. Every knee bows to him, and every tongue acknowledges him.
And after Satan’s fall, again, after another long span of time, as only he knows—the one who created the worlds and arranged the times.
For the times, years, months, weeks, and days of this perceptible world of ours had not yet been arranged.

In the world of spiritual beings, these do not exist at all. And if someone says that the interval from the creation of the heavenly powers until Satan’s fall was a period of about twenty thousand years,
or thirty thousand, or more, and likewise that the interval from Satan’s fall until the creation of humanity was that long or longer,
he is neither confirmed nor shown to be wrong, since there is no other human being who knows the time precisely enough to confirm or refute him.
But we do know this: after a long span of time, the Creator wished to establish
the second world, just as it had previously been determined in his mind, neither more nor less. Nothing is new to God.
Rather, he knows precisely everything that is going to happen, as though it had already happened, passed, and gone.
So when he wished to create humanity, for the reason we mentioned above, he planned first to prepare a dwelling place for humanity, and then to create its inhabitant.
He prepared the dwelling place in this way, from the matter that had previously been created and already laid up at the creation of the spiritual beings, as we said above in the preceding chapters.
For it had been created and laid up for this purpose, since he knows everything.
Matter consists of the four elements, which themselves are constituted from four qualities, the parents and sustainers of this world and everything in it.
These are cold, heat, moisture, and dryness. There is nothing beyond these, nor anything apart from them.
Each element is composed of two qualities. The elements themselves are these:
air, fire, water, and earth. Air consists of heat and moisture. This sustains life and well-being.
Therefore it is the [?] and the breath of life of all living creatures. And everything that consists of this mixture and combination of heat and moisture
gives life and sustains it, brings health, and preserves well-being.
For this reason, this nature—that is, the combination of heat and moisture—has been called and named good, goodness, and continued existence.
Earth, however, has a cold and dry nature, the opposite of heat and moisture, and brings the dissolution and destruction of existence.
This is the opposite of life, good, and goodness. It has been called and named the death of life and the dissolution and destruction of existence.
And what is opposed to the goodness of this world, dissolves and destroys its well-being, and brings death to its life, is its evil.
For the absence of goodness is evil. It has now been established that a hot and moist nature is goodness and life,
and a cold and dry nature is evil and death. Now take note and keep these things carefully in your mind.
Fire, however, is hot and dry by nature. It sustains in one way and destroys in another.
Because it is not life and subsistence in the strict sense, nor entirely death and destruction, its nature—that is, hot and dry—was called sickness.
Water, in turn, is cold and moist by nature. Likewise, this nature too is neither subsistence nor destruction. It too
was called sickness. Now let us see how the Creator fitted these opposing natures together,
and united their opposition through [?] and great longing, and made and arranged this whole. For heat is the opposite of cold,
and moisture of dryness. Air disperses earth, and water extinguishes fire.
How, then, did the creative power, wise in everything, unite these things that oppose, consume, and destroy one another,
and fashion from them this beautiful order and all these astonishing variations that surpass the power of understanding? First, then,
the union of these elements took place as follows. Air is hot and moist, and it was joined to fire, which is hot and dry,
and to water, which is cold and moist. Thus, the heat of fire on one side,
and its moisture with the moisture of water on the other side. Earth, however, is cold and dry:
its coldness with the coldness of water, and its dryness with the dryness of fire. In this manner and through this compatibility the elements were united,
and from them came a mixture of matter, from which everything within [?] the curtain of this [?] was made and established, according to this height, as we depict here.
And so, according to God's will, the elements were united and fitted to one another. From them came a mixture of matter, which is the earth
that divine Scripture says God created. We also describe another manner of association and union among these elements.
We see, then, that every union, association, and mixture comes about and is completed in this world through a compatible attraction.
From their mingling through a natural, loving attraction, many complete and beautiful activities and beings are brought forth.
For example, the union of male and female takes place through a passionate attraction, which is natural love.
From it their own kind is born, propagated, and multiplied, and from it comes the beauty of
continued existence. Everything in creation has a mutual compatibility and attraction, in the very same manner as the attraction of male to female;

and together with that with which they unite, beautiful kinds and activities are completed and established through their union. In this same manner, the natures of the elements have a mutual compatibility and attraction. Through it they were united by attraction and brought matter to completion,
from which everything was established and completed. Hear and understand how this happens. Dryness, then, is strongly attracted to moisture
and is very compatible with it, and coldness with heat. But if heat is joined to heat, they do not produce subsistence,
but harm and destruction. Likewise, coldness joined to coldness, and moisture to moisture,
and dryness to dryness: from the union of these, no beautiful order of existence comes about at all.
but injury and damage, as when someone's body suffers from a fever caused by red bile.
We know from experience that this illness arises from hot, dry humors, so we compound medicines for it from cold, moist substances that counteract the illness.
In this way we heal the body and restore its well-being. Likewise, when someone's body suffers from paralysis,
which arises from an excess of phlegm that has accumulated in the body—and this humor, that is, the phlegmatic bodily fluid,
we know from experience to be cold and moist—we compound medicines for it from hot, dry substances that counteract the humor.
In this way we heal the suffering body, and it regains its well-being. Now let us consider the natural properties of the elements as well:
although they seem to be opposites, their opposition is itself what sustains them.
Earth, then, is cold and dry. Its dryness is moistened by the water for which it longs,
and its coldness is warmed by the heat of fire through the sun's rays. This union and mutually desired association take place,
and through them every kind of beneficial activity involving seeds and plants and the ripening of fruit is sustained and brought to completion,
as is the entire existence of this bodily life. But if water were added to water, or fire, and air to air, and dust to earth,
they would not bring anything into being. Nor, if we treat a hot illness with a hot medicine, does healing result.
Understand many other things in the same way, as the saying goes: “Give a wise person an opportunity, and he will become still wiser.”
Thus the creative power, wise in everything, arranged and created the natural properties of the elements very well and fittingly,
from heat and cold, moisture and dryness. What is hot, then, longs for what is cold, so that it may be refreshed by it; and what is dry thirsts
and yearns for what is moist, so that it may be softened and moistened by it, as in this diagram that we draw here.
Through this kind of passionate longing, like a natural love, the elements were fitted together and united with one another,
as in the longing of male and female. Thus they were united in a natural, harmonious, mutually desired union,
and constituted matter, from which everything came into being and was brought to completion. As for the union in that first diagram that we drew and outlined above,
we heard and learned about it from others before us. But this other, mutually desired and harmonious union we discovered through our own contemplation,
just as we also know from experience the nature of the elements and the humors, their longing for one another, and the well-being that results from this union of which we have spoken.
Now you, discerning readers, may accept what seems good to you. Prefer, however, what follows the order of the natural properties,
as the wise Creator arranged them and defined their limits. In this pattern the four elements were fitted together and united with one another,
through the longing that their Maker placed in their nature. From them matter was constituted, which is “the earth.”
It was “formless and void,” that is, the elements were mingled with one another and hidden within one another.
And they were in a bottomless abyss, and darkness was over the surface of the abyss, because light had not yet been created.
For the illuminating element of fire was hidden and mingled with the other elements and was not visible at all.
Even now, the nature of fire is hidden and concealed in stones, iron, wood, and the heat of material substances, and is not visible at all,
until the human being, the image of God, brings it into the open through the skill of his knowledge.
Thus matter remained, from the time it was created together with the spiritual beings, formless and empty, mingled and disordered. And earth, fire, and water—
all were mingled together with air in a disordered state. The air moved according to its nature,
and set the rest of the elements in motion. The earth's dust, together with the stones in it, was mixed with the moisture of the water,
and was poured this way and that by the movement of the air, which set matter in motion.
But the power, that is, the nature of fire, was concealed in them, as we said above. It was kept hidden in the nature of earth and stones.
The remaining elements were strengthened by the nature of fire and held together.
Thus the elements tumbled against one another and rubbed against one another, having no rest from movement.
Because of this, the stones rubbed against one another and became smooth from that time onward, just as happens when rivers flood.
For when the water rises above the islands and the [?] in the rivers and along their banks, the stones rub against one another.
Through this tumbling and striking against one another, their protruding parts are worn away, and they remain smooth, rounded stones.
This is what happened in that mingling of the elements. Because the earth and stones were mixed with water, they lay together,
and the mixture was soft. The air within them set them in motion.
The stones rubbed against one another and became all these smooth stones on the surface of the earth and beneath the earth, as well as what is called garomma [?],
that is, those smooth stones that are mixed with dust and hardened at the command of God, who separated moisture from dryness,
that is, earth from water, as we are going to explain. This is the cause of these smooth stones found in the earth and beneath the whole earth.
In various places they hardened and joined together, and from them came heights, ridges, and things resembling mountains.
And so they have remained until today. If someone should think that perhaps these things came into being at the time of the Flood,
we say that the Flood came upon the surface of the earth from above and destroyed everything on it. The air remained as it was, and the earth continued in its firmness.
The elements did not mingle with one another as they did in the beginning, before they were separated (dissolved), when they were formless and empty.
Even if earth and water did mingle, they mingled only a little, on the surface of the earth.
The depths of the earth and the foundations of the mountains were not shaken at all, nor was the earth ruined and laid waste.
If that flood had rushed down like a mighty torrent and poured out over the earth, it would have torn through it and hollowed it out.
It could never have been inhabited again. But first the Lord broke open the streams below and made them gush out.
The waters rose and covered the earth. Then he released the downpours from above, and water poured down and emptied out upon water.
In this way the earth was preserved and remained spread out and firmly established through the command and providence
of the one who is wise in everything, the maker and fashioner of the worlds. Thus the elements were joined and mingled with one another, and the mass of matter was molded, which is the earth itself.
And so it remained as it was, with expanses and mountains that cannot at all be measured or known by us,
until God wished to fashion this world, put it in order, and adorn it for humanity, which he was going to create, so that people might be inhabitants and temporary residents in it for a time.
Then humanity would be transferred to that place for which it was created,
and would ascend and inherit the throne of the one who fell. From there it would rise still higher, to where that one had desired to exalt himself presumptuously and before the proper time.
That is, if he had persevered in the order of his ministry, humbled himself like an obedient servant, and kept his master's command,
then certainly, after a time, whenever his master, creator, and maker wished, he would have granted him freedom
and raised him to the exalted rank of sons. But because he did not endure and persevere, and instead acted presumptuously and exalted himself to seize it in his arrogance, lawlessly and tyrannically,
he was overthrown and cast out of his place, and fell a great fall, like lightning from heaven. For this reason humanity was created: to take up his ministry
and inherit his throne, and from there to be raised to that greatness which the rebel who fell had wished to seize.
Now it lies within our own will as human beings: if we are willing, make an effort, and keep our Lord's command,
we will be deemed worthy of that exalted, indescribable honor and will delight in being with our Lord. But if we are negligent, we will fall even from our own honor
and be tormented with that rebel. We pray and plead that we may be saved and delivered from sharing his lot and keeping company with him,
and that we may rejoice and delight with our good Lord and merciful God, through his grace and his abundant mercies, forever and ever. Amen.
With these words the fifth chapter of the fourth discourse is completed, through God, who gave strength and help.
The fourth discourse is completed. In it there was discussion of the scribe and the book, and of the truthfulness of the book of Genesis concerning creation,
and of the creation of this world—how it came about and from what it was constituted—and also of the world of spiritual beings and their orders,
the fall of Satan, the reason for humanity's creation, and how the opposing elements were joined together and became the matter from which everything visible in this creation was constituted.
We now write the fifth discourse, on the formation of this world, its arrangement, and the many differences within it.
It contains seven chapters. Chapter One, with God who grants wisdom: On the beginning of the ordering of this creation,
and on how light was created and what it consists of. In these four discourses that have been delivered up to now,
In them, all the things that a rational human being [?] needs to know were discussed.

And after he had been instructed and had gained wisdom through knowledge of the truth, and had become convinced and believed, from nature and experience, that this whole universe has a Lord and Creator,
and that he is its ruler and caretaker, able to do everything, [and how the worlds were created and put in order,] and why humanity was created, along with the many subjects discussed above,
which perfect a person in knowledge, understanding, and especially faith, so that it is impossible to doubt the truth or refuse to accept it.
And all these things we have discovered and learned through contemplation of nature and from nature itself.
In it there is also discussion of God, insofar as a created being can know and comprehend its Maker, and discussion of all divine matters.
From them a person learns what our nature is, what it comes from, and for what reason we were created.
A person is instructed rationally and wisely in divine and human matters, and in knowledge of spiritual beings and what they are like.
And when he has been instructed and perfected in these things, and his spiritual senses have been brought together, and he has recognized his own dignity,
and understood the order of his freedom, his self-determination, and his rationality, from this point onward let him hear and understand the ordering of this world from the beginning:
how it was fashioned and ordered by the wise Creator, and how it was adorned and clothed in splendor with many wonderful beauties and varieties.

And now, from this point we make a new beginning [?], with the creation of light, just as the glorious Creator himself, the uncreated Light, began with created light in his radiant and illuminating work of creation,
he who illuminates the world with his beautiful and glorious light, which darkness cannot comprehend at all. We speak as follows:
Suppose, then, there is a great and powerful king who has a beloved only son, heir to the kingdom.
He wishes to arrange his betrothal and hold a great wedding celebration and banquet for him, to rejoice in him and satisfy his heart and his desire,
because he expects him to become heir to his kingdom, his many possessions, and his inexhaustible wealth.
First, he prepares and makes ready beforehand everything needed for the wedding and the invited guests, and a splendid chamber for the bridegroom,
and an adorned bridal chamber for the bride. He prepares spacious rooms and lofty, magnificent dining halls,
and hangs lamps and lights in them. An adorned bridal chamber. He prepares spacious rooms and lofty, magnificent dining halls,
and hangs many lamps and lights in them, so that people can see and enjoy the beauties of the dining halls, with gilded ceilings fashioned with
skillful craftsmanship, with splendid pictures on the walls and doors, of every kind and every color;
with curtains, garlands, and silks stretched across the courtyards and everywhere; with rugs and carpets (that is, coverings) spread over the floors of the rooms;
with provisions of food of every kind and every variety, with clear wines and other pleasant and cheering drinks;
with perfumes and aromatic herbs that delight the sense of smell; with various kinds of music, zithers, lyres, flutes, and [?] and [?];
with blossoms, flowers, blooms, and roses and lilies of every color; with dancers and entertainers.
And the rest of the [?] and [?], with flowers of different kinds, many flavors, and fragrant colors.

With attendants, [?], bakers, cooks, and the rest of those who provide comfort; with decorated mounts and splendid carriages for carrying supplies and for the convenience of the riders, in glory, honor, and grandeur;
Together with all the other provisions and necessities required and suitable for the bridegroom, the bride, and the invited guests and those called
From near and far. When he has arranged and prepared all these things, he then calls the bridegroom and lodges him in his room.
He brings the bride into her bridal chamber, and sets out and prepares food, delights, and luxuries for the betrothed couple,
And also for all the wedding companions and invited guests. They begin to eat, drink, enjoy themselves, and rejoice at the great and splendid wedding feast.
When the day draws to a close, he lights lamps, candles, and lanterns for them, and makes the night more splendid than the day.
When they wish to go out for recreation, he brings them decorated mounts and splendid carriages.
They ride some of them in procession and for recreation, and load others with food and supplies for their needs and comfort.
In the same way, that good Father, glorious King, and gracious Lord, when he wished to bring joy to the glorious bridegroom, the human being, and to his betrothed bride, his spouse,
And to hold a great wedding feast for him in this world, and to make him heir to his heavenly kingdom and his abundant, inexhaustible wealth,
So that the human being would be his son and God would be his Father, first arranged and prepared for him a room and a glorious bridal chamber,
And a splendid and beautiful dwelling: this wonderful world, filled with every variety of things.
He stretched out this splendid canopy for him and built this lofty, royal vault for him.
He hung the light-shining stars in it like lamps, and placed the two great lights, the sun and the moon, for him on the lampstand of the zodiac.
He made this pleasant air blow for him, for the breath he needed [?], and provided rain, dew, and showers to refresh him
And to water his gardens and fields. He made birds and winged creatures fly in the air, of many kinds and varied colors, to delight him and to sing and chirp with their voices

And melodies before him, to cheer him. He spread out the earth beneath him for his comfort, and planted in it gardens and orchards with every kind of blossom and flower, roses and lilies, for his enjoyment.
He made steeds and mares for him, tall and splendid, magnificent in stature, for him to ride and travel in procession.
And camels, mules, and donkeys to carry his loads, and flocks of sheep, lambs, and kids to nourish him richly.
And oxen and izbaraks—that is, buffalo—to plow and open up the earth for his cultivation, and the wild animals in the mountains to leap before him and delight him.
And the sea and dry land together were to serve him, the human being, to offer him gifts and bring him tribute.
Then he created and formed the human being in his image and likeness: a rational power, a composite being, a bond in whom all created things are gathered together.
With this purpose, God first created the world, adorned it, and made it splendid.
He filled it and stored up in it every good thing and every variety of things, and then created the human being in the image of his majesty.
At the end of all his creations, like a glorious bridegroom and a beloved son, and a prince of sovereign royalty.
And heir to all the treasures and riches. He established him as lord and ruler, freeborn and exalted.
He entrusted all visible creatures into his hands and placed in his nature intellect, understanding, wisdom, and knowledge, to know hidden things and reveal secret things,
and to understand spiritual things; and, after a time, to renew him and further bestow on him a great and glorious [?], lasting and imperishable,
so that he would become heir to the eternal kingdom. Now a great stillness and silence lay over all the heavenly powers,
and they were in great fear and dread from the time of Satan’s great fall.
While they were still, the elements too were silent in their mingled state, while the earth itself was formless and void,
and darkness was over the surface of the abyss of unformed matter, while the living and life-giving Spirit of God hovered over the surface of the waters.
And suddenly a command and a sovereign gesture went forth from the divine Being. God said, “Let there be light.”
Together with that gesture, light came into being like a swift flash of lightning. That matter was illuminated, with its mingled elements, lying formless and void in a dark state.
Thus was the first form of created substance and the beginning of the ordering of creation.
It was fitting for that eternal and essential Light to begin the ordering of creatures with light.
Darkness did indeed precede the creation of light. Nevertheless, that darkness was not a thing.
Light, however, is a thing, and it was created by the word of God. Darkness is not a thing, nor a creature, nor a being,
but an absence, like an empty place in which there is nothing at all. That emptiness is an absence, not a thing.
Therefore, let those who place darkness before light understand and consider in what manner and sense they should understand it. They are not companions
or equals in definition and nature—light and darkness. Nor is it a case of one thing preceding another, but of nothing preceding something.
This thing is called new and first, not a later thing, because the term “later” is used of something coming after something
equal to it in definition. Light, however, is a first thing, which no other thing preceded.
Therefore darkness has no existence at all and is not called a thing, but the absence of something.
It has therefore been established that, in the creation of this world, light preceded all visible creatures.
And if you say, “But matter itself, that is, the earth itself, preceded this light, since it was created together with heaven itself, that is, the creation of spiritual beings,”
we answer this difficulty by saying that the entire nature of created things was created and came into being in a single instant.
When God created [heaven and earth in the beginning, nothing new at all came into being afterward. God is not] [?], nor does his nature lack anything at all.
Nor is there any reasoning process or other thought at all in his nature. Rather, his thought is one, and his knowledge is perfect and complete, knowing everything before it comes into being.
Everything that was to be created, he created at the very beginning, in a single instant, as Holy Scripture says:
“In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” All the orders of spiritual powers were made and established within “the heavens.”
And the whole nature of humanity, the rest of the living creatures, and all visible things were contained within “the earth,” in that matter compounded from the elements.
And these remained like this for many stretches of time, which God alone knows. When he wished to arrange and order this world,
he took from that very matter and made and fashioned all visible creatures, like a potter who takes from a mixture of clay that has already been kneaded and left to mature,
and fashions many vessels for various uses. This created, material light itself was also concealed and hidden within the elements, in the nature of fire.
And when God commanded that there should be created, material light, it was concealed and hidden within the elements, in the nature of fire.
And when God commanded that there should be light, light revealed itself, and the elements shone [?] from the nature of fire that had been concealed within them.
Now, first you have learned that this light was created, even though the statement that it was created comes after the mixing of matter, when God says that there should be light: this was created,
even though the statement that it was created comes after the mixing of matter, when God says, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
But it had previously been created together with matter, in the nature of fire, which is one of the elements of matter.
Rather, however, the account concerns this world and its arrangement, that is, its ordering.
And this account concerns the arrangement of created things, or is called the ordering of existing things.
But the whole creation was created and completed by a single word, as Holy Scripture says: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” In this statement he included all things
in heaven belonging to the angels, and all things on earth belonging to human beings.
But when the Creator wished to order this visible world and arrange the things within it, from the mixture that already existed, which is matter, namely “the earth,”
the wise architect, master carpenter, and chief craftsman took some and began to arrange existing things and put the world in order.
As the beginning of everything, he made and arranged light. He commanded the nature of light, and it illuminated the elements.
For this reason, light is said to be first among the created things in the arrangement of this world. This is true and certain. Light exists and is spoken of as something.
But darkness is not so at all. It neither exists nor is spoken of as something. Rather, as we have said, it is the absence of light.
It has neither existence nor a distinct reality, since God did not say, “Let there be darkness,” [and there was darkness,]
as he said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. For this reason, light has existence and a distinct reality,
just as goodness and truth also exist and have a definition, existence, a nature, and a distinct reality. But evil is not so at all.
It has neither a definition, nor existence, nor a nature, nor a distinct reality. Rather, it is an intrusion through the absence of goodness.
It then acquires existence, just as darkness is spoken of and recognized through the absence of light, because the light has been hidden.
Otherwise, it does not exist and is not spoken of. Thus it has been established that neither evil nor darkness exists by nature.
Light came first in the creation [?] of this world. As for our practice of beginning in the evening to welcome the day that dawns,
we do well. This is certain and true. We will explain and establish these matters further when their time comes.
“And God said,” it says, “Let there be light, and there was light. And God saw that the light was good.”
“And God separated the light from the darkness.” His separating them means this: when light is visible, there is no darkness.
When a place is deprived of light, it is called darkness. “And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night.”
The whole span of daytime and the whole span of the absence of light, which was called night, were called one day. Now understand,
and consider the glorious order that the wise Creator and illuminator of the worlds created: he began with light in arranging this creation.
He formed this light from the element of fire.
For, as we have said, he made and formed all the creatures in this world from matter that had previously been created.
For he created in a single instant the nature and substance of all things—the spiritual beings in heaven and the bodily beings on earth—as the one who knows everything from the beginning.
This is expressed in the statement of Holy Scripture: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.”
In this sentence he encompassed all the creatures God created. “The heavens” means all the hosts of spiritual beings,
and “the earth” means the matter consisting of the four elements, which had previously been created and laid out like a lump of dough rising.
Now the skilled craftsman began to fashion from it vessels for the needs
of this world's continued existence. First, then, he created light from the element of fire. The light would spread out for about twelve hours,
and then it would withdraw and remain invisible likewise for about twelve hours.
Then it would appear again and give light. In this way the first three days were completed,
until the fourth day, when the sun and the moon and the stars and the moon and the stars were created. With these things the first chapter is completed, through God, who gave strength and help.
Chapter Two of the Fifth Discourse, with God who gives wisdom. On how the heavens were stretched out and what they are,
and what the firmament above us is. After Holy Scripture says, “And there was evening”—this is the end of the daylight of the first day of the week—
“and there was morning, one day.” That is, from the time light was created, it was reckoned as the morning of the first day of the week. This morning is the evening of the second day.
On the morning of the second day, God said, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it separate water from water.”
“And God made the firmament and separated the waters below the firmament from the waters above the firmament. And it was so.”
“And God called the firmament Heaven.” On this second day, God separated the nature of air from the elements and established it in its lofty position.
And it separated the waters below the firmament. These are the elements of water and earth.
They were still mingled with one another. Because of their weight, they remained below and were positioned in the middle of this circle of the firmament.
This place in the middle, the center, was called the lowest part of everything. Air surrounds it on every side, like the white of an egg surrounding the yolk.
And the celestial sphere above the firmament, which is the air, is like the shell of an egg, surrounding everything on the outside.
Within the single revolution that the Creator assigned to the celestial sphere, the firmament was enclosed beneath it. Earth and water, because of their weight, remained in the middle of everything.
Like the yolk of an egg. This place was called the lowest, that is, the innermost part of everything.
Outside it, as mentioned above, is air, surrounding it evenly on every side, like the white of an egg.
Outside this, that is, above it, the fiery ether was placed. Above this is the firmament, that is, the orbits of the celestial sphere.
Above them all, those waters above the heavens were spread out and stretched taut: that blue which is seen above the stars.
These are the waters above the heavens of which Scripture speaks. The Creator arranged them like a curtain.
And like the shell of an egg, which surrounds everything on the outside. Within it, the firmament of air is enclosed like the white.
And the waters below the firmament, together with the earth, are inside everything. These are the upper waters whose interior the Creator opened, arranging this whole universe within it.
He ordained that they should revolve swiftly and rapidly, faster than the speed of lightning,
so that through their swift revolution, like a wheel, they would be compacted and made firm, and would not spill this way and that.
It is like someone taking water in a vessel with a handle, grasping the handle, and swinging it around, up and down.
Through the speed of the revolution, the water is compacted inside that vessel.
Not a single drop of it spills at all. So too the waters above all the firmaments of heaven, through the swift momentum of their rapid revolution,
do not spill at all, but are compacted and made firm at the command of the wise Creator. And through the powerful, swift momentum of the revolution of that upper sea,
the entire region of the celestial sphere revolves along with it, from the boundary of the waters down to the fiery ether above this air that we breathe and that surrounds us.
And that region of the celestial sphere, in which the stars are arranged and ordered, is, I think, a subtle substance.
Some say that the substance of the celestial sphere and the stars is something different, apart from the four elements already mentioned,
and is called a fifth element. But they are not correct, nor does it exist independently.
One reason is that, in the creation of heaven and earth, nothing else was mentioned except heaven and earth.
Another is that, inside the waters and outside the air and fiery ether, there cannot be another substance apart from these.
And another is from the influence that comes upon us from the revolution of the celestial sphere and the aspects of the stars toward one another.
And the extension of their rays into the sphere of the moon, and their transmission toward us through the moon’s own rays.
We have established that the nature of the celestial sphere and of the luminaries within it comes from these elements themselves, and not from some other nature.
We will explain these things again in detail below.
There are also some who say that the nature of the celestial sphere and of the luminaries comes from the element of air alone.
This too is inaccurate, as we will show with the help of God, who guides us.
In this expanse outside—that is, above—the earth, the element of air was separated and stood apart by itself.
It became a channel for the breath of life, to sustain the life of all flesh among the living creatures on earth.
The elements of water and earth, however, were still mingled together, with the expanse of air outside—that is, above—them.
It was called heaven because it is above us. The plural form, “heavens,” was used because the expanse has many spheres.
As we will show. With these words the second chapter is completed, through God, who gave strength and help.
Chapter Three of the Fifth Discourse, with the help of God, who gives wisdom. On what the celestial spheres are like, and how they are bound
to one another, and how many they are. The wise Creator, who created the human being in his image and likeness,
placed intellect, understanding, and knowledge in his nature, so that he might comprehend and know many wonderful and profound things—not only those things that his outward eyes see,

his ears hear, and his hands touch. Rather, through his inward senses he distinguishes and understands hidden and concealed things, through that spiritual nature of his soul, which is free, rational, and capable of knowledge,

and is clear and subtle in its nature. From experience he learns everything, and from visible things he knows hidden things. From the visible creation he comprehends and comes to know the hidden Creator.
In this same way, when the human being examined the revolution of this wonderful celestial sphere, experienced its many variations, and compared them with subtle understanding,
using the intellect he has from his Creator, he clearly grasped the whole wonderful order of the revolution of this glorious celestial sphere.
From the opposing movements and variations that occur in it, we have established that it is not just one sphere, but many.
It is arranged by the wise Creator not in one region, but in many spheres. And these principal ones, which encompass all the spheres,
are two, intertwined and set upon one another. They are also bound to one another in a greatly wonderful way.
Their intertwining and connection with one another do not become entangled; rather, their movement proceeds in order and measure.
Nor do that intertwining and the point of their connection with one another remain in one place.
Rather, it has a hidden law that can be known precisely through nature, measurement, and unchanging number. And this knowledge of the hiddenness
and concealment of something unseen we have learned from many observations of eclipses—that is, the darkenings that happen to the sun and the moon.
We will explain these things clearly below. With these words the third chapter is completed, through God, who gave strength and help.
Chapter Four of the Fifth Discourse, through God who gives wisdom. On whether there is anything hidden in these celestial spheres that is not visible to the eyes.
It certainly exists, and it must be known through experience and study over many periods and a span of years.
We human beings have established with certainty that in these celestial spheres there are boundaries, divisions, places, bonds, and nodes.
We must certainly know them so that we may gain knowledge of times, the cycle of years, and the limits of months, weeks, days, and so forth.
The entire celestial sphere has therefore been divided around its circumference into twelve towers, which are called zodia, that is, signs of the zodiac.
A certain natural activity has been assigned to them, which [?] in these places.
And also from the arrangement of the fixed positions of the stars. These are as follows: first, Aries for Nisan,
the month, because the sun travels through it in the month of Nisan. Second, Taurus for the month of Iyar. Third, Gemini for the month of Haziran.
These belong to the spring season. Fourth, Cancer for the month of Tammuz. Fifth, Leo for the month of Ab.
Sixth, Virgo for the month of Elul. These three, in turn, belong to the summer season. Seventh, [?], that is, the Scales, for the month of First Tishri.
Eighth, Scorpio for the month of Second Tishri. Ninth, Sagittarius for the month of First Kanun. These three, in turn, belong to the autumn season.
Tenth, Capricorn for the month of Second Kanun. Eleventh, Aquarius for the month of Shebat. Twelfth, Pisces for the month of Adar. These three belong to the winter season.
These twelve signs encompass the entire circuit of the celestial sphere's rotation. Their length is measured along the curvature of the celestial sphere.
Their breadth extends from above to below, so as to include all the spheres, that is, the firmaments of heaven.
Above, it extends very widely, but the farther it descends, the narrower and smaller it becomes. It is like the shape of a wheel, whose outer circumference is broad.
The farther it goes inward, the narrower it becomes, until [?] the center, that is, the point in the middle.
Each zodion, that is, sign of the zodiac, has been divided into thirty parts. Each part has been divided into sixty minutes.
Each minute, in turn, has been divided into sixty seconds, and each second into sixty thirds, continuing in this way as far as possible,
because of the immense extent of the celestial sphere. Each sign is also divided into three decans, that is, faces.
Each face, that is, decan, consists of ten parts, that is, degrees. They also divide each sign into five bounds.
The bounds are not equal. There is a bound consisting of eight degrees, that is, parts.
There is a bound consisting of seven degrees, and a bound consisting of six degrees, another of five, and another of four,
as established by the ancients who were highly practiced in calculating the celestial sphere. There are also two places in the celestial sphere
that are bonds, that is, nodes, where two celestial spheres intersect, that is, overlap one another.
The nodes are diametrically opposite one another, positioned evenly opposite one another like a [?]. Between one and the other there are six signs of the zodiac.
That is, portions of those 180 degrees on this side, and likewise six other signs of the zodiac on the other side.
So that half the circuit of the zodiac lies evenly between these nodes. One node is called the dragon’s head, that is,
Anabibazon. The other is the node of the dragon’s tail and is called Catabibazon.
These are essential points in the zodiac that are not visible to the eyes, but are apprehended by the mind, and certainly exist.
When the sun and moon are positioned at one of them in conjunction, an eclipse of the sun occurs.
When the sun is positioned at one and the moon at the other at full moon—that is, when the moon is full—an eclipse of the moon occurs.
We explain these things clearly below. All these things that we have mentioned—that is, the division of the twelve signs of the zodiac,
and that of the decans, that is, the faces, and the boundaries within each sign, and the size of a portion, that is, a degree,

likewise the fine subdivisions and the triplicities, and so forth, and these nodes of the dragon’s head and tail, together with the remaining other points that exist in the zodiac and are not visible—
are not known through eyesight, but are apprehended by the mind.

Through exact and precise calculation they are known and learned accurately, without any error at all. Through gifts and revelations from God, and through experience over a long time, all these things became known to human beings.
It was absolutely necessary that they should be known, because times, years, months, and the changes of winter, summer, spring, and autumn are ordered according to them.
Otherwise, human beings would have passed their days like irrational animals, without knowledge of times and seasons.
With these things the fourth chapter is completed, through God who gave strength and help.
Chapter 5
The fifth chapter of the fifth discourse, with God who grants wisdom.
On how many firmaments, or regions, the celestial sphere has. Glory to him, the Creator and wise Orderer of the worlds and created things.
For everything that he created and established in his wisdom, full of distinctions and abounding in great wonders, represents something and [?] a hidden mystery within it.
In all the mysteries, patterns, natures, elements, worlds, and created things, visible and invisible, his power is active and his wisdom is seen, and they proclaim his glory to one another.
Just as he established in heaven ten orders of spiritual beings, powers and commanders of powers, so he divided and marked out the celestial sphere above us into ten regions.
Each is called a heaven, and the one above it, the heaven of heavens. The waters above them all are called the waters above the heavens,
that is, the waters above the firmaments. He arranged them into three firmaments, with three regions in each firmament.
In each region there is a numbered multitude of stars. But in the tenth they are without number and invisible because of their lofty elevation.
Above them all is that great, boundless sea, representing the exalted, boundless, and unlimited divinity.
First, beyond the air that surrounds us, that is, above
Above our heads is the fiery ether that separates us from the firmaments above. The first quarter, that of the moon, contains three ordered spheres.
The first is the one in which the moon travels, corresponding to the order of angels in the first rank.
The second is the one in which the planet Hermes travels, who is Nebo, that is, Utarid. It corresponds to the order of archangels.
The third is the one in which the planet Belti travels—Aphrodite, that is, Zuhara.
It corresponds to the order of principalities. The second firmament, which is the middle one, belongs to the sun, like the middle assembly of spiritual beings.
In its first sphere, which is the fourth, the sun travels. It corresponds to the order of authorities.
The second, which is the fifth, is the one in which Karig [?] travels, who is Ares, Mirrikh. It corresponds to the order of powers.
The third sphere of this middle firmament, which is the sixth sphere, is the one in which Bel travels, who is Zeus, that is, Mushtari.
It corresponds to the order of dominions. As for the third firmament, called that of Cronus, Cronus travels in its first sphere, which is the seventh.
It corresponds to the order of thrones. In the second sphere, which is the eighth, the bright stars travel, numbering one thousand one hundred and twenty.
It corresponds to the order of cherubim [?], with their many luminous eyes. The third, which is the ninth sphere,
is where those higher stars travel that cannot be numbered. It corresponds to the order of the six-winged seraphim.
Above these is the tenth firmament, called the zodiac. It contains stars without number and without limit.
Because of their exceedingly great height, they are concealed and can be seen only as a pale glow, like a thin cloud,
like that whiteness seen in the Milky Way. This high firmament bears a very close resemblance—
the tenth [?], the zodiac—to that exalted order of the morning star who fell.
He was above all his companions and was the crown of the ten—that is, the completion of the ten—for he was the crown of the other nine beneath him
and the one who completed their number. Just as, to our knowledge, the higher stars in the zodiac have neither limit nor number,
so we do not know the quantity or number of the powers in the rebel's order. And just as these higher stars are dim and cannot be seen
except as something like a pale cloud, so too those hostile powers
became dim and were darkened, deprived of the light of divine knowledge. And just as the Milky Way appears like a sort of rift in the firmament of the zodiac,
so heaven, in which they had been stationed and stood, was torn open, and they fell like lightning into the lowest Sheol of the outer darkness of ignorance.
Above these ten spheres and firmaments of the heavens and the heavens of heavens,
nothing further is known except that great, limitless, boundless sea of waters
above the firmaments [?], which depicts and symbolizes the greatness, exaltedness, and limitlessness of the eternal Being.
And if no boundary or limit is known for the great sea, the Ocean, although it certainly has an end and a boundary, since it is bounded within the air,
and limited by the earth, then that indescribable sea which surrounds everything beyond the entire extent of the firmaments of heaven and the regions of the zodiac,
and is situated in that exalted and invisible height—how great, then, is its vastness! How boundless it is! It cannot be limited at all.
It cannot be measured, comprehended, or bounded. It has neither end nor limit. It is that abyss above which cannot be conceived,
a lofty and exalted depth which human knowledge cannot comprehend at all. And if this sea, although it is created,
merely portrays an image of the greatness of that adorable, uncreated, and eternal Being, then that Being, the essence of [?], exalted and hidden and above every mind and thought—
how astonishing is its incomprehensibility! How glorious is its exaltation! How knowledge is bewildered by investigating it!
How all minds are astonished and all thoughts bewildered by the impossibility of investigating the thought of its boundlessness!
Great is our Lord and greatly to be praised. The nature of the eternal Being cannot be investigated. It cannot be comprehended or conceived. It cannot be measured at all.
It cannot be limited at all. It cannot be expressed at all. Rather, let it be honored and praised in silence. With these words the fifth chapter ends, through God, who gave life and helped.
Chapter six of the fifth discourse, with God who grants wisdom. On what the sun, the moon, and the rest of the stars are; from what they came into being; what their nature is;
how they are arranged; what their usefulness is; where their places are; and what their activity and their entire governing order are.
In the account of creation, the creation of trees, plants, and seeds precedes the creation of the stars.
The appearance of dry land, the separation of the waters to one side, and the basins of the seas were likewise arranged earlier, before the lights appeared.
But since we began from above to explain each of the things that came into being and the arrangements of created things,
and have spoken about the firmaments of heaven and the circuit of the zodiac, we should next take up the entire arrangement and governing order of the zodiac
and speak about the lights arranged in it. Then we will explain and speak about the things below the firmament, and about the [?] within this air.
Then, when we reach the earth in this same sequence, we will speak about it and everything within it and upon its surface, as divine grace grants us wisdom.
First, let us set down the holy words of Scripture concerning how the lights and stars were created.
Then we will speak about them. And God said, “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to separate day from night.
Let them serve as signs and for seasons, days, and years, so that they may shine in the firmament of heaven and give light upon the earth,
and rule over day and night.” And it was so. God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day,
and the smaller light to rule the night, and the stars. God placed them in the firmament of heaven to give light upon the earth,
to rule over day and night, and to separate light from darkness. And God saw that it was good.
For we have already said above that divine Scripture speaks with us as with children, telling us things that we can hear, understand, and know.
And look: it recounts all these things and tells us that the living God said, “Let [?] be, and let [?] be.”
That it happened in this way, with one created thing being formed and then another after it—we should not understand it this way.
Rather, they were all created, formed, and brought into being in a single instant—all these things that we could scarcely recount in a million years through an explanation spoken by mouth,
or understand and know by hearing with our ears. In God's mind they exist in reality, complete and finished in a single instant.
With a single gesture he gave the command when he wished, and all created things came into being and stood there, formed, finished, and complete.
And in the nature of his being there is no duality, nor any number at all, nor any before and after.
Rather, he knows them all together, both those that have already come into being and those that will come into being forever, with their measure, number, quality, and quantity.
But for us human beings, it is not at all possible to know these things

except over a long period of time, measuring, taking their capacity, and counting in sequence—one, two, three—in numerical order, and hearing the account in a lengthy discourse, one word at a time and sentence after sentence.
It is like someone who is in a very large house full of different things, and it is dark as night.
Suddenly the light of a lamp enters the house. As he looks around, he sees many things and wants to tell others what he has seen throughout the house.
But he cannot describe as quickly what he saw in a single instant. Instead, he recounts one thing at a time.
After every one or two sentences he speaks, he rests, catches his breath, and draws breath. Then he speaks again.
Likewise, the listeners cannot hear everything all at once, but only as it is recounted in sequence, word after word.
So too holy Scripture speaks with them in sequence, as things can be spoken and heard. And those things that came into being and were formed in a single instant
it is compelled to teach us over a long period of time. Think in this way about all these things that it says about God.
Again, then, we ought to learn from where and how human beings were able to comprehend, know, and learn precisely the law

of the stars, the order of the circuit of the constellations, their natures and influences, and the rest of the knowledge concerning these things that are high above and exist in the firmaments of heaven,
at the distant limits and in the depths below. Could all these rational branches of knowledge, these astonishing forms of wisdom,
and this magnificent skill have been learned without divine activity? Certainly not!
The nature of created beings cannot possibly comprehend and know these things without the gift of divine Wisdom, which herself [?], made, and formed all created things,
and placed in human nature a rational and intelligent soul capable of receiving knowledge about all these things.

And the human being is truly called, and truly is, the image and likeness of his Creator, since it has been placed in his nature to comprehend and investigate knowledge about everything that has existed, exists, and is yet to come into being.
And all these things are learned through constant experience and practice.
The learning and knowledge of the entire law of the stars were discovered by the Babylonian Arameans, that is, the Chaldeans, who live in the southeast of the inhabited world.
For all the land in their regions is sandy, and the paths and roads leading from region to region and from city to city cannot be recognized,
or from village to village, because the winds blow and obliterate the paths with that loose, scattered sand. That region is also very hot, and the sun scorches it during the day.
The inhabitants of that region—that land—are forced to walk and travel from place to place at night, so that they will not be scorched by the sun’s intensity.
Because there is no clearly marked path to be seen, they take the stars as their guides and travel by them wherever they wish.
Through their constant observation of the stars throughout all the changing seasons of the year, they began to learn something of the laws governing their courses and movements.
And so, little by little, through persistence over a long time, they learned the entire system and circuit of the zodiac.
In that eastern region there was a man among the descendants of Noah’s sons called Joniton.
Through his understanding, this man withdrew and chose a quiet life for himself. He went and lived alone in a desolate wilderness, quiet and free from every sound and every distraction.

He constantly watched the expanses of heaven and studied the stars and the luminaries that mark the changing seasons. He was filled with great wonder and praised the wise Creator who ordered all these things.
And so, through his stillness and solitude, and his separation from all the noises, sounds, and turmoil of the world,
and through his freedom from every occupation and the serenity of his heart, free from all concerns, through his constant observation of the zodiac and his study of the stars, there was given
to him the gift of knowledge concerning the entire system of the stars and the circuit of the zodiac.
From time to time, people from that region would come to him individually and receive enlightenment and instruction from him about such matters.
They would write down and record these observations and matters in a book, as a reminder and a source of knowledge, so that they would not be forgotten.
Thus, little by little, they learned the entire system of the stars, which is called astronomy in Greek.
As time passed, they gained still more knowledge, because they constantly observed the zodiac and studied the stars.
Because they did not yet have any other field of study apart from constantly watching the zodiac, those Chaldeans learned the art.
They recorded in books the movements and courses of the stars, their effects and natures, and the whole system governing them:
how they were created and ordered by the wise Creator to serve as signs and to mark seasons, distinguishing times and their changes,
according to the particular property placed in their nature, by which they act, like the rest of creation.
Afterward, time passed, and corrupt people arose whose minds were corrupted through ignorance and the influence of demons. They went astray concerning the stars and mistook one thing for another.
They imagined that the stars were rational beings and possessed freedom and self-determination.
Little by little, Satan led them astray until they imagined that the stars were creators and makers.
They gave each one of them the name of a god and began to serve and worship them, setting up statues in their names and placing images on walls and columns.
They set up likenesses of them, poured out offerings to them, burned fragrant incense before them, and offered sacrifices.
Satan too would sometimes speak through one or another of these images, misleading people through them, announcing future events to them and revealing hidden things.
He would hasten to proclaim news of things that had happened in distant places. He would put a thought into their hearts and reveal it to someone else.
By such things he has misled many people down to the present day. But discerning people, firmly grounded in the knowledge of the truth,
are not deceived at all. Instead, they know them precisely as they are—that is, in their actual order, nature, and properties,
and in the condition in which the Creator created, fashioned, and arranged them: what they are and why they exist.
That is, to serve as signs and mark seasons, to give light by day and by night, to bring about changes in the air, to make crops grow, and to ripen fruit,
and to bring about many changes in the earth’s natural condition. These and similar things the Creator naturally placed and fixed in them as characteristics and properties,
as with the rest of creation—trees, fruits, roots, soils, and stones—and not through their own will.
Nor are they rational beings in another sense, namely, because they submit to divine commands and obey his will.
Rather, this applies to all created things: living things, rational and irrational beings, and solid and insensible things.
Everything in creation acknowledges the Creator and submits to his command. Truly, their created form is beautiful, and their place is exalted and glorious.
Through the unchanging character of their laws and their course over these many thousands of years, they are known to have a nature that is exceedingly glorious, clear, and pure.
Their created form is exceedingly beautiful. Nevertheless, they are created and made things. Their nature contains properties that never change, not through an act of will, but by nature,

like trees, roots, stones, and soils, in the nature of each of which God placed a particular property and an action directed toward something, to meet the needs and requirements of the world’s continued existence.
Moreover, there is the great mystery of God’s foreknowledge: God concealed in their nature hidden knowledge and indications of things that are going to happen,
whether in the air and the firmament, or on the earth, and among bodily kinds [?], or in the bodies of rational human beings.
God also placed in them certain profound indications of things he knew beforehand, just as he knows everything that is going to happen,
whether in people’s deeds, words, or thoughts, according to their own will, through the exercise of their freedom and their control over themselves.

He knew these things beforehand as the one who knows everything, not as things done under compulsion. He placed knowledge of them in the nature and properties of the stars. And for those who are discerning and wise in divine truth,
these indications show and disclose the greatness of God’s wisdom and his foreknowledge.
They do not negate human freedom and control over oneself. Listen, then, to how this is so. Suppose someone says that a certain person was born at a certain time.
Those trained in this discipline of astronomy look and examine it. They learned it through experience and constant practice over a long time, and [?] from it the calculation of this knowledge,
that this person is going to be such and such. Some of the things they indicate concern his body, such as conditions and distinguishing marks,
complexion, large size, small size, quickness, slowness, firmness, flabbiness, strength, weakness,
beauty, ugliness, shrewdness, simplicity, sharpness of mind, confusion of mind, and strong desire.
And modesty, excessive anger, [and cowardice,] courage, arrogance, contempt, and foolishness.
And simplicity, and many similar things that arise from the body's temperaments. He has learned these things accurately through experience.
But knowledge belonging to the soul—that is, the will, which is the movement of freedom and self-determination—
whether he attends to and governs all these things rationally, and not like livestock or wild animals;

and whether he conducts himself as a rational human being and recognizes his dignity and the excellence of his nature, created and made in the image of his Lord and the likeness of his Maker, dealing with all these things rationally and according to
his Lord's will—or rather, conducting himself and thinking as is right for everyone. He restrains desire and calms anger,
humbles arrogance, gives wisdom to foolishness, and subdues the body's agitation, along with the rest of these things.
But if he is negligent and gives these passions what they demand, he becomes like the rest of the livestock and wild animals that have no reason.
The body is composed of the elements and is subject to astral fate.
For this reason, all these incidental and natural conditions are imprinted upon it by astral fate itself.
But the soul's nature does not consist of the elements that are subject to astral fate.
Rather, it is above and beyond astral fate and the material elements: something spiritual, pure, and subtle, like the nature of spiritual beings.
It knows and commands astral fate and subjects the elements to itself; they do not subject it to themselves, because it is not bound beneath a material composition made from them.
Therefore, thoughts, movements of free will, and words that come out of the heart through the movement of the tongue,
through the combination of sounds, and the actions of the hands performed voluntarily and rationally—through which sin and righteousness are judged—
these belong to the self-determination of the rational and intelligent soul, and not to the conditions affecting the body, a composite living creature.
But because the soul is bound and joined to the body, it is drawn along with it into its fears, and everything belonging to the body is also said to belong to the soul.
For the soul is its governor, like a charioteer governing a horse; the body does not govern the soul.
Likewise, a horse cannot force the will of the charioteer who holds its reins, even if the horse tries to leap this way and that according to its nature.
But the charioteer, because he holds its reins, does not let [it go. And if he lets it go] and is negligent, it leaps over some mound
or off a cliff, and both of them fall and are broken. The charioteer is held responsible for the entire disaster.
Think of the soul in the same way. Again, we reveal another mystery before those who discern the truth. Tell me, brother:
Everything that a human being who will be born after a hundred years, or a thousand, or more, is going to do, or say, or think—
does God know all these things beforehand or not? Certainly he knows them all before they happen. And how can we know them?
We know these things from the revelations of prophecy, which is given freely by grace to individuals for the arrangements of divine governance.
Or from its companion, prophecy, which is given and becomes known after much effort, practice, and learning.
It is hidden in the knowledge of the stars by the will of the Creator, who is wise and exalted in foreknowledge.
But it is not because God knew beforehand what a person would do or what would happen to him, and made these things known,
through the movements of the stars, as astrologers determine beforehand
and announce what is to come, that these things must necessarily happen by compulsion.
Rather, because they were certainly going to happen through the exercise of freedom and self-determination, voluntarily and not by compulsion,
he who knows everything, rules everything, and can do everything knew them beforehand. And where he wishes, he allows freedom to fulfill its will,
as he knows in the depth of his unfathomable judgments. And if you say, “The Lord does whatever he wishes, and changes and abolishes things,
and strikes and heals, and gives life and puts to death,” it is true that this is so. But he does not only now will these things.
He has already willed everything that he wills, and all these things are complete and fulfilled in his mind. He does not only now consider
and then will something, as we do in our limitations, since at every moment we think of something new, will it, and carry it out.
Far be it from that knowledge, wise in everything that has happened or occurred in creation, or is still happening or [?],
whether in deed, in word, or in thought, not to know these things perfectly, as though they had already happened, even before the foundations of the world.
Everything that he has willed, from the beginning of the creation of the worlds forever and ever, is complete and fulfilled in his knowledge,
and is not new. There is absolutely nothing new to that perfect knowledge, wise in everything.
Even if someone changes his thoughts tens of thousands of times in a single day, and tens of thousands of times sins and turns back in repentance, and becomes rich and becomes poor,
and does something and regrets it, God knew all these things beforehand perfectly, just as they happened. Nothing at all escapes his knowledge.
So those who say that the Lord does whatever he wishes, and abolishes and changes things as he pleases, are not thereby exalting God.
Rather, they greatly diminish that complete and perfect greatness: he is still forming wishes, like children who want something today,
and tomorrow abandon it, learn something else, and want something different. Far be it! So the message of the stars and the indications that the Creator placed in their nature do not abolish freedom.
Rather, they establish and confirm it. They announce beforehand whatever freedom is going to do through its own self-determination.
The same is true of the changes that happen to a person, whether voluntary or forced,
whether accidental or natural, throughout the whole span of his life. The Creator placed certain signs in their nature that announce these things beforehand.
It is not because this is in the nature of the stars that it is necessarily fated to happen, as we have said many times. Rather, because it was going to happen in
every case through the choice of free will, the Creator knew it beforehand and placed it in their nature.
Just as, then, we know that winter is coming, and that there will be rain and cold, snow and ice during it, and that afterward spring will come,
and then summer and intense heat: these things certainly do not happen because of our foreknowledge.
Rather, because they are certain to happen, we recognize them beforehand from experience as things that are going to happen.
An even greater example is that of sailors and seafarers who observe the atmosphere days in advance,
and, through certain signs they possess, which they have previously learned from experience over time,
know beforehand and announce changes in the weather, the blowing of the wind, clouds, storms, and the sea’s calmness and agitation.
It is not because they predict and decree these things that they must inevitably happen under compulsion.
Rather, because they are certainly going to happen naturally, they have known them beforehand, predicted them, and announced them from experience.
Again, suppose a gardener has thousands of trees in his garden, and someone comes to him in winter, when the trees are stripped of leaves and fruit,
and are dark and ugly to look at, like dry sticks. The gardener explains to that person the characteristics of the different kinds of trees:
that this one will bear white figs, this one black figs, this one red figs, and this one sweet pomegranates,
and this one sour ones, this one soft ones, this one [?], this one apples, and this one [?].
And this one peaches. He explains the kind of fruit and its varieties, its differences, its color, smell, and taste,
and its size, whether large or small, and its quantity, whether abundant or scanty. And when the fruiting season comes,
everything certainly happens and comes to fulfillment just as the gardener announced beforehand. Now, these things did not happen because the gardener knew and decreed them beforehand.
Rather, because they were certain to happen naturally, he knew them beforehand from experience.
The matter of the stars is the same. Because a person is going to do this or that by his own will and through the exercise of his freedom,
or because things will otherwise happen to him through compulsion, nature, or chance, the wise Creator knew beforehand and placed certain signs in their nature.
But there is no randomness at all—that is, no lack of discrimination. Nothing happens randomly; rather, everything is under God’s care, command, and governance.
Not even a single leaf falls from a tree, nor does a single hair fall from a person, an animal, or a bird,
without God’s knowledge and care. God’s care, governance, and foreknowledge do not abolish freedom.
Rather, they all the more confirm, demonstrate, and establish freedom. Likewise, the sign of foreknowledge
that God placed in the nature of the stars does not abolish either of these:
neither freedom nor providence. Rather, they all bear witness to one another, confirm one another, and establish one another.
The foreknowledge contained in the stars confirms and bears witness that freedom truly possesses authority over itself, in the image and likeness of the Creator.
And astrology knows beforehand, like prophecy, what free will is going to do within its own domain of authority, and nothing else.
And both bear witness to and confirm divine providence and its governance, which is wise in everything, through which they stand, move, and exist.
The world does not proceed and conduct its course by chance or spontaneously. And the fact that divine providence sometimes constrains free will,
or prevents it from fulfilling its will, although it greatly desires and is fully prepared to act as it wishes,
and sometimes allows it to [?] and fulfill its will as it desires—this confirms both, namely, free will and providence.
Otherwise, if free will always carried out its will, this would be thought to be an inherent property of it,
rather than something voluntary. Everything would be a matter of chance and happen of its own accord, rather than under the Lord’s providence.
But when free will is sometimes constrained and sometimes not, this wonderfully and clearly makes known that both exist with sovereign authority.
Nevertheless, both the fact that free will is constrained from time to time and the fact that it is sometimes allowed to fulfill its will,
are all known beforehand, complete, and fulfilled in God’s foreknowledge:
when providence allows free will to fulfill its will, and when it constrains it and does not allow it.
And, as the one who knows everything, he placed indications of all these things beforehand in the nature of the stars.
And the foreknowledge of the stars confirms free will and providence. It is not because it announces beforehand those things that are already known,
and are still going to happen in actuality through free will and providence, that it has [?] become primary.
Rather, free will precedes all these things, and providence follows free will.
Sometimes it constrains it, and sometimes it does not. The foreknowledge in the stars comes last of them all, concerning things that are going to happen in any event.
And it announces them beforehand, like prophecy. Again, it is not because prophecy foretells future events that they necessarily happen and are carried out because of it.
Rather, because they are going to happen in any event according to God’s incomprehensible judgments,
prophecy knows them beforehand and announces them. And when prophecy has sometimes failed and has not stood,
