this happened so that free will and providence might be confirmed, not because prophecy is untrue or in any way deceptive.
This was already known in God’s foreknowledge: where prophecy was going to be nullified and would neither stand
nor be fulfilled. Sometimes free will, too, nullified prophecy, as in the case of King Hezekiah.
And sometimes providence nullified both free will and prophecy, as in the case of Jonah and Nineveh.
God knew all these things beforehand, that they would happen in this way. And the knowledge that he placed in the nature of the stars,
which announces future events beforehand, encompasses all these things and is never nullified, constrained, or brought to failure.
For what is natural inevitably happens and is fulfilled, like winter, which is inevitably going to come.
And summer too, and trees inevitably producing particular kinds and varieties of fruit, and things like these.
And not voluntary things, such as free will and providence. For it reveals the things that are inevitably going to happen,
and not those that are prevented by free will or providence. Those things that are prevented and never happen at all are not counted as anything,
but as nothing, because they did not come about, did not happen, and do not exist.
As for the character of prayer that truly is prayer and rightly bears that name: it is a second God.
It commands like a king and acts with authority. The power of prayer is great and beyond expression. It compels the will and nullifies freedom [?].
It changes natures and creates new things. In short, like God, it has authority over everything, to speak and bring it into being.
Prayer also commands the heavenly powers like a master—that prayer which truly possesses the qualities proper to prayer.
The conscience of the person offering it bears witness to it through courageous confidence, without any wavering of mind at all.
This prayer commands the zodiac, and it slows down; the luminaries are restrained in the speed of their course. Indeed, it says, “Sun, stand still in Gibeon,
and moon, in the valley of Aijalon,” and so forth. And, “As the Lord lives, before whom I stand, there will be neither rain nor dew upon the earth until I say so.”
Such confidence and courage are bestowed upon the heart by pure and true prayer.
Again we ask: did God know beforehand the things he was going to do through Moses the Great, Joshua son of Nun, and Elijah the Zealous,
and for King Hezekiah and the Ninevites, and things like these, or not? Certainly they were in his knowledge before the world came into being,
exactly as they happened. Yet it was not because God knew beforehand that they were going to happen that they necessarily happened under compulsion.
Rather, because they were inevitably going to happen, whether through free will
or through providence, by compulsion or voluntarily, by chance or by nature,
the one who knows everything knew them beforehand, as though they had already happened and passed away. Now understand it this way: these very things,
these things that happen, are said to precede God's knowledge, even though his knowledge knew them beforehand.
But it knew them beforehand as things that were going to happen, so that ignorant people who deny free will might not be emboldened.
And hence, all the things that are going to happen, whether through human free will or through divine providence,
whether through nature or through what is regarded as chance, or through the purpose of prayer, God certainly knew them beforehand.

And if he also placed signs of all these very things in the nature of the stars, so that discerning people might learn from them the exact details of everything, is that a great matter, or something objectionable,
or does it conflict at all with the knowledge of the truth? I do not think so. And if you say that the Lord can change natures and the seasons of summer and winter,
And I believe that he can do whatever he wishes, and things greater and more numerous than these.
But before any of these things came into being, he knew beforehand that he would change and do such and such. He did not newly conceive of doing them as though he had lacked knowledge of them.
Everything is complete and perfect in God's knowledge. He never newly wills anything that he did not already know by his very being.
Let whoever reads these things understand, and let him not attribute deficiency, inadequacy, or weakness,
or inability, to that blessed, perfect, and complete nature of the eternal and sovereign Being.
And if he cannot clearly understand this depth of meaning and subtlety of thought, let him acknowledge his own ignorance and not blaspheme the incomprehensible greatness,
thinking that, as a believer, he is glorifying God by saying, "There is no fate; rather, the Lord does whatever he wishes, changing and abolishing such and such."
O you who are wise in your own eyes! He does not now will anything that he did not know beforehand and will from eternity.
Rather, he has willed everything that he will ever will, and everything is settled, complete, and perfect in his knowledge.

And God's will did not precede events so that such and such should happen by compulsion and inevitably, as though we should suppose a fate that abolishes freedom. Rather, because whatever the event might be was going to happen,
whether through free will or through providence, as we have said at length, the one who knows everything knew these things beforehand and placed signs of them in the nature of the stars.
And he granted true knowledge of them to the wise and discerning, so that they too might know them accurately beforehand,
and make them known to others, and all become witnesses to God's foreknowledge. This knowledge resembles prophecy,
as we said above. And does prophecy, because it foretells and makes future events known beforehand, therefore abolish free will
and establish fate? Far from it! Rather, because these things are going to happen, whether through free will or through providence,
it knows them beforehand through divine knowledge and foretells them. Free will confirms providence, and providence confirms free will.
And true knowledge of the stars confirms God's foreknowledge. And the foreknowledge
of God confirms all these things and abolishes none of them.
From chapter six. On why some stars are called good and others evil,
although they have no free will; why they are called wanderers; and why all religious communities have warned against and forbidden the study of them.
As for some of them being called good and others evil, this is the reason.
First, we say that they do not have free will to do good or harm by their own choice.
Rather, it is because of their nature that they have been named good and evil. Listen to how this is so; pay attention and understand.
Everything that preserves the continued existence of this world, such as life, health, a favorable balance of the air, abundant crops, and plentiful fruit,
is called, and truly is, its good. And everything that is destructive and ruinous,
Such as death, unhealthy air, the spoiling of fruit, the destruction of crops, and things like these.
These are the evil of this world. Other injuries, such as illnesses and minor losses,
are called harms. Through experience we have learned and become certain about the nature of these four elements that sustain this world:
that everything among all the natural things in the world that has a body, and all animal flesh [?].
For example, the element of air, which is warm and moist, is the sustenance and breath of life. Whenever the air remains pure in its nature,
which is warm and moist, it produces a well-balanced constitution, health, life, and the preservation of crops and fruit throughout creation.
But when certain vapors rising from the earth mix with it,
or the smell of decay and mildew from varieties of plants, seeds, and herbs growing in water, such as [?], [?], rice, and millet—because water remains continually over them,
they produce decay and mildew, and their smell mixes with the air, corrupting its nature and causing illnesses, swellings, jaundice, and much destruction.
Again, the element—that is, the nature—of earth is cold and dry.
When it remains by itself, without any of the elements of water or air mixing with it,
it destroys the life of every body buried in it. Likewise, everything that is cold and dry produces death.
The nature of death is cold and dry, because it is the opposite of what is warm and moist,
which is the nature of life. We have therefore become certain that what is warm and moist, producing life, is a good thing and is called good.
Likewise, what is cold and dry, producing death, is an evil thing and is called evil.
But those things that are mixtures of these natures, such as what is warm and dry or moist and cold,
produce neither death nor life, but they do produce illnesses. For this reason they were named
harmful natures. And through experience over a very long time, we human beings have learned about these stars:
that some of them are warm and moist by nature, such as Zeus and Aphrodite.
They called them good by nature, not by their own choice. Cronus is cold and dry, and they called him evil.
Ares, however, is warm and dry, and they called him a harm, that is, harmful. As for the sun and the moon,
because they sustain all the genera and species of natural things in creation, they called them rulers and governors.
For the sun warms and ripens, and dries up the decay and rottenness caused by excessive moisture, as well as mildew. The moon, in turn, moistens, irrigates, and makes natural things grow,
and, as it were, waters them and cools them from the excessive heat they have acquired from the intensity of the sun’s rays.
And again, those things that become excessively moist from the moon’s rays, the sun in turn purifies, dries, and warms.
And through these activities of these two great lights, all the natural kinds in creation grow, are sustained, and are preserved.
For this reason they called them rulers and lords; also because the sun is greater and more glorious than all the stars.
And the moon, because it is the lowest of all the lights and close to the earth, and its rays spread out and act upon creation.
Its nature is cold and moist. But it has no light or rays by its own nature; rather, its light comes from the sun.
Its nature mixes with the nature of the sun, or of one of the stars that casts rays upon it.
Thus its rays act in a mixed manner. And if you ask how the nature of the stars was tested and became known,
we say that it was from their rays. And as for how their rays became known, listen. We have observed that when the stars face the moon or one another,
in conjunction—that is, their joining one another, when two or more are situated in a single degree—
or when they are in sextile, which is a sixth, or square, which is a fourth,
that is, when there are three signs between them, a quarter of the zodiac; or in trine, which is a triangular configuration,
that is, a third of the zodiac, which is four signs; or in opposition, which means that half the zodiac lies between them,
that is, six signs—when, then, they face one another in these configurations,
they cast their rays upon one another. And when they face the moon and cast rays upon it,
the moon’s own rays, received from the light of the sun, spread over created things and act according to the nature of the star that faces the moon and casts its rays upon it.
If it is one star, they act according to its nature; if two or more, they act in a mixed manner. There is much to say about these things.
But indeed, it was from configurations and effects like these that human beings came to understand the natures of the stars.
They called some of them good, some bad, and some harmful. And when the rays of the good and bad stars mix,
and are cast upon the moon and spread over creation, because they mix in the air, they are called mixed.
As for the star of Nabu, which is Hermes, that is, Mercury, the Creator made it a marvel in its nature: it is mixed.
And according to the nature of whatever star has its rays mixed with it, its own nature also becomes like the nature of that star.
This is the reason they are called good and bad: because of the properties the Creator placed in their natures,
as with all the other natural kinds—that is, trees, fruits, roots, stones, soils, and the other kinds of things—
whose ability to do good, that is, to help, and whose ability to do evil, that is, to harm, lies in their nature,
and not in their will, that is, the exercise of their freedom. For they do not possess these things, because they are not rational beings or masters of themselves,
but bound and subject natures, appointed for signs, seasons, and indications, like the rest of created things.
Each one was established for a purpose, and the Maker laid down a law for them, with order, regularity, measure, and permanence.
It never passes away or changes. Thus he established them forever and ever. As for their being called wanderers, this is what it means.
Everything that moves and travels is called a wanderer—not because it goes astray, but because it travels straight ahead.
For example, someone might say, “So-and-so is wandering in such-and-such a desert,” meaning that he is traveling and moving [?] straight ahead without turning back.
These are the seven stars called wanderers: the sun, the moon, Cronus, Zeus, Ares, Aphrodite, and Hermes.
Because they continually travel and move through the zodiac straight ahead without turning back, they are called wanderers.
For they wander, as the saying goes—that is, they travel eastward without ever reversing direction, while the zodiac passes, or revolves, westward.
These stars, however, wander and travel through it in the opposite direction, straight ahead—that is, eastward.
Because the revolution of the zodiac is swift and very rapid, the axle of its sphere revolves quickly. But each of the stars, according to the breadth
of the circuit of its sphere within the axle of the zodiac [?], completes its course.
The moon, because its circuit is narrow and it lies inside all the stars—that is, below them, above the fiery ether—
travels, moves, and passes around, or circles, the entire zodiac in thirty days.
The circuit of Hermes is above the moon, and it travels, or revolves, around the entire sphere of the zodiac in six months.
Aphrodite, or Beltis, who is the morning star, has her circuit above Hermes. She revolves around it in more than eight months.
But because the sun’s rays have a certain influence from these two stars, Hermes and Aphrodite, they continually travel with the sun.
Sometimes they are ahead of it in the west at evening, or again behind it in the east, appearing at dawn.
Aphrodite can never move farther from the sun than a zodiacal sign and a half [?]. Hermes, however, moves only as far as twenty-five parts, or degrees, from the sun.
There is a certain power in the sun’s rays that turns them back toward it.
As we said, sometimes they are ahead of the sun and appear in the evening in the west, and sometimes, again, they are behind it
and appear at dawn. These three are below the sun: Aphrodite, Hermes, and the moon.
These other three—Ares, Zeus, and Cronus—are above the sun, that is, Aphrodite, Hermes, and the moon.
These other three—Ares, Zeus, and Cronus—are above the sun. Whenever the sun moves away from one of these three upper stars,
four zodiacal signs ahead of it, the sun casts rays upon it from a trine and turns it backward. Thus it remains turned backward,
that star, until the sun travels through another four zodiacal signs. Then it again casts rays upon that retrograde star from behind it,
from a western trine. Then that star resumes its forward course and travels according to its appointed order, by the will of its Creator.
As for the sun, the reckoning of years and seasons is based on it. It produces winters and summers and the other changes.
For every three hundred and sixty-five and a quarter revolutions of the zodiac, the sun makes one circuit of the whole zodiac.
That is, it passes through each zodiacal sign in thirty days. A day, however, is one revolution of the entire sphere of the zodiac.
During this revolution of the entire circumference, the sun advances one division, that is, one degree.
Every four years, that quarter is accumulated and becomes one complete day.
It is added to the days of February, and that year has 366 days and is called a leap year.
Ares, which travels above the sun in the fifth orbit, or firmament, traverses the whole sphere of the zodiac
in eighteen months, which are a year and a half. As for Zeus, since its sphere is wider—for the higher one goes, that is, the farther outward, the wider the sphere—
it travels in the sixth firmament and circles, that is, crosses, the whole zodiac in twelve years,
each zodiacal sign in one year. As for Cronus, which travels in the seventh circuit, its firmament is very extensive and wide.
It traverses the whole sphere of the zodiac in thirty years. That is, it spends two and a half years in each zodiacal sign.
The distance that the moon travels in its own circuit in one day, Cronus travels in one year, because of the breadth of its circuit.
In the eighth firmament, the one above Cronus, travel the bright stars, which number one thousand one hundred and twenty.
Because their circuit is so wide, it takes seventy years to traverse one division, which is one degree: one of the thirty divisions of a zodiacal sign.
The ninth circuit is exceedingly wide because of its height, that is, its outward position.
Along the circumference of the sphere of the zodiac, the stars in it barely [?] one division, that is, one degree, in a hundred years.
So that circuit of the crown of the zodiacal signs, in which tiny stars appear like whitish clouds,
is vastly wider and greater! Yet the movement of the stars, each in its own circuit, is swifter than a whirlwind.
How great, then, is the [?] of the breadth of the outer circumference of this sphere of the zodiac! It cannot be measured or calculated.
For the stars, which fly like a whirlwind, do not traverse one of the 366 divisions of the whole sphere in a hundred years.
In how many thousands of years, then, would they traverse its entire extent, if the world were to endure and not pass away?
In thirty-six thousand years they would barely traverse the entire extent of the ninth circuit of the zodiac. How much greater and wider, then, is the tenth!
The human mind cannot comprehend it at all. What, then, of that great sea of waters above the heavens,
which is stretched like a curtain over all created things, above, that is, outside all the heavens of heavens,
and, like the shells of an egg, encloses within itself all the firmaments and circuits of this circumference of the sphere of the zodiac?
And within this is the whole expanse of the air; and again, that is, below it, this whole creation—the dry land and the boundless seas set in the earth.
How great, then, is that upper sea, which appears like a dome and holds everything within it! Can the mind comprehend it?
Or can any thought at all conceive of it? It is utterly impossible. Oh, what an indescribable marvel! How glorious is your creative power!
O wonderful Maker, wise in everything! When even one of your creatures cannot be measured or comprehended at all, can you—
the Creator and Maker of them all—be encompassed by anyone? Who can describe you? Who can speak about the incomprehensibility of your being?
There is nothing to say or speak, but only to marvel at your works and praise the great power of your being at all times. Amen.
Concerning, again, the fact that all religions have rejected knowledge of the stars and condemned the teaching of astrology, that is, discourse about the stars.

This is the reason. They acted very well and knowledgeably, gave strong warnings, and prohibited believers from acquiring knowledge of astrology, because not everyone is capable of this branch of knowledge, and scarcely one in a thousand knowledgeable people
can enter into these depths and understand the subtlety of the things we outlined above.
Because of their ignorance and simplicity, they do not understand the precise nature of the subject from its beginning
or what its underlying cause is. Instead, they look at the outcome and final result of the teaching.
And when they hear astrologers calculating by their art and telling someone beforehand about future events, they marvel.
They suppose that fate is compulsory and inevitable, and they deny free will, saying:
“Since these things are now allotted to happen inevitably, what use is free will?”
They do not understand precisely that what is foretold is what free will itself is going to do [?], by its sovereign choice and its own authority,
and not something compulsory that forces free will. The same is true of prophecy.
Yet the religions also say that when someone hears from astrologers what lies ahead for him, whether good things or bad,
he becomes negligent and does not give thanks for the good things, and if he prays and pleads concerning the bad things. And they are quite right about this.
They acted very well in prohibiting believers from this teaching. If simple believers could understand these deep and precise matters,
they would understand and know that free will, too, must not cease from its own activities or become negligent at all, as the religions have commanded,
but must take constant care, do as much good as possible, and put an end to evil.
For all the [?] under heaven praise the doing of good and condemn the doing of evil.
This is righteousness, and this is sin: namely, the things that one's own authority does through the exercise of its freedom, which is the will.
But the things that happen and take place [?] through sovereign and [?] chastisement—whether killings, strangulations, or drowning in water,
or burial beneath buildings, mounds, and pits, or captivity, or the destruction of fruit and crops.
Whether severe pains or various illnesses, these are not properly called evils, but corrective disciplines for the evil that is sin
arising from free choice. Furthermore, all religious confessions are foreign to the teaching of astrology.
For it is very extensive, deep, and subtle, and requires attention, perseverance, and much study.
Even if a person's life lasted a thousand years, it would not be enough to learn completely and know precisely all its movements, influences, and indications.
People would be occupied with it to the exclusion of other teachings that benefit the soul and bring it close to God. A person's prophesying and knowing future events,
whether through the gift of prophecy or through the teaching of astrology, does not help that person if it is not accompanied by good deeds.
For prophecy speaks through the mouths of sinners, outsiders, and unbelievers because of God's unfathomable arrangements and judgments. They are not justified by this.
Rather, this becomes a cause of judgment, punishment, and grave accusation against them. Yet there are also many uneducated and innocent people,
simple by nature, through whom prophecy speaks, although they themselves do not understand its purpose and power. On this account they are neither justified nor condemned.
But those who understand the power and purpose of prophecy and do not do good
are justly condemned. Those, however, who do the good things that prophecy commands are praised.
Likewise, there are many who, through their natural acuteness and the composition of their temperament, grasp the power of astrology, its movements, and its indications,
and through the great attention and study they devote to it.
But if they do not perform the good deeds that everyone approves and all religious confessions praise, they are despised and condemned
and are held accountable to a stricter judgment. The purpose and power of religious confession is faith that does not inquire.
Faith is a spiritual understanding that the soul apprehends naturally, from what is naturally implanted in its living, rational, and spiritual nature, which is higher than the nature of the zodiac.
The soul knows the zodiac, but is not known by the zodiac. The zodiac, however, rules over the elements within it—that is, beneath it—and acts upon them.
The soul's nature does not come from a combination of the elements, but from a subtle spirituality that is not material at all.
The zodiac does indeed rule over bodies composed of the elements, act upon them, and speak about them.

Because the soul is bound to the body, it is subjected along with the body's nature to the elements that gave rise to it. But if the soul is watchful and clear, and remains in the nature in which it was created,

it is not at all subjected to the body's nature. For the body desires what harms the spirit, namely, what fattens and thickens the body, such as nourishment, rest, [?], sleep, sexual intercourse, and indulgence.
These things dim the mind, darken the heart, blind the understanding, and harm the spirit. Therefore, whenever the stars indicate something, they indicate something about the nature of the body,
which is composed of the elements upon which those stars act. And because we [?] call a person by one part of that person,
[sometimes by the body,] sometimes by the soul, whenever the body suffers, whether from illness or from a wound, we say, “So-and-so is suffering,”
although the soul is neither sick nor disturbed. Yet because it is bound to the body, it necessarily suffers with the body's suffering, although its nature is higher than material sufferings.
Again, whenever the soul suffers from distress or sadness caused by some troubling news, or over someone who has died, or over some loss,
or thinks contrary thoughts and pours forth [?], or, again, is joyful and glad, thinks rightly, and pours forth true teachings,
both kinds of things are said of the whole human being—even these material things—and not of one part of the person.
Therefore, let this easily understood point be firmly established and accepted by everyone: the stars indicate what happens to the body because they act upon the elements.

[But they have no influence at all over the soul, because the soul’s nature] is higher than the elements, the stars, and the constellations. Through its independence and the movement of its freedom—that is, its will—the rational soul can alter natural dispositions
and constrain the body’s characteristics. Most people, however, are bound like animals to the body’s characteristics, according to the constitution and composition of their temperament.
They have not trained themselves rationally so that they can constrain natural dispositions and correct the habits and characteristics they have acquired over a long time,
whether from the body’s temperament, from the place where they were brought up, or from the company and teaching in which they were trained,
or from other such things. Only a few individuals can govern themselves rationally
and correct the habits and characteristics with which they have become imbued and which have become firmly established in them over a long time.
Scarcely one person among many thousands can be found who knows these things and has become wise through knowledge of the truth. For such a person there is no law.
He is not bound under any law at all. Rather, he himself lays down laws and establishes regulations and judgments,
and pours forth [true] teachings and explanations of hidden and secret things, because his heart has been purified and his understanding made clear,

and his mind has been enlightened. He has become established in the nature in which he was created, has become divine, and has been raised to spirituality, because his soul has been united with its Creator.
Therefore, the leaders of all religious communities acted and conducted themselves very well in prohibiting simple people and the general population from studying astrology,

for the sake of the uncultivated, the uneducated [and most people are uncultivated and uneducated], and the fleshly, lest they suffer harm in their faith and begin to doubt the sovereign freedom they have
from their Creator. But for those who are wise and knowledgeable about the truth, there is no law.
For they have grasped the truth, which itself taught and established laws and judgments. “The law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the lawless and sinners,” and so forth.
From chapter six. Concerning the purpose of the stars and where their positions are,
and what their signs of the zodiac are, and the rest of their entire order. Their usefulness is this:
by observing them, the directions of east, west, north, and south are known, as well as the directions from which the winds blow.
They also indicate the times and hours of days and nights, mornings and evenings, and the changing seasons of the year: winter, spring, summer, and autumn,
as well as the complete year itself, the boundaries of the months, the division of [?], and the numbering of days. Travelers also set their courses by them,
especially those whose journeys and travels are on the seas. Were it not for the indications and signs they have in the stars,
they could not sail the sea at all, nor would they come through safely. The divine writer, the great Moses, spoke well about them.
That God created them and appointed them as signs and for seasons, days, and years. Moreover, from their positions relative to one another,
through careful observation of their nature and composition, we recognize cold and heat.
We anticipate the blowing of winds, storms, and whirlwinds and take precautions in making use of them and in our activities at sea, on land, and in every undertaking.
Furthermore, the Creator placed in them reliable and unmistakable signs,
in that he did not arrange them in rows like the rows of a vineyard, nor make them equal in light and radiance,
or, as one might say, all of the same appearance and size, in one firmament and arrangement.

If they had been arranged in this way, they could not have been distinguished from one another at all. Their positions and boundaries would not have been known, nor would the times, watches, and hours of the night have been known.
Nor could anyone have traveled at night, either by sea or by land. Much confusion and bewilderment would have resulted from this.
Indeed, even the world's cycle would not have continued. But because the Creator, who is wise in everything, arranged them differently,
in their shapes, differing appearances, sizes, brightness, radiance, dimness, and all their other characteristics, they became distinguishable and precisely known to us.
Just as we recognize and distinguish many people by their features, so too do we distinguish livestock and wild animals,
and also regions and places on earth by their heights, depths, plains, valleys, and so forth.
Likewise, we know how to distinguish the positions of the stars, their boundaries, and the time of their movement from the differences in their appearances and individual characteristics.
We have also learned their sizes and heights. And these things
are known precisely through the art of geometry, that is, the measurement of the earth. We will explain this below,
when we speak about [?], with the help of the Lord who grants wisdom. Through this art one can come to know how high the mountains are, and also the number of the stars,
their size and quantity, and many wonderful and glorious things.
We can also discover and calculate the number of the stars through the art of arithmetic, that is, the art of numbers.
The Phoenicians discovered it because they were continually engaged in trade and numerical calculations for buying and selling.
Over time, as they became practiced in numbers, they discovered it and set it out systematically in books, and it became an exalted art.
There is another of the intellectual arts called music, that is, the harmonizing of melodies.
The Thracians of Greece discovered it. Because they loved songs and refrains, they learned to compose different melodies,
and made it an excellent art. For there are four exalted intellectual arts on which the whole course of the world depends.
One is astronomy, which the Chaldeans discovered, as we have shown above.
Another is geometry, which the Egyptians discovered in the land of Egypt, as we will show; and there are arithmetic and music, as we have said.
The positions of the stars are as we said above. First above the fiery ether is the sphere of the moon.
Its height extends from the boundary of the ether to the boundary [?] of the sphere of Hermes, which is above the moon.
A measured and known number of parasangs, made known to us through the art of geometry.
Such is the height of the sphere in which Hermes travels, above the moon. Above this is the sphere in which Aphrodite travels.
It is not as high as either of these. Above it is the fourth sphere, in which the sun travels. It is much higher than those we have mentioned.
For the sun itself is also much larger than all the stars. Above [?], Zeus travels.
This one is much higher than these, because it is also much larger than all the stars, second only to the sun.
Above Zeus, in the seventh sphere, Cronus travels. This sphere is very high, extending to the boundary of the many bright stars.
It is very large, but a little smaller than Zeus. Above this, in the eighth sphere, travel stars numbering one thousand one hundred and twenty.
This sphere is many times higher than those preceding it.
Above these, in the ninth sphere, travel many stars that cannot be numbered. This sphere is one and a half times as high
as the sphere of the bright stars below it. In the tenth sphere, that of the circle of the zodiac signs, the visible stars travel.
This is much higher than all the other spheres. Then, above this, stretches the great sea of the waters that are above the heavens.
The zodiac signs belonging to the stars were assigned by the ancients as follows: to the sun, which is the great and royal luminary,
the sign of Leo was given. To its west, on its boundary, the sign of Cancer was given to the moon, which is the lesser luminary.
To these two great luminaries one zodiac sign each was given, and to each of the remaining five stars two signs, as follows.
To Hermes, who is above the moon, Virgo was given on the sun’s eastern boundary, and Gemini on the moon’s western boundary.
To Aphrodite, who is above Hermes, Libra was given on Hermes’ eastern boundary.
And Taurus, in turn, on Hermes’ western boundary. As for Ares, who is above the sun,
Scorpio was given to him on the east, on Aphrodite’s boundary, and Aries, in turn, on Aphrodite’s western boundary.
As for Zeus, who is above Ares, [?] was given to him on Ares’ eastern boundary.
And Pisces, in turn, on Ares’ western boundary. As for Cronus, who is above Zeus,
Capricorn was given to him on the east, on Zeus’ boundary, and Aquarius, in turn, on Zeus’ western boundary.
Both of Cronus’ zodiac signs were placed together, opposite the sun and the moon.
For this reason, every placement in opposition—that is, diametrically opposite—is unfavorable.
The decans, that is, the faces, are also assigned as follows: the first face of Aries to Ares, and the second to the Sun, which is below Ares.
The third to Aphrodite, who is below the Sun; and the first face of Taurus to Hermes. And so on, one after another, to the end of them.
The bounds, and also the portions—that is, the degrees—of the zodiacal signs, are reckoned in another way, except for the Sun and Moon, to which no bounds have been assigned.
The portions, that is, the degrees of the zodiacal signs, are also assigned in succession to all seven planets, beginning with the first degree of Aries, assigned to Ares.
The second is assigned to the Sun, and so on in succession to the end of the twelve zodiacal signs. The days are divided as follows.
Sunday belongs to the Sun, and the night leading into Monday to Zeus, because the first hour of that night falls to Zeus.
Monday belongs to the Moon, and the night leading into Tuesday to Aphrodite. Tuesday belongs to Ares, and the night leading into Wednesday to Cronus.
Wednesday belongs to Hermes, and the night leading into Thursday to the Sun. Thursday belongs to Zeus, and the night leading into Friday to the Moon.
Friday belongs to Aphrodite, and the night leading into Saturday to Ares. Saturday belongs to Cronus, and the night leading into Sunday to Hermes.
The hours of day and night are likewise divided among all seven of them, beginning with the first hour of Sunday.
Each takes an hour in succession, one after another, night and day, until the end of the week.
Whichever one is assigned the first hour of the day or night is reckoned to possess that day or night.
Their symbols are these: the Sun [?]; the Moon [?]; Cronus [?]; Zeus [?]; Ares [?]; Aphrodite [?]; Hermes [?]. Gold is assigned to the Sun.
Silver to the Moon; quicksilver to Hermes, that is, Utarid; copper to Aphrodite, that is, Zuhara; and iron to Ares, that is, Marit.
Tin to Zeus, that is, Mushtari; and lead to Cronus, that is, Zuhal. All this was ordered and arranged by the Creator, who is wise in everything,
in groups of seven, as we shall see in the discourse on the earth, through the Lord who gives wisdom. These few things we have said on the subject of the stars.
Anyone who is interested and wishes to learn more about them should read the books on the art of astronomy and praise their Creator and the one who set them in order.
We mean those on astronomy, not those on astrology.
For astronomy, that is, the law of the stars, teaches about their order, their movements, and the rest of their laws.
Astrology, however, that is, discourse about the stars, gives advance indications concerning destinies, future events, and portents.
The religious communities do not accept this, and the leaders of the religious communities did well to set limits, because it is profound and not everyone can grasp it.
It also seems to conflict with freedom and to abolish it. Many of those who trained in the art of astrology,
because they were not sound in the confession of their faith and were not wise in the knowledge of the truth,
and did not have the gift from divine grace to distinguish truth and certainty from falsehood and error,
went far astray, erred, and turned aside from the path of truth. They supposed that the seven planets were makers rather than things that had been made.
And they are lords, not subjects. These wretched people did not understand that it is utterly impossible for there to be many gods,
[and many lords and rulers]. Otherwise, the world could not stand at all, as we showed above in the first discourse.
And so, in their error, they practice divination by the stars through the activity of Satan.
They offer them libations, sacrifices, incense, and other kinds of offerings supposedly suited to the nature of each one,
along with much misguided and empty worship. Others set up images and likenesses for themselves out of solid gold and silver,
bronze, stone, and wood, and worshiped them as living, rational beings possessing authority and governing power. Demons, too, would speak through these images from time to time,
display illusions and apparitions, announce future events beforehand, and perform many actions that seemed to those wretched people to be wonders, great
and glorious deeds. They thought that these beings and the stars were doing, performing, speaking, and displaying all these things.
Through this they strayed from the truth and from knowledge of the one God. They led many astray and harshly and tyrannically persecuted those who would not be persuaded by them.
Thus many sects arose within the science of astrology itself, in conflict with the truth and with one another.
For this reason, all the religions of all the nations utterly rejected the teaching of astrology, and they did very well to do so. There is no need for it,
because not everyone is competent in it or able to grasp its precise details. But the study of the laws of the stars, astronomy, is good and does no harm.
It does not conflict with religion at all. There is a great need for it, and it is required in every respect,
because through it the years, the cycles of time, the changing seasons, the months, the weeks, and the whole order by which this world is maintained become known.
The religions do not reject this at all, because they use it to determine times, seasons, and festivals for the maintenance of their religions and for other purposes.
Concerning the nature of the stars and the zodiac: of which elements it consists,
what views people have held about this, and which view is accurate. Everything that is visible to the eyes and audible to the ears,
perceived by [?], and felt by the hands necessarily consists of and is constituted from the four elements—either from all of them,
or from three, or from two. It is impossible for anything below those waters that are above the heavens, and within the zodiac,
not to consist of [these] elements, unless it is a spiritual nature, such as angels, souls, and demons.
The nature of these beings cannot be seen, heard, touched, or perceived at all. The stars, however, are visible to the eyes,
and the activity of their nature is known from their rays to derive from the very nature of the elements.
They are, however, the refined part of the elements. That is, [the] clear and fine substance found in the nature of fire, air, and water:
from these the Creator made these individual bodies of the stars. Not one of them consists of the nature of earth.
As for the moon, whose globe is dim and dark, we think that it is the sediment of that clear and fine substance from the elements out of which the stars came into being.
All that sediment was gathered into the orb of the moon by the will of the Creator.
So too the human being is a small world and the bond joining all the worlds and created things.
That is, everything is summed up and gathered together in human nature. The image and likeness of the human being’s Creator is recognized in him.
The nature of his soul comes from the world of spiritual beings and the nature of the angels. The whole human being, his composition and his structure, resembles the zodiac and its luminaries,
and the earth, mountains, seas, rivers, trees, and animals, as we shall clearly show below.
When a human being receives nourishment from material food derived from the elements that constitute his body, that subtle power of the food is sent to the liver,
like that pure power from the elements which is sent to the zodiac. The liver, in turn, dissolves and clarifies the subtle substance it has received.
It sends the pure substance to sight, hearing, and [?]—or rather, to the brain, the king of the bodily organs, in which the senses are fixed and established like the stars in the zodiac.
And that other sediment which also comes from the subtle power of the food received by the liver,
it sends to the spleen, which is sustained by it—by that sediment of the subtle substance of the food.
It is like the sediment that comes from the subtle purity of the elements and is gathered into the orb of the moon.
This is why it is dim and formed this way. Thus the orb of the moon is the spleen of the zodiac,
in which are gathered the density and sediment left over from the purity of the elements,
from which the stars were formed. Others say that the stars are constituted from the element of air alone.
But air alone cannot be held together and gathered unless there is something else to hold it, because its nature is inherently mobile.
For example, air is thought of as being in a leather bag, that is, a wineskin; or a bottle, a jar, or any such vessel may be [filled] with it.
Likewise, air is held in every bodily nature and kind: in stones, pieces of wood, trees, fruits, grasses, animals, birds, and the rest.
All these are constituted from all four elements, and the elements themselves hold one another together.
Thus air alone cannot be held together so that stable individual substances come into being from it,
unless other elements are present with it, so that they hold one another together.
Thus it is neither true nor possible that the stars consist of the nature of air alone.
Nor are they a fifth element or anything else. Rather, they come from those very elements of the matter from which this whole universe was constituted.
The purity and subtlety of the elements of air, water, and fire were gathered together by the will of the Creator, and these stars came into being from them.
Their residue, in turn, was gathered into the orb of the moon. This is why it is so dim and dark by nature.
The moon’s light does not belong to it by nature; rather, its light comes from the sun.
And when they come together in the conjunction called synodos, the moon passes beneath the sun’s rays,
and gives light upward, toward the sun. As the sun moves farther away from it little by little, it casts its rays upon it,
and the moon shows light until it stands diametrically opposite—that is, directly opposite it. Then, when the sun faces it from this distance,
it casts abundant light upon it, and its light reveals half its sphere. To us it looks something like a sieve. But this is not the moon’s actual shape.
Rather, it is a round sphere, like a round melon that is smooth and round. Its dimensions are very great.
Yet although it is very large, it is much smaller than all the stars. But because it is much closer to us than all of them, it appears so large.
Aphrodite is the same size as the moon, while Hermes is much smaller even than the moon. The sun, however, is much larger than all of them.
It is also many times larger than the earth, the seas, and the dry land. Ares is larger than the whole earth—one and a half times its size, it is said.
Zeus is much larger than all of them, after the sun. Cronus is smaller than Zeus.
Orion’s Dog is as large as Zeus. Because of their very great height, they appear so small to us.
Yet they are indeed very large. People have learned this precisely through the art of geometry,
that is, land measurement. All the stars, the sun, and the moon are spherical and round.
The places visible on the moon when it is full are like valleys, ledges, and hollows. They cast shadows and appear to us in this way.
Just as there are valleys and hollows on the earth, so there are on the moon. The earth itself, together with the basins of the seas, is entirely spherical,
as we shall see with God’s help. With these things the sixth chapter is completed, through God who strengthened and helped us.
Chapter Seven of the Fifth Discourse, with God who grants wisdom. On the cause of an eclipse, that is, the darkening of the sun and the moon,
and from what this happens, and how. The sun’s eclipse, that is, its darkening, is caused by the moon.
When the moon is positioned directly beneath it, it hides it from us. Just as a cloud passing through the air hides the sun from us,
so too does the moon. The moon’s eclipse, however, that is, its darkening, is caused by the earth.
When the moon rises and stands diametrically and directly opposite the sun, the earth comes between them and blocks the sun’s rays from the moon.
The darkness visible on the moon is the earth’s shadow. But as for what the cause is, and why
the moon is not darkened by the earth’s shadow every time it becomes full and stands opposite the sun, but this happens to it only from time to time;
likewise, why the sun is not darkened every time it comes into conjunction with the moon when the moon stands beneath it, but only from time to time;
and why sometimes the entire disk of one of them is darkened, sometimes both, and sometimes half or a third,
or again less or more—we shall speak precisely about all these things, with God who grants wisdom, who in his wisdom arranged and set bounds
All these things. The shape of the zodiac [?] is like two circles that overlap and intersect one another.
These two places where they join one another—that is, their intersections, where they overlap—are called nodes.
One is the dragon’s head, and the other is its tail. They lie directly opposite one another, like an eye.
There is no width on either side at these places; rather, they are very narrow. These nodes do not remain in one place,
but pass and travel backward through all the signs of the zodiac. Each of them stays in a sign for less than one year.
When a conjunction occurs [?] and they are positioned together at one of these nodes, because there is no latitude at that place in the zodiac, the moon stands directly beneath the sun.
It blocks the sun’s rays from reaching the earth. If the conjunction—that is, the coming together of the sun and moon—occurs exactly at the center of the nodes,
the whole sun is darkened. But if it occurs near the node, and not at the node’s center, not all of it is darkened, but only portions of it:
either half its disk, or more, or less. What appears dark to us is not the sun, but the moon,
which has taken its position beneath the sun and blocked its rays from reaching the earth. Likewise, when there is a full moon—that is, when the moon is full—
as it stands diametrically opposite the sun, if they take their positions at these nodes, each at one,
the earth necessarily stands midway between them and blocks the sun’s rays from reaching the moon.
It casts its shadow upon the moon, and the moon is darkened: either all of it or less, or half of it or less.
But if, when a conjunction or a full moon occurs, they do not take their positions at these narrow nodes,
they have no latitude on either side; no eclipse occurs for them. Here we draw the figure so that it will be clear to the readers.
The head node: Anabibazon.
The tail node: Catabibazon.
Now pay attention to this figure. This is the shape of the two circles of the zodiac. The sun travels around one of them,
and the moon around the other. When a conjunction of the two luminaries occurs at one of these nodes,
the sun is necessarily darkened by the moon, which is positioned directly beneath it and blocks its rays from reaching us.
Nevertheless, the air remains bright because the sun’s rays are spread through it, since the sun’s disk is much larger than the moon’s—a thousand times larger.
The moon’s disk cannot conceal the whole sun from all the air. But it is concealed from the earth, and daylight grows dim.
If the conjunction takes place at the node itself, the whole sun is darkened—that is, covered by the moon. What appears to us without shining
is not the sun, but the moon. But if the conjunction occurs a little outside the node, less than the whole sun is covered.
If it is a little farther still, only half of it is covered. But if the conjunction takes place still farther outside the node, some portion of the sun is covered.
Likewise, when there is a full moon, that is, when the moon is full, if the sun is positioned at one node and the moon at the other, at the very center of the nodes,
the whole moon is completely darkened by the earth’s great shadow, which blocks from it the rays of [?]. But if the luminaries are positioned a little outside the nodes
at the time of the full moon, when the moon is full, it is not entirely darkened.
We know these things clearly from astronomical calculation, as each year we make a new calculation concerning the configuration of the whole year.
If an eclipse of one of the luminaries, or of both of them, occurs in that year, we know it beforehand from calculation.
We calculate the one above the earth and discuss it. But we do not discuss the one that occurs below the earth.
Nor do we perceive it. From calculation we can know at what hour the coming eclipse begins, and how much of the luminary is darkened,
and how long it takes for the darkening to reach completion, and when the darkness begins to clear [and how much time passes from when the darkness begins] until it clears entirely,
and what the luminary looks like when it is darkened, and in which sign of the zodiac and at what degree. God has granted human beings knowledge and understanding of all these things.
The stars too, when they are positioned with the moon at one of these nodes, are covered by it, whether they are among these seven,
or among the higher stars fixed in the circle of the zodiacal signs—that is, in the path along which the seven travel through the zodiac.
And when two of the seven stars themselves are positioned at one of these nodes, the higher one is covered by the lower until it passes beyond it.
Venus covers Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and the other stars that are positioned with it at the same minute of arc at one of these nodes.
This is because it is below them. It too is covered by the moon, because the moon is below it. Jupiter, in turn, covers Saturn, which is higher than it, and the other stars.
Saturn too covers whatever is above it when it comes together with it at one of these nodes.
In this coming together, which we call a conjunction, although they are positioned together at the same minute and degree,
each is nevertheless far above the other, as we showed above concerning their firmaments, their circuits, and their spheres.
Praise, worship, and thanksgiving belong to the one who created, established, and ordered them, for he alone knows the exact truth about all these things.
Human beings, however, through experience over a long time and much study, have been able to learn these things through the grace that gave them wisdom from nature itself.
From Scripture we have heard that God created them and appointed them as signs and for times and seasons. Another passage of Scripture says:
“He counted the stars and called them all by name.” And again it says, “Praise the Lord from the heavens, and praise him in the heights,”
that is, all his angels and all his hosts. And again, “Praise him, sun and moon,
and praise him, all stars and light. Praise him, highest heavens, and waters above the heavens. Let them praise the name of the Lord,
for he spoke and they came into being; he commanded and they were created. He established them forever and ever. He gave a law that does not pass away.”
Throughout the holy Scriptures they are called hosts, and many people have held many opinions about them.
But here we have set down the precise truth, something accepted by all confessions.
Rather, by discerning people who are wise in the knowledge of the truth, not by ignorant people who are wise in their own eyes and bring accusations without understanding.
With these words the seventh chapter ends, through God, who gave strength and help. To him belong glory, honor, and worship forever and ever. Amen.
The fifth discourse ends, through God, who gave strength and help. In it he spoke splendidly and at length about the creation of light and the stretching out of heaven,
and about the waters above the heavens, the firmaments of heaven, the shape of the zodiac, and the stars, their nature, their behavior, and their movement,
and about eclipses of the sun and moon, and the entire order and revolution of the zodiac and the stars.
Next, the sixth discourse, about the things beneath the zodiac: what the fiery ether beneath the firmament of the moon is like,
and about this air and its changes, the seasons of the year, dew and showers,
and everything that happens in this air surrounding us. It contains seven chapters. First chapter, with—with God, who grants wisdom.
On what lies beneath the whole zodiac and the regions of the stars, and what the fiery ether is like, and why.
Glorious is your providence, our good God, wise Creator and generous Provider. Your works are wonderful, and your creations cannot be comprehended.

Anyone who, out of overflowing love, dares and ventures to speak about the glorious wonders of your creative work is like someone who enters the deep abyss of the great sea and is covered by the waves,
and sinks among the billows. If your power does not reach him and your help does not accompany him,
if your grace does not guide him and give him wisdom, and your right hand does not lift him and bring him up, he sinks and drowns within the confines of the deep sea.
There he is tormented and tossed about without end. The wonders of our Lord and Creator, who is wise in everything, cannot be comprehended.
As we have often said, even if someone [?] lived for a thousand years studying and learning about these things,
he could scarcely grasp a few small fragments of true knowledge about all things that exist, as they actually are and have been fashioned
by the wise Craftsman of creation. But if someone is discerning and humble, faithful, and upright in the good practices [of virtue],

he is made wise by heavenly grace, and his mind is enlightened because of the purity of his heart, the clarity of his thoughts, and the cleansing of his mind from all ugly passions, material concerns,
and the empty cares of this world. A person like this is truly made wise by God in the knowledge of the truth.
When he perceives this, he despises all material things, and all the wealth of this passing world counts as dung to him.
He seeks only the things to come, which are true and endure in eternal life. May we all be found worthy of them through the grace of our Lord. Amen.
Let us concern ourselves with these things, my brothers, and acquire them—that is, the upright and good practices of virtue,
which bring us near to the knowledge of the truth and unite us with our Lord, who is good and wise and rich in everything:
how he created and fashioned all these glorious arrangements for our sake alone, for us human beings.
He stretched out for us this glorious curtain and lofty vault, and decorated this splendid bridal chamber for us.
He arranged and placed within it all these good things and comforts beyond measure, and enclosed one thing within another.
He bound them together, fitting and ordering them with great craftsmanship, wise in every respect.
All these immeasurable and incomprehensible distinctions—everything was established and completed with a single gesture, in an instant.
He made the covering of this glorious vault from loose, fluid, flowing waters.
He also established its stories from water and wind, and adorned it with many lamps.
He suspended glorious lights in it to give us light by day and by night, and appointed them to distinguish times and seasons for us.
He yoked them to the revolving wheel of the zodiac, moving swiftly and with great speed, without rest or pause.
From this swift revolution, the heat of the element of fire was kindled.
The whole force of this fiery heat was driven inward from the entire circuit of this wheel above us.

From within, that is, from below, this air surrounding us pushed it back and restrained it, so that it would not come farther inward, reach our vicinity, and scorch us. Thus it was compressed from both sides,
according to the will of the Creator, who is wise in all things: from above, by the great force of the swift revolution of the zodiac,
and from below, in turn, by the force of the air's powerful blast. Thus it was restrained, compressed, and held back.
It stood in the middle, occupying the region from the boundary of the firmament—that is, the orbit in which the moon travels—
to the boundary of this air that reaches us and surrounds us. It was named the region of fire, or the fiery ether.
No fleshly creature can pass through it at all. It is above us by a distance of parasangs known in number and measurement,
for we have been able to measure these heights through the art of geometry.
This first story above us was constituted from blazing fire and was called the fiery ether. Above it is the orbit of the moon,
and so on, one above another, up to the highest, which is an unfathomable sea. The Creator—whose name is worshiped and praised—roofed his chambers with water and fire.
How wonderful is his creation! With these words the first chapter is completed, through God who gave strength and help.
Chapter Two of the Sixth Discourse, with God who grants wisdom. On what lies below the ether,
what this air is like, and what the meteors are—that is, the fiery streaks seen in the air at night.

Although God is almighty and above the order of nature, and can change natural substances and preserve them without destruction or confusion, he has not made any use of these powers in the ordinary course of things.

Rather, he established and defined everything in an orderly way. Through this very harmony and beauty of arrangement, the world stands, is preserved, and is carried along, and times and seasons revolve.
And these elements, the fathers of the inhabited world, from which everything was established, are like the four corners [of a house].
And like four elements that rule and govern, and like four tent ropes holding the tent covering.

He established them, each within its own boundary and in the place allotted to it by its nature, as was appropriate for it. In this way they hold creation together so that it does not tilt to one side and fall into ruin.
Fire, because it is vigorous and light and constantly tends upward and rises,
was assigned the highest position, and an elevated region was marked out for it, the one called the fiery ether.
Air, in turn, which is also light and moves this way and that, pushed the element of fire upward.
Leaving the heavy elements below, it occupied the middle region and was confined within this entire surrounding space.
It surrounds earth and water as the white of an egg surrounds the yolk, as we said above, in the second chapter of the preceding discourse.
Thus air occupied the region below the fire [?], and it is pushed this way and that by some other force
and a much denser and harder substance, which pushes it here and there. It is like someone taking a board and pushing the air with it, producing wind and a breeze.
Likewise, when vapors rise from the earth, they push the air aside and occupy its place. And when that air is driven and pushed,
a blowing wind results, in proportion to the greater or smaller amount of vapor. If the vapors are abundant and dense because of the great force coming out of the earth,
they push aside all the air in the region where they rise. That air is pushed in the direction in which the vapors drive it.
A violent blast and powerful storms result. In this way they push along with them the air ahead of them, continuing and increasing until they become powerful winds.
If they pass over high mountains and northern regions, they bring cold blasts.
If the terrain over which they pass consists of level plains, low-lying deserts, and southern regions, hot and fiery blasts come.
If they blow from the east, they produce moisture; and if from the west, likewise, according to the position of the region and the regions beyond it.
From those regions beyond it, the winds bring a potency corresponding to the climate of the region. That potency mixes with the air, and it is inhaled
by human beings and animals, and acts upon them according to its nature, producing either health and the preservation of life, or sickness and harm,

and even death and destruction, according to the constitution of their bodies and the climate of the region where they live, [and the season in which they find themselves,] and according to the size, habit, way of life, and occupation of each individual.
If those currents of air displaced by the vapors come from temperate regions and clean mountains, and from places where there are no pools of water, marshes, or [?],
[but rather] clean and clear terrain, the air produces health, strength, and firmness in bodies, makes fruit flourish, increases crops, and is beneficial in many ways.
But if these winds come from plains full of marshes, [?], and lakes,
and from places where there are dense forests and thickets of trees, willows, slender reeds, and rushes,
and abundant grass and thick meadows, all the air coming from regions like these is very bad, causing sickness and harm.
And in general, regions with abundant water, forests, meadows, numerous streams, pools of water, and lakes,
[The air] in them becomes foul because of the vapor rising from the decay of the thick grasses of the meadows, willows, and similar things.
If the owners of these places can clear them of such things, uprooting and removing all the dense growth of grass and willows and the thick woods beside the water,
and the rotting vegetation in the water and along the shores of lakes, rivers, pools, and watercourses [?], they benefit greatly from doing so.
The foul air and disease are removed from them. Thus, all winds and violent gusts are the air itself being compressed and driven by exhalations.
It rushes wherever the exhalations drive it. These exhalations rise very high and reach as far as the fiery ether.
Then they turn back. Many phenomena arise from these exhalations that rise from the earth,
according to their mixture and the lands from which they rise. Through the air and the fire of the ether, they are refined and acquire strength and many active properties.
First, seven kinds of dew arise from the exhalations that rise from the earth.
The first consists of rain, drizzle, and watery dew. The second is what is called mercury, for this too is a dew produced from watery exhalations.
They rise, as we shall explain clearly below concerning this. The third dew is manna, which is called arura [?].
The fourth is what is called tarangil [?]. The fifth is what is called sharakusk [?]. The sixth is honey, and the seventh is ladanum, that is, ladin.
These seven dews that descend from the sky have their origin in the exhalations that rise and collect in the air.
They acquire strength, turn back, and descend in places suited to them. They remain on rocks, trees, and grasses.
Those who understand these things collect them skillfully and use them for many needs and purposes.
The exhalations also carry the dust of the earth upward with them, and then it mixes
with them and sometimes descends with snow and rain. These change to resemble the dust that rose with the exhalations, and their color becomes red,
or yellow, or white. Sometimes, too, that dust mixes with manna and other substances that descend like dew through the power of the exhalations.
The violent gusts that arise from the displacement of the air through the force of the exhalations occur in many forms.
Some of them come from nearby, from mountains or plains.
Those that come from the mountains are strong and cold because of the nature of the mountains, and because the exhalations are greatly compressed within the mountains owing to their solidity.
They emerge in great quantities through cracks in the rocks, because they gather and increase and come out through ravines, valleys, and fissures,
and similar places, wherever they can and wherever they find outlets. They become very dense and powerful
and drive the air forcefully. That is why the gusts coming from the mountains are harsh and violent.
The gusts that come from the plains, however, are neither very strong nor cold,
because the exhalations continually rise from the soft earth and are not held back, accumulated, and multiplied as they are within solid mountains.
For this reason they are not as strong or as cold as those that come from the mountains.
There are also other winds, strong ones that come from very far away, from all regions of the world.
There are four principal ones: the east wind, the west wind, the north wind, and the south wind.
Between these there are also other winds from the corners, two from each corner, making twelve in all.
They have names that are familiar to those who travel in ships and go down to sea—to sailors and pilots.
Their entire cause is the exhalations that drive the air in every direction, so that it blows either strongly or weakly.
And if you ask where the exhalations from the earth get the strength to drive the air so powerfully
and produce such harsh and violent winds, we say that the exhalations have so much strength that nothing in creation can restrain them.
For when they gather in great quantities in the lower cavities of the earth, they shake it like a hammock.
These movements, tremors, and disturbances in the earth occur because of the exhalations. For these movements and tremors
are caused by their gathering in great quantities beneath the earth, in deep cavities. And when they do not find spacious outlets,
they shake that earth, rock it, strike it, break through it, rise upward, and drive the air. You can recognize this from the fact that winds are frequent during the periods and days of earthquakes.
If it is winter, the earthquake becomes severe and powerful, rocking the earth and jolting it, because the surface of the earth has hardened
and become compacted, and the fissures and vents through which they had previously been rising continually have [?].
Thus they immediately gather, increase, and grow dense within the earth. Then they force their way through and shake the earth
and the seas and mountains, coming out and descending. For this reason the earth is broken open, split, and subsides in many places.
Many hills and heights are brought low and swallowed up within the earth.

The sea too is shaken and thrown into turmoil, and its waves rise very high from the force of the dense exhalations that rise from its lower depths, from the deep cavities of the earth above which it arches.
The sea itself is driven and tossed this way and that. Sometimes it overflows and goes beyond its boundaries, damaging and devastating many places.
Sometimes it retreats, and places within it that have never seen the sun are exposed.
Great wealth is found there, spilled long ago from ships that sank there.
Then either the sea returns once more to its place, if the earth that was shaken and raised settles down,
or it remains like that forever, if the earth has been raised beyond its normal position by the force of the exhalations.
There are some wise people in the world who, when building cities, dig into the earth, going down as far as the water. Over the water they build long, spacious vaulted chambers.
Above these they build still other vaulted chambers, leaving openings to the sky in them, so that when dense exhalations rise from the earth,
They pass easily through the water pipes, because they displace the water naturally present and pass through in its place. When they reach those broad conduits,
those vapors pass easily through them from one to another.
In this way they rise into the air and ascend without greatly shaking the ground [on which that city is built], and the buildings are not damaged.
Buildings, walls, and towers are built over those conduits, as I myself have seen in many cities,
especially along the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, but not in Constantinople or in the western regions either.
In summer, however, the vapors do not become abundant beneath the earth, because the earth’s surface is [?], soft, and cracked.
Whenever the vapors gather, they rise before they become abundant, and nothing holds them back.
Even if they shake the earth, they shake it only slightly, not violently as in winter.
Buildings on the plains suffer greater damage, and most of them are swallowed up in the earth.
For when the earth is jolted and moves in an earthquake, it settles, spreads out, and splits open because the soil is soft.
But in solid mountains and wherever there is hard rock, the ground does not settle or change.
For this reason, the buildings there remain firm and are not shaken.
Furthermore, the vapors that rise from the earth mix with many substances and change the color of each substance to their own color.

For this reason, snow and rain become red or yellow, according to the color of the dust that rose with the vapors and mixed with the dew, rain, and the other kinds of things, according to the will and command
of the wise Creator. But if someone among those who are wise in their own eyes says
that all these things happen as the Lord wills and his command decrees, he does not say this with knowledge of the truth.
God does not now will some new thing that he did not know about. Rather, he willed it beforehand, and everything is determined in his knowledge.
As we said above in the discussion of the stars and in many other places, whoever says these things thinks that he is exalting God.
He is not exalting him, but greatly diminishing him. Things that can be perceived, and whatever is still to happen, whether through God or through the free will of rational creatures,
whether in deed, word, or thought—God knew them all beforehand, before he created a single one of the worlds.
When he created the worlds, he connected one thing with another, made known the causes of everything, and gave knowledge concerning the certainty of the whole truth.
He has never changed natures, nor does he newly change anything that he had not intended to change and only thought about afterward.
Far from it! Rather, he knew everything beforehand in a single instant, and he himself gave knowledge and understanding concerning all these things.
Otherwise, how could we have known all these things, apart from the working of his divine grace?
From the chapter on shooting stars, that is, the fiery darts that appear at night high in the air.
As we said above about the vapors that constantly rise from the earth, some of them rise from below, from the earth’s lower recesses.
Some rise from the surface of the earth, from smoke and fires; and moisture, when heated by the sun’s rays, all turns into vapor and rises.
Likewise, vapors constantly rise from seeds, fruits, and various species. Vapors rise from all the activity on earth.
As they rise into the air, they receive another power from the air and from the sun.
They become different kinds of dew, serving many useful purposes. As for those vapors that are oily,
when they reach the fiery ether, they flare up and burst into flame in the air. They increase, grow, and linger in the air according to the greater or smaller quantity of vapor.
The flame of the vapor spreads along with it. People suppose that it is a star, but this cannot happen at all: a star cannot move from its place.
Rather, as we said, these are oily vapors. When they reach the fiery ether, it catches hold of them and blazes. These events also occur frequently during the day,
but they are not visible, except during flashes of lightning, which are seen in times of storms. For the causes of lightning and thunder also come from vapors, as we shall show with God’s help.
With this, chapter two is completed, through God, who gave strength and help.
Chapter Three of the Sixth Discourse, with God, who grants wisdom. On the arrangement of the clouds called dark clouds, and what causes them to increase and become compact.
And how, in turn, they disperse. As we showed above, the vapors that rise from the earth are the cause of everything that takes place and happens in this air.
Concerning the clouds that gather in the air, it must also be understood that they are the watery vapors that rise from the earth and from the waters.
They gather in the air, and when the vapors come near the fiery ether, they can rise no farther.
Thus, as the vapors rise, the clouds increase, thicken, become compact, and grow, until they occupy a great expanse of the air.
If moist or warm winds come upon them, they are further strengthened by the moisture, driven by the warmth, and compressed.
They quickly send down rain. But if a cold, dry wind strikes them, it scatters them in every direction. When they are dispersed from there,

they do not perish altogether, because it is not possible for anything at all to pass outside the sphere of the fiery ether. Even if something were to pass beyond it, how would it pass through the other firmaments?
Or how could anything at all pierce, break through, and cross that upper sea? Nothing can pass above the fiery ether at all, neither vapor nor air,
nor anything else made from these elements. Rather, everything returns to its own nature: air to air,
fire to fire, earth to earth, and water to water. Nothing at all is taken away from the elements, nor is anything added.
Rather, they remain in the quantity, weight, and measure in which God created them, until he wills to renew them.
These remarks are sufficient concerning clouds and dark clouds: what causes them to gather and thicken, and what, in turn, causes them to disperse and scatter.
With this, chapter three is completed, through God, who gave strength and help.
Chapter Four of the Sixth Discourse, with God, who grants wisdom. On where the flashes of lightning and the sound of thunder come from, and what produces them.
In spring and autumn—that is, the months of Tishri—many thick vapors rise from the earth and the seas.
This happens especially in spring, because there is much moisture in the earth and because at that time the sun is rising from the south.
Its rays increase over the world, and the earth grows warm at that time and sends up many vapors, which thicken in the air.
They become clouds and press against one another, rising through the force of the vapors that multiply and push them upward.
From the great force of the clouds striking that fire, they give out powerful sounds, and crashes [?] are heard. And there flares up
a blaze from that fiery substance within these densely packed clouds, producing the sight of these flashes of lightning.
That sound of thunder comes from the force of the fire that blazes in the clouds, crackling and rolling about.
When they are densely packed together from every side—from below by the vapors that rise continually and press against one another, or push upward toward that fiery ether,
and also by the air, from whichever direction it blows—it further thickens the clouds, packs them against one another, and pushes them upward. In this way they are compressed beneath the ether.
Through the force that presses and pushes them, they strike and come into contact with the ether, giving out the powerful sounds of thunder.
Flashes of lightning are seen when those watery vapors in the clouds blaze up.

From time to time, certain bursts and a mighty force emerge from these collisions and descend powerfully to the earth with a swift rush. Whatever this force falls upon, it passes through it like wind through the air,
and like fierce fire passing with a violent rush through soft, dry material. Nothing at all stops that force.
Instead, it passes through the solid substances of iron, stone, and earth like lightning through the air.
It damages and destroys the material through which it passes more thoroughly than fire burns wood and consumes its particles.
If it strikes iron, it melts, separates, refines, and smooths it until it is thin, so that, if that iron is found, a sword or some kind of blade can be forged from it.
Whatever body it strikes, it cuts it like [?] being cut, because of that great force which passed through the iron in the blink of an eye,
melting and smoothing it cleanly. Vapors are the cause of all these things. In the season of [?], they rise abundantly from the earth, more than from the sea.
In the season of the Tishri months, they rise from the sea more than from the earth, because the earth has dried out throughout the summer and many vapors have risen from it.
All the vapors that form clouds in the air are watery in nature.
Those that rise from the sea do not come from the sea’s salt water, but from the fresh water that enters the sea,
either from rivers on land or from rains that fall upon it. These waters are released again as vapors and separated from the salt water,
