like gold from copper. Thus water rises as vapor and descends as rain, and every substance returns to its place,
and every substance to its own element. Nothing increases or decreases. As for the fact that clouds are numerous in spring,
and sometimes during the season of [?], rain too is especially abundant and falls at that time.
This is its cause: as the day grows hot and the earth warms up, it sends up many vapors. The sea does the same. And especially
they increase after midday, after the sun begins to decline. Because of the great heat that presses upon the earth and the seas, they send up many vapors, which increase in the air.
They gather until the ninth hour and increase, and the clouds grow thick and bring down rain at that time.

Because of the thickness and density of the vapors, they are driven together forcefully, and the clouds are compressed and bring down downpours, violent rains, and large drops that in a single hour produce streams and torrents that cannot be crossed.
But these violent rains do not last long, because they fall rapidly and abundantly, and the clouds are emptied.
In winter, however, this does not happen in the same way. Instead, the vapors rise little by little.

For there is no heat in the sun’s rays to warm the earth and make it send up thick and abundant vapors, so that they press against one another and are compressed beneath the ether, bringing down violent rains.
Instead, gentle and steady rains fall then. As long as the vapors rise and are strengthened by the southern and eastern air,
rain falls without stopping. But if the vapors are held back and do not rise, or dry air blows upon them from the north or the west,
depending on the location of that region, the vapors are scattered, the clouds disperse, and no rain falls. This process resembles the bowl of a cooking pot set on a fire,
filled with water or any kind of cooked food, and covered with a lid. Vapors rise from it and gather on its lid.
When they settle on that lid, they grow hot and drip. In the same way, vapors rise from the earth’s vessel and from the boiling caused by the sun’s fire.
They rise and gather beneath the fiery ether, which is the world’s lid. There they are compressed and descend upon the clear earth,
as from a lid into a pot. The reason there is no rain in summer is that, as soon as the vapors rise from the earth or the sea,
they are quickly dissipated by the intensity of the sun’s rays and return again to their own nature.

Sometimes, however, the vapors increase and overcome the sun’s heat. They rise and thicken in the air, and the clouds grow strong and bring down rain and drizzle. Likewise, the dews that descend at night
come from these same vapors: as they rise from the earth, air blows upon them
and pours them out over the lands, the grasses, the crops, and the leaves. Especially in places near the sea,
dew is very abundant in winter and summer, particularly in places such as the region of Egypt and the whole land of Egypt, Palestine, Phoenicia, Syria, Cilicia, Pisidia, and Bithynia,
and all the regions near the sea. For in summer the vapors rising from the sea because of the sun’s heat are abundant, and there blows upon them
a western wind, which pours them out over these lands. Through this dew, the crops and fruits of these regions grow especially well.
Sometimes the vapors are dry and produce neither rain nor dew.
Instead, they merely cloud the air, which grows dark because of their abundance, and it looks as though some smoke has gathered over the earth like a mist.
This is a sign for you: when the air is clouded by dry vapors, after the days of that mist,
strong winds blow, because the air is being cleared of those thick, dry vapors. Breezes are more frequent at night.
For when vapors rise, none of them is dispersed, because there is no sun at night. When they become abundant, they drive the air to another place.
And winds blow from there onward. That is, the air itself is driven by the vapors, as by fans, and produces these gusts.
There are also harmful, very thick vapors that rise from cracked and desert lands at midday in summer,
because heat enters the heart of the earth and brings them up through the cracks in the ground.
If a person or an animal happens to be there in that land at these times, they die immediately,
because all the air is driven away from that place by the density of that harmful vapor.
When no air remains for them to breathe, they weaken and lose their lives, like someone who descends into a newly opened pit
in which thick vapor has been trapped and no air remains. He loses his life immediately because he has been deprived of breathing air,
which is the breath of life. This harmful [?] vapor, when driven by the air and spread over the ground, destroys crops and fruit.
It causes diseases, much damage, and blights from scorching heat. That is, the scorching wind destroys living things and is opposed to life.
When people see crops and grasses on which blight has descended and which a scorching wind has struck, they should not enter them at all,
nor harvest them. Nor should they allow any of their livestock or cattle to enter them or eat any of them at all,
because they cause illness and death. Even the animals themselves recognize them: they catch their scent from a great distance and do not approach them.
Such crops and grasses should not be left standing, because their smell and the air that passes over them cause illness and death.
They should be burned promptly. Those who burn them should stand at a distance, on the side from which the wind blows,
so that they do not breathe in their smoke. Even if grain remains in the ears of those crops,
it must not be kept in the expectation that [?] will fall on it and the blight will be washed off it, and that it can then be gathered.
For even if it is washed a thousand times, it is never cured; rather, it causes illness and death. And when you see abundant, lush, tall grass,
or grass near water, marshes, lakes, and pools, do not graze sheep or cattle there at all, nor live nearby,
because these places cause illness and are harmful. But high, open places, especially those with an open outlook to the east, south, and west,
and particularly those with an open outlook to the south, are very suitable for living in.
But places that are enclosed and low-lying are not suitable at all, nor are those that face north,
especially where there are many woods and thickets beside the water, and where there are dense, damp meadows.
All these are harmful and cause illness. With this, the fourth chapter is completed through God, who gave strength and help.
The fifth chapter of the sixth discourse, with God who gives wisdom. Further concerning rain and dew, and concerning manna.
And from what cause snow, hail, ice, and things like these arise.
In the chapter before this one, we spoke briefly about rain, dew, and fine droplets, which come from the element of water, which neither increases at all nor decreases.
At times water rises as vapor here and there. Some of it rises high, thickens, and accumulates beneath the ether.
When it is compressed there, it is squeezed out and falls. Some of the vapors are poured out over other, dry lands, which become moist and bear fruit.
Some of the vapors also rise through the earth’s cavities and collect in hard places. They accumulate, find an outlet, and gush out in springs and fountains, according to God’s will.
For this reason, springs and fountains are especially plentiful in mountains and highlands, because these are hard and solid, and the vapors do not disperse in the heat.
Instead, they are held back and confined beneath their hard mass, like vapors from a pot beneath a lid.
Thus mountains and highlands are set upon the earth like a skull upon a body and like a lid upon a pot.
When the vapors gather and accumulate, they become large quantities of water and gush out through the outlets, cracks, and cavities they find in the earth and mountains.
The vapors that rise from plains and deserts and from porous, soft lands rise into the air and gather beneath the ether.
If they have strength and rise in great quantities, they accumulate, press together, and are squeezed beneath the ether.
They become drops, and rain falls. In spring and autumn, there are sometimes heavy rains and large drops.
There are floods and inundations, because the earth grows warm and sends up abundant vapors.
Because of their strength, they rise rapidly, press against one another, and are squeezed beneath the ether, and heavy rains fall.
If dry northern air blows upon these large drops, it hardens them, and they freeze in the air above.
When they fall and reach the earth, this is the cause of hail and sleet. And it is not directly above that place that
hail is formed from that cloud; rather, sometimes that harsh northern wind brings it from far away.
Wherever that wind dies down, there that hail or heavy rain is discharged. Snow, however, forms in winter for the following reason.
Abundant vapors rise when there are harsh, dry northern winds.
The vapor freezes in the air itself while it is like thin smoke. Then portions come out toward one another
and become large and small flakes. This is a sign for you: after snow, the air clears and the weather becomes clear and bright.
Frost and ice also form because of the northern wind, when weak, thin vapors rise from the surface of the earth
and lack the strength to press through, overcome the air, and rise. Instead, they turn back, are poured out upon the earth, and become dew.
Toward morning, when the air is colder, that dry northern air freezes them, along with all the pools of water.
Sometimes, when the air becomes especially harsh, dry, and cold, it freezes great rivers and the shores of the sea.
And it hardens many kinds of things. But when the south wind, which is warm, blows, it loosens and melts the hardness of ice and the other things.
This is the cause of hail, snow, and ice. Now we speak also about thunder and lightning.
Because the clouds are compressed by the abundance of vapors and their upward propulsion by the air, which is itself pushed by the lower vapors,
and it compresses the upper vapors, which have gathered, thickened, and become dense clouds,
the force that pushes them makes them strike that fiery ether, and they shriek and crackle. That mighty sound of thunder comes from the collision of the clouds and winds.
And that fierce blast of the ether, and the [?] of fire and the flash in the clouds coming from the ether, are seen immediately.
The sound, however, is delayed because of the distance from that height. At the same time, rain falls because of the compression of the clouds, which are squeezed and send down rain.
If rain does not fall after lightning and thunder, know that mercury descends at those times. And because the vapors are hardened still more by the action of the air,
this substance called mercury is formed. Its nature and composition come from watery vapors and from western and northern air.
It descends over the whole creation as something fine and invisible, and mingles with the substance of the earth like a male with a female.
From this mixture all solid bodies are formed: I mean gold, silver, copper, and tin,
and lead and iron, as well as precious stones and the other kinds of things that come out of the earth.
We will speak about these clearly and at length in another discourse below, when their time comes, if our Lord wills.
Know this, then, with certainty: when thunder and lightning occur, rain comes at the same time.
Not everywhere, however, but where the vapors have gathered and the clouds have [?], even though lightning can be seen
from a great distance. And if neither rain nor hail falls, mercury is certainly descending, though it cannot be seen at all.
However, the air becomes colder at those times when mercury descends.
Hail comes from large drops that descend from the clouds after they are squeezed beneath the ether.
Then they freeze because of the north wind that blows high above.
These drops also stick to one another and become large pieces of ice, like walnuts and almonds, and elongated in shape.
They fall in every sort of shape. Snow, however, is those vapors themselves hardening and freezing in the air before they reach the region beneath the ether.
As the particles join one another while flying through the air before that north wind, they grow heavy together, descend gently to the earth, and pile up.
As for frost and ice, as the vapors rise from the surface of the earth, the harsh air pours them back onto the surface of the earth and hardens them.
Thus frost and ice form according to the will and command of the wise Creator. All these things are for the benefit and preservation of creation.
Hail frightens, terrifies, and disciplines wrongdoers. It also kills creeping creatures and moths that damage crops and fruit.
Snow and ice cultivate the earth and renew it, so that it gains strength like soil that has been manured, grows rich, and produces fruit.
They also suffocate, destroy, and wipe out mice, locusts, and vermin—that is, [?], crawling pests, [?], and blight.
And all such things that harm and damage crops. They also provide many other hidden benefits that we neither understand nor recognize.
As he alone knows—and blessed be his glory. Here ends chapter five [of discourse six], through God, who gave strength and help.
Chapter six, with God who gives wisdom. On what causes the changes of the seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—and how they occur. God's great power is sufficient for everything.
But his wisdom has no divisions; it has made great wonders and many variations in all created things and their arrangements.
So that the great wisdom of the one who orders everything, who is wise in all things, may be known, and so that we may marvel greatly at this.
And as he is marveled at, he is loved [and as he is loved], and he draws to himself those who love him truly and without divided loyalties.
Who, when he considers all the beings, arrangements, and natures of creation, and looks at them and examines them discerningly with the hidden eye of his mind,
And understands the great power concealed in them and the spiritual contemplation hidden within them, does not become astonished
And marvel at the Creator, who is wise in all things? And as he marvels, he is drawn toward a love that unites and cannot be comprehended.
Blessed is he whose judgments cannot be comprehended and whose ways cannot be traced. One of the men of God said:
“What God is to things perceived by the mind, the sun is to things perceived by the senses—that is, bodily things.”

That is, God placed in the nature of this sun a great bodily power of action, so that, through the magnificence of the effects it produces in all the bodies of living creatures, in the earth, and in the waters, it resembles
God, who holds everything, governs things perceived by the mind, and cares for things perceived by the senses. This is how this sun acts, the great light, the king of the lights—

Or rather, of all created things. It orders seasons and appointed times. By it and from it the years and their boundaries are known. It distinguishes the months, marks out the weeks, and counts the days.

From it all the hours of daylight are known. It brings about the changes of the year in a greatly wondrous way. When it stands at the midpoint of its course through the zodiac, it makes day and night equal.

It makes the air temperate, pleasant, and springlike, warming the earth so that it sprouts grass and brings forth plants, like a hen that warms [?] and brings living creatures into being within them. This happens when it stands at the midpoint of its course, which is the sign of Aries.
This is the house of Ares, the planet that travels in the firmament above the sun and is the fifth.
And for this reason it is the house of exaltation and beneficial influence of [?], that is, [?]. When it is positioned here after the cold and damp winter,
It makes the air good and temperate, warm, moist, and mild, sustaining life and preserving health.
This is the season that is good and beneficial for things perceived by the senses, more than all the other seasons of the changing year.
Afterward, the sun again ascends along the upward part of its course and rises to the highest degree, which is the end of the sign of Gemini.
And it comes near us, because the seven climatic zones of the inhabited world are on the northern side of the earth.
And when the sun ascends to the high, northern degrees of its course, it comes near the climatic zones of the inhabited world.
And it warms them and makes them hotter because its rays fall on their heads. In this way it immediately brings about the change to summer and heat.
For its course extends much farther above the earth and is shortened below the earth, because it has inclined toward the north.
That day grows longer, and its duration becomes one and a quarter times that of the day at the equinox, about nine equal hours.
The entire night and day comprise eight parts. That long day in this middle climatic zone—that is, our fourth zone—lasts [?] parts, and the night three parts. And the farther you go north or south,
the lengths of the days and nights vary because of the earth’s inclination, that is, the elevation of its middle.
For it is spherical and round, like the shape of a melon.
When the sun enters the beginning of the sign of Cancer, its course turns toward the south, until it reaches the end of the sign of Virgo, which is the ear of grain.
Then the day becomes equal [to the night, as at [?], and the day lasts] twelve hours, and the night twelve hours [equally].
The sun’s heat also diminishes in our region, because the sun has moved away from directly above our heads. And the farther someone goes north through the climatic zones
that are inhabited, the colder those places are. And the farther one goes south, the hotter they are, because of the sun’s nearness and distance.
When the sun descends to the lower, southern degree at the end of the sign of Sagittarius, that day consists of three quarters, or parts,
that is, nine equal hours, like the summer night at the beginning of Cancer. This winter night consists of five parts,
that is, fifteen hours, like that summer day. The sun’s heat diminishes greatly because it has moved very far away from us.
Its rays warm us from the side and do not descend upon us from directly above our heads so as to warm the earth.
As a result, vapors increase, rise, gather in the air, and are held there. The air too is pushed by them and moves back and forth, and the cold increases.
The vapors grow stronger, the clouds become dense, are squeezed, and send down rain. The air and natural things grow cold, and winters occur.
This is the cause of these changes that occur in creation: they all arise from the sun’s approach and withdrawal.
It is also the cause of the completion of the year: when it completes its circuit around the entire circle of the zodiac, the year is completed.
And if someone investigates intelligently, it is the cause of all the formations and things that come into being from the elements.
It ripens the earth, and the earth produces gold, silver, copper, and the other material substances. It [?] stones, makes them clear, and makes them shine.
And they acquire varied, brilliant colors, along with other powers and many marvelous effects that they produce.
It ripens fruits, makes seeds rich, causes growth, and preserves. It brings everything into being. It gathers and dries up mud and decay.
It clears away the filth, corruption, and mildew in creation. As it is said, nothing is hidden from its heat.
For its power enters and acts in all the natural things in this world. And where there are northern regions on which its rays do not fall,
its power nevertheless enters those places through the [?] on the other side and through the air, as well as into places that are interior and very far below.
And downward into the earth, the sun’s power descends, penetrates, and acts to a depth of one parasang, which amounts to four miles.
Likewise, upward in the air, it acts for one parasang and no farther, because its power is weakened by the coldness of the air and the northern winds.
And because there is no earth or surface there upon which its rays can fall, becoming hot and giving heat.
Rather, they are weakened along with them, and their activity diminishes because of [?].
When the sun itself descends into the southern quarter, it warms the region beyond the middle of the earth and makes summer there, but winter for us.
Again, when it is summer for us, it is winter for them, because it moves farther away from them. And whether there are human beings in that region
or animals, we know. Nor is it dry land or sea.
For the whole earth, together with the seas and depressions in it, is divided throughout its entire spherical form into five parts, as in this diagram that we draw here.
PICTURE ON PAGE 241
Now imagine, according to this diagram, that the earth is round and spherical, and divide it into five parts: one in the middle,
another to its north, another to its south, and two others at the extremities of the earth: the northern one beneath the North Pole,
and the southern one beneath the South Pole, which is not visible to us. This region is dark and does not see the sun because of the elevated curvature of the earth’s spherical form.
It is also very cold because of the sun’s distance from it.
Whether it is dry land or sea, no one knows at all, unless he is a prophet who sees by the Spirit of God and knows hidden things.
On this side of it is a southern region beyond that burning, uninhabitable land, and because of the sun’s passage.
That region beyond the middle of the earth should be temperate, like this northern region in which we live.
It is divided into seven climatic zones. Winter there is summer here with us,
because the sun draws nearer to us and moves farther away from there. Likewise, winter here with us is summer there.
But whether it is dry land or sea, we do not know at all, unless human beings or animals live there.
But because a human being cannot cross that burning, sandy land, in which there is no grass or tree at all,
nor any mountains or hills, but only a desolate, scorched wilderness continually set ablaze by the sun’s constant passage over it.
Great serpents live in it. By day they go down into deep holes in the earth, and at night they come out and swallow one another.
Day and night are always equal there, because it is the middle of the sphere.
The sun always passes above it as it revolves with the zodiac, though it also inclines a little to this side and that in summer and winter.
But it remains near and does not produce much variation. In the region above the middle of the sphere, on its southern side, however, it is as it is with us.
Thus its changes occur: summer, winter, spring, and autumn, and nights
and days. But we think that summer there is hotter than summer here,
because the sun travels through the lower regions of its celestial sphere at the time when it is winter here and summer there.
Again, winter there is also colder than winter here, because during winter there, which is summer here,
the sun travels through the upper regions of its celestial sphere and is very high and far from the earth. If it were not so high above us during summer,
I think we could not survive the intense heat that would scorch us. Likewise, in winter,
if the sun did not descend and come close to the earth and warm it greatly, we could not survive then either, because of the severe cold.
This is why the earth’s interior, springs, and fountains grow warm in winter: the sun is close to the earth and warms it from the south,
while here the cold strikes it from above and confines that heat within its interior.
Through this we have become convinced that that southern region is uninhabitable,
because summer there is very hot, and winter there is colder still. Were it not for these divine arrangements, not even
this region could be inhabited by a human being or any other animal.
But through tempered heat and measured cold, he who is wise in everything has wonderfully governed and ordered the seasons.
The entire inhabited world is confined to this portion situated in the middle of the northern region, between the scorched land at the earth’s middle beneath the sun
and that dark northern corner beneath the North Pole.
Within this portion, seven belts, that is, climatic zones, are distinguished, and the entire inhabited world lies within them.
It is bounded on its four sides, and no one can possibly pass beyond these impassable boundaries.
To the east, beyond the land of China, there are dense forests that are utterly impossible to cross.
To the west lies the Ocean, the great and impassable sea. To the north, again, there is that dark and cold region,
and to the south, the scorched land that lies at the middle of the sphere, over which the sun continually passes.
Know that the sun cannot shine equally upon the entire inhabited world at one time, because of the earth’s spherical shape and the shadow cast by the slope of its rounded elevation.
When it is morning in China, it is still midnight here in Media and Assyria, and evening in the west, in inner Spain.
The reverse also happens in the same way, and there is no place to which the sun is closer than to another.
Rather, just as it is high above us when it stands over our heads at midday, so it is equally high in every place when it stands above it.
For the earth is situated in the midst of the air and is suspended at God’s command like a bird in the air. The air surrounds it on every side, encircling it like the white of an egg around the yolk.
As we said above and will say again below, we have now established that only one of the earth’s five parts is inhabited.
The other four are empty and uninhabited. Two of these are the dark and cold regions: the northern and the southern.
These are equally dark and cold, as we said. The northern region is colder because of the sun’s height in the summertime.
However, the dark region does not extend as far in the north as in the south, because when the sun rises to the upper limits of its firmament in Cancer,
it shines farther into that northern region. In the south, however, when it descends into Capricorn,
it travels along the lower limits of its firmament and is lower and closer to the earth than when it is in Cancer.
It warms the earth more intensely, but it cannot shine far over that southern region. Thus the dark region there is much more extensive than in the north.
However, it is not as cold as the northern region, because the sun is closer to the earth and warms it more intensely. The power of its heat reaches as far
as that place. For during our winter, which is summer there, it is close to that southern region, and at that time the region is not as cold as the northern one.
But during our summer, which is winter there, that southern region becomes [colder],
because of the sun’s rising higher. Likewise, the region on this side of it, situated between it and the scorched land,
during our summer, which is winter there, has a winter colder than the winter we have here, because of the sun’s rising higher.
The summer there is also much hotter than our summer because of the sun’s descending lower, as we also said above.
Because of these changes, that region is uninhabited, even if it is indeed dry land.
This inhabited part is one of the five parts of the earth’s surface—that is, of the upper half of the sphere.
This side where we are is considered upper from our perspective. But the earth has no above or below, because of the spherical shape of the [?],
which constantly revolves above it in a circle. The whole earth is said to be below—that is, inward, in the middle.
The side of the earth’s surface opposite us also faces the sun as we do, and the sun is just as high and elevated above it as it is on our side.
We do not know whether it is sea or dry land. And in this temperate part opposite our inhabited region, below, on the side opposite us,
we do not know whether any human being lives there, or anything else.
In the same way, divide that other side of the earth’s surface in your mind into another five parts, equal to these in every respect, so that there are ten parts altogether.
Our inhabited region is only one of these ten parts of the earth.
The seas [?], however, are included together with the lands, because they are bounded together within the spherical shape—that is, the roundness—of the earth.
The sea is much larger and more extensive than the dry land. For, like an island in the sea, it is exposed and visible because [it rises] above the waters.
Think of the whole earth in this way: the waters of the seas surround it, and the elevated places are exposed and visible.
Wherever there were suitable conditions and a temperate climate, there was habitation for humans and animals. Or consider the earth in another way.
Picture in your mind the earth, together with the seas in it, as a round sphere, like a round [?].
In your mind, draw bands around it. Let one band encircle its middle. This is the one beneath the sun.
Another band lies south of the middle one. This too is uninhabitable, as we showed above.
A third band lies north of the middle one.
In its upper half lies this entire inhabited region, bounded on the east and west as we showed above. Consider these three bands
as three parts, and the other two extremities, the northern and southern, as the two ends of a spindle or a melon.
Now, in half of the section north of the middle one lies the entire inhabited region comprising the seven climatic zones of the whole world.
In them there are many thousands of cities, countries, and regions,
whose inhabitants have not even heard of one another or have any knowledge of one another, because of the distance between them.
And if this one-tenth portion of the earth is so broad and extensive, out of the whole earth and the seas surrounding it and within it,
how great, then, must its size and extent be! Then how much greater and more extensive is the air that surrounds all of it on the outside and rises to this great height, as far as the ether!
And the fiery ether itself, beyond the air and the earth—how much greater, larger, and broader it is!
Think in the same way and picture in your mind all the firmaments of heaven. How much greater each one is than the one beneath it!
How much greater, then, it is than the earth! And the sun and each of these great heavenly lights—how great is the size of each one!
For although they are set at that immeasurable height, they shine and are visible to the whole world.
If they were not exceedingly great, beyond measure, they would not be visible to the whole world from that lofty height.
What, then, must be the immense size of the zodiac, in which and beneath which all these heavenly lights are arranged?
And if the earth, which is like a point in the middle of a vast sphere, cannot be measured or delimited at all,
then what must be the measure of the breadth, size, and extent of these lofty and exalted spheres?
And if these cannot be measured or delimited, then who would dare say anything at all about that great sea of waters above the heavens, or comprehend it or define its limits,
or reach the end of knowledge of these things? Oh, how wonderful are your works, Lord, and how very deep are your thoughts!
Your knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is too mighty, and I have not the strength to attain it. And as I falter and fail to comprehend, I cry out:
Oh, the depth of the riches and knowledge of God, exalted in his being, whose judgments no one can probe,
and whose ways cannot be traced! With these words the sixth chapter is concluded, through God, who gave strength and help.

Chapter Seven. With God, who gives wisdom. Why the changes of the seasons come gradually and in an orderly way, and do not occur suddenly, one after another. “The heavens,” it says, “declare the glory of God,
and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands. Day pours out speech to day, and night reveals knowledge to night.
There is no speech or language where their voice is not heard.” Just as, when someone sees a lofty and splendid tower, adorned with buildings and crowned
with walls, and completed with upper rooms, with many strong and sturdy structures on the outside,
and inside, in turn, still more splendid furnishings, delightful ornaments, beautiful objects,
magnificent equipment, inexhaustible wealth, possessions beyond measure, and countless troops, together with an abundance of many other things,
he then reflects in his mind on the great wisdom and abundant knowledge of the craftsman who arranged all these things.
The craftsman becomes very great in his eyes, and he praises the greatness of his knowledge and the abundance of his wisdom:
how his mind grasped how to arrange all these things. He becomes certain in his heart and believes in his mind, without any doubt,
that this splendid structure of that adorned and delightful tower, in which every good thing is stored, certainly has a craftsman and builder.
He does not think of it as something that arose of its own accord, like a mountain height situated in some place and filled with dense trees,
but believes that all these things were certainly arranged by an intelligent craftsman.
From their splendor and their marvelous character, he also concludes that their craftsman is very wise and lofty in knowledge.
Likewise, every person who possesses understanding, when he looks and thoughtfully examines this [?] of heaven stretched out above us,
and the ordered ranks of these firmaments, the rows of heavenly lights and the orderly course of their movement, and the hours and seasons and their changes,
together with the abundance of beings, arrangements, natures, genera, species, and distinctions in this world, marvels and is amazed, and becomes certain that indeed
all these splendid things have a craftsman and arranger, and that this craftsman is wise and lofty in knowledge,
whose knowledge cannot in any way be measured or comprehended, nor can his great and richly varied wisdom be bounded:
how he created, arranged, and established all these marvelous, astonishing, splendid, and indescribable things,
each one of which, if the mind examines it, leaves it astonished and bewildered; and how, after creating and arranging everything,

he cares for and governs it, and is concerned for the preservation and continued existence of everything, like a shipbuilder and its pilot who, after constructing it and completing it with every kind of equipment it needs,
holds its rudders in his hands and steers it with great vigilance and much care.
So this wise craftsman and mighty master architect, after stretching out this curtain and setting up this splendid vault and filling it with every furnishing and necessary equipment,
holds its rudders carefully, steers it vigilantly, and governs it attentively.
He extended its days and set limits to its nights. He appointed different seasons for its continued existence and preservation.
If it were spring all the time, seed would neither grow nor reach maturity, and fruit would neither grow plump nor ripen. If it were summer all the time, there would be withering
of everything from the heat; it would be scorched, destroyed, and come to an end. And if, again, it were winter all the time, no living creature would survive,
neither human nor animal nor bird. And if these changes occurred and arrived rapidly, one after another, the world likewise could not endure,
and no living creature would survive. If, for example, there were winter weather today, and tomorrow hot summer suddenly arrived,
the bodies and constitutions of humans and animals, and seeds and trees and everything else, would be ruined.
And if, again, there were hot summer weather today, and tomorrow winter suddenly arrived,
the constitutions and bodies of humans and animals would likewise be ruined. No living creature could survive or endure at all.
But the Craftsman, wise in everything, arranged and ordered things so that one season would follow another slowly and gradually.
Between the seasons of winter and summer he placed other seasons: spring and autumn, that is, the Tishrin months.
This was so that the changes would follow one another little by little, until bodies and constitutions became accustomed to cold and heat, without being harmed and ruined.
He divided them into four seasons, and each season consists of three months, differing to provide an adjustment that sustains and preserves life.
The spring season consists of three months, differing to provide an adjustment that sustains and preserves life.
The spring season begins with April, which is still a little [?] and close to the other month of the winter season, March.
The beginning of April itself is cold, like the end of March. Its middle is somewhat mild, and its end is milder still.
June follows it. Its beginning likewise resembles the end of May. Its middle is hot, and its end is hotter still.
After these three spring months, which contain nine changes, comes the summer season. Its first month is July.
Its beginning closely resembles the end of June, the last month of spring. The middle of July is hotter, and its end is hotter still.
After it comes August, which is the height of summer and ripens the fruit. Its beginning is likewise intensely hot.
Its middle is the same, but at its end the heat diminishes in intensity. The beginning of September is likewise hot.
Its middle is less hot, and its end less hot still. Then cold spells and cooling breezes begin.
Thus the three summer months are completed in nine changes. The middle one is more intensely hot than all the others.
Now see how great a distance there is between this scorching, ripening heat of August and the harsh, biting cold of January. If one occurred immediately after the other,
everything in the world would be ruined at once. But the Creator provided and arranged for the weather to grow warm little by little,
so that bodies would become accustomed to it, seeds would grow, and fruits would [?], ripen, and become sweet.
But if heat suddenly overtook them, they would be scalded while still tender, and the fruits, leaves, and blossoms would grow hot, dry up, and fall. Nothing at all would grow.
But little by little they grow, become stronger, and develop substance, so that when the weather grows hot they can withstand the intensity of the heat and ripen well.
Then, after that intense heat, a breeze blows over them again and refreshes them, so that the fruits and produce soften and become sweeter.
Their sweetness becomes pleasant and delicious. The grapes and pomegranates soften, their moisture increases, and their skins split.
After these things comes the autumn change, which is also intermediate between summer and winter, just like the spring change.
Its first month is October. The beginning of this month resembles and is close to the end of September, the last month of summer.
The middle of October, however, is a little cooler, and its end cooler still. The same is true of November and December.
In this way the cold comes little by little, without causing harm, like someone traveling in a ship.
Although he neither walks nor exerts himself, the vessel carries him from place to place. Little by little he reaches where he wants to go, without noticing it.
In this way the seasons and times carry the world, conveying it gently from one change to another without its noticing.
Then the winter change begins, and the cold increases little by little until February, which is the height of winter.
From its full moon onward, that intense cold diminishes again, and the time of the spring change draws near once more.
In this way the seasons revolve and the changes are ordered through the great care and wonderful providence of the Craftsman who is wise in everything.
Little by little, as we have said, for the continued existence and preservation of this world and of all the natures and beings within it.
And from these wise arrangements [and others like them], these wonderful changes, the cycle of the seasons, and the ordering of the times,
the setting of boundaries for years and months, the moderation of the rains, the gentleness of the showers, and the fact that storms do not persist,
the severity of periods of violent lightning, mighty thunder, and driving rain, and the short duration of tremors, earthquakes, and shakings,
and from many wonderful things like these, we know and are assured beyond doubt that this world has a Lord and Governor.
He himself created it, fashioned it, and established it. He provides for everything within it and cares for it wisely,
perfectly and rationally. He has no opponent, no partner, and no equal. Rather, he alone is one power and authority,
nature, will, lordship, and governance. He can do everything, fills everything, and suffices for everything.
And if this sun, which is one of his creatures, exercises the power of its nature in this way and penetrates solid bodies, the earth, the seas, and all created things,
and nothing is hidden from its heat, then how much more can the power of God, the Creator of the sun and of all created things above and below, accomplish everything
and suffice for everything! Without doubt he is one, the Lord who holds everything and governs everything, who himself created and fashioned everything.
He cares for, provides for, and orders the seasons through his great and all-powerful wisdom. And although they change so gently, little by little and gradually,
the seasons, through his great and all-powerful wisdom—and although the seasons of the year change so gently, little by little and gradually.
Look, these changes bring about much destruction, and in human bodies they cause pains, diseases, and fevers of various kinds.
And in trees, blossoms, and crops there is much blight and damage, and likewise among the rest of the animals and the birds.
So if the changes happened suddenly, to what destruction would the world be abandoned!
Glory to the craftsman who is wise in everything! How wonderful and glorious his ordering of things is! It is like a glassworker,
who makes and fashions many different vessels from glass. At the very moment when he completes and finishes a vessel,
while the body of the vessel is still fiery, he first places it in the middle chamber of the furnace, above the place where the fire blazes.
If, at the very moment when he finished the vessel, he were to set it away from the heat of the fire, it would immediately break and be ruined.
Instead, he skillfully places it in the middle chamber, where the fire is not as intense as in the lower one, which is blazing,
where the glass was melted and the vessel was worked and fashioned. In this way he arranges and places there all the vessels he makes.
When he finishes his work and gets up from his labor, he closes all the doors of the furnace chambers and seals them with clay, so that air will not enter and ruin the work.
He leaves it throughout the night and the following day, while the heat subsides a little and the fire dies down.
Then he first opens a small opening at the back of the furnace, and after a while a little more. He does not hurry,
but is patient, so that the work will not be damaged. In this way he proceeds skillfully throughout the day, until the furnace gradually settles down.
Then he brings the work toward the door of the furnace’s middle chamber. He brings it nearer little by little as the heat subsides.
Then he takes the vessels one by one and arranges them on top of the furnace. In this way he manages things with his knowledge and [?] all the work.
Again, whenever he wants to melt glass for working, or to return a glass vessel to the fire, he manages things and works in the same way.
Little by little he brings them toward the heat. First he places them in the middle chamber, where the reflected heat of the fire is mild,
and afterward [?] a gentle fire. Little by little he increases its strength through his craft, without hurrying. In this way he skillfully completes his work and preserves what he has made.
In just this way that mighty architect and wise craftsman of created things acted and provided for them.
He ordered the times, the seasons, and the changes of the year with abundant knowledge and great wisdom, for the well-being
and preservation of this world, which he created and established in his goodness. He himself had no need of it, but did so for the benefit of the creatures he had made,
for their advancement and growth in virtue and upright conduct, so that through these things they might rise in knowledge and enter more deeply into true wisdom,
and draw near to the dwelling of his majesty, and be illuminated by the rays of the radiance and splendor of his majesty’s glory.
To him belong, and are due, praise, thanksgiving, and worship in all the worlds that his lordship has created and established,
forever and ever. Amen. Here ends the seventh chapter, through God who gave strength and help.
The sixth discourse on the knowledge of truth is complete, through God, who gave strength and help.
It contained seven chapters, in which all [these] things that occur beneath the zodiac, in the ether and in the air, and down to the earth were splendidly discussed.
The seventh discourse on the knowledge of truth, explaining the kinds of birds and the species of flying creatures, and the kinds of fish and all the creatures that move in the water;
and the nature of the earth and its many variations, and the formation of material substances, namely gold, silver, copper, and so forth;
and mineral deposits, that is, mines; and hot springs, and other gushing springs, and bitumen and pitch;
and the kinds of trees and the species of fruits and seeds, and wild animals and livestock. It contains five chapters.
Chapter One. With God, who gives wisdom. Why the kinds of birds and flying creatures exist, and where they come from.
And what benefit they provide, and what their meanings are. For concerning these too, in the account of creation,
as the holy book of Genesis says, which the great Moses wrote according to what he received from God, after the creation of the sun and the moon and the rest of the stars,
which were created on the fourth day, the kinds of birds and flying creatures were created, as well as the kinds of fish
and all the creatures that move in the water, on the fifth day. But the creation of trees and seed-bearing plants preceded these too.
For seeds and all vegetation were created on the third day by the Creator, who is wise in everything and orders created things.
But we, as we said above, wish to proceed in order and speak about each created thing individually.
We first began with things that are intelligible and invisible, and then went on to speak about the creation
that is invisible, beginning above, with the waters above the heavens. Then, in succession, we spoke about all the firmaments of heaven,
and about the heavenly lights, and then about the fiery ether, and about this air and all its variations and movements.
And because birds and flying creatures fly in the air, it is fitting for us to explain them first,
and then descend to the earth and speak about it and everything in it. In the account of creation, however, the Spirit of God arranged things well and instructed the writer:
first, trees, seeds, and grasses were created, and the waters were gathered into basins, and from them were distributed through rivers.
Then birds and flying creatures were created to dwell in the trees and feed on their fruits.
Fish too, and all the creatures that move in the water, were created from the waters themselves, to swim in them and live in them.
Likewise, livestock and wild animals were created after these, so that as soon as they were created, formed, and brought into existence, they could begin to graze on grass
and be nourished. For this reason grass was created beforehand, to be their food and sustenance.
And because all these things were created for humanity, to be of use to human beings and supply all their needs, everything was created and prepared beforehand.
Then the human being was created and found everything needed and everything useful already available and laid out, as for a king.
Lord. Blessed is the wise Creator! How great and wonderful are his works, and how glorious are his creatures!
After the things belonging to the fourth day were completed, there was evening and there was morning, which was the morning of the fifth day:
God said, “Let the waters swarm with living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth, across the expanse of the heavens.”
God created the great sea monsters and every living creature with which the waters swarmed, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind.
God saw that it was good. God blessed them and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth.”
As we said above, it is like a king who wishes to hold a wedding feast for his beloved firstborn son.

First he prepares spacious halls and stores in them the necessary provisions of food, drink, and entertainment, along with various kinds of music and harpists, to delight the invited guests and those reclining at the feast.
In the same way, this heavenly King first arranged and prepared everything humanity needed, as for a bridegroom and a son of [?],
before creating him and bringing him into being. First he stretched out this lofty canopy for him
and erected this magnificent and glorious dwelling for him. He planted these splendid gardens for him and filled their trees with desirable fruit.
He made abundant rivers gush forth for him, and made springs and fountains of plentiful, clear water flow for him.
In the height of his canopy he arranged a multitude of shining lights, and he lit two lamps for him, blazing with powerful light,
to give him light by day and by night. He also confined and gathered vast waters for him in deep, fathomless seas, so that he could ride upon their backs, tread confidently upon their waves,
swim boldly among their billows, and complete his journeys and travels amid their mighty surges.
He also made their depths swarm with countless creatures, varied in their kinds and species
and in their flavors, to provide him with nourishment and delights lavishly and splendidly. In his wisdom he also made and created great and mighty sea monsters [?]
and whales of enormous size, together with immeasurable Leviathan, full of wonder and an astonishing sight, for many purposes and various reasons.
There is much to say and explain about them. Afterward he continually guards humanity, the image of his majesty,
and saves him from their harmfulness, so that not one of them has any power to injure him without a signal from his command. Thus he filled the seas with swarming creatures and kinds of fish,
animals, snails, turtles, crabs, and many other creatures beyond limit or number,
all for humanity’s use in many activities. For if we began to speak about these things,
even briefly and in a very limited way, neither would the paper suffice nor would words be adequate.
One of those wise in God, speaking through the Holy Spirit, rightly said: “Here is the sea, great and wide, in which there are countless swarming creatures,
living creatures both great and small. Ships travel upon it, and this Leviathan, whom you created to laugh at.”
That is, because of his enormous stature and vast size, the tremendous weight of his body prevents him from turning this way and that [?].
But he is set in the depths of the seas like a great, heavy mountain that is not easily shaken.
This represents that spiritual dragon, the devil. For although he is great and powerful, a spiritual being with many heads—
that is, evil schemes, tricks, and deceptions—and is always alert and diligent in causing harm, busily struggling,
never ceasing or resting from wrongdoing, nevertheless God has given those who fear him, who keep his commandments and do his will,
strength and power to trample on his neck, crush his many heads, laugh at him, and mock his tricks,
to undo his schemes, break his traps, and cut through his snares and nets.
Blessed is our good Lord and mighty God! He has enriched us with his gifts and poured out upon us an abundance of his blessings.
This great, terrifying, and drowning sea he has filled, storing up in it for us useful things, necessities, and things beyond all counting:
various foods and abundant nourishment, and countless creatures useful for many purposes—for healing limbs,
bones, and bodies that are weakened and debilitated; for the purposes and needs of kings and rulers;
for dyes, various colors, and brilliant royal purple from shellfish, and brilliantly colored scarlet, along with all the other things.
He has also brought up for us from the lowest depths of the seas splendid pearls of great value, whose beauty greatly amazes those who see them.
They say that in the depths of the sea there is a certain shelled creature belonging to the family of shellfish and snails.
It resembles two little boats joined together. In the month of Nisan it stirs, grows warm, and opens like a pair of doors.
It rises and floats on the surface of the seawater, and by God's will a drop of dew falls into it, in proportion to its size, whether large or small.
Then lightning flashes upon it, and its force makes it close, while [?] within it from its light, together with that drop of dew.
It grows heavy, descends again, and settles in the depths of the sea. It grows like a living creature for as long as it remains in that place.
There are skilled workers accustomed to diving into deep water. They descend skillfully, plunge into the depths, and draw up the splendid pearl, becoming rich from its price.
All their needs are met. The pearl closely resembles the true faith.
The orthodox faith in one God is one, and nothing can be added to it or taken away from it,
just as nothing is added to the splendid pearl or taken away from it. Divers bring the pearl up from the depths of the sea,
and discerning people establish the faith from the depth of knowledge and through diving into the Holy Scriptures.
Virtue, however, resembles gold and silver, which can receive additions, increase, and bring wealth.
So too with the virtue of upright conduct: the more you add to it, the greater your spiritual wealth becomes, and the more abundant your treasury grows.
But faith is in one God—Mind, Word, and Spirit—an essential, eternal, and sovereign Trinity.
Nothing can be added to it, because there is no other God besides the One. Nor can anything be taken away from it, because there are no measures or numbers in the Godhead.
Although we speak of three persons, we do not count them one after another, saying, “One, two, three.”
The sovereign Trinity is not like that—not one followed by another. There is no first or second within it.
Rather, it is all one being, one eternity, one sovereignty, one nature.
One power, one will, one lordship, one kingdom [?], one governance. Nothing can be added to this true faith.
Nor can anything be taken away from it, just as a pearl is one in its beauty and its nature. Blessed is he who gave us a pearl that can be seen and understood.
Amen. Who can grasp the great blessings and the many benefits that our good Lord has prepared for us in the sea, on dry land, in the air, and in the depths?
After the many things he created and gathered for us in the seas and rivers—many kinds, varied species, and different natures—there is much to say and discuss about them.
Again, great wisdom and its wonderful care [?]. And he brought up for us from the sea winged birds, many kinds and countless different species.
All of them are useful for our needs and serve us. Some are raised among us and in our presence, such as chickens, geese, and ducks,
to produce offspring and hatch chicks for the enjoyment of our meals, and to wake us at times during the night and keep watch over our guard posts.
Such is the nature of geese: they are very alert even to a faint, tiny sound, and as soon as they notice the slightest thing,
they become agitated, cry out loudly, and wake the people of the place so that they get up and see what the noise was—that is, the chirping—that occurred.
Through this, many cities, fortresses, houses, and places have been saved from theft.
There is also the splendid kind of peacock, adorned with every sort of beauty, which he gave us for the delight and enjoyment of our sight.
He clothed them and decorated them with varied colors that astonish those who see them:
like gold, like purple, like [?], like green, and like white, together with a multitude of different, bright, and radiant colors.
All the craftsmen of kings cannot combine such splendid and brilliant colors.
It is as though they were all formed from liquid gold and overlaid with gold. And as the peacock struts about here, displaying its beauty and delighting those who see it,
it stirs hearts and minds to praise the Creator of these splendid wonders.
Again, the Maker appointed some birds to chirp for us early, so that we rise from our beds for our work and our tasks,
or rather, to praise the Creator of the morning and the one who dispels the darkness of night. Swallows chirp and warble in measured rhythms.
Sparrows chirp from their nests. Other birds take wing and fly; others coo and flash brightly.
Others are intent on mating. Others gather flock after flock and soar above us.
Still others travel from place to place in even greater numbers, thousands and tens of thousands. Others pick insects, flies, and gnats from our fields.
Others are set against locusts to drive them out of our fields. Others catch creeping things, mice, and flying insects on our land.
Others live among us and watch for snakes and [?]; wherever they see them, they quickly carry
them off so that they do not harm us. At night, too, they stay awake and keep watch to protect us.
When someone stirs at night, they honk and rattle their beaks, making their thunderous cries heard to guard our houses against break-ins and thefts.
Others count the hours by beating their wings, making known to us the times of day and night.
Others coo at noon and urge the weary toward sleep and rest in the intense heat.
Others call out in the trees, sending forth ringing cries and varied sounds to delight our hearing.
Others fly through the air in flocks upon flocks and make the seasons known to us.
Some of them rejoice in spring and appear to us. Others live near us in the height of summer.
Others appear to us at the beginning of winter. Others come to us from other lands during the season of intense cold.
Others delight us throughout the day. Others call at evening time and announce the end of the day.
When it is a winter day and the sun cannot be seen at all, we can recognize all the times of day from them.
Especially at evening time, when you see many of them springing from their nests, we can recognize all the times of day.
Especially at evening time, when you see many of them springing from their nests, flying about, chirping, and calling to one another,
know for certain that evening is near and that these birds have gone out to their nests to prepare to spend the entire stretch of the night.
Late in the evening, others begin to coo and make their voices heard, as though calling us to sleep and rest. Other flying and creeping creatures
chirp gently, as though rocking us to sleep, like a mother who rocks her infant and sings to it to make its sleep pleasant and help it fall asleep.
Others call in the very middle of the night and awaken us to praise and thanksgiving to the one who gave the night for rest from labor and toil.
Thus they are all yoked together in our service, like diligent servants who neither slumber nor sleep.
Others soar and rise to lofty heights. Others move about on the face of the earth, with us and among us.
We can also see others that are hunters and birds of prey by nature, which, when captured and raised among us,
grow accustomed to us and attach themselves to us. They no longer leave us, and they hunt others of their kind for us.
They snatch prey from others and bring it to us. Others act as singers and lyre players for us all day long.
They chirp, chatter, and twitter, flying and soaring around us with pleasant warbling, sweet songs, and delightful melodies
that bring comfort. Human beings cannot compose such sweet sounds and delightful warbling.
And whoever looks at them and examines them carefully, and applies himself spiritually to the contemplation hidden and concealed within them,
sees the adorable Maker in their very nature, behavior, and colors, and comes to know him through his great power at work in them,
and through his care for them—in their kinds, their individual beings, their colors, and their wonderful, glorious, and clearly defined forms,
and in all their other distinctive properties. But someone might think superficially and say, “What benefit is there in these things?
Look, even innocent children [?] know and recognize them all. I do not count this as knowledge.”
Yet a person gathers much spiritual knowledge and gains clear wisdom from examining and studying these things and the other beings and structures of creation,
when he applies himself with understanding, together with stillness, prayer, and a heart free from thoughts and empty concerns about passing affairs.
Why should I multiply words? He comes to know the Creator himself through his creatures. With these words the first chapter ends, through God, who gave strength and help.
Chapter Two of the Seventh Discourse, with God who gives wisdom. On the nature of the earth and the many differences within it:
in its soil and stones, and [?] the minerals derived from them and their distinctive properties;

and on what the substances derived from the earth were formed from, and how they were formed—that is, gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, and iron; and on minerals, that is, things extracted from the earth,
such as sulfur, arsenic, bitumen, alum, natron, salts, and precious stones, together with the other things derived from the earth. This chapter, which is divided into many sections, is placed [?].
Let us return to Holy Scripture and listen to the divine words concerning creation. It says that on the third day God said,
“Let the waters beneath heaven be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear.” And it was so.
God called the dry land Earth, and the gathering of the waters he called Seas. And God saw that it was good.
So that this chapter should not become excessively long, beyond what is necessary, we have already spoken about the gathering of the waters and about the swarming creatures and fish within them,
and about the birds that God created and brought forth from them. Although he made these from the nature of water,
nevertheless, fish and birds, and everything that lives, crawls, moves, and sustains life—both animal life and plant life—are constituted from all four elements.
And everything animate and inanimate, trees, crops, grasses, and everything that exists in the world
cannot be constituted except from the four elements. Yet in a particular thing there is more of one element or of two
than of the others, according to the mixture and composition that the all-wise Maker has worked together and blended. His power extends throughout them all, and his will is at work.
When God said, “Let the waters beneath heaven be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear,” by this statement he again distinguished the waters above heaven
from the waters beneath heaven. Those above heaven he stretched out like a curtain,
and harnessed them like a wheel in swift rotation. By his command he made them solid, so that they would never spill out or
sway this way and that, but would be like a wheel set upon upright supports, held firmly on every side, and turning evenly like an eye.
Thus he fixed it and set its limits. He also yoked all nine spheres of the zodiac to that swiftly moving force, as far as this fiery ether.
From the heat of that swift revolution it caught fire and blazed up, and heat spread from that swift revolution into this air around us.
Thus, by the will of the Maker, it was confined to that place, just as he had set its limits.
Thus everything was ordered, created, and established within the wondrous bosom of those waters above the heavens.
Others have said that rationality belongs to the nature of these revolving heavens above us.
They say this because of their motion. Everything that moves, they say, moves out of longing.
Where there is longing, there are desire and will, and these indicate rationality.
We, however, make no judgment on this. Nevertheless, we say that everything that moves of itself has rationality in its nature.
For example, the soul moves of itself and moves the body rationally—not like irrational animals, which move naturally rather than rationally.
But anything moved by something else cannot properly be called rational.
What is properly rational is that which moves of itself, independently and freely—or rather, in a divine manner.
For everything that governs itself and possesses freedom is in the image of God. But concerning heaven and the zodiac,
we cannot say such things. For if it possessed freedom and rationality, it would move of itself.
Thus many would have gone astray and supposed that the revolving heaven itself was the God and ruler of all, just as some people did go astray and lose their way from the truth.
But if heaven has another mover, who moves it by his power and the command of his will, while he himself has no other mover,
and no one is the cause of his motion, but he moves of himself, and in himself lives and moves in his own being,
moving everything that lives and moves, then he is the God of all and the ruler of all, and he has neither opponent nor equal.
Nevertheless, concerning the lights in the firmament, we have heard Holy Scripture call and name them hosts.
But how and in what manner are we to determine whether they possess a subordinate rationality,
or possess some other nature? We do not understand this, since they are situated in an exalted place, very high and far above us.
We cannot make any definite judgment about them at all. But this we know for certain: they are subject to the command of their Creator,
like all the rest of creation, and the properties they possess are implanted in their nature, as with trees, roots, and the rest of natural things. And by nature
they are subject, like all created things, and not by choice, like angels and rational human beings.
These remarks suffice, together with the many things already said about the lights and all the firmaments beneath those waters above the heavens.
And God said to it, “Let the waters beneath the heavens be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear.”
And so, at the signal of the command, these two elements, which had been mixed together, were separated:
the water from the earth. The waters gathered in the depressions and hollows that God had marked out for them, and dry land appeared here and there,
like islands in the middle of the sea. The sea is one: that great sea whose end has not been found. It is the great Ocean,
which borders all the western regions and extends northward as far as the dark region beneath the North Pole.
To the south, a gulf branches off from it and spreads throughout the whole region of Ethiopia,
that is, inland from the countries of the Abyssinians and Nubians, as far as the entrance of Dush [?]. It extends eastward and joins the great sea of India.
Another gulf branches off from the Ocean and enters the western regions of the Britons of England, reaching as far as Italy.
It spreads southeastward along the regions of Syracuse and Carthage, and along Lombardy and Sicily.
It extends as far as the area opposite Alexandria and the regions of Libya and Egypt. It turns toward Palestine and Phoenicia, along Tyre and Sidon, and descends to Syria.
It turns toward Cilicia, Bithynia, and Pisidia, as far as Asia and the entrance to Byzantium, which is Constantinople.
Again, from the west, it comes from the regions of Italy as far as the regions and islands of Bithion [?].
It comes along the regions of Calabria and the Venetians, as far as Corinth and Euripus, and passes along Thessalonica.
It reaches again the entrance to Byzantium, opposite Ephesus, the chief city of Asia.
In this sea, whose circuit we have traced, there are large islands: Cyprus, Sicily, Crete, Rhodes, Samos, Mytilene, and Chios,
and many other small ones. This sea passes through the entrance in front of the imperial city, which is Byzantium, and flows out into the northern sea.
From the boundary of Byzantium it goes from the west toward the northwest, along the whole region of Thrace, as far as the great river Danube, which is the Pishon, one of the four.
Inland from there are the countries of the Bulgarians, Scythians, Slavs, Vlachs, Serbs, and many different peoples.
From where the river Danube enters that northern sea of which we have spoken, the sea extends along the regions of the Hungarians and stretches toward Great Russia.
On its shores live the Khazars, Alans, Cumans, and Oghuz, as far as the Turks, opposite the passes through the high mountains
in the recesses of the north, beyond which the peoples of Gog and Magog are confined, as far as the dark region in the north.
Again, this northern sea turns toward the regions of the Iberians and toward Trebizond.
It runs a little eastward, then turns southeast toward the gulf of Sinope.
On its shores are Gangra, Colonea, Nicomedia, Heraclea, and great Ilium, which was destroyed.
Its boundary comes back again to the narrow entrance in front of Byzantium. Now the Red Sea, through which the Israelites crossed,
is a gulf of the southern sea. Its ends and boundaries are close together, and for this reason it is called the Sea of Suph. Its bed is red clay.
The sand on its bottom—for this reason it is called the Red Sea. Most of its stones and rocks are lodestone, which attracts iron.
For this reason, the boats and ships that travel on it contain absolutely nothing made of iron.
Neither nails nor a rudder nor [?], nor anything else made of iron at all. Instead, their boats and ships are constructed by other ingenious methods.
As for the great sea of Oceanus, many have ventured to sail into it and have traveled about for many months.
Yet no end or boundary has ever been found. There are a few islands in it, some inhabited by people and others with no one on them,
but only strange animals that are not seen in other lands. There is the island of Gades,

where Hercules, the mighty man and prophet of the pagans, erected those three statues famous throughout the world, and lofty pillars, supposedly as a memorial to himself, so that his memory might [?] throughout all the generations of the world.
He erected these statues at the boundaries of the inhabited world.
If a ship happens to be driven that far by the force of the wind, the sailors give up hope of their lives,
because they cannot return from there on account of the slope of the sea.
This man devised this and expended all that great labor, over a long time, with the toil of a great multitude and vast expenditures of wealth beyond counting or weighing.
He made and erected these astonishing statues so that his memory would not be forgotten in the world, although there is no benefit [?] from all that great toil.
How is it, then, that we, idle and lazy as we are, do not make an effort to leave [for ourselves] a good memory in the world through good deeds and upright conduct,
as our forefathers did, who conducted themselves properly? In this world they distinguished themselves, were praised, and acquired a good name.
The memory of their victories was recorded as a good remembrance until the end. And in the world to come they will inherit
the heavenly kingdom and life that does not pass away. May we too be worthy of these through their prayers. Amen.
There are also many seas in this inhabited earth, which the wise Creator hollowed out for human needs, as means of assistance.
Some provide habitation and protection, since they contain islets and islands suitable for people to live on.
Some form boundaries around lands like walls and protect them from enemies.
Others are full of many living creatures to sustain this temporal life.
On some, because of their extent and location, people travel easily and quickly here and there by sailing and voyaging in ships.
Those whose waters are salty serve to temper the air of the region, [because the air of the region] that comes from the salt seas
is very beneficial and protects the lands near the seas from putrefaction and decay. Just as salt preserves bodies so that they do not rot and perish,
drawing out their moisture and preserving them for a long time, so too salt water preserves the lands near it.
No region can be more than fifteen days’ journey from the sea. And where a region is excessively damp,
The Creator prepared and established a salt lake there to help sustain the lives of its inhabitants. In all the seas and lakes there are many kinds of swarming creatures,
except for the Dead Sea, which is in the region of Palestine, a day's journey beyond Jerusalem, where the River Jordan enters and is swallowed up.
It flows out of the Lake of Tiberias, which is fed by Manon and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus,
together with the other rivers that descend from Senir and the mountains around it. One stream flows out of this lake and is called Jor.
Another, called Dan, comes from the southeast and joins it. For this reason it was called Jordan, after the names of both.
This points to the great mystery that took place in the Jordan, where the union of divinity with humanity was confirmed
by the voice that testified from above and the Spirit who appeared in the bodily form of a dove. This Jordan enters that dead [?].
As for this sea, because of the great wickedness committed in that land, it became polluted and defiled and died,
when the Lord rained fire and sulfur from heaven upon Sodom and Gomorrah and the whole region around them.
After the burning fire, the destruction of the people and all their possessions, and this severe trial and bitter punishment by fire,
so that through fire that land might be cleansed of the great and hateful wickedness that had polluted and defiled it,
the mighty Judge then covered it again with floods of water. And because sin is dead to God
and does not live in him, the body of water that covered that defiled land also remained dead
and unfruitful. Nothing living moves at all in that lake. Instead, it continually spews up black bitumen and foul-smelling pitch and casts them onto its shores,
to shame its defiled and licentious inhabitants and to bring fear and trembling upon all the peoples under heaven,
so that such great wickedness should not even enter people's thoughts—wickedness that uproots and destroys those who practice it
and bitterly torments the generations after them. In this way the wise Ruler has arranged many lakes everywhere,
some of them fresh and some salty, for the sustenance and use of human beings.
This is enough about the basins of the seas and lakes. But let us think of all the earth's sea and dry land as spherical, not flat.
For this reason, whenever ships are driven by the violent force of the wind and pass beyond those pillars erected by Hercules, that mighty and renowned man,
the sailors give up hope of their lives, because they have crossed the boundary of the western edge of the earth's surface
and have slipped onto the downward slope, and can no longer return. As we said above,
the whole earth—that is, all the seas and the dry land—forms one round sphere.
They are situated in the middle, like a point at the center of a circle, and air surrounds them as the white of an egg surrounds the yolk.
Above the air are the celestial spheres of the zodiac, revolving in circles without ceasing. And the earth is [?] in the middle, a great wonder.
And there is no above or below, because everything revolves in a circle. And if it were possible for people to live over the whole surface of the earth,
people and animals would live there with all their feet standing on the earth and their heads upward, toward the air.
Understand this word “upward” that we use as meaning “outward,” because everything outside the earth’s spherical body is described as above, or outside.
First there is air, and outside this, surrounding it, ether; and outside, that is, above the ether,
are the firmaments, one above another, as we have shown above. As for the earth, its divisions are five regions:
one is the central region, which is scorching and uninhabitable because the sun passes above it; and the region [?] to its south,
of which no one knows what it contains. Nevertheless, we suppose that whether it is land or sea, it is uninhabitable.
For during our winter that place is very hot, because the sun comes close to that land,
as it descends to the lower level of its firmament. During our summer, on the other hand, that place is very cold,
because the sun moves away from it and rises to the upper level of its firmament. This is why the interior of the earth is warm during our winter:
the sun warms it by drawing near, while the cold above, which occurs in our region, confines the warmth within the earth.
The warmth drives out the vapors, and they rise abundantly in winter. This is why the rains are plentiful. And because the sun is far away, the vapors do not
disperse and descend to the earth until they increase, gather together, and reach the ether. They become heavy and turn into drops, and rain falls.
During our summer, the same applies to our region. Because the sun is far away, being high above the earth, it warms only the surface of this region,
while its depths are cold. This is evident from the waters that spring from the earth’s cavities,
which are cold in summer and warm in winter. The same is true of the vapors that rise from cracks in the mountains
and from fissures and cavities in the earth, which are cold. The third region of the earth is the southern one,
which is dark and lies beneath the South Pole. The fourth region is this inhabited one in which we live,
which the ancient sages divided into seven climatic zones, like bands extending lengthwise from east to west.
Its width extends from the boundary of the central region, which is the scorching land, to the boundary of that northern, dark region
beneath the North Pole. This is one-fifth of the earth’s surface, amounting to one-tenth of the whole sphere.
This region, which was divided into seven climatic zones, they marked out in its entirety into three regions, according to the following scheme:
from the shore of this sea, the Hellespont, in which lie the islands of Sicily, Crete, Rhodes, Cyprus, and the others,
as far as the western limit of Ocean, the great sea, it was called Europe. In it are the lands of Spain and the great cities of the West.
Its boundary follows the shores of Ocean southward, to the land of Maaph [?] and of those with slit noses, and comes to Libya, Syracuse, and Carthage, as far as
to this sea of islands. It runs along the shores of this sea as far as Lombardy, Calabria, and Bandia.
Within it lie the whole land of Italy and great Rome, Germany, England, Brittany, Poitou, Francia, and Provence,
