and many other lands. Toward the north it extends as far as the land of the Bulgars, Scythia, the Slavs, [the Wallachians,] the Serbs, the Hungarians, the Cumans, the Oghuz, the Russians, and the Khazars, as far as the Alans,
and the Cumans, and the remaining lands to their west. As for the southern region of Libya, its boundary begins in the west, from the land of the people with slit noses,
and from the south of the Sea of the Hellespont. It comes opposite Sicily and extends toward the entrance to Cush, as far as the land of the people of Clysma.
It descends into the lands of Ethiopia, among the Nubians, Abyssinians, and Zanj, as far as Taif, Nigra, the Himyarites, Tabaristan, and the people of Khuzestan, as far as India.
Then it rises again through the eastern lands, on the southern side, and comes to Elam, Media, Chaldea, Assyria, and Mesopotamia.
It extends again toward the west, across all Arabia and the desert inhabited by the Arabs, as far as Palmyra in the desert.
Within it lie the lands of Phoenicia, great Damascus, Homs, and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, extending as far as Syria.
Within it lie Palestine, Ashmun, Midian, the lands of Egypt, the Red Sea, and Mount Sinai,
and the remaining lands of Egypt. This region is hot because it is close to the middle of the earth.
[The northern region of the inhabited world, called Asia.] The region of Asia, in turn, lies on the northern side of the inhabited world.
Its boundary begins at the seacoast of the narrow strait in front of Byzantium.
Within it lie Ephesus, Troas, Bithynia, Phrygia, Pisidia, and Cilicia, as far as Syria. The high mountain Amanus marks its boundary.

This begins at the sea near great Antioch in Syria and is called the Pig’s Head. It runs through the Black Mountain and passes the land of Tagra and Arabissus on its northern side, with Marash on its southern side.
This mountain extends toward the east. To the north lie Armenia and Persia, extending as far as Samarkand and Bukhara,
and Sarazm, Kashgar, and the land of Gog and Magog, as far as China and the eastern extremity.
To the south of this mountain lie the city of Ghazni, Sistan, Chinistan, and the great river in the east,
and the land of Isfahan and Iraq, extending as far as Mosul, Amid, and their surroundings. These are reckoned as part of southern Libya.
The area inside the mountain belongs to Asia. Its boundary then rises again from the western region

and from the north, passing across all Sistan as far as the high mountains of the peoples of the north. Beyond these mountains Alexander confined the shameful and filthy nations of Gog and Magog: the Turks, the Cumans, and various nations with hateful customs, who are defiled
and eat the carcasses of every kind of animal, the creeping creatures of the earth, and every abomination.
Outside them, between these two high mountains, stands the Gate of Gates, which Alexander made through the skill of his wisdom, confining them behind it.
The people of the Iberians hold this gate, and from there the boundary of their land extends as far as Armenia.
It then goes westward as far as Alania and passes through Trebizond.
which lies on the northern seacoast and goes up into Cappadocia. It passes through Galatia, Phrygia, and the remaining regions as far as great Nicomedia.
It continues as far as the entrance before Byzantium, where we began. This is the region of Asia on the northern side of the inhabited world.
The differences found in soils and stones all result from the action of the sun and depend on the location of the place:
whether it is a plain, mountains, hills, depths, valleys, slopes, foothills, rivers, or land that gushes with water, springs, and streams;
and on its nearness to or distance from the sun—that is, whether it is near the east, south, west, or north;
or near the great sea or smaller seas, or whether the place is hot and dry or cold and moist.
In all these things the sun's action is more powerful, as we said above. It acts on the earth, heating and drying it.
The air cools it, and water likewise cools and moistens it. The earth itself acquires different qualities according to the influences acting upon it.
Among these there are many differences, beyond counting or any description that could encompass their multitude.
Through this action the earth and the deep recesses within it are cooked.
It produces many kinds of substances that have various effects, bringing healing or disease to human bodies.
Some of them strengthen and help, while others harm, destroy, and kill.
Some of them act on solid bodies such as gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, and iron, affecting their entire nature and composition. There are also others, namely these:
such as sulfur, arsenic, magnesia, marcasite, alum, natron, ochre, and prasinum.
And precious stones such as jacinth, emerald, carbuncle, calf's-eye, jasper, and the rest;
and lapis lazuli, malachite, Armenian stone, Jewish stone, and many others described in the writings of physicians.
Smiths, founders of gold and silver, and glassmakers also know them,
as do makers of fine seals. There are other substances as well, some of which come from aquatic animals

and the beds of seas and rivers, such as pearls, coral, shellfish, and many things like these, which the divine command has established for the help, use, and sustenance of human beings, and for the sustenance and preservation of the whole world,
to the praise and thanksgiving of the good Creator, the Provider who is wise in everything and almighty.
We should explain to discerning people the primary and effective cause of all these differences, products, and minerals that the earth brings forth,
as the Caretaker, wise in everything, has ordered and arranged them—he who cares for his creatures and whose power is in everything.
There is no place or region that can be known or conceived where he is not present, in all the worlds perceived by the mind or the senses.
He is like the soul that is in the body: it moves it, strengthens it, preserves it, and directs it.
The cause is as follows. Listen, discerning people, and understand. Gather your minds together out of distraction.
Everything God created and made, whether animals, plant-like animals, or trees and plants, he created male and female.
Through this mingling the world continues and endures. The origins of everything and the continued existence of this world come from these four elements:
water, earth, air, and fire. There is nothing outside these four natures.
I mean the hot, the moist, the cold, and the dry. Vapors continually rise from the earth.
From these vapors many kinds of things are formed: I mean rains and dews, manna and juniper, camelthorn manna, cotoneaster manna, and labdanum,
and mercury. All of them are called dews. There are seven of them, descending from the air, although their origin is in the earth,
which gives off vapors. The air and the sun act upon them according to the location of the region. These kinds of things are formed and descend, and all are grouped together as dews.
As we said, they are these: first, rain, drizzle, and watery dew; second, honey; third, manna, which is juniper; fourth, camelthorn manna;
fifth, cotoneaster manna; sixth, black labdanum; seventh, mercury. All of them are compounded and formed from all the elements,
but mercury alone comes from the nature of water and air. This is the subject of our entire discussion. Now listen to how this happens.
The nature of water continually sends up vapors. These vapors are acted upon in the air and condensed, and from them is formed the substance
called mercury. It continually descends from the air onto the earth. This substance, formed from water and air at the Creator’s command, is male.
Earth, again—that is, soil—is cooked within the depths of the earth by the action of the sun, whose rays continually fall upon it,
and becomes sulfur. This sulfur exists throughout the earth, in soil, in stones, and in [?]. There is no place at all in the earth where sulfur is not mixed in.
In certain places, however, the sun’s action is stronger because of the region’s location, and a large cavity and abundant sulfur are produced.
There are also many variations in the sulfur itself, likewise because of the strength of the sun’s power acting upon a place according to the region’s location.
All the many variations likewise result from the strength of the sun’s power acting upon a place according to the region’s location.
All the variations come from vapors. This substance is formed from these two elements, soil and the sun,
that is, earth and fire. It is sulfur, and its nature is female. It is mixed throughout the earth, as we have said.
The male substance formed from water and air, namely mercury, continually descends, sinks into the earth, and mingles with sulfur wherever it is found.
From this mingling of the two, all the solid bodies in the world are formed, foremost among them these seven, which are named after the seven planets.
I mean: the Sun, gold; the Moon, silver; Aphrodite, that is, Beltis, copper;
Zeus, that is, Bel, tin; Cronus, that is, Kaiwan, lead; Ares, that is, Nergal, iron; Hermes, that is, Nebo, electrum.
[Electrum] is a body that unites with other bodies, becoming like the nature of whatever body it unites with.
Likewise, the planet Hermes takes on the nature of whatever planet it mingles with: that is, with good planets it is good, and with evil planets it is evil.
Male with the male, and [female] with females; hot with the hot, and cold with the cold, and so on.
These seven bodies are formed in the earth, and the power of mercury acts in them. How this happens we will show later.
It is not only these bodies that arise from the mixture of mercury and sulfur,
but also all the varieties of stones and earths: precious stones and those possessing powers and active properties,
those we mentioned above and many that we have not mentioned and that are unknown to us. All these, and every kind that comes out of the earth,
are from mercury and sulfur. All the kinds occur in groups of seven,
as discerning men have investigated and established with precision and care. Now these seven bodies,
the primary bodies and the chief of all bodies, are gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, iron, and electrum. They are formed as follows. Gold, which is the sun, is formed in this way:
Where there is a temperate place and wholesome air, and a little of the sun’s heat predominates there and abundant sulfur is cooked in it, gold is formed when mercury mixes with the sulfur.
If it is a little hotter, hard, red gold results. If its heat is less, pale, soft gold results.
They mix a little copper with it, one part for every thousand, to remedy and correct it. But if, again, the sun’s heat is reduced
considerably, that body becomes silver. This is how silver, which is the moon, is formed. If the place is temperate and wholesome,
and heat does not predominate there, silver results. This body is close to gold in its nature, but differs in color and weight.
It is not hot like gold. How copper, which is Aphrodite, is formed. If the place is one where heat predominates more strongly and it is dry,
its sulfur too is harder and hotter. When mercury mixes with it, red copper is formed. There are differences both within copper itself and within all the bodies,
according to the location of the place and its constitution. How tin, which is Zeus, is formed. Likewise, if the place is colder and wetter,
its sulfur too is not very hot, and it is white. When mercury mixes with it, tin is formed, and it is called a paralyzed body,
like human bodies in which cold and moisture predominate and which become paralyzed.
In the same way, this body too remains weak and paralyzed. It is called paralyzed silver, being paralyzed by cold.
How lead, which is Cronus, is formed. When a place has a bad constitution, and the place is bad and its vapors are thick and cause disease for many reasons,
the sulfur that is cooked and formed in that earth also becomes badly [?] and thick. When mercury mixes with it,
it produces this body of lead. It is called leprous silver. Just as bodies that have a bad constitution
develop the disease called leprosy, so this body of lead is formed in the same way.
How iron, which is Ares, is formed. When a place is situated in the mountains, and cold and dryness are abundant [in it],
the vapors that rise from the lower depths of that earth are also cold and dry.
Likewise, the sulfur formed there is cold and dry. When mercury mixes with it, it produces this substance, iron.
Even within this substance there are many varieties: hard iron and soft iron.
And Indian iron, which is called steel. Likewise, the place where it is deposited is mountainous, and there is much coldness and dryness there.
The vapors rising from the lower recesses of that land are also cold and dry.
Likewise, the sulfur formed there is cold and dry. When mercury mixes with it, it produces this substance, iron.
Even within this substance there are many varieties: hard iron, soft iron, and Indian iron, which is called steel. Likewise.
There are many varieties among all the substances: silver [?], copper, tin, lead, and iron as well.
All these variations arise from the combination of mercury and sulfur, from the location of the place and its climate,
and according to the nature of the vapors rising from it, in accordance with the command and will of the Creator. For all these substances, and many others,
the wise Creator fashioned for human needs and the maintenance of the world. They did not come into being by chance through these processes,
but through an ordering [?] that is wise in every respect and beyond human understanding, since everything was created and established in a single instant by the almighty command.
His power is in them all, and they are in him, as we said before.
How the substance called electrum comes into being, which resembles the nature of the planet Mercury. Glory to that wise Creator, whose images are portrayed by all his creatures.
By his own will, he became like us and all his creatures in everything except sin.
This substance called electrum is a composite substance, sometimes made of gold and silver, and in various places of other substances.
Some of these people compound, while the natures are preserved without confusion in this composite union.
So too with Christ, who is united from divinity and humanity and appeared as one person, and is also one incarnate nature.
Sometimes this substance, electrum, is found already compounded in the mines themselves, like gold and silver, or like silver and iron.
Thus it comes from the mixture of mercury and sulfur and is useful for many purposes, to the praise of the wise Creator. How and from what there come into being
and are formed fine gems and precious stones. As for their nature and the names of each of them, we are not now concerned with speaking or writing about these,
nor about their properties and the action of each one, or about their beauty, value, and similar matters,
but only with a general and concise account of their formation. The divine book of Moses mentions them as twelve precious stones,
those placed on the breast of the high priest when he commemorated the twelve tribes of the Israelites before the Lord.
They also portray a great mystery, because three kinds among them are especially beautiful and costly:
jacinth, carbuncle, and emerald. These portray the adored and glorified Trinity, while the other nine portray the nine orders of the heavenly powers.
Those who are arranged in three congregations in heaven, to the praise of the Trinity,
which is holy. Now all of them are formed from mercury and sulfur. They are formed in a clear and temperate place,
where the sun acts well and with moderation, and pure, exceptionally clear vapors rise from it.

By God's will, all these precious stones were formed and came into being, as did the other substances, such as lapis lazuli, malachite, zinc oxide, soot, alum, orpiment, marcasite, magnesia, natron, and the rest.
All of them were formed from mercury and sulfur according to the will of their Maker.
Although some of them were formed from the beginning and exist like rocks in the mountains and valleys, and some along riverbanks,
most of these splendid stones are found in the region beneath the sun's course, in that burning land which cannot be traversed by day because of its intense heat,
or by night because of the dragons and numerous snakes found in that region.
Skilled people devise many ingenious methods, extract some of them, and become very rich.
Many ancient philosophers have spoken about these things, as have writers on natural phenomena and minerals.
They have dealt with each one individually. We, however, have shown their cause and how they all originated.
By Mar Jacob
Glory to the Father, in whom we began with confidence;
and worship to the Son, in whom we proceeded peacefully;
thanksgiving to the Spirit, in whom we finished without disturbance.
The nature of the three is one, without division.
Just as the sailor rejoices
when his ship has [?] the harbor,
so the scribe rejoices
at the last line he writes.
With the help of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one true God, this life-filled book of the Cause of All Causes was completed, just as

we found it in the exemplar, by the hands of the wretched, sinful, and lazy man named Aziz, a subdeacon, son of the priest George, from the village of Bashiqa in the region of Mosul, a Syrian, Jacobite in faith.
It was written in the holy church of Saint Shmuni in Bashiqa, in the Christian year 1882 [?], in the month of June. On its twenty-third day this book was completed for [?], the Armenian from Mosul.
And may Mary, the Mother of God, and all the saints be remembered. Yes and amen.
This was completed with the help of our Lord.
Again we write a little about the elements and their union, in the meter of Philor [?], that is, Phimuni [?], which has seven beats. We will now speak about the four elements, and also [?].
How, although they are opposed, they are at peace and in harmony with one another. Fire is opposed to earth; water is not friendly to fire. Water, whether exposed or enclosed,
air diminishes and consumes. Do not suppose that the heat of fire consumes the water in a pot. Rather, through the abundance of the flame, air burns away its moisture.
Although these elements are strongly opposed to one another, the Maker composed from portions of them a single vessel full of wonder.
He united, blended, and mixed the opposing things, and made peace between them. In creation he fitted them together so that they would sing praise. He brought dust from the earth,
and water from the [?]. He mixed fire with air and composed the living human being. Then they came into being and were united. Listen, discerning one.
To each element the Eternal One, its Creator, gave two powers. Although in the account they amount to eight, there are four distinct qualities.
For one element takes from its companion and is then combined, so that cold is united with cold, and then it is completed. It also keeps the opposing quality away.
Then let us speak [?] about both sides. Earth is by its nature dry and cold. Water, in turn, is like it:
cold, but also moist. Air, in turn, has a moist and hot constitution. Fire, as it was created, is hot and dry.
Now [?] toward their union, and unite them properly. Combine them without difficulty, with knowledge, like a discerning person. Earth
is united with air through fire, by heat. Fire is united with water through earth, by dryness. Air is united with earth
through water, by coldness. Water is united with fire through air, by heat. Opposing elements are not united in their own forms.
Every opposing element is united through an intermediary, and through portions taken from one another it is united without disturbance.
Among the inner and outer things, some convey things such as these; and there are inner and outer things that do not convey things such as these.
Fire is dry, and it is also hot. Unless air is between them, it is not united with water.
Earth, which is cold, and air, which is hot—one would not approach the other unless water were between them.
For this reason we said that they do not receive things such as these. Fire is united with air because it is light and moves,
since both of them are mobile and light. Air is united with water through the mobility of both. Water is united with earth
through the heaviness they possess, because they tend downward together: both of them are heavy. And so that you may gain understanding through these things,
I have drawn them in diagrams, so that when you look carefully, you may see their proper union. Look at the elements in red,
and in black at the powers they possess. Through the beauty of the writing you will learn the truth and benefit. The horse is red,
and its [?] is not black, but its rider is black. It receives its paths from hands, upon white earth.
Bearing the beauty of colors, it runs, moves on, and shows that it does not fear [?]. The eagle that rests upon its head
examines created things. It accepts no other garment, for its covering is mysteries upon mysteries. Its clothing and its movement are [?].
And esteem it above others. Look at its beauty and reflect on it, for a lovely gift is offered to you. Examine riddles carefully.
And do not be in the dark about puzzling matters, for through these and things like them, they will call you a learned man.
This short extract from the Book of the Cause of All Causes is finished—that is, this whole [?], as we saw in the exemplar.
Finished.
